Initial Verses: I bow to the horse-headed deity (Hayagrīva), whose luster is like the snowy mountain, who is adorned with garlands of *tulasī*, who bestows the lofty eloquence of Sarasvatī, who is composed of knowledge and bliss, whose form is like pure crystal,
and who is the foundation of all sciences.
We worship Hayagrīva. || 1-1 ||
We worship that form of Lakṣmī, who has the bird as her seat, who is the support of compassion, who is adorned by the moon, and who is the stainless moon, sun, and fire. 1–2.
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and Vedānta,
who is proficient in all the scriptures,
who knows the essence of all philosophical systems, and who has mastered the traditional sources of dharma.
One who has conquered the senses and conquered the physical basis, who is no longer subject to passion and hatred, who abides in the fourteen-limbed yoga, and is devoted to higher discernment. (1–4)
Commentary:
We pay homage to the Goddess Śrī, whose friend the Divine One sports with by casting the dice of Brahmā and others upon the variegated board of the three *guṇas*.
For those seeking the jewels of reality within the great ocean of the Lakṣmī Tantra,
this commentary, the Tattvaprakāśinī, strives to provide assistance.

1. "Namaḥ" (salutation) is the designation of the distinguished means; "to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa" is the designation of the distinguished goal. "To the eternally faultless one" is the refutation of the suspicion that Nārāyaṇa, as the material cause of the world, might be subject to modification.

The distinction between the bound and liberated souls has been stated. By the phrase "for the sake of the cause of the entire world," the Upaniṣadic doctrine of being both the non-different instrumental and material cause, as well as the distinction from the eternal soul, has been stated.
By the word "for knowledge" (jñānāya), the perfection of the multitude of qualities conducive to being the cause of the world is expressed.

The attribute that defines its essential nature (*svarūpa*) has been stated. By the term "to the waveless one" (*nistaraṅgāya*), the absence of the six waves (*ṣaḍūrmi*) and the distinction from consciousness (*cit*) which is subject to constant transformation have been stated.
2. Regarding "of such a kind" (*īdṛśam*) and so forth: it means having the form of the letter *ī*. Regarding "stainless" (*akalaṅka*) and so forth: [the meaning follows].
The statement that [the mantra] has the form of vowels, consonants, and pervasive letters (vyāpakākṣara) expresses that it is the very nature of the Goddess’s speech.

As it is said in the *Prapañcasāra*: "The sixteen are declared to be called vowels (svara), the twenty-five are called consonants (sparśa), and these ten are the pervasive letters (vyāpaka); they consist respectively of the natures of the Moon and Fire."
Thus:
In ancient times, when the sun was pierced by Svarbhānu, it attained the state of being a burner [of darkness].
The source of all austerities, a mass of splendor, and free from all ailment. || 1.5 ||
[He saw] the sage Atri, endowed with the three qualities, established in the three groups [of life], immutable, performing the morning twilight worship, and having offered oblations into the fire.
She was the most eminent lawful wife among those devoted to their husbands and possessed of great fame;
yet, for another reason, she was the mother of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
Constantly praised by the gods, ever-peaceful, eternal, and ascetic;
she was wise, a knower of all duties, and always devoted to her husband. (1.8)
Having heard various discourses on dharma from her husband,
Anasūyā spoke these words preceded by a prostration.
Anasūyā said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, my protector, Lord of the World!
From you alone have I heard those various kinds of dharmas."
And there are various types of knowledge, distinguished by their fruits, forms, and so forth;
among these, the dharma of the Blessed One has been upheld by me as preeminent. (1.11)
As you have been recounting those various discourses connected with the teachings of the Blessed One, the supreme majesty of Lakṣmī has been indicated here and there. (1.12)
Because it is a secret and because you were not asked, you have not revealed it;
nevertheless, I desire to hear that supreme majesty of Lakṣmī.

For whatever is the intrinsic nature of that Goddess, whatever her essential form, whatever her origin, whatever her measure, whatever her support, whatever her means, and whatever her fruit— || 1.14 ||
Therefore, O best among the knowers of Brahman, I wish to hear this from you, so that through the yoga of its realization I may have fulfilled my purpose. (1.15)
"Show me that path; I have approached you, O Lord, teach me!
Having heard these words of hers, the Blessed One Atri spoke: (1–16)
Atri:
O knower of dharma, O practitioner of dharma, I have been rightly and well enlightened today.
Previously, when questioned by me, you did not disclose what ought to have been said. (1.17)
O auspicious lady, you are worthy to hear the supreme majesty of Lakṣmī, which is eternal and resides within the hearts of the series of the Upanishads. 1-18.
Formerly, sages dwelling on Mount Malaya were devoted to dharma;
they had heard the Sāttvata wisdom from Nārada, who has the vision of the gods.
They questioned the Lord Nārada— who was like Brahmā himself and a knower of the duties pertaining to the Blessed One— regarding this very same matter concerning the eternal Lord.
The Sages said:
O Blessed One, we have heard from you that the Sāttvata is the refuge of pure being (sattva).
The pure Dharma of the Blessed One has liberation as its sole characteristic and fruit. (1) Note 4:
"In fourteen" means by means of devotion, ritual placement, and yoga.
5. Regarding the word "pierced" (viddha), one should refer here to what is stated in the 260th chapter of the Anuśāsana Parvan of the Mahābhārata.
6. By the phrase beginning with "beyond the three qualities" (atriguṇa), the etymological significance of the name of the great sage Atri is revealed.

7. "Brahmā," and so forth. Formerly, the three forms [of the gods] endeavored to test the chastity of Anasūyā. Enraged by this, she turned them into two-year-old infants. Thereupon, propitiated by her queens, she restored them to their former state; such is the Puranic account.
The relevant discourse should be connected here.
11. The Dharma of the Blessed One. The Dharma of cessation has the attainment of the Blessed One as its fruit.
13. Regarding the phrase "because it was not asked": the injunction intended here is that one should not speak to anyone unless asked.

16. Regarding the phrase "to him who had approached": the intended meaning of the Vedic text is that "to him who had approached, that wise one duly proclaimed that knowledge of Brahman in its true essence. Regarding the word "path" (*panthānam*): it means the correct means (*sadupāya*), as in the common saying, "The path is that by which great men have gone."
21. *Sāttvata* means that which takes refuge in *sattva*; the meaning is that *dharma* has the quality of *sattva* as its sole primary constituent.
(p. 3) In that exposition of the true meaning of reality, the majesty of Lakṣmī is supreme.
It has been indicated here and there, but it has not been fully revealed because it was not asked for. || 1.22 ||
We desire to hear this very thing which enables one to cross the ocean of worldly existence;
may your lordship explain to us the entire majesty of Padminī.
We bow our heads to your feet, which deliver one from the cycle of worldly existence. O Sage, please instruct us; we have sought refuge in you for a long time.
Nārada said:
"I have been well enlightened today, O sages of firm vows;
being pleased, I shall now relate the eternal Lakṣmī-tantra."
There that goddess is seen in the fullness of her own form, qualities, and majesty—
the lotus-born queen of Padmanābha, who is like a lotus-pond.
Formerly, when Purandara was overcome by the curse of Durvāsas,
the three worlds were deprived of the study of the Vedas and the utterance of the vaṣaṭ-call, and their prosperity had fallen away.
When the host of gods was impoverished, when the Dharma was emaciated and nearly extinguished, and when the Grandfather (Brahmā) had gone together with the deities to the Ocean of Milk—[variant:
having entered the Ocean of Milk]. (1–28)
Having performed intense and great asceticism for many divine cycles of years, when Janārdana, the Lord of the World and God of Gods, was awakened to enlightenment— 1-29.
When the matter had been reported by the Grandfather (Brahmā) to the God,
the gods churned Śrīroda according to the path then commanded [by him].
When the Pārijāta tree, the best of horses, the lordly elephant, the host of Apsarases, the Kālakūṭa poison, the Vāruṇī wine, and likewise the nectar had emerged. (1–31)
Immediately thereafter, when the goddess rose from the great ocean together with the moon,
she stood upon a lotus in the lotus-naveled one’s chest.
When she had looked upon the host of gods who had attained glory, and when she had not looked upon the host of Daityas who had been utterly defeated in the past; || 1.33 ||
When Purandara had attained complete sovereignty and was rejoicing,
Bṛhaspati approached him and spoke these words in private.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Purandara, I shall awaken you at the proper time; listen to these words, for the nature of Fortune has already been explained to you through positive and negative concomitance.
O Lord of the great ones, your greatness extends through her;
may your supreme state of sovereignty never fall away. Therefore, O Lord of Gods, strive accordingly and seek refuge in Padminī.
For this is indeed the root of the highest good; for this is the supreme goal. (1.37)
Note: By this, the etymological derivation of the word *sāttvata* is also indicated. For example: *sattva* refers to the quality of goodness (*sattvaguṇa*).

That which possesses this is *sattvataḥ*. The suffix *tap* is used here in the sense of possession, as in the case of words like *parvata* (mountain). [The term *sāttvata*] is derived from *sattvata* itself.
Regarding the term "Sāttvata": its explanation is "the pure Bhāgavata dharma.
Regarding the word "for a long time" (ciram): the intended injunction is that one should not speak [this] to someone who has not resided [as a disciple] for a year.

25. *Lakṣmītantra* is the name of the work. It will be stated right here (in verses 44–52) that this *tantra* was taught by extracting the essence from the root *Lakṣmītantra*, which consists of one hundred crore verses. 27. Regarding "In the city," etc.: this is a narrative (*ākhyāyikā*).

This is to be seen in the first part of the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*. It is the cause of the absence of Vedic study and the *vaṣaṭ* call, as well as the loss of prosperity. 28. *Nisaṃtate*: the meaning is "interrupted."

33. By means of this positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that the casting of a glance by the Goddess Lakṣmī is the cause of all prosperity. Regarding the positive concomitance—“when X exists, Y exists”—the illustration is “as among the gods. Regarding the negative concomitance—“when X is absent, Y is absent”—the illustration is “as among the Daityas.”
The illustration: He will state this very subject immediately thereafter, in verse 35. (p.
4) Root-text:
She alone is the eternal Goddess, the true intention of the Vedas;
she alone is the life-breath of the worlds, and she alone is the activity of the worlds.
For this indeed—[as in the Āgama, Bhāgavata, and Liṅga Purāṇas]—is the very desire of the worlds; she is knowledge, both supreme and inferior.
She alone creates at the proper time; she alone protects the three worlds. (1–39)
At the end, she withdraws the world while remaining established in its respective causes;
without propitiating this Mother of the worlds, how can there be greatness? (1.40)
This indeed is that abode of Viṣṇu from which the ascetic does not return;
this is that supreme consummation of the Sāṃkhyas who have realized the Self. (1.41)
This is that final goal of the yogins, having reached which one does not grieve;
this is the final goal of the Pāśupatas, and this is the destination of those who know the Vedas. (1.42)
This eternal conclusion of the entire Pañcarātra is she;
this goddess Nārāyaṇī abides as the very self of Nārāyaṇa. (1.43)
She is both distinct and non-distinct from them, like moonlight from the cold-rayed moon; she is manifested through those various distinct cognitions and diverse scriptures. (1.44)
This one supreme Goddess alone is worshipped in many ways;
therefore, O illustrious one, go for refuge to her who is born from the lotus.
Having propitiated the Queen of Viṣṇu through various specific austerities and diverse auspicious observances, stabilize your own prosperity.
With her face bright with grace, this Goddess will lead one to her own state;
she is the bestower of desired objects and grants even the desires of those who long for them. (1.47)
Thus addressed by his preceptor himself, Śakra,
desiring to propitiate her, went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk. (1.48)
There, making his dwelling at the foot of a *bilva* tree, he performed divine asceticism;
standing on one leg, observing silence, like a piece of wood upon the ground, subsisting only on air. (1–49)
With his eyes, arms, and face turned upwards, self-restrained and with a controlled mind,
he performed most difficult ascetic penance for a thousand divine years.
At the concluding bath of that penance, that goddess born from the lotus,
the consort of Viṣṇu, with a gracious countenance, appeared before his sight.
Beholding with his eyes the supreme Goddess, the Mother of the worlds, standing before him, Śakra was filled with the utmost wonder. (1.52)
Then, overwhelmed and with palms joined in reverence, Balarāma’s slayer, the subduer of Pāka,
prostrated himself and praised Śrī, the lotus-dwelling goddess, with a hymn.
Note:

38. Regarding the phrase "of the Śrutis": the meaning is that, according to the statement "I alone am to be known by all the Vedas," He is the ultimate terminus of the purport of all the Vedas. Because there is no separation between the two, [He is not different from them].
There is a contradiction in the statement.

39. Even according to the established doctrine that the status of being the cause of the world is unique to Brahman, because that [causehood] is of the nature of His power and is non-separately established from Him, that which is produced by the power [is also Brahman].
The designation of being "created by the Possessor of Power" (Śaktimat) is indeed appropriate. This will be explained very clearly by the Goddess herself [in verse 44].
She establishes, through the terms "separate" and "not separate," the very point stated in the preceding verse regarding her abiding as the self of Nārāyaṇa.

When there is a desire to isolate a property from its substratum—which are not established as separate—the property is designated separately; but when there is no such isolation, it is designated by way of its substratum. For example: "white color" and "white cloth."

47. By this [work], the attainment of liberation in the form of the supreme state within the grace of the Goddess, as well as the incidental attainment of the fruits of the three aims of life, are described.
Thus ends the first chapter.
Seeing him who had attained a state of absolute solitude and was established in sincere devotion, the Mother of the worlds spoke these words: (1.54)
Śrī said: "O child Śakra, O observer of noble vows, I am pleased with your austerity.
Choose a boon, O highly fortunate one; what desired thing shall I do for you? (1.55)
Śakra:
O Goddess, today the fruit of my asceticism, self-restraint, and observance has been attained immediately, since the Blessed Lady has been seen by me. (1.56)
Or if a boon is to be granted by you to me, O Supreme Goddess, then tell me, O Mistress of Gods, what kind of nature you possess, O Goddess.
O Goddess, what are your means of valid cognition, what is your support, and what are your methods? To whom do you belong, and of what nature is your relationship with him? (1.58)
And whatever else is to be known by you, augmented by various scriptures—O Goddess, tell me all that; I am seated before you, please teach me. (1.59)
Thus propitiated and enlightened by him, Padmā, with a heart full of affection like a milch-cow toward her calf, spoke to the subduer of Pāka (Indra).
Śrī said: Listen, O illustrious Śakra, to who I am, in what manner I exist,
by whom I belong, and what kind of relationship I have with him, O slayer of Vṛtra.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Descent of the Scripture" (or "The Illumination of the Foundation of All"), in the *Lakṣmītantra*, which is the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra* (or *Śrīpañcarātra*) Tantra.
The second chapter.
Śrī said:
There exists [that state] characterized by the experience of infinite bliss free from all suffering.
The supreme self is that whose state the wise behold as the highest. || 2.1 ||

Someone might be the self of some, and someone else the self of others; yet for that person as well, there would be another—and so on. But where this series comes to an end, there [the self] is established. (2.2)
The supreme Self has been declared to be the further shore of every path;
that reality which is traditionally known by the name "I" is proclaimed to be the Self. (2–3)
I, whose nature is undivided, am designated as the Supreme Self (Paramātman); this entire universe, consisting of both the sentient and the insentient, is embraced within me. (2-4)
That eternal supreme self, the state remembered by me as "I am He," is the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, who is considered the supreme Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). (2.5)
Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Viśva, and Viśvarūpa—thus he is proclaimed.
This entire world is pervaded by him through the sense of "I-ness. (2–6)
In reality, there is neither an entity nor a non-entity that is not pervaded by the "I-sense" (ahaṃtā). Whatever is grasped as "this-ness" (idaṃtā) is pervaded by the "I-sense.
This [Self] is entirely quiescent, eternally changeless, and primordial.
Ananta is devoid of limitations such as space, time, and so forth. || 2-8 ||
It is called "Great Abundance" because that pervasion is vast;
it is Brahman, the supreme abode, whose meditation is without support. It is like a waveless ocean of nectar, radiant with the six divine qualities.
That one Reality is a mass of consciousness, peaceful, and free from rising and setting.
Because its power is non-different [from it], that is called the non-duality of Brahman;
its supreme power is like the moonlight of the cool-rayed moon. (2.11)
Note:

1. By the phrase "free from suffering" (*nirduḥkha*) and so forth, [the Lord's] possession of both characteristics is indicated: being the opposite of all that is to be abandoned (*nikhilaheyapratyanīkatva*) and being a mine of infinite auspicious qualities (*anantakalyāṇaguṇākaratva*).
This refers to the Supreme Self (paramātman).

2. "The Self" (ātmā) means the Controller (niyantṛ). Regarding the word "this" (eṣa), the word "establishment" (vyavasthā) is to be understood as the ellipsis. It "establishes" (vyavatiṣṭhate), meaning it pervades;
thus, the connection with the preceding [text] is that "He is the Supreme Self."

3. Regarding the phrase "of the paths" (*adhvanām*): in comparison with the path pertaining to the three aims of life (*traivargika-adhvan*), the supreme path is the path to liberation (*mokṣa-adhvan*), such as that beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*). The meaning is that he reaches its further shore (*pāra*), the goal to be attained;
for there is the scriptural statement: "He reaches the end of the path, that highest step of Viṣṇu. [The phrase] "of the paths, O Lord of the paths" (*adhvanām adhvapate*)...
The citation from scripture here is: "I" (aham). The meaning is that he who is the object of the notion of "I" is the Self (ātman).

4. Regarding "unlimited" (anavacchinna): the meaning is that he who is perceived through the function of the word "I" as extending without limit—due to the absence of delimitation by substance and so forth—is the Supreme Self (paramātman).
6. And Śakra says elsewhere: "O Mother, this world of moving and non-moving beings has been pervaded by you and by Viṣṇu.
7. Regarding the phrase "as this" (*idaṃtayā*): the meaning is that the entire world is perceived as the referent of the word "this" (*idaṃśabdārthatayā*).
10. By the words beginning with "nistaraṅga" (waveless), the state of the Blessed One as both quiescent and emergent is described. He states that very point:
"quiescent. 11. Regarding "the non-duality of Brahman": this is because [Brahman] is characterized by the I-consciousness (*ahaṃtā*) whose power is not established as separate from itself.
The meaning is that Brahman, distinguished by that [power], is the one and only reality. (p. 7) Root-text:
The Goddess, who exists in all states, is non-separate from and identical with her own self.
I am that eternal ego-consciousness of that Brahman; I am she. (2-12)
Hari is remembered as the Self of all beings, having become the "I";
I am the eternal ego-consciousness of all beings. (2.13)
By whatever nature the eternal Vāsudeva exists, I am declared to be that very nature which serves as the companion of that God. (2.14)
Brahman consists of both existence and non-existence; therefore, that is the eternal state.
From it arises the Lord Nārāyaṇa, while Bhāva is Lakṣmī, and I am the Supreme (Parā).
Therefore, that eternal Brahman, known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, is pervaded by the sense of "I," and thus the object denoted by "I" (the ego-sense) is established. (2-16)
And that sense of "I-ness" (sāhaṃtā) is proclaimed to arise from the object of the notion of "I" (ahamartha);
for they are inseparable from one another and are mutually concomitant. (2.17)
Know that the relationship between me and my Lord is one of identity;
for without the sense of "I," I, being indefinable, cannot be established. (2-18)

Without the referent of "I" (ahamartha), the sense of egoity (ahaṃtā) cannot be established as it would be without a substratum; its nature consists of both being and becoming, and it is the object of both the collective and the individual. (2-19)
In the world, both the hidden and the manifest are contemplated [or analyzed].
When there is no unfolding, that Supreme Goddess is the non-unfolding *ahaṃtā*. (2.20)
Having embraced the entire universe, it abides within Brahman;
its manifestation is like that of the ocean at the rising of the moon. (2.21)
At that time, I am the power of Nārāyaṇa, characterized by the desire to create;
that which is called a "nimeṣa" (moment) of that Supreme Self is [the duration] for the act of withdrawal. (2.22)
I am indeed that Śakti Nārāyaṇī, characterized by the desire for sleep;
yet, as I arise from the Lord of Lakṣmī when He Himself awakens with the desire to create, [I manifest]. (2.23)
Unobstructed and uncontracted sovereignty unfolds;
that supreme knowledge is Brahman, which is all-instructing, all-seeing, and free from affliction.
Likewise, the egoity whose nature is knowledge is omniscient and all-seeing.
The supreme form, consisting of knowledge, belongs to both Brahmā and myself.
The remainder—sovereignty, valor, and so forth—is the eternal attribute of knowledge.
The internal form "I" is proclaimed (or determined) as the very form of knowledge. (2.26)
The nature of the illuminator and so forth is characterized by being like a crystal and such;
therefore, the nature of consciousness belongs to both me and Nārāyaṇa. (2.27)
Note:
By means of an illustration, he states that His own essential nature is non-separable from Him—“like the moonlight,” etc.
By the phrase “not departing even in all states,” it is shown that Sītā existed as Rukmiṇī during the state of being Rāghava.
Regarding the birth of Kṛṣṇa, as well as in other incarnations of Viṣṇu, the statement of the great sages—that she is inseparable from Him—is recalled.
16. The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman is indeed endowed with Śrī, and not devoid of Śrī.

The point is this: although both Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa remain as the remnants of the sacrificial offering (*ātmahaviḥśeṣita*), there is no possibility of a duality of the *śeṣin* (the recipient of the remnant), because—as in the case of the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* and other offerings—it is the qualified entity alone that constitutes the object of the injunction (*uddeśya*), and that [qualified entity] is singular.
18. "Nirupākhyo" means devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*). In the world, every object is [designated] as "this is such-and-such."
The meaning is that [the Goddess] is established only by way of specific modalities (*prakāraviśeṣa*), and not as being devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*).
22. It was previously stated that the Goddess has the nature of power (*śakti*); now her divisions are described:
the power of the desire to create (*sisṛkṣā-śakti*) and the power of the desire to sleep (*suṣupsā-śakti*). By the first, there is creation; by the second, [dissolution].
And dissolution occurs. In that regard, regarding the eternal manifestation (*nitya-vibhūti*), only the first [power] is operative;
as for the second, its utility lies solely in the playful manifestation (*līlā-vibhūti*).
24. Among the six qualities such as knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth, knowledge is the attribute that defines His essential nature (*svarūpa*); the others...

The distinction is that the qualities (*guṇas*), however, are the specific qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) whose essential nature has already been defined. This very point he will state later: "The remainder—sovereignty, valor, and so forth—is the attribute (*dharma*) of knowledge.
The meaning is that it is the attribute of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) called knowledge.
"The supreme sovereignty of mine, which consists in the non-obstruction of the root [power] as it arises—
that is called 'Icchā' (Will) by the learned in the various scriptures on the principles. (2.28)
That state of mine which is the primordial nature (prakṛti) of the world is called my Power (śakti);
that absence of fatigue in me while creating is intended as my Strength (bala). (2.29)
The support of an effect is also declared to be its power;
those who are skilled in the true nature of things say that such support is provided by a portion of that power, through both the capacity and the possessor of capacity. (2-30)
Even though I am the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), I am always free from modification;
for water quickly abandons its own nature when it arises as curd. (2.31)

Even while the world exists, that transformation does not exist in me, who am eternally the primordial nature (prakṛti). The absence of modification is my power; this is the opinion of those who know reality. (2.32)
Vikrama is said to be valor, and it is remembered as a portion of sovereignty; for it is my lack of dependence on auxiliary causes in the performance of all undertakings. (2.33)
Those who know the truth declare that *tejas* (splendor) is the sixth quality;
some describe *tejas* as the capacity for overcoming others. (2.34)
Some, who are experts in the principles of that splendor, employ it for the sake of sovereignty;
these five are the pure streams (or manifestations) of knowledge. (2.35)
These six qualities, beginning with knowledge, constitute my sixfold power (ṣāḍguṇya), which is my very body;
thus, this is my ten-thousandth part (kalā) arising from the desire to create.
The entire class [of beings], consisting of both pure and impure natures, has been encompassed by her;
therein, O Lord of the Gods, I shall explain the path that consists of purity alone. (2.37)
That form of the Supreme Lord is radiant, characterized by the sequence of the six qualities—both manifest and unmanifest—and assumes fourfold forms. (2.38)

[The state of the conceptualization of qualities (guṇas). This wonderful path is threefold: that which is superimposed through the conceptualization of qualities, that which is characterized by the sequence produced by the manifestation of qualities, and that which consists of qualities made manifest as forms. (2.39)
The three pairs of the six [qualities], which those who know them call "knowledge" and so forth,
have their fourfold nature analyzed both in summary and in detail. (2) By means of the distinction between the combined and the individual, [the nature] of the qualities...
When those three ages are intended to be expressed, that is my state of fourfold nature (caturātmatā) within Śāntā. (2.41) Note: Caturātmatā refers to the fourfold nature. (ī.)

28. "Desires" (iccheti): It should be recalled here that the sovereignty-nature of the power of the desire to create was previously described in the twenty-fourth verse; for the desire to create is indeed the wish to emanate.

29. The Goddess's state as the primordial nature of the universe is not due to her essential nature (*svarūpa*), because if it were so, the consequence would be that she is subject to modification (*vikāritva*).

However, it should be understood that [Brahman exists] as having the sentient and insentient principles as its own modes (*prakāra*). For this alone is the way in which Brahman serves as the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the world:
namely, being devoid of modification (*vikāra*), while there is transformation (*pariṇāma*) in the aspect of the mode according to the manner previously described, and not [in the essence].

Because it is accepted that [the Self] is the aspect of the qualifier (*prakāryaṃśa*). To maintain the absence of modification by accepting transformation (*pariṇāma*) only in the essential nature (*svarūpa*), which is the qualified (*prakārin*), is not tenable, as it fails to account for the capacity to bring about the impossible. For this very reason, [it is said]: "But Māyā is Nature (*prakṛti*)."

Regarding the word "vidyāt" (one should know), the view of some is that the meaning is the state of being the material cause (*prakṛtitva*) within *māyā*, which serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Lord.
36. Regarding "udyati": the meaning is "having attained rising."
37. Creation is twofold: pure creation (*śuddhasṛṣṭi*) and impure creation (*aśuddhasṛṣṭi*). Among these, the pure [creation] is devoid of the three *guṇas* and consists of pure *sattva*.
Some maintain that because it is self-luminous, it possesses non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*); others hold that it is indeed inert (*jaḍatva*). Of this very [pure creation]...

The term "eternal manifestation" (*nityavibhūti*) is used [for this]. However, the impure creation, which consists of the three *guṇas* and is insentient in nature, is designated as the "pastime manifestation" (*līlāvibhūti*).
38. Not only is the eternal manifestation alone the pure creation; rather, those who shine forth therein [are also included].

It should be understood that the manifestations (vyūhas) known as Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are likewise [to be considered in this manner]. Among them, the sequence of the six attributes (ṣāḍguṇya) is not clearly manifest in the first, Vāsudeva; however, it should be known that in the subsequent manifestations, they appear to some extent in successive order.
39. In some of those arrays (vyūha), even without observing the fundamental forms of the qualities (guṇa), there is a construction of qualities based on conceptualization (kalpanākṛta).
Those who contemplate reality declare this to be the fourfold nature of Śāntā. (2.42)
From the state of peace and supreme peace, there is my unfolding (*unmeṣa*) within the triad of form and the other [senses].
That primordial fourfold nature of mine is manifest in sequence and is formless. (2.43)
Waveless, indescribable, devoid of being yet the very essence of being, imperishable—this unfolding known as pure existence-consciousness is my primordial, undeviating state of peace. (2.44)
In the former state, within the self of Saṃkarṣaṇa known as the power of manifest knowledge, every modification exists within me like a mole on the forehead. (2.45)
Therefore, the wise, through the power of knowledge, know me as Saṃkarṣaṇa;
then, as I unfold further, I myself assume the state of agency.
At that time, they call me Pradyumna, the illuminator of all objects.
The *yuga* is the form that vibrates within that [state] of sovereignty and vigor.

Then, by that power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), having attained possession through the desire to act, it is joined with and designated as "Aniruddha" by those learned in the principles (*tattva*). (2.48)
Those states of mine—deep sleep, dreaming, and waking—are in succession;
they are my three powers known as innate nature, consisting of consciousness and sovereignty. (2.49)
Manifesting separately through the triad of principles, they are proclaimed as the triad of qualities: strength, vigor, and likewise splendor. (2.50)
The absence of defects such as fatigue and the like is known as the subordinate factor of knowledge and so forth.
Thus, for me, who experiences the distinction between these two states— the quiescent and the arisen— (2.51).
The surging of the waves of my own dharma does not lead to division, just as that of the ocean;
for I generally abide in the performance of my duties through this creative power (kṛtyā). (2.52)
In that regard, that pair of qualities is said to be my own form;
therefore, O Lord, Saṃkarṣaṇa is proclaimed as the power of knowledge (jñānabala). || 2.53 ||
Pradyumna is sovereign power (*aiśvarya*) and valor (*vīrya*); Aniruddha is potency (*śakti*) and splendor (*tejas*).
[The first (Ḍ): But the First One possesses the sixfold attributes indivisibly, existing as non-different from the reality of Brahman. (2.54)
Just as a single actor assumes various distinctions of costume and gesture through qualities such as conciliation, generosity, cruelty, and heroism, so too does [the soul]. (2.55)
Note:
Due to the lack of perfect unfolding (*samyaganunmeṣāt*), there is no knowledge of [the object] as consisting of qualities (*guṇātmatayā*).
However, in some cases, because of unfolding in succession (*krameṇonmeṣāt*), there is manifestation in succession (*kramādabhivyaktiḥ*); but in other cases...

The sequence is that through the extreme manifestation of the qualities (guṇas), there is a thorough cognition [of reality] by means of the qualities themselves. 45. "Like a mole" (tilakālaka): just as in the bodies of living beings a particular small, dark-colored spot like a mole is seen in some very limited corner, so too is the entire phenomenal world (prapañca).
The meaning is that he resides in one part of me. He is called Saṃkarṣaṇa because he draws [all things] together; thus his name is etymologically significant.
Herein lies the full manifestation of knowledge and power. 47. He whose splendor (dyumna)—meaning strength or brilliance—is preeminent; thus his name is etymologically significant.
Because he is the creator of the universe, there is here the manifestation of *vīrya* (prowess) and *aiśvarya* (sovereignty).

48. Regarding "Aniruddha": he is the protector; here there is the manifestation of *śakti* (power) and *tejas* (splendor). And so they have recorded: "Vāsudeva is supreme due to his sixfold qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*); he, O Lord, is the object of enjoyment for the liberated."

From your powerful awakening you are Saṃkarṣaṇa; through your sovereign power and heroism, you take away [evil] and spread the scripture. As Pradyumna, O Blessed One, you lead forth creation and dharma. And as Aniruddha, maintaining the quality of goodness (sattva), you protect it by thus manifesting yourself in your emanations.
"O Sovereign of the Stage!

(49). Regarding "deep sleep," etc.: Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are the presiding deities of deep sleep and the other states respectively; Vāsudeva, however, is the presiding deity of the fourth state (*turya*)—this is the distinction.
This very division is indicated in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad by the names Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Turya.
51. Regarding "the quiescent and the risen": the state of quiescence is the state of Paravāsudeva; the state of the risen is...
The state of manifestation (*vyūhāvasthā*). Therein also (p.
10): "In that same way, though she is one, she is indeed 'I' through qualities such as the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and so forth [knowledge, sovereignty, etc., according to E]."
Out of a desire for the welfare of the world, I worship the true being of Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others.
[In due order (ī. the benefit for living beings occurs gradually through dissolution, creation, and maintenance;
furthermore, there is another purpose consisting of the scripture, the meaning of the scripture, and its fruits. (2.57)
One should perceive the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth within the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) as well;
the Vibhava form, however, consists of infinite forms, with Padmanābha at its head, belonging to the All-pervading Lord.
The detailed account of Aniruddha has been shown in that Sāttvata [Purāṇa]; even the worldly worship of those whose selves are permeated by the Blessed One [is described there]. (2.59)
Through the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantras and the lords of mantras, she too possesses a body composed of the six qualities;
[in this descent of the worship of Parā and the others,] within these four forms of mine at the conclusion of the worship of Parā and the rest.
The states beginning with the fourth (turya) are to be known; this is the path of purity.
The difference between the Vyūha and Vibhava [forms] is to be understood through slight distinctions.
But now, O Śakra, listen to my [explanation of] the path that is both pure and otherwise. || 2.61 ||

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Pure Path" (or "Pure Creation"), in the *Lakṣmītantra*, which is the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. [Note: Variants A, B, C, Ḍ, and F omit the title; variant Ṅ reads "Pure Creation."]
Note:
The first array (vyūha) consists of the states of the quiescent and the arisen; the distinction is that the other three consist of the eternally arisen state.

57. Saṃkarṣaṇa is the agent of dissolution and the instructor of the scriptures; Pradyumna is the agent of creation and the promoter of the meaning of the scriptures; Aniruddha is the agent of preservation and the one who brings to fruition the results of the meaning of the scriptures—such is the division of their respective functions.

58. Having described the arrays of others, the manifestations (vibhava) are now discussed here. There are many manifestations such as Padmanābha and others; even the Fish, Tortoise, and so forth are included here among the incarnations (avatāras).
59. *Arcā* refers to specific images installed in temples.
Thus ends the second chapter.
Chapter Three.
Śrī said:
"I am she who is eternally faultless, endowed with boundless auspicious qualities; I am named Nārāyaṇī, that supreme Vaiṣṇava reality. (3.1)
I am not remembered as being delimited by space, time, or form;
pure consciousness alone is my form, and sovereignty and the like are my qualities. (3.2)
The division therein exists solely by virtue of its own sovereignty;
that division which consists of the nature of the powers of consciousness and lordship is what has been described.
Now, another [division], namely the unfolding of the powers of consciousness and lordship, [is discussed].
By my own rising power, which is inconceivable and always beyond the reach of questioning or command. || 3-4 ||
By his will, another form was produced within the triad beginning with knowledge,
just as the clear juice of sugarcane attains the state of molasses.
In the same way, knowledge, which is essentially pure, assumes the nature of *sattva*;
likewise, my sovereignty becomes *rajas*, and my power also becomes *tamas*.
O Śakra, these three qualities are designated as "the triad of qualities" (traiguṇya).
In the process of creation, that triad of qualities revolves with rajas as its predominant factor. (3.7)
In the state of maintenance, that [power] has sattva as its predominance; but in withdrawal, it has tamas as its face.
O Purandara, I am the primordial one, consisting of consciousness, and all-pervasive. (3.8)
Presiding over the qualities (guṇas), she brings about creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
though herself devoid of qualities, she presides over these very qualities by her own will.
I alone set in motion the wheel, which consists of the forms of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Śakra said:
"Having established the two modes within the three ages beginning with the Age of Knowledge (or the three qualities, according to Āṅ. and Ī.),..."
For what purpose do you proceed with the distinction between the pure and the impure? O Lotus-born One, what is the mutual relationship between these two injunctions? (3.11)
"Being asked this by me, speak; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One. Śrī said:
"My sovereignty is not to be commanded; my own will alone is the cause of it. (3.12)
Note:

2. Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the attribute that defines its own nature (*svarūpa-nirūpaka*). The meaning is that the other five attributes are qualities that constitute the nature once [knowledge] has been defined.
3. He states that even this differentiation is produced solely by my will: "By its own sovereignty," etc.

4. "The other" means that previously, in the pure creation, one unfolding (*unmeṣa*) was mentioned; now, in the creation consisting of the impure three qualities (*traiguṇya*), there is another unfolding—this is the meaning.
5. The meaning is that the triad consisting of knowledge (*jñāna*) and the others was transformed into the nature of the triad beginning with *sattva*.
6. He states this very point with the words "tadvat" (in the same way): the sense is that knowledge arose as *sattva*, sovereignty as *rajas*, and power as *tamas*.
7. The term *traiguṇyam* is formed with the suffix *ṣyañ* in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), just as in the case of *cāturvarṇyam*.

9. Regarding the phrase "even though devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇāpi*): since the sixfold qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*) were mentioned previously, the word *nirguṇa* here means "devoid of the mixed qualities consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. By the expression "by the desire of the Self" (*ātmavāñchayā*),...

It is thus stated that, at the beginning of the creation of the world and so forth, play (*līlā*) alone is the motive. As the venerable Bādarāyaṇa said: "But as in the world, it is mere play" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.33). [p. 12] Root-text:
Even the great are deluded in this matter; nevertheless, hear the truth from me:
for I always exist in the state of both the Ruler and the ruled. (3.13)
Nārāyaṇa is to be known as the Lord, and I am his lordship;
but that which is to be ruled over, O Purandara, is to be understood as both the conscious and the unconscious. (3.14)
The power of consciousness (cicchakti), however, is supreme therein; it attains the state of the enjoyer.
The non-conscious sphere (acid-pada) consists of the objects of enjoyment, the instruments, and the locus for that [power]. (3.15)
That power of consciousness (cicchakti), eternally pierced by beginningless ignorance (avidyā) set in motion by me, has attained the state of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtā). (3.16)
Due to the connection with the notions of "I" and "mine," the intellect indeed identifies itself as the Self;
that is ignorance (avidyā), which indeed undergoes disappearance when [the Self] is realized through knowledge (vidyā). || 3.17 ||
Then the power of consciousness (cic-chakti), free from egoism, shall attain my own state;
that Vidyā, established on the pure path, possesses forms such as the Supreme Manifestation (paravyūha).
Out of compassion, I, who perceive the true nature of knowledge, set this forth;
for this relationship of the protected and the protector exists between two injunctions. (3.19)
The first kind protects, and the other kind is protected;
thus it has been told to you, O Śakra. What more do you wish to hear?
Śakra:
For what purpose do you act in the relationship of lord and subject? Tell me: how many varieties are there of the subject, and what is its nature in that regard? (3.21)
Śrī said: This nature of mine and of Nārāyaṇa is not to be questioned;
for I am the Lord, and that eternal God is the one to be ruled by me. (3.22)
The object of His lordship is declared to be twofold, by way of being either conscious or unconscious.
Here, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) takes the form of the enjoyer, and she bears the nature of consciousness, which is my own form.
The power of the insentient (acid-śakti) is considered to exist in three ways through the objects of enjoyment, the instruments, and the locations.
And that third stage of my expanding power is remembered as a "knot" (parvan) by the wise. (3.24)
Even though these two powers, consisting of consciousness and unconsciousness, are distinct,
they are nonetheless my eternal forms by virtue of my own sovereign freedom.
The power of consciousness (cic-chakti) is stainless, pure, consisting of consciousness, and of the nature of bliss;
yet, pierced by beginningless ignorance (anādy-avidyā), it thus certainly undergoes transmigratory existence. (3.26)

Even though the power of consciousness (acicchakti) is insentient, impure, subject to transformation, and composed of the three qualities (triguṇa), this [universe] is merely my own manifestation through the exercise of my own sovereign will. (3.27)
Just as a comet, though blazing, may itself be possessed by smoke, so too do I, though my essential nature is pure consciousness, resort to the state of insentience. (3.28)
Unassailed by conceptual construction, unafflicted even by words, and likewise untouched by the artifice of mental visualization, I thus abide as the insentient self. (3.29)
For although the nature of consciousness is undivided within and without all objects,
it nevertheless appears differentiated through the collection of various limiting adjuncts (upādhis).
"Sovereignty alone is my cause; I am not subject to any inquiry.
Knowing me thus as one of such power, you will become a Buddha. (3.31)
Note:
13. The relationship between the pure and the other [impure] creations is stated as "the Lord and that which is to be ruled.
This means the relationship of the protector and the protected.

28. Just as a comet, though its inherent nature is fire, assumes the form of dark smoke, so too I, though my essential nature is consciousness, have attained the state of non-sentience (acidbhāva); this is the meaning.
29. "By means of the adjunct of meditation" (ādhyānopadhineti) means by means of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of my own will.
Or rather, the meaning is "for the sake of the object of meditation. (p.
13) Mūla-śakra says:
How indeed do you create the worlds endowed with both pleasure and pain? Non-creation would be better, or else let creation consist of nothing but happiness. (3.32)
Śrī said:
Having observed the accumulated karma—composed of both the existent and the non-existent—of individual souls pierced by beginningless ignorance, I bring about a mixed creation. (3.33)
Śakra said:
O Goddess born from the Ocean of Milk, how could you possess autonomy if you ordain happiness and suffering only after taking karma into account?
Śrī said:
"When I perform my tasks, that act of performing is considered [the action]. Furthermore, the agent's dependence upon an instrument does not constitute a violation of his autonomy. (3.35)
I am faultless and independent, not situated within the sphere of questioning;
I divide myself manifoldly through the categories of agent, object, action, and so forth. (3.36)
"No cause for this sport need be sought here; remain thus steadfast.
Śakra said: "Whether it be so or otherwise, O Goddess, such is your sovereignty."
Tell us the manner of creation; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One! (3.37)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Three Qualities" (the mixed creation), in the *Lakṣmītantra*, which is the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Note:
As he will state—“the stages of rest for meditation” (4.24).
32. Regarding the phrase “non-creation”: here [it refers to the idea that] “impelled by compassion, he would create only happiness alone.”
The statement from the Ślokavārttika should be remembered.
Thus ends the third chapter;
[now begins] the fourth chapter.
Śrī said:
I am like the stainless sky, consisting of consciousness and peerless bliss;
I am named Nārāyaṇī, and my nature is such as that of Hari. (4.1)
I am neither quiescent, nor active, nor even intermediate; I am of the nature of consciousness (cidātmikā).
Such is the true form of Hari Viṣṇu, the Self of all. (4.2)
Of that which is of a single, non-variegated form, yet frequents the path of conceptual construction—of that, I am non-variegated, bearing its form, and have attained equality in every respect. (4.3)
In those two, the very nature of consciousness has arisen as a certain unfolding;
it is a fraction [of that] which is [as vast as] ten million times ten million times ten million times ten million.
The desire to create is indeed that very form; "I perform the desired creation. With one portion, I truly exist in the form of the pure sacrifice. (4-5)
Just as the light of a vajra-jewel radiates in all directions,
so does this path consisting of purity radiate from me in every way. Like the cloudless sky, it has the nature of a motionless ocean.
From my form, which is a mass of pure consciousness, a pure creation proceeds.
It is free from latent impressions, devoid of activity, eternally blissful, pure, the self of all, and supreme.
Knowledge is first manifested; he is called Saṃkarṣaṇa. (4.8)
That sovereignty which is independent of any other cause in the creation of the universe—that was my lordship; I was Pradyumna, the Supreme Person. (4.9)
That power of mine which, possessing variegated forms, is latent and omnipresent, and remains unimpeded, is proclaimed as Aniruddha. (4.10)
These gods, the lotus-eyed Puruṣas, who possess the powers of wisdom and sovereignty and are the agents of creation, maintenance, and destruction, are my very form. (4.11)
Resembling a waveless ocean, comparable to the sky when all clouds have vanished—this is my primordial form, O Vāsudeva, who desires to create, whose very nature is mine. [Ā.ṅ.
In its entirety, it possesses knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor.
When they open their eyes simultaneously, he is then called Vāsudeva.
Upon the manifestation of their power of knowledge, Saṃkarṣaṇa is proclaimed;
he sustains the entire universe from himself like a sesame seed within its husk. (4.14)

Its name is indeed "Power" (*bala*), and from that it is designated as Vedānta. When the manifestation of valor and sovereignty occurs, he is celebrated as Pradyumna. Valor is freedom from transformation; therefore, he is unchanging.
For when the power and splendor [of Śakti] manifest, he is called Aniruddha (the Unobstructed). || 4.16 ||
Moreover, its luminosity is independent of anything else and is indeed unobstructed;
therefore, the scripture shines forth from Saṃkarṣaṇa alone, like the sound of a thunderclap. (4.17)
Since all ritual action originates from the god Pradyumna,
they declare that the entirety of the fruit of such action arises from Aniruddha.
For here Aniruddha creates, Pradyumna protects what has been created, and the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa devours that which was both created and protected. (4.19)
These gods themselves always bestow their grace through the acts of creation, preservation, and dissolution, as well as through the fruits of the teachings and dharma.

Even if there is the manifestation of only a single quality, nevertheless all these six qualities are neither deficient nor excessive; they all proceed from the eternal Vāsudeva. Their limbs, minor members, intellect, and so forth, are not considered to be composed of the material elements.
Their divine and eternal body consists of the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) itself.
O Lord of Heaven, no real distinction between these should be contemplated by a wise person;
that distinction was established through the power of conceptual construction for the sake of accomplishing various specific effects. (4.23)

Sovereignty is not other than knowledge, nor is power other than that; these, O Śakra, have been conceived by me as stages for resting in meditation [objects of meditation, according to Ā.B.C.Ḍ.]. First there is the thing, then its existence, then the object, and finally the action.
This fourfold nature should be known to exist at all times within all entities. (4.25)
Having divided myself fourfold by means of myself in the forms of Vāsudeva and others, I abide pervading everything, always through my consciousness.
The gods, beginning with Vāsudeva, each divide their own body threefold and again threefold in the form of Keśava and the others. (4.27)
This other array, known as Pañcarātra, consists of these twelve gods stationed for the guidance of time and its effects. (4.28)
For the benefit of the worlds, the expansion of the all-pervading Lord Hari, who is unceasing, is known as his manifestation (vibhava), such as Padmanābha and others.

That wherein the Lord of the World, entering again and again, effects the welfare of the world—consisting of gods, humans, and so forth—that should be known as another form of manifestation (vibhava). (4.30)

The image (arcā) is that form of the Blessed One created for the welfare of the worlds by gods, sages, ancestors, perfected beings (siddhas), and others, or created by himself; it consists of pure consciousness. (4.31)
Thus, this pure path has been briefly demonstrated to you;
now listen as I describe another path, that of the three qualities (traiguṇya). || 4.32 ||
That knowledge which was previously described manifests through sattva;
sovereignty through rajas, and power as well through tamas. (4.33)
In that state of creation, rajas predominates and revolves;
the two qualities, sattva and tamas, remain on either side of it. (4.34)
That which was previously described by me as the ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part—by a portion of its ten-millionth part, I emit the universe. (4.35)
I am Mahālakṣmī, the primordial source of all; I am the Great Sovereign consisting of the three qualities.
Presiding over the quality of passion (rajas), I perform the desired work of creation. (4.36)
Bearing the two divine states of Agni and Soma, characterized as female and male,
she whose every limb was beautiful acted out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Four-armed and large-eyed, resembling molten gold, she bears a citron, a mace, a shield, and a vessel of nectar. (4.38)
Note:
19. Here, the agency of creation is attributed to Aniruddha and the agency of preservation to Pradyumna;
whereas previously, in the second chapter, the agency of preservation was attributed to Aniruddha and [the agency of creation to Pradyumna].
And the status of being the creator of the universe has been mentioned; however, that should be understood as referring to another *kalpa*.

22. Here, "intellect" (*buddhi*) refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). By the statement, "These [elements] do not consist of the elements," the passage from the *Śāntiparvan*—namely, "The body of this Supreme Self is not a configuration composed of a collection of elements"—is [referred to].
It has been recalled.

24. Regarding "meditation" (*dhyāna*): the meaning is that a distinction is conceptually constructed therein in order to provide objects of focus according to the inclinations of the lay practitioners (*upāsaka*).
27. Thus, all twelve [forms], beginning with Keśava and ending with Dāmodara, which constitute the various internal manifestations (*vyūha*), are to be meditated upon.
30. By the phrase "beginning with gods and humans," [it is implied] that Dattātreya, Bādarāyaṇa, and others are also included.
The state of being a different manifestation is to be meditated upon. 31. By the word "itself," the images situated in self-manifested sacred fields (kṣetra) are included.
36. By this [verse], [the state] during the stage of being the creator of the world of the three qualities (triguṇa-jagat) is [indicated].
(p. 16) I am known as Mūla-Mahālakṣmī, beautiful in all my limbs;
I am Mahāśrī, Mahālakṣmī, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍī, and Caṇḍikā.
Bhadrakālī, as well as Bhadrā, Kālī, Durgā, Maheśvarī, the Goddess of the three qualities (triguṇā), the consort of the Lord, and likewise the supreme Bhagavatī.
These designations and others as well have been recorded by me there in many ways;
I shall now describe those various others in their entirety, arising from the application of modification.
I perceive the entire world, its merits and demerits, its deeds done and left undone;
she who is great and venerable is proclaimed everywhere as Mahālakṣmī. (4.42)
She is called Mahāśrī because she is to be resorted to by the great;
she is Caṇḍī as the beloved of Caṇḍa, and she is considered Caṇḍikā because of her fierce nature.

I am auspicious in form and benign; I am Kālī because I bring about the reckoning (kalanāt) of the virtuous, and I am also proclaimed as Kālī because I possess the form of Time (Kāla) for my enemies. (4.44)
Because she simultaneously ordains both the good and the evil for friends and enemies alike, she is celebrated as Bhadrakālī, whose nature consists of the wondrous qualities of Māyā. (4.45)

She is Mahāmāyā because of her greatness, and she is considered Mohinī because she deludes; she is Durgā because she is difficult to attain, and also because of her practice of protecting her devotees. (4.46)
Because of my application [of means], I am called Yoga and Yogamāyā;
I should be known as Māyāyoga because of my application of knowledge to men. (4.47)
Because I am the embodiment of the six perfections in their entirety, I am remembered as Bhagavatī;
because of my union with the sacrifice of the Blessed One, I am the consort of the Blessed One.
Because of its vastness, it is known as Vyoman (the Sky); because of its filling [all things], it is known as Purī (the City).
Because it is the nature of both the transcendent and the immanent, I am known as Parāvarā (the Transcendent-Immanent).
I am called Śakti because of my power; I am the Queen because I always delight [or cause to reign].
Because I am eternally free from all modification, I am proclaimed as Śāntā (the Peaceful). || 4-50 ||
From me the universe is produced; I am celebrated as Prakṛti (Nature). Resorting [to all], I am the one to be resorted to; I destroy the evil of the virtuous. (4.51)
I hear their piteous cries, and by my qualities I pervade the world;
I lie within all beings, and I take delight in those of meritorious deeds.
I am always praised by the gods, and my body is indeed Vaiṣṇava;
seeing these qualities in me, those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāntas [worship me]. (4-53)
Those who know the application of the conjunction of qualities designate me as Śrī;
such as I am, I am eternal, possessing all forms, and everlasting.
Note:
It is understood that during the *daśā* [period], she is designated as Mahālakṣmī.
45. Regarding "the wonder of *māyā*": by this, it is stated that the meaning of the word *māyā* is its quality of being marvelous.
It exists. By this, the assumption that the word *māyā* has the meaning of "falsehood" is refuted.

47. Regarding the phrase "through the application of knowledge": by this, the meaning of "knowledge" for the word *māyā* is stated, based on the statement of Yāska: "Māyā is *vayuna*, which is knowledge."
The explanation of the phrase "I manifest through my own *māyā*" as meaning "through my own volition" (*ātma-saṃkalpena*) is also based precisely on this [scriptural authority].
48. Regarding "from the connection with sacrifice": this is established by the injunction, "In the connection with our husband’s sacrifice."

Form (rūpa) is to be understood as the sacrifice of the Lord, consisting in the protection of those who have taken refuge [in Him]. In this regard, her union occurs through [the devotee's] human effort and so forth.
51. The verbal roots are *śri* in the sense of "resorting to" (*śrayaṇe*) and *śṝ* in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsāyām*).

52. The verbal roots intended here are *śru* in the sense of hearing, *śrī* in the sense of pleasing, *śī* in the sense of sleeping, and *ram* in the sense of sporting. Regarding the explanation of the letter *śa* in the name *Śrī*: "She lies within" (*śaye'ntar*). Regarding the explanation of the letter *ra*: "I sport" (*rame'ham*).
53. Explanation of the letter *ī*: "Īḍitā" (the praised). The verbal root is *īḍ* in the sense of "to praise. The meaning is that it is the body or form of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.

Presiding over the three qualities, I am proclaimed as the "Threefold One" (Triguṇā). Driven by the desire to create, I have set forth for the sake of the creation resulting from the imbalance of the qualities.
Having the luster of molten gold and adorned with ornaments of molten gold, I fill this world, which was devoid of light, with my own splendor. (4.56)
In the past, in order to fill that entire empty world with myself, I assumed another form consisting solely of darkness. (4.57)
She became a woman with a slender waist, resembling crushed collyrium, her excellent face adorned with fangs, possessing large eyes set between those fangs.
Her great arms were adorned with a sword, a skull-bowl, a head, and a shield; she wore a necklace of headless trunks and bore a garland of serpent-heads upon her head.
Having come into being, that most excellent woman, characterized by the quality of darkness (tāmasī), spoke to me:
"O Mother, give me a name and a ritual act of naming; salutations, salutations to you! (4.60)
Śrī said:
I spoke to that woman of beautiful hips, that most excellent of women belonging to Tamas:
"I shall grant you names which correspond to your various deeds. (4.61)
Mahākālī, Mahāmāyā, Mahāmārī, Hunger, Thirst, Sleep, Blackness (or Craving), Ekavīrā, and the insurmountable Kālarātri. (4–62)
These names of yours are to be explained by means of these very names;
he who studies them, having understood your deeds through these [names], attains happiness. (4.63)
Considering this first creation to be insufficient, I then bore a form resembling the moon, consisting of the manifestation of pure being (sattva). (4.64)
Holding a rosary and a goad, and bearing a lute and a book, she became that excellent woman; for then I gave her that name and performed her consecration.

Mahāvidyā, Mahāvāṇī, Bhāratī, Vāk, Sarasvatī, Āryā, Brāhmī, Mahādhenū, Vedagarbhā, Dhī, and Gī. (Ā.B.C. read "vedabhāgāścagaśca dhīḥ" erroneously; the correct reading is "vedagarbhā... gīśca dhīḥ"). 4–66.

The actions of one who is characterized by goodness (sāttvikī) should be in accordance with her name; her deeds are marvelous. We three are proclaimed as the Mothers, the sustainers of the world. (4.67)

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Mahālakṣmī," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, which is the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. [In some versions, the title is omitted; others read "The Illumination of the Two Creations."]
Fifth Chapter. Root-text: Śrī said: [B.]—
She who is that primordial *Ahaṃtā* of Hari, possessing all forms, eternal, whose nature is pure bliss and consciousness, and who has attained equanimity in every respect. (5.1)
Desiring to create, I, though possessing only a very small portion of my own bindu,
brought forth a pure creation whose form was composed of the fullness of the six divine attributes.
I, whose own nature is never abandoned, am known as Mahālakṣmī through my own tiny drop (or: through my own self), revolving through the three qualities. (5.3)
In that state, I am the Great Goddess Mahāśrī, whose nature is predominantly *rajas*; and that aspect of mine which is of the form of *tamas* is known as Mahāmāyā. (5.4)
That which is my form as Sattva is known as Mahāvidyā;
I and you two are the beloveds, and thus we three are powerful.
Having created three kinds of suitable pairs, that mental pair of mine was of beautiful form. (5-6)
Know that this Hiraṇyagarbha— lotus-eyed, beautiful, and seated upon a lotus— was born within me from a portion of Pradyumna as a mental creation.
Dhātṛ, Vidhi, Viriñci, and Brahmā are remembered as Puruṣa;
Śrī, Padmā, Kamalā, and Lakṣmī are proclaimed there as Nārī.
Born from a portion of Saṃkarṣaṇa through the emergence of Mahāmāyā, he was a pair consisting of a male and female;
he was three-eyed, with all limbs beautiful, and that person there was born of the mind.
He is Rudra, Śaṃkara, Sthāṇu, Kapardin, and the Three-eyed One;
there also reside the Lord of the Three Vedas, Bhāṣā, and likewise Vidyā and Akṣarā.
She is to be known as Kāmadhenu; she is both that woman and the cow Gaurī, who is Sarasvatī herself.
She is born from a portion of Aniruddha and originates from the Great Vidyā.
That which is the mental couple: therein Puruṣa is Keśava, Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vāsudeva, and Janārdana. (5.12)
Umā, Mahādevī, Gaurī, Satī, Caṇḍā—there, that auspicious woman was Satī;
by my command, she became the three wives of Brahmā. || 5.13 ||
Gaurī is the beloved of Rudra, and Ambujā is that of Vāsudeva;
she is the manifestation of passion (rajas), darkness (tamas), and goodness (sattva). || 5.14 ||
This first section, consisting of that triad of pairs, has been told to you;
I shall now speak of the middle section concerning the qualities—listen to this.
Having come together with Bhāṣā, Viriñca produced the cosmic egg;
by my command, Śaṃkara, along with Gaurī, split it open.
Note:
Herein, the first verse describes the state of tranquility (śāntāvasthā); the second verse describes the state of emergence (uditāvasthā);

the third verse describes the state of the three qualities (traiguṇyāvasthā), which is designated as Mahālakṣmī; and the fourth verse describes the state in which rajas predominates (rajaḥpradhānāvasthā).

Mahāśrī is another synonym for Mahālakṣmī. Due to her predominance of *tamas*, she is the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*) mentioned in the preceding chapter; due to her predominance of *sattva*, she is the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) mentioned in the fifth [chapter].
15. Regarding "the first mountain": from the portion of Pradyumna, there is a mental creation of the Rajasic Lakshmi—namely Virinchi and Shri.
From the Tamasic Mahamaya, the root...
(19) Keśava protected that very Pradhāna, which was the effect of the Creator within the egg, together with Padmā. (5.17)
This middle section of the qualities has thus been proclaimed;
I shall now speak of the third section, so listen to it here with a one-pointed mind. (5.18)

Indeed, that which is the primary principle within the egg, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, is the triad of qualities (traiguṇya), primordial nature (prakṛti), the ether (vyoman), inherent nature (svabhāva), the womb (yoni), and the imperishable (akṣara). (5.19)
Having thus liquefied this reality known as the Unmanifest, the Blessed Lord Hṛṣīkeśa, together with the goddess Padmā and with Vidyā, [proceeded]. (5.20)
Having entered into the yoga of sleep, he performed his immersion in the waters;
she who is called Mahākālī became that very sleep characterized by darkness (tāmasī). || 5.21 ||
O Purandara, as he was lying there, a lotus then emerged from his navel;
at that time, it was called a "lotus" (paṅkaja) even though it was not born of mud (apaṅkaja).
[Kālā E.ī. Its names are Jalādhikaraṇa, Padma, Ādhāra, Puṣkara, Cakra, and Puṇḍarīka. (5.23)

Śakra said: "The principle of consciousness and non-consciousness has been explained; consciousness is proclaimed as *cit*, and non-consciousness is said to be the three qualities (*traiguṇya*). What other [principle] is remembered as Time (*kāla*)? (5.24)
Śrī said: "The insentient portion is the other [aspect], Time; the three qualities (guṇas) are remembered as the other.
As for that which was previously mentioned as the triad within the sixfold group (ṣāḍguṇya), it consists of strength and so forth. (5.25)
This very [Prakṛti], in the form of Time, revolves throughout the process of creation;
while this [Prakṛti] itself is unchanging, that triad of qualities (traiguṇya) is subject to transformation.
This dual nature, consisting of both time and non-time, is proclaimed to be insentient;
it belongs to my Goddess Mahāśrī, who creates manifold beings. (5.27)
This time, which consists of me, always exists as the instrument;
therefore, from that lotus composed of time, which arose from the navel of Viṣṇu. (5.28)
Brahmā, consisting of the Veda, was born together with the triple Veda (Trayī), he who is the powerful Hiraṇyagarbha mentioned previously as the source of Lakṣmī. (5.29)
She who was born from Mahākālī is known as the triple Veda (Trayī);
this couple was produced from the lotus at the navel of Viṣṇu.

The lotus, the pair born from the lotus [i.e., Brahmā and his consort], and likewise Dharma and the others— this triad together is declared by the ancient sages to be the great transformation characterized by tamas. (5.31)
The division is threefold: Prāṇa, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Buddhi.
Its greatness is proclaimed because it supports the lotus, the male, and the female. (5.32)
Note:

From the portion of Saṃkarṣaṇa, the mental creation consists of Rudra and the Trayī. From the Sāttvika Mahāvidyā, through the portion of Aniruddha, the mental creation consists of Viṣṇu and Gaurī. Thereafter—

The meaning is that this takes the form of a conceptualization of couples: with the *rājasī* [form] of Viriñci (Brahmā) and the *tāmasī* of Trayī; with the *tāmasī* of Rudra and the *sāttvikī* of Gaurī; and with the *sāttvika* of Viṣṇu and the *rājasī* of Śrī. Regarding the phrase "the middle joint," it was [created] by the Creator.

The creation of the cosmic egg; its splitting by Rudra; and therein, once again, the creation of the primary principles (pradhāna) within the egg by Dhātṛ—meaning that its preservation is carried out by Viṣṇu. 18–The third section: from the lotus-navel of Viṣṇu, [the birth] of Hiraṇyagarbha together with the three Vedas (trayī).

Manifestation: the navel-lotus, that which has arisen from it, and the pair—these three together are called the "Great" (mahat). From that, in the sequence beginning with the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), there is the creation of the phenomenal world (prapañca); this is the meaning.
25—“The triad” means the nature of power (*bala*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and valor (*vīrya*).
27—“Time” refers to moments (*kṣaṇa*) and so forth; “temporal” (*kālya*) refers to that which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and the collection of its transformations.
31—“The pair born from the lotus” refers to Hiraṇyagarbha and the triple Veda (*trayī*).
32— (p. 20) Vitality (prāṇa) is the fundamental quality of the vital breath, while determination is the quality of the intellect (buddhi).
Dharma and its opposite, adharma, and so forth—the pair—is considered a quality (guṇa) of the Person (puruṣa).

Dharma is described as the highest quality, consisting of knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty. Since dharma and the others are primary, adharma and the rest are proclaimed [as their opposites]. (5.34)
The Great One enters him and impels him toward his own creation;
from that Being thus impelled, the ego (ahaṃkāra) was born. (5.35)
He who was previously called Śaṅkara, born from Mahāmāyā, had Gaurī as his wife; she was born here as Abhimati. (5.36)
Having entered this ego (ahaṃkāra), I impel it toward creation;
it then became threefold at first through the intermixture of the qualities (guṇas).
The source of the elements (bhūtādi) therein is composed of tamas; hear from me all about it:
from the source of the elements comes the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), and from that subtle element arises sound. (5.38)
From the mere sound-element impelled by me, the mere touch-element came into being;
and from the touch-tanmātra, impelled by me, [the gross element of air arose]. (5.39)
Then there was the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra); and from that, impelled by me, the primordial form appeared, followed thereafter by the subtle element of taste (rasa-mātra).
From that [subtle element] which was cast forth by me as the measure of taste, when it was agitated, taste was born;
from that, when impelled by me, the subtle element of smell also came into being. (5.41)
"The pure odor has arisen"—this is the classification of the derivative elements (bhautika).
Others [classify] the subtle elements (mātrās) as the subtle elements (sūkṣmabhūtas) and the gross elements (sthūlabhūtas). (5.42)

Sound and the others are declared to be qualities; however, those which are sound and the others that constitute the emission of the gross elements are not other than the qualities of sound and the rest. (5.43)
Quiescence, ferocity, and delusion—these are its threefold nature; they exist in subtle beings as the manifestations of the unfolding of sattva and the other qualities. || 5.44 ||
Therefore, their state as mere [subtle] essence is proclaimed for those subtle [elements];
however, in other cases, they possess grossness because they bestow pleasure, pain, and so forth. (5.45)
The three states of the gross elements alone are proclaimed,
according to their divisions as subtle, born of the ancestors, and abundant. (5.46)
The various external objects, such as jars and the like, are called "abundant.
The specific features produced from semen and blood are known as those born of the father. (5.47)
The subtle forms of the five elements, however, are those that reside within the subtle body; thus has the creation arising from the *bhūtādi* been described in its proper sequence. (5.48)
Of egoity (ahaṃkāra), there are two portions based upon rajas and sattva.
The sattvic portion of these two is called vaikārika; the other portion is called taijasa by the wise. Listen now to this creation of theirs.
From the *vaikārika* ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the cognitive faculties (*dhīndriya*) such as the ear and the rest arose. (5.50)
Note:
*Hiraṇyagarbha* and *buddhi* are distinct entities.
33—Regarding the word "puṃsaḥ": it means "of Hiraṇyagarbha."

34—Regarding the phrase "yasmāt" (because): the opposites of dharma and the other qualities are to be understood as adharma, ignorance (ajñāna), non-detachment (avairāgya), and lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya).
36—The quality of egoism (ahaṃkāra) itself is designated by the term "abhimati" (self-identification); this is another name for it.
38. It should be understood that *bhūtādi* is another name for *tāmasa-ahaṃkāra*, *vaikārika* for *sāttvika-ahaṃkāra*, and *taijasa* for *rājasa-ahaṃkāra*.
48. From the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), both sound and the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*) were produced.

From the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*), touch and the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*) are born; from the subtle element of form, form and the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*) are born; from the subtle element of taste, taste and the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*) are born; and from the subtle element of smell, smell is born—such is the process here. However, the Sāṃkhyas [maintain]:
They state that all the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) arise from *bhūtādi* alone.
However, according to the Upaniṣadic system, the subtle element of sound arises from *bhūtādi*, and from that, space (*ākāśa*) [arises] (p. 21). This is the fundamental [view].
The organs of action, beginning with speech, proceed from the Taijasa [ego].
From both of these, moreover, arose the mind, which possesses both the faculties of cognition and action. (5.51)
The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—these they call the five sense organs; this power is of my own nature. (5.52)
Speech, hands, feet, as well as the organ of generation and the anus—these they call the five organs of action; this power is of my own nature. (5.53)
That power of consciousness which has come down to me through a succession of lineages, having presided over the faculties of perception, operates upon the objects of the senses. (5.54)
And that power of action which has come down to me through the lineage of succession, having presided over the organs of action, proceeds toward what is to be done. (5.55)
Sound is considered the object of the ear, and hearing is considered its activity;
touch is considered the object of the skin, and touching is considered its activity. (5.56)
Form is the object of the eye, and seeing is considered its activity; taste is the object of the tongue, and tasting is considered its activity. (5.57)
The object of the nose is odor, and its function is considered to be smelling;
the functions of this [organ], as well as those of the ear and the others, with respect to their objects, are hearing and so forth. (5.58)
The perceptions and so forth are now described; that is the apprehension of the mere substratum (dharmin).
These are: space, lightning, the sun, the moon, and likewise the earth. (5.59)
That which is declared as "relating to the deities" (adhidaiva) pertains, in order, to the pentad beginning with the ear;
that which is declared as "relating to the elements" (adhibhūta) consists, in order, of the objects of sense beginning with sound.
This pentad beginning with the ear is proclaimed as internal (*adhyātma*).
The creation of the ear and the other senses from the *sāttvika* [aspect] is in comparison to [the creation of] ether and the other elements.
Therefore, the pentad beginning with the ear is said to be elemental (*bhautika*) according to the sequence.
The object of speech is sound, and its function is considered to be the act of speaking. (5.62)
The taking up of what is to be taken is considered the function of the hand-faculty; going to what is to be gone to is considered the function of the foot-faculty. (5–63)
The blissful state of the generative organ is considered its bliss, and emission is considered its activity;
the object to be emitted is that of the anus, and evacuation is considered its activity. (5–64)
The group of four beginning with the hand consists of the five sense objects;
their presiding deities (adhidevas) should be known by the wise in this order: Agni, Indra, Viṣṇu, as well as the First One (Brahmā), Prajāpati, and Mitra.
Sound, which is indeed the object of speech and the other [senses], consists of five elements. || 5.66 ||
That is declared to be the *adhibhūta*; speech and the rest are called the *adhyātma*.
But the mind is the common agent in both of these pentads. (5.67)
[Regarding the group of cognitive faculties, Ātreya says: "The mind expands this conceptualization through the group of cognitive faculties.
Conceptualization is a manifold construction, and that is said to be the qualifier. (5.68)
The connection with a property (dharma) is said to belong to the property-bearer (dharmin).
This conceptual construction (vikalpa) is to be known as fivefold, by way of substance, action, quality, and so forth. (5.69)
The person is [designated] as "staff-bearer" due to conjunction with a substance; as "white" due to connection with a quality;
as "going" due to connection with an action; and as [a mere] "person" due to the persistence of the universal. (5.70)
Note:
From that [sound-tanmātra] arises the touch-tanmātra; from that, air; from that, the form-tanmātra;
