from that, fire; from that, the taste-tanmātra; from that, water; from that, the smell-tanmātra.
Therefore, it is said that "the earth was born.

51—In this regard, there is a conceptual distinction made that the organs of cognition arise from the *vaikārika* [sāttvika] aspect, while the organs of action arise from the *taijasa* [rājasa] aspect. However, according to the followers of the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣadas*), all the organs [arise from the same source].

They declare that [the mind] originates from *vaikārika* [sattva]. Likewise, according to the Sāṃkhya school, the mind possesses the nature of both types of sense organs; however, in the Upaniṣadic system, it possesses only the nature of a cognitive organ (*jñānendriya*).
59—Perception (*ālocana*) is the clear apprehension of the attributes of sound and so forth, without [the intervention of] conceptualization.
It is the apprehension of the mere object; yet even that is indeed indistinct. And they say:
"There is indeed an initial non-conceptual cognition which is mere observation (*ālocana*).
(p. 22) [Root Text]
"‘This is Ḍittha,’ ‘due to the conjunction with words’—this fivefold state exists.
And the mind, through the groups of organs of action, expands this volition. (5.71)
That which is the fall from indifference is called "volition" (saṃkalpa) and "exertion" (udyoga);
and by means of the ego (ahaṃkāra), there is a state of abiding within both these categories. (5.72)
This [individual] functions within the group of sense organs through egoism (abhimāna). The association with space and time belonging to the knower is proclaimed as egoism. (5.73)
"Today this object appears before me"—in this way the object is perceived;
yet it proceeds with such intensity through the group of the organs of action. (5.74)

But passion (saṃrambha) is proclaimed to have volition as its precursor; the intellect (buddhi), situated within the group of the organs of perception, functions through determination (adhyavasāya). (5.75)
Intellect (buddhi) is declared to be the determination of objects;
the ascertainment of objects is proclaimed to be certainty (niścaya). (5.76)
The intellect operates with effort upon the group of the organs of action;
thus, this thirteenfold instrument is to be known by the wise. (5.77)
The external is to be known as tenfold, and the internal organ is said to be threefold;
these twenty-three are proclaimed as the transformations (vikāras) of Virāj.
The ten organs and the three [internal faculties] are subtle components that arise from the gross;
this is proclaimed as the subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra) of Virāj. (5.79)
The individual emanations and subtle bodies—[the various distinctions]—are established for each individual soul;
they, being born from their own source, cease upon the liberation of the souls. (5.80)
These twenty-three principles, having arisen through mutual assistance, produce the cosmic egg (aṇḍa)—namely, those beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas. (5.81)
Then that golden egg came into being, possessing a radiance equal to the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Prajāpati, the god Virāj, who has four faces.
And Virāja was born as Manu; from that Manu, the Mānavas are said to have descended.
From them, Marīci and the others [were born], and from them came this entire world of moving and unmoving beings. (5.83)
This manner of my arising has been shown to you only in brief.

Although the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is pure by its very nature, is inherently stainless, it experiences suffering arising from birth, old age, and so forth, because it is constricted by beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*). (5.84) Abiding therein, it undergoes that [suffering].
When, through connection with pure consciousness and through the accompaniment of pure action, one shakes off that ignorance, then one enjoys bliss [which is infinite]. (5.85)

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Primal Creation" (or "The Creation of the World beginning with Brahmā"), in the *Lakṣmītantra*, which is the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra* (or *Śrīpañcarātra* / *Śrīpāñcarātra*). Chapter 5.
Note:
"The object is as if it were the consciousness of a child, a mute person, and so forth.
(82) — Here, the previously mentioned sequence of emanation is stated by synthesizing it with the creation of Manu and others.
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
The sixth chapter, the Root.

Śrī said: Obeisance to that primordial I-consciousness of Hari, who is like a waveless ocean, a great sea of the bliss of consciousness and the six perfections (ṣāḍguṇya) in their full and steady state. (6.1)
I, being thus pure, have in some instances attained a state of swelling;
I am the Goddess characterized by the desire to create, autonomous, and whose essence is Being-Consciousness. (6.2)
For seven days, the supreme power of Viṣṇu, who consists of the three qualities (guṇas), entered into the state of the six sheaths as Māyā, Prasūti, and Prakṛti. (6.3)

The cosmic egg and the bodies of living beings—these are designated as the six sheaths. That supreme desire of Viṣṇu to create, which has arisen from his sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā), [is the first]. (6.4)
That power is the first sheath (kośa), which sets the pure path in motion;
"sheath" (kośa) is a synonym for "nest" (kulāya), possessing another name for the body. (6.5)
In this first pure treasury, characterized by the first unfolding, the supreme Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, the master, was indeed the Ego-maker (Ahaṃmānin). || 6.6 ||
There, a smooth transformation exists like a mole or a freckle;
that goddess who is his ego (ahaṃtā) is I myself, the supreme Saṃkarṣaṇī.
She who is endowed with the power of consciousness is thus designated as Śrī;
that which is her manifestation is celebrated as Pradyumna. (6.8)
The god Pradyumna, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), abides in the state of intellect (buddhi) as the deity who presides over the sheath of power (śakti-kośa) belonging to the god Saṃkarṣaṇa. (6–9)
The aggregate of the enjoyer and the enjoyed remains dissolved therein;
it is that which is known as the "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) of that deity who has become the mind. (6.10)
I am she named Sarasvatī, who manifests through the power of heroic sovereignty;
that which is my unfolding is proclaimed as Aniruddha. (6.11)
I am established in the function of ego-consciousness for that Saṃkarṣaṇa;
these three ancient gods are Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others. (6.12)
Those proclaimed by the names Jīva, Buddhi, and Ahaṃkāra are not deities composed of material nature (prākṛta), but rather consist of pure consciousness. (6.13)
Of the primordial, manifested Lord Vāsudeva as he sports, these [forms] are designated by various names according to their performance of specific tasks. (6.14)

All of them are said to possess the six qualities, and all of them are the Supreme Persons; [they arise] from the great ocean of eternal bliss, which is full and steady in its sixfold attributes. (6.15)
The simultaneous manifestation of the six qualities by virtue of their functional activity—
that which came into being is Vāsudeva, the first-conceived manifestation (vyūha). (6.16)
My peaceful nature is indeed Ahaṃtā; she is proclaimed as Śakti.
The gods reside within the sheath of Śakti, where the three [E.ī. are conceived. (6-17)
That which is the "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) of Aniruddha, designated as "delight" (rati), is that very goddess Mahālakṣmī; she is called the sheath of māyā. (6.18)
Note 3:

Among the six sheaths known as Śakti, Māyā, Prasūti, Prakṛti, Brahmāṇḍa, and Jīvadeha, the Śakti-sheath is that which initiates the path of purity. Within that very [sheath] reside Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others.
The manifestation of the three:
8—Śrī is the queen of Saṃkarṣaṇa; Sarasvatī is the queen of Pradyumna; Rati is the queen of Aniruddha; and Śānti is the queen of Vāsudeva.
18 – Impure Creation, beginning with the Sheath of Māyā (p.
24): The root [verse] states:
"The unfolding of Mahālakṣmī, which is designated as the *guṇas* of Māyā..."
The two great vidyās of Mahākālī are thus fully proclaimed. || 6.19 ||
The third treasury of mine, named Prasūti, which consists of Mahālakṣmī, Mahāmāyā, and Mahāvidyā, is now recited. (6.20)
There were three pairs here which were previously mentioned by you;
having made the primary matter (pradhāna) like water, the Supreme Person (puruṣottama) lies upon it. (6.21)
She is declared to be Prakṛti, the source (yoni), whose essential nature is the equilibrium of the guṇas;
she indeed gave birth to the cosmic egg within herself in the beginning, O Viriñca.

Regarding this, some who are experts in the treatises on the principles (tattva) declare it to be primordial nature (prakṛti), along with the cosmic egg that has been fashioned by [the principles] beginning with the Great One (mahat) and ending with earth. (6.23)
That is called the "Cosmic Egg" (Brahmāṇḍa), wherein Brahmā became the Virāṭ;
it is the body of living beings here, endowed with limbs and minor members. (6.24)
This sixth method of the treasury has gradually become diminished;
these six descents of mine, which were once full, have been fully described. (6.25)
In the first sheath, the Lord Himself exists in three ways as the ego;
in the other five sheaths, various kinds of individual souls (jīvas) reside. (6.26)
They experience various states arising from the distinction between the auspicious and the inauspicious;
these include the three divine ones and their three pairs,
as well as the incarnations of those [goddesses] and [their consorts] that are remembered within the Egg.
But these, created by his own sovereignty, are not at all subject to the power of karma.
Those bodies of both [types] are proclaimed to be non-material (aprākṛta).
Others, from the gods down to the stationary beings, exist within the five sheaths (pañcakośa).

Those living beings who, occupying various states, transmigrate through the power of their karmas—these, by virtue of the ripening of auspicious karma, lead their office (*adhikāra*) to its exhaustion. (6.30)
Having attained an abundance of knowledge and having destroyed their impurities through yoga, they gradually ascend the sheaths; once ascended, they do not fall.
From Satyaloka onwards, those who have ascended to whichever stage they reach do not return; they either remain there or proceed further upward. (6.32)
Śakra said:
"O Goddess born from the Ocean of Milk, O Consort of the Lotus-navelled One!
Who indeed is this so-called *jīva*? Tell me that; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One! (6.33)
Śrī said: "I am the primordial, perfect I-consciousness of Hari; I am that supreme sovereign of all.
O bull among the gods, my four states are remembered as being true. (6.34)
The knower is one kind; within that, the internal organ is another;
the external organ is yet another; and the fourth is the plane of objective existence. (6.35)
The cognizer is declared to be consciousness; he is said to be my contraction.
For I am that which has attained non-limitation by space, time, and so forth. (6.36)
In the *Mūla*, it was previously stated that Mahālakṣmī possesses the quality of *rājasa* and is the cause of the creation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
[This refers to] the *prasūtikośa* (the womb of manifestation) of Rājasyā Mahālakṣmī and Tāmasī Mahāmāyā.
It is of the nature of a conjunction between that [power] and the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) characterized by sattva.

21—Three pairs are described in the fifth chapter by the seven verses beginning with the seventh. Primordial matter (pradhāna) itself is called the "sheath of nature" (prakṛtikośa). In the Upaniṣads, these natures—which are the source of illusion (māyā)—are referred to by the names "darkness" (tamas), "the unmanifest" (avyakta), and "primordial matter" (prakṛti).
Regarding the term *vyavahāra*: 30—*adhikāra*. The sūtra of Bādarāyaṇa states: "The persistence of those who hold office lasts as long as their office."

35. The cognizer is the individual soul (jīva). The internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is threefold, consisting of mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), and ego (ahaṃkāra). The external organs (bahiḥkaraṇa) are the organs of knowledge—(p. 25)—the sense organs. The root [organs]...
Out of very freedom itself, I assume contraction while not abandoning my own nature;
therein, that first contraction is proclaimed as the "subject" (pramātṛ). (6.37)
Just as the universe remains dissolved within me, who am the conscious self (cidātman), so too does it abide within the subject (pramātṛ), like mountains reflected in the interior of a mirror. (6.38)
The cognizer attains a state of oneness, duality, triplicity, and fourfold division; [six, seven, and five (Ā.B.C.)]—that is, a state of seven, five, and three forms.
For by means of light, he is one with himself, yet through the power of the grasped and the grasper, he becomes manifold.
That [reality] possesses a twofold nature and a threefold nature, by way of being the essence of cognition, form, and activity. (6.40)
The state of consisting of seven pentads is established in the abiding of each respective principle (*tattva*).
Śakra asked: "O lotus-eyed one, what are those principles, how many are there, and of what nature are they? (6.41)
"Being asked this by me, tell it; salutations to you, O one born from the ocean! [Padma] Śrī said:
"The ten elements and the voids, distinguished as gross and subtle... (6.42)
Through the distinction between knowledge and action, there are the three internal organs;
as well as primordial nature (prakṛti), procreation (prasūti), illusion (māyā), and the qualities of goodness, passion, and darkness (sattva, rajas, tamas).
Time, destiny, power, the person, and the supreme ether—these are the principles that the Sāttvatas study as the Blessed One. (6.44)
Śakra said:
"I have heard the truths from the lotus of your mouth;
explain these to me, O Goddess; salutations to you, O Sarasīruhā."
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Six Sheaths," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra* (or *Śrīpañcarātra*).
Note:

[The senses] are of ten kinds in the form of the organs of action. The "planes of existence" (bhāvabhūmikā) constitute the manifold expansion of objects of knowledge. 39—The four divisions are the states beginning with waking.
Thus ends the sixth chapter.
The seventh chapter. Śrī said: [Śrī said, B.]—
Therefore, O Śakra, I shall explain to you in due order the sequence of the principles (tattvapaddhati).
This sequence of principles is said to be pure, impure, and mixed. (7.1)
He has the appearance of a cloudless sky, resembling an ocean without ripples;
he is the great ocean of eternal bliss, characterized by pure and autonomous consciousness. (7.2)
Free from the limitations of form, place, time, and so forth—[and free from qualifying attributes]—the eternal Supreme Self is to be known as the Blessed One. (7.3)
Her supreme egoity is such an eternal lordliness—Nārāyaṇī, the supreme, subtle, free from conceptual construction, and stainless. (7.4)
He is a great ocean of knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor;
indeed, he is the first manifestation of the six qualities occurring simultaneously.
He is designated as twofold by virtue of being both existence (bhava) and the essence of existence (bhāva).
Here, Vāsudeva is "existence," while the state of being Vāsudeva within him is "the essence of existence."
I am that eternal Goddess known by the name Śānti;
the manifestations (vyūhas) beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa, which consist of that [Śānti], have been described previously. (7–7)
And the three, O Lord of the Gods, constitute the fourfold nature; these four are the reality beyond all principles (nistattva), the supreme reality which is the denotation of the Blessed One. (7–8)
But the sky is the supreme void, designated as the supreme ether,
wherein the Lord, having divided himself by himself along with me in that place— || 7–9 ||
The eternal Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, sports with Ramā;
that region, where the six divine attributes manifest, is the supreme ether (paramāmbaram). 7.10.
The Puruṣa is the eternal enjoyer, all-knowing and facing in every direction; from him, all the eternal individual souls (jīvas) emanate as partial manifestations. (7.11)
Even at the time of dissolution, those whose nature is action enter this supreme man;
this is my state as a mother, which was previously described by me to you. (7–12)
Mahālakṣmī is declared by the wise to be the principle of Śakti;
Niyati is Mahāvidyā, and Kāla is proclaimed as Kālī. (7–13)
The triad of qualities is declared to be sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Sattva is remembered as being of the nature of happiness, transparent, producing knowledge, and light.
Rajas should be known as being of the nature of suffering, mobile, passionate, and impelling.
Darkness (tamas) should be known as having the nature of delusion (moha); it is heavy, black, and restrictive. || 7.15 ||
O Vāsava, Māyā, Prasūti, and Prakṛti—this triad of natures was previously explained to you. (7.16)
Note:

The thirty-five principles (tattvas) mentioned in the preceding chapter are now described in reverse order. Among these, the principle of the Blessed Lord (Bhagavat-tattva) is first described here; and the principle of the Blessed Lord is the state of tranquility (śāntāvasthā).

The secondary Vāsudevas, the states [of manifestation], and the arrays (vyūhas), as well as the Goddess who is non-distinct from them—these constitute the *nistattva*. The meaning is that it has emerged from and transcends the other principles (*tattvas*). He expresses this very point by saying, "the supreme principle."
10— By describing the Supreme Space (*paravyoman*) as having the nature of the manifestation of the six attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*), its non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*) is intended;
however, there is also a position that maintains its inertness (*jaḍatva*).
The fundamental elements are ten in number, and likewise the cavities are thirteen;
these twenty-three were clearly explained by me in the past. (7)
Therefore, this contracted subject of mine, consisting of pure consciousness, remains always like a mirror, with the flood of all principles flashing within itself. (7.18)
Now listen with a focused mind to that which constitutes its fourfold form:
the first is proclaimed as the Mother, consisting of emptiness, occurring at the onset of fainting and other such states. (7.19)
[B. omits this line. Therefore, the mother is proclaimed to be composed of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*) in deep sleep;
for it is the vital breaths alone that expand within a person during deep sleep. (7.20)
In cases such as fainting or being struck by poison, even the vital breath (prāṇa) ceases;
at that time, there remains only the existence of one's own self (svātmasattā), and thus the person is void.
The third, measuring eight purīs, is proclaimed as the mother in the dream state;
[it consists of] the vital breaths, the elements, actions, the organs, and the three qualities. (7.22)
Prior latent impressions and ignorance are known as the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka), which is the subtle body;
for in the dream state, it moves about at will by means of the internal organ alone. (7.23)
The embodied soul, exerting itself with its own body, has entered the waking state.
Listen now to me regarding this fourfold nature of the person, as well as its threefold nature. (7.24)
The contraction of those whose nature consists of knowledge and action is indeed threefold;
for that [contraction] possesses a threefold form—listen now to this explanation of it. (7.25)

Through *māyā*, there is the contraction of knowledge; through lack of sovereignty, the loss of action; and through incapacity, atomicity (*aṇutā*)—thus, in its essential form, it is designated as threefold. (7.26)
"He is minute, he is an agent of something, and he is a knower of something"—this has already been explained previously regarding his dual nature as well as his single nature. (7.27)
Thus, having reached the state of the Mother, it has been proclaimed with its specific distinctions. Now, O Śakra and others, hear from me concerning the state of the internal organ as well. (7.28)

I am indeed consciousness, free-willed, having attained self-awareness by itself; and having abandoned that state of consciousness, I have subsequently descended through the stages [of manifestation]. (7.29)
The *caitya* is the contraction; the mind (*citta*) is said to be the internal organ (*antah-karaṇa*).
That triad consists of the intellect (*manas*), the faculty of discernment (*buddhi*), and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). (7.30)
Conceptualization, determination, and self-conceit are the functions [of the mind]. The mind conceptualizes the object, and the ego-sense conceives "I. (7.31)
And the intellect, presided over by consciousness, always determines;
the intellect is said to be the "internal self" (adhyātma), while determination is the "elemental" (adhibhūtaka).
Note:
"Of others.
11. Hiraṇyagarbha is the Puruṣa who is the aggregate of individual souls (jīvasamaṣṭi) and is immutably situated as the enjoyer (bhoktṛkūṭastha).
18. Thus, having defined the thirty-five principles introduced in the forty-second, forty-third, and forty-fourth verses of the sixth chapter,
right there—
Beginning from the verse "tadayam" up until the end of the chapter, he describes the four states of the self introduced in the thirty-fifth verse.
[Verse 22: "Consisting of only the eight cities. The word *mātra* signifies either measure (*pramāṇa*) or exclusivity (*kevala*).
The meaning is "devoid of external activity. The eight cities will be mentioned in the subsequent verse.
23—*liṅgam* refers to the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*).
26—*kriyāvyayaḥ* means the incapacity to perform desired actions; [this is what is meant] by *ānaiśvaryam*.
In the sense of "the state of being without a lord" (*anīśvara*), the suffix *pyañ* causes the *vṛddhi* strengthening of both syllables.

By the statement that [the soul] is "of the nature of an atom" (*aṇurūpa*) due to the contraction of its own form, one should not think that the soul's inherent nature is that of being all-pervasive (*vibhu*).

Since its nature as an atom is established by numerous means of valid cognition, it should be understood that the specific description here of its atomic form is intended to indicate its lack of omnipotence, lack of omniscience, and so forth. This very point is explained by the phrase "due to that very incapacity."
28. In the preceding chapter, the second state of the internal organ was indicated; it is explained here. (p. 28) Root-text:
The Knower of the Field, together with the presiding deity, is reflected upon the mirror of the intellect.
Likewise, the sense of "I" (ahaṃkṛti) is the internal aspect, while self-conceit (abhimāna) is the elemental aspect.
Furthermore, Rudra is proclaimed as the deity with respect to the divine (adhidaiva), while the mind is proclaimed as the self with respect to the self (adhyātma).
Conceptualization (vikalpa) is the elemental sphere (adhibhūta), and the moon is its presiding deity (adhidaivatam).
Vitality (*prāṇa*), exertion (*saṃrambha*), and intention (*saṃkalpa*) are the qualities involved in the performance of action.

Vitality is said to be effort (*prayatna*); exertion is called pride (*garva*). (7.35) [F. omits this line; E. and I. omit this line; B. reads: "Exertion, which consists in the state of possessing fruit, is called pride."]
Pride regarding the nature of one's ownership of the fruits [of action] is called *saṃrambha*;
the wise declare that mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is the departure from indifference. (7.36)
This second state, pertaining to the internal organ, has been explained by me;
for from that [state], the "I" belonging to the internal organ falls away from its form. (7.37)
Having gradually attained the state of torpor, it is designated as the external instrument;
indeed, the external instruments have been explained by me previously. (7.38)
But when the organs of knowledge are active, the mind and the others proceed;
the eye perceives the object, and it is the mind that conceptualizes it. (7.39)
The ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), situated in the conceptualization of perception, conceives "I am.
Then, having reached a determination, the intellect (buddhi) presents it to the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). (7.40)
However, regarding the activity of the organs of action, the sequence is traditionally held to be reversed; for the acts of speaking and so forth follow after volition and the like. (7.41)
All the distinctions concerning the internal [senses] and so forth have been previously explained here; this third [category], consisting of the external organs, is now described. (7.42)

Now listen to me regarding this fourth limit, which indeed has the nature of the object of measurement (*meyarūpa*). That object of measurement is twofold, established by way of the external and the internal. (7.43)
External objects such as blue, yellow, and so forth, as well as internal states such as pleasure and pain—I have become solidified through these four modes. (7.44)

By means of the objects of conceptual construction arising from my own mind, I had forgotten even that which is directly perceived; [now I am restored] by the instruction of a true teacher, following correct reasoning. (7.45)

When I am clearly dissolved within that object of knowledge which is to be scrutinized by the wise—even while being an object of knowledge—then, having likewise dissolved this entire state of being consisting of the nature of the cognizable; (7.46)
Then I myself am that independent, full consciousness in the state of light;
thereafter, being transparent and more transparent, I am designated as the instruments (of perception). (7.47)
Then, within the Mother, I shine forth as utterly pure and consisting of pure consciousness.
Contemplating both my ascent and descent, one whose mind is fixed on Me, whose life-breath has gone unto Me, attains My state of being. (7.48)

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Knower and the Instruments," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra* (or, as the case may be, the *Pañcarātra*, the *Pāñcarātra*, or the *Pañcarātrasāra*). The eighth chapter: Śakra said—
Salutations to you, O one born from the ocean; salutations to you, O one born from the lotus;
salutations to you, whose abode is the lake-born flower, O consort of Nārāyaṇa.
The incarnations of yours that have been mentioned in the *Pañcakosa*—O Lotus-born One, you should explain them in detail to me as I ask. (8.2)
For what purpose are they, of what kind are they, how many are they, and what is their nature?
O Goddess, tell me the truth, for you are all-knowing and eternal. (8.3)
Śrī said: It is without waves, indefinable, unshakable, incomparable, formless, non-manifest,
without categories, indivisible, free from conceptual construction, and undisturbed.
Unchanging and undisturbed. || 8 - 4 ||
There is one Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, who is void, pure, and free from affliction.
Whatever is seen here, heard, or inferred—[B. omits eight lines from here]—is that alone.

The world— comprising the moving and the unmoving, the subtle and the gross, the sentient and the insentient— is characterized by existence and non-existence, and its specific nature is to be fully understood through the three means of valid cognition. (8.6)
All this is indeed the unsurpassed Brahman, Nārāyaṇa— [I am you]—
a mass of pure, independent consciousness, whose bliss is free from ignorance.
The divine, supreme end of the path,
which consists of both being and non-being, exists in two ways through the state of the possessor of power (śaktimat) and power (śakti).
That Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, is the possessor of power; I am that very being. That Nārāyaṇī is my power; I am the ego-consciousness (ahaṃtā) whose nature is existence.
There is no place where that which has come into being exists without me;
there is no place for me where that which has come into being does not exist. (8.10)
In one way and indeed in two ways, we two are designated as the cause of all things by those various scriptures that have reached the further shore of the ocean of reality. (8.11)

In some cases creation has existence as its ultimate; in some, it has becoming as its ultimate; and in others, it has both becoming and existence as its ultimate. The wise man is not deluded by this. (8.12)
For when Nārāyaṇa alone descended due to the business of the gods, I was there with him, sharing in his very nature. (8.13)
And when I alone descended out of a desire for the welfare of the gods, that Lord who is the referent of the term "I" became manifest within me through my sense of selfhood. (8.14)

When we two descended equally with the desire to accomplish the work of the gods, we both remained as one another's counterparts, consisting of the nature of existence and non-existence. *Note:* [The reading "dvayau" is supported by manuscripts A, B, C, and Ḍ.]

The Root [Śrī said]:
I am the goddess Nārāyaṇī, devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
my nature consists of knowledge, bliss, and action, and I am composed of knowledge, bliss, and action. (9.1)
For me, there is no separation from him, nor for him from me; indeed, it is impossible to bring about such a state, whether at any time or in any place. (9.2)

And by the power of their respective functions, those two possess forms that are both ordinary and wondrous; through the strength of their own yoga, they exist together with their own selves, and yet also independently.
Brahmā and the others, compelled by the power of his asceticism and yoga, granted an excellent boon to the Daityas and others who were causing the destruction of the world. (9.4)
Assuming such and such forms, we two, though eternal, move about for the sake of the gods' business, desiring to bring about their respective pleasures. (9.5)
Having concealed my true nature through illusion by means of my own splendor, I have indeed descended myself with the desire to destroy those various [demons] who seek to annihilate them. (9.6)
In the beginning, I was remembered as the Goddess Mahālakṣmī, the Supreme Sovereign;
and then, by way of form, I became twofold: Kṛṣṇā and Brāhmī. (9.7)
This supreme form of mine, through the differentiation of the three qualities (guṇas),
is Mahālakṣmī, O Śakra, during the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara.
Born for the welfare of all the worlds and the gods, she is the crusher of Mahiṣa;
those who are but fragments of my power have entered the bodies of various deities. (9.9)
Having come together, O Lord of the Gods, they became my form, which was supremely beautiful,
as well as whatever weapons belong to the gods.
The powers of that [weapon], possessing its form, became my weapons;
praised by the gods, I slew Mahiṣa in an instant. (9–11)
Then the Mahiṣāntakarīsūkta, which bestows all accomplishments, was likewise seen by the goddess, as well as by the gods led by Indra and the ṛṣis. (9–12)
"O Lord of the Gods, the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas recount his birth, his prowess in battle, and his hymn of praise in great detail. (9–13)
Praising, meditating upon, or even bowing down to that Goddess of such power, one constantly obtains the fruit of eternal sovereignty. (9.14)
That goddess who is called Yoganidrā of Hari, she who is difficult to overcome—
know me to be that eternal goddess, the very body of Mahākālī. (9–15)
For at that time, Madhu and Kaiṭabha were deluded by her;
consequently, they were slain by Viṣṇu, the God of gods, through the granting of a boon. (9.16)
O Purandara, that hymn beginning with "Viśveśvarī" was formerly seen by Brahmā for the purpose of praising me, the Goddess Yoganidrā. (9-17)
This is indeed that Vaiṣṇavī Māyā, the Great Kālī, who is difficult to overcome;
when brought under control by praise, she brings both the moving and the unmoving worlds under the control of the one who praises her. (9.18)

The origin, the life-story, and even the hymn of praise of this Goddess are maintained [or meditated upon] by the exponents of Brahman for the welfare of all beings. O Śakra, during the Tāmasa interval, she is indeed the supreme Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā).
"Then indeed I was born from the body of Gaurī as Kauśikī. || 9.20 ||
For the sake of slaying the wicked Daityas, as well as Sumbha and Niśumbha, and for the protection of the worlds, she was a benefactor to the gods. (9.21)
Those powers of mine which reside within the bodies of the foremost of gods assumed their respective forms and indeed rendered me assistance;

Having withdrawn all those entire droplets of mine into myself.
"O Goddess, remover of the distress of those who seek refuge, be gracious to me"—thus she spoke, after having slain Sumbha and Nisumbha. (9.24)
The hymn named Nārāyaṇī-stuti is supremely beautiful;

When worshipped with devotion, she bestows omniscience;

"Origination, heroic prowess in battle, and praise— this triad is recited by the ancient brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences. (9.27)

"Born in the family of Nanda the cowherd, originating from the womb of Yaśodā—I, Sunandā Vindhyavāsinī, shall destroy them both. (9.29)
Furthermore, descending upon the surface of the earth in an exceedingly fierce form,

And as they devour those fierce Vaipracitta great Asuras,
their teeth will become red, resembling the blossoms of the pomegranate tree.
Then all the deities and the mortals in the world of men, praising me, will constantly address me as Raktadantikā (the Red-toothed One). || 9.32 ||
In that very interval, O Śakra, during the fortieth yuga,
there occurred a drought lasting a hundred years on all sides, and there was no water.
"Remembered by the sages, I shall be born upon the earth not from a womb;

O Śakra, men will call me "Śatākṣī" (the Hundred-eyed One);
then I shall pervade the entire world with those born from my own body. (9.35)
"I shall nourish [them] with auspicious, invigorating vegetables that sustain life;
therefore, O Vāsava, the gods will then praise me as Śāmbharī. (9.36)
And right there I shall slay the great asura named Durga;
thereafter, I shall attain renown on earth as the goddess Durga.
O Śakra, by praising, meditating upon, worshipping, and bowing to Śākaṃbharī during the twilight hours,
one quickly attains inexhaustible delight arising from food and drink. (9)
And in the fiftieth cycle of four ages, she was entreated by the sages on the Himalayas; having assumed both a beautiful and an exceedingly terrifying form, [she appeared]. (9.39)
"I shall devour the Rākṣasas for the sake of protecting the sages;
then all the sages, with bodies bowed in reverence, will offer praise to me. (9.40)

For the praise of this [Goddess], the hymn beginning with "Namo Devyai" was seen by Brahmā and all the gods; it is excellent, granting all desires. (9.47)

O sinless one, [I shall describe] the births of this Mahālakṣmī,

"By my power, he enjoys good fortune and fame;
