The Tenth Chapter: The Root Text – Śakra.
Obeisance to you, who are the very fruit of the labor of churning the Ocean of Milk; obeisance to the enemy of Madhu’s sister, obeisance to you, the source of nectar. 10.1.
Those categories beginning with "existence" (bhāva) have been heard by me from the lotus of your mouth; now I desire to hear the categories beginning with "becoming" (bhava). (10.2)
"O Lotus-seated One, salutations to you! Please tell me, as I have asked: what are the forms of those Vaiṣṇava incarnations, and how many are they said by the wise to be in the lotus? (10.3)
Śrī said: "O Śakra, alas! I shall tell you the various ways in which your answers are surpassed;
how many of your Vaiṣṇava incarnations there are, and of what nature they are. (10.4)
The sixfold policy is the stainless Brahman—faultless, undecaying, and eternal;
it possesses all powers, is free from affliction, and is the meditation upon the supportless. (10.5)
That indeed first unfolds from the state of the possessor of power and power;
Nārāyaṇa, the supreme deity, exists as the possessor of power.
"I am the steadfast power (Śakti) of that All-pervading Lord, performing all his works;
we two manifest in many forms for the sake of the world. (10.7)
Just as I have previously explained to you my abiding in various manifestations, now hear from me as I describe the transformations of Viṣṇu, who is himself changeless. (10.8)
Resorting to my own power, that most wonderful primordial nature, which is non-material, incomparable, and blazing with inconceivable majesty— (10.9)
The Lord of the World arises for the welfare of the world through a threefold form:
first, by means of his supreme form, and then by means of his manifested forms.
Likewise, the all-pervading Lord, desiring to bestow grace upon his devotees, assumes various states through the form of phenomenal manifestation. (10-11)
Furthermore, he assumes a supreme body that is incomparable and indescribable, which nourishes the entire universe with a splendor equal to ten million full moons. (10–12)
With two arms, he has eyes like lotuses, and his two hands display the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*),
as well as a discus and a conch shell depicted in lines.
It was marked [with auspicious signs], situated upon feet free from change, supremely beautiful, and adorned with its own six qualities, neither deficient nor excessive. || 10.14 ||
With limbs perfectly proportioned and beautiful in every part, he was adorned with white ornaments that resembled the surging waves of nectar. || 10-15 ||
This single divine form, known as the Supreme, is the transcendent Vaiṣṇavī, which is unswerving through the sound of Acyuta and others that have become rays and are formless. (10.16)
Those who have attained perfection in yoga worship her, who is established in the heart and resides in the fourth state (turyapada).
Now, I shall describe to you her second form, the Vyūha. (10–17)
Having divided himself fourfold according to the distinctions of the directions starting with the east,
the Lord abides on the path of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) through the divisions of Vāsudeva and the others. (10–18)
The configuration of the primordial form is indeed remembered as being the same for all;
the first form possesses six qualities arising from the pairs beginning with knowledge. (10.19)
The other forms have been described by me previously;
[that form] which possesses the radiance of a thousand fires, suns, and moons, and is characterized by bliss and vibration (ānanda-spanda). || 10-20 ||
O Vāsava, know that the state of deep sleep (sauṣupta) is the seed of all actions and their mental constructs; it is their abode, and it is the first among the fourfold nature. 10.21
Then, even in his own dream-state, the Lord likewise divided himself by himself through the distinctions of the directions—east and so forth—assuming the forms of Vāsudeva and the others. (10.22)
Through the division of concise and detailed descriptions of the qualities, the Supreme Person [is described] with most wonderful forms resembling white, red, and golden clouds. (10.23)

Through forms equal to the primordial matter (prakṛti), it abides in a fourfold manner, bestowing the fruit of liberation and experience, and bringing about the destruction of the seed of worldly existence. || 10.24 ||
The second is the fourfold nature (cāturātmya), which is beautiful with its abundance of nectar;
then, in the state of waking, the Lord [appears] through the distinctions of white, red, and so forth.
With four arms and noble limbs, marked with the conch, the discus, and other symbols, their bodies variegated by various banners, they are designated as Vāsudeva and the others. || 10.26 ||
Having divided himself by means of various arrays, the All-pervading Lord remains there by his own playful power;
therein is the primordial form of the Blessed One, possessing the luster of snow, the kunda flower, and the moon.
Four-armed, with a gentle countenance and eyes resembling lotuses, clad in yellow silken garments, and adorned with the Garuda-bannered standard. || 10.28 ||
With his primary right hand he grants fearlessness to those who are afraid,
and with his left hand, likewise disposed, he holds an excellent conch shell.
With his other [left] hand he holds the Sudarśana discus,
and with his right hand a heavy mace resting upon the surface of the earth.
One should thus contemplate Vāsudeva in the space before one:
having the form of a peak of vermilion, with a gentle face and four arms. (10.31)
His garment resembles the flax flower and is marked with the palm tree;
it is identical to that of the Primordial Lord by means of his two principal hands.
One should contemplate Saṃkarṣaṇa in this manner on the right side: holding a plough in his hand and a pestle in his other hand, while the mace is in the hand of the one who holds the discus. (10.33)
He possessed the luster of a multitude of fireflies appearing on a rainy night,
was clothed in garments of red silk, and was adorned with the dolphin-bannered god of love.
The third supreme lord has a gentle face and four arms;
O great-minded one, his two principal hands are identical to those described previously.
In the left [hand] he holds a Śārṅga bow, and in the right, five arrows;
in the other [left] part, one should contemplate Pradyumna—thus it is proclaimed. (10.36)
Resembling the Añjana mountain, clothed in beautiful yellow garments, four-armed, large-eyed, and adorned with the mark of the moon. || 10.37 ||
One should first contemplate his pair of hands as being like those of the primordial [deity];
then, in order from the right, one should visualize a sword and a shield in two of them.
One should contemplate Aniruddha as being situated in the northern quarter;
all of them wear forest garlands, are marked with the Śrīvatsa,
and are adorned upon their chests with the Kaustubha, the king of jewels.
The unsurpassed Lord, who possesses a fourfold nature, is established in the state of waking. || 10.40 ||

One should contemplate that divine [deity], who effects persistence, origination, and dissolution, and is endowed with all instruments; it is he under whose teaching the universe abides. Furthermore, the threefold fourfold nature [of the Self] exists within the triad of states beginning with deep sleep.
Clearly manifest in that fourth state (turya), the supreme reality abides as the goal indicated by the qualities.
This second form of Viṣṇu, known as the Vyūha, which desires to emit the worlds through knowledge, action, and other powers, has been described by me. (10.43)
Now behold the third form of Viṣṇu, called Vibhava, situated in the center of the universal abode, the performer of various forms and actions. (10.44)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Supreme Vyūha," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra. || 10 ||
The Eleventh Chapter.
Root Text—Śrī [B: Śrī said]:
Faultless, beyond dependence, desireless, blameless, and eternal;
Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the glorious one, the Supreme Self, the eternal;
whose form is eternally composed of the six divine attributes, the supreme Brahman, the imperishable, the highest.
Of him, I am the supreme power, eternally possessing his attributes.
Know me to be that which follows all beings, faultless and imperishable;
I am she who accomplishes every task for Viṣṇu, whose form is immutable. (11.3)

By means of her own self, she constantly expands herself through entities consisting of both pure and impure aspects, manifesting the various divisions of Hari’s manifestations, such as the supreme form (paravyūha) and others.
Taking up the pure sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), she fashions herself accordingly;
by that means, she immediately assumes various forms appropriate for her manifestations (*vyūha*) and so forth.
I shall reveal to you the supreme mode of the Lord;
I am the very activity of that Lord, of this there is no doubt. (11.6)
For whatever action is performed by me, it is said to be performed by him;
indeed, I am considered the active instrument of that God. (11.7)
Thus, O Śakra, having manifested the supreme form and the arrayed form, now behold the third form, known as the Manifestation. (11.8)
The four stages beginning with the Fourth (turya) and ending with the waking state (jāgrat), which have been described,
are pervaded by [the Vyūhas] beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with Aniruddha.
In each and every state, the fourfold self (cāturātmya) has been proclaimed by you in its various forms, both unmanifest and manifest, exactly as it was described.
From one manifestation to the arising of another manifestation, from the first step until the end of the next step, he fills every intermediate space with his splendor. (11.11)
A mass of splendors, worshipped, unmanifest, and devoid of form, he is called Viśākhayūpa, strengthened by various forms of knowledge and other virtues. || 11-12 ||
O Śakra, from each of those respective states, the fourfold manifestation of forms beginning with Vāsudeva indeed emerges in succession.
Thus, when the array of states of waking is manifested from the state of dreaming, the Great Taijasa is worshipped at the end of the waking state, arising from the state of dreaming. || 11-14 ||
Note 2:

Since the words *brahman* and *akṣara* are also used to refer to primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), the qualification "supreme" (*param*) is added to exclude those meanings.

12. Viśākhayūpa is a specific form of the Blessed One, radiant and composed of light, appearing in the shape of a pillar within the extraordinary divine world. Therein, from the lower portion up to the upper portion, there are four joints (*parva*).

In sequence, these are presided over by Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Vāsudeva, bearing the distinct marks of the conch, discus, and so forth, which are respectively very clear, clear, somewhat clear, and indistinct. On each joint (parvan),
on all four sides in order starting from the east, the emanations (vyūhas) beginning with Vāsudeva appear in succession.
They shine. Thus, this division was indeed taught by the Blessed One himself for the sake of the objects of meditation for yogins.
(p. 38) Root—
The Blessed One Viśākhayūpa is that god, a treasury of splendors;
for whatever exists from the fourth [tattva] up to the end of the dream state—[or, according to the variants: from the fourfold nature (cāturātmya) and so forth]—is he. (11–15)
In him, who is endowed with various sovereign powers, the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) is well-established;
taking all that divine [power], preceded by pure consciousness,
he divides himself by means of his own self into forms such as Vāsudeva and the others.
Furthermore, at the time of dissolution, there is nothing except for the fourfold form. (11–17)
Indeed, this Viśākha-yūpa manifests through his power;
those gods, Padmanābha and the others, are considered to be of the nature of that power. (11.18)
Padmanābha, Dhruva, Ananta, Śaktīśa, Madhusūdana, Vidyādhideva, Kapila, Viśvarūpa, and Vihaga. (11–19)
He whose nature is the boar, he who has the face of a mare, Dharma, Vāgīśvara,
he who lies within the single ocean, and likewise he who has the form of a tortoise. (11.20)
The Boar, the Man-Lion, and likewise the Seizer of the Nectar;
the Lord of Śrī with a divine body, the Embodiment of Beauty, and the Sustainer of the Nectar. (11.21)
The conqueror of Rāhu, the slayer of Kālanemi, and likewise the one who carried off the Pārijāta tree;
the Lord of the World, the tranquil-souled Dattātreya, the Great Lord. (11-22)
The Blessed One reclining on a banyan tree, as well as the one with the body of Ekaśṛṅga;
the god Vāmana of dwarfed form, the all-pervading Trivikrama. (11.23)
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and likewise Kṛṣṇa;
Rāma bearing the flaming axe, and another Rāma who is the wielder of the bow;
the Lord Kalki, the knower of the Vedas; and the Sovereign who reclines upon the underworld (Pātāla).
These thirty-eight deities, beginning with Padmanābha and others, are thus considered. || 11-25 ||

These manifestations of the omnipresent Viśākha-yūpa, appearing according to their respective functions, are known as the *vibhavas*; and their function is characterized by non-confusion (*asaṃkara*). (11.26)
Between the pure and impure paths, Padmanābha is established;
other gods, beginning with Dhruva, are manifested within the temple of the universe.
Their forms, weapons, powers, and various other modes [are likewise present].
All that is established in the Sāttvata; it has been shown to be a mere designation. || 11.28 ||
The branches are proclaimed to be Vāsudeva and the other forms of the all-pervading Lord;
the blessed Lord Viśākha performs that [sacrifice] by means of his extended arms as the sacrificial post.
Then, from the four branches, three [names] beginning with Keśava and ending with Dāmodara have emerged; that is called another manifestation (vyūha). (11.30)
For from those very branches, a triad of three— Śrī and the others— has emerged,
corresponding to the previous triad, as well as the emergence of the Śaktis.
This applies to all the deities, beginning with Parā and ending with Vibhava.
O Lord of the Thirty-three, these forms consist of the pure sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya).
Whatever weapons the gods possess, such as the discus and the conch,
as well as their various ornaments and diverse garments— 11.33.
O Lord of the Gods, there are banners of various forms and splendors such as white and others, as well as diverse vehicles beginning with the Truth (Satya). || 11.34 ||
The powers (śaktis) bestow experience and exist in various forms; they constitute the entire group of internal organs as well as all their respective functions. (11.35)
And whatever common instrument there may be shared with other men,
know all that to be fashioned from the sixfold policy, O slayer of Bala.
Note:
This is a conceptual construction (*kalpita*). Its detailed exposition is to be found in the *Sāttvata-saṃhitā*.
19—These very deities, acting as the presiding lords of the consonants (*vyañjana*), [reside] right here together with their respective consorts (*mahiṣī*).
They will be explained in the twentieth chapter. (p. 39) Root-text:
I am that which consists of pure consciousness, fully endowed with the six qualities.
In whatever manner and in whatever way this [being] desires, I become exactly so for him. (11.37)
Indeed, my existence does not occur without the God of gods;
nor indeed does the existence of the god Viṣṇu occur without me. || 11.38 ||
Thus we two have attained oneness, yet we remain established in a twofold state;
let us assume whatever various forms are required here and there according to necessity.
Śakra said:
O Daughter of the Ocean, salutations to you; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One!
What purpose does the Lord have for the distinctions such as the supreme manifestation (paravyūha) and the others? || 11.40 ||
Śrī:
For the sake of favoring living beings,
out of compassion for her devotees.
The manifestations of the God of gods occur through various distinctions, such as the *paravyūha* and others. (11.41)
Śakra:
O Goddess, beloved of the God of gods, salutations to you, O lotus-born one! For the sake of favoring devotees, may you alone be the sole consort of Hari. (11.42)
Śrī:
O Śakra, the various accumulations of merit gathered by living beings—those beings do not accumulate them at all simultaneously in any way whatsoever. (11.43)
For indeed, due to the manifestation of his past merits, a certain man among humans is sometimes beheld by the illustrious Kamalākṣa as he is being born. (11.44)
At other times, pure intentions are distinct, such that one person is different from another;
thus, a difference among qualified aspirants arises according to the gradations of their merit. (11.45)
Discrimination regarding the knowledge of the Lord's true nature may be dull for some, middling for another, or divine for yet another. (11.46)

Since such differentiation is established solely through the diversity of the Lord’s grace, the conceptualization of him as the Supreme (para), the Manifested (vyūha), and so forth, occurs in accordance with their respective functions. (11.47)
It is performed by the God of gods, who presides over me,
for the sake of those who have perfected the principles of yoga, so that they may attain authority within the Supreme Self (parātman).
For those of middling capacity, who are engaged in the yoga of mixed practice, there is the meditation upon the manifestation (vyūha).
For those whose minds are devoid of discernment regarding forms such as Vaibhāvī and the rest, [there is delusion]. (11.49)

Having observed the disparity in the qualification of his devotees—who are afflicted by the notions of "I" and "mine" (or ignorance regarding "mine")—with respect to the Supreme Lord, he... || 11.50 ||
It assumes various states designated as the "external array" (paravyūha) and so forth;
thus, O Śakra, these [forms] consisting of both natures have been shown to you in brief. (11.51)
The manifestations of myself and of Nārāyaṇa, which culminate in existence and non-existence,
reside within the group of sheaths arising from me— both the pure and the impure.
Today you have shown us our state— both separate and together, as well as absolute.
Having thus known me in this manner, as one who is perceptible and universally acknowledged, || 11.53 ||
Having constantly worshipped her, who possesses various natures, through diverse means, one transcends the latent impressions of afflictions and karma and attains my own state. (11.54)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Vibhava," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the Śrī Pañcarātra. || 11 ||
Note: The afflictions (kleśa), actions (karman), and latent dispositions (āśaya) will be discussed in the immediately following chapter.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter.
Twelfth Chapter: Root Text – Śakra:

If the eternal individual soul (*jīva*) were merely your pure power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*), how could it be touched by afflictions, karma, and latent impressions (*kleśa-karma-āśaya*) within the lotus [of the heart]? (12.1)

What are the afflictions (kleśa), how many are they said to be, and what is their nature? What kind of action (karman) is it, and of what sort? O Goddess, what is that which is called intention (āśaya), and what fruit is traditionally taught for it? || 12.2 ||
O Daughter of the Ocean, tell me this; salutations, salutations to you!
For indeed, O Omniscient One, no one other than you is able to speak of this. (12.3)
Śrī:
I am the goddess Nārāyaṇī, pure and consisting of self-willed consciousness;
I am the independent, faultless Śrī of Viṣṇu, who never departs from him. (12.4)

I have fashioned my form in two ways through the distinction between the Lord and that which is to be ruled; and that which is to be ruled, being distinct from Me, exists in two ways solely by virtue of My own freedom.
The power of consciousness (cic-chakti) is one, designated as the enjoyer (bhoktrī), while the other consists of the objects of enjoyment (bhogya) and so forth;
by means of the distinction between Kāla and Kālī, it has been divided into two kinds by me.
In that regard, the power consisting of time is both deluding and binding;
this very nature (prakṛti), along with its transformations, is the power of consciousness (cicchakti) that is bound by it. (12.7)
That form by which the power of consciousness, having attained the state of an enjoyer, becomes afflicted—that affliction is to be known as fivefold; hear from me its names as well. (12.8)
Darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, and indeed that which is called utter darkness—
this fivefold ignorance is the supreme destination of darkness.
Although the power of consciousness is unattached, pure, and immutable,
it bears the form of the self as if pierced by it, owing to its own stainlessness.
Śakra said:
I perceive as if obstructed the attachment of the power of consciousness to afflictions;
my mind seems to be deluded today—O Lotus-born One, cut through that delusion! (12.11)
Śrī is independent, the cause of all accomplishments (siddhis), and here she is wondrously manifold.
I am the eternal goddess Śakti of Nārāyaṇa, ever-manifested.
O Lord of the Thirty-three, these five functions of mine are eternal:
concealment, as well as creation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
"Anugraha" is declared to be my fivefold activity.
O Śakra, hear from me the explanation of these activities according to their functions. (12–14)
In that regard, the concealment of one's own nature is proclaimed to be the manifestation of something else; for my own pure power of consciousness is indeed designated as the "enjoyer. (12-15)
That power of mine by which [the soul] exists under the sway of Prakṛti is called my power of ignorance (avidyā-śakti), known as "concealment" (tirobhāva). || 12-16 ||
This divided form of mine was manifested by me through my power of true resolve;
that first descent of mine which was described to you previously—[that is this]. (12-17)
The power of consciousness (cicchakti) is thus proclaimed by the wise as the individual soul (jīva);
its differentiation is said to arise solely from the force of my own freedom (svācchandyavaśa). (12.18)
And as for this form of my *caitya* which was fashioned by you with a resolve of truth—that very act of unification is indeed performed by me through the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). (12.19)
That supreme power is ignorance (avidyā), known as concealment (tirobhāva).
It has five stages; learn from me what they are:
darkness (tamas) is the first stage, and its name is indeed avidyā.
The notion that there is a living soul in a shrine that is non-self and devoid of intrinsic nature— || 12.21 ||

That which consists of "mineness" (svatā) and "I-ness" (ahantā) is remembered as *tamas* and *avidyā*. And when an object of consciousness is grasped through "I-ness," the pride (*māna*) that arises therein [is also a form of *tamas*]. (12.22)
The great delusion called *asmitā* (I-am-ness) is the second stage of affliction; it is the attainment of a state of oneness between the knower and the known through ignorance (*avidyā*). (12.23)

That latent impression (vāsanā) which, caused by the sense of "I-am-ness" (asmitā), is the cause for the recollection of pleasure, is designated by the terms "delusion" (moha), "egoism" (asmitā), and "great delusion" (mahāmoha). (12.24)
That passion and the object of passion constitute the third knot of affliction;
it is the cause for the recollection of suffering, which is established by the latent impression of egoism. (12.25)
That hatred and its object constitute the fourth stage of affliction.
[F: omits three lines from here] For one who desires to abandon suffering through yogic means and likewise desires to attain happiness, || 12.26 ||
That terror which arises in the midst due to obstacles is called "blindness";
it is the fifth stage of affliction, known as *abhiniveśa* (clinging). || 12-27 ||
Having perceived the body as the self, he then attains identification with it; thus, he desires to obtain that which is pleasurable and likewise wishes to abandon that which is otherwise.
Fearing obstacles to that [attainment], the conscious being (the embodied soul) practices its remedy for the sake of obtaining the desired and for the destruction of the undesired. (12.29)
Whatever action this [person] performs, consisting of three types and having a threefold nature—that action has been described by the virtuous who are experts in Sāṃkhya and Yoga. (12.30)

The pleasure produced by that, as well as the pain and that which consists of both pain and pleasure, is declared to be the threefold ripening (vipāka) by those learned in the treatises on reality. (12.31)
Impressions (*vāsanā*) are said to be latent dispositions (*āśaya*), born from afflictions, karma, and their maturation; for they reside within the internal organ and extend everywhere. (12.32)
Latent impressions (vāsanās) are constantly produced by the five stages of affliction;
likewise, latent impressions are the cause for the commencement of similar [actions], and action is likewise [the cause] of latent impressions. (12.33)
The latent impressions of pleasure and so forth are produced in three ways by the ripened fruits;
thus, they are characterized by four marks known as afflictions and the like. (12.34)
The binding of the sheath of the individual soul is known as concealment;
by this very power, the souls bound to me are eternally held fast. (12.35)
My powers of creation and the rest proceed in an uninterrupted stream;
that power of mine, the power of creation, is twofold according to my sovereignty over purity and impurity.
Having distinguished it, that [power] has been shown to you; it exists again in sevenfold form, yet one part is incessantly employed in the ritual action pertaining to Prajāpati.
Other [emanations] arise from the six sheaths, appearing at their respective times;
furthermore, within the sequence of creation arising from primordial nature (prakṛti), the process of manifestation is to be known as threefold. (12.38)
According to their distinctions, they are the real (bhāvikī), the inferential (laiṅgikī), and the elemental (bhautikī);
just as it is in the seed of a nyagrodha tree, so it is in the primordial nature (prakṛti) consisting of the three qualities (traiguṇya).

That state of the Mahat and the rest is called the creation of objective existence (bhāva-sṛṣṭi); it is the subtle body (liṅga) which is created by me through the distinction between the collective and the individual. (12.40)
And likewise, the Virāj is born from the linga of other beings;
it consists of the twenty-three principles, beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas. (12.41)
The objects of the senses residing within the subtle body (liṅgadeha) are proclaimed to be the Virāj; as are the collective totality of the elements and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). (12.42)
Those various portions of that which exists in three ways, which are established within each individual soul,
and those which were previously described as the subtle forms of even the gross elements— || 12.43 ||

These eighteen individual manifestations—namely the afflictions, actions, latent impressions, and vital breaths—are designated as the subtle body (liṅga), which serves as the substratum for the hosts of individual souls. 44.
For the powers of consciousness (cic-chaktayaḥ), residing in the subtle body (liṅga), transmigrate in such a manner;
however, this occurs only as long as pure divine knowledge has not arisen in those who live by their virtuous deeds. (12.45)
These signs of living beings cease to exist at no other time;
as for the Virāj, the gross body which has the Brahmāṇḍa as its other name. (12.46)
Furthermore, there are four other kinds of bodies for embodied beings.
This is my elemental creation; such is the contemplation of creation. (12.47)
The third of my powers is called *sthiti* (stability), which was previously mentioned to you;
I shall describe its true nature—listen to that from me, O Śakra. (12.48)

That which is the first moment of creation and that which is the moment of the desire to withdraw— the interval between these two is what is called "the act of stabilization" for those who abide therein.
That supreme power of my own, which is my capacity for persistence, exists in various forms—
both as Viṣṇu, the god of gods, and likewise as myself.
That state which has been described is declared by the contemplators of reality to be the first;
the second is proclaimed by the lords of the Manvantaras. || 12.51 ||
The third [power] consists of the sons of Manu and the Kṣudras; thus it is fourfold.
The fourth is the power of withdrawal (saṃhṛtī-śakti); hear now its divisions. || 12.52 ||
That which is the constant destruction of beings such as those born from a womb is the eternal dissolution;
O Śakra, any other is known as the occasional dissolution.
That third [form] is said to be the natural (prākṛtī) one, pertaining to the three worlds, caused by the sleep of Brahmā,
and resting upon the principles beginning with the Great One (mahat).
The fourth, however, is the spiritual (prāsūtī), and its object is the Unmanifest (avyakta).
That which is called the fifth is the illusory one (māyī), while that which pertains to the sphere of procreation is the sixth.
The sixth is to be known as Śakti, which has Māyā as its object;
the seventh is declared to be absolute, the dissolution of yogis within me.
Then the subtle bodies of the virtuous cease to exist.
O Śakra, this sevenfold withdrawal has been described by me;
the fifth is called "grace" (anugraha).
Listen to this explanation of Śakti, the primary power. || 12.57 ||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Powers of Concealment and the Like," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*. 12.
Thirteenth Chapter. Root Text—
Śrī.
O Śakra, my fifth power is known as being of the nature of grace; O child, I shall now describe this very power to you according to its true essence.
Pierced by ignorance and brought under the sway of egoism and the other afflictions, they are concealed by my very power known as concealment (tirodhāna). (13.2)
Falling from the high to the low, they spring up again from the low;
bound by three kinds of bonds, they revolve through the three states of existence.
Staying amidst the embers of saṃsāra, being cooked by their own karma, they take pride in happiness while constantly suffering, overcome by ignorance. (13.4)
Chasing after those origins which distinguish between the moving and the unmoving,
they are variegated by their own causes, which consist of ever-newer and newer beings. (13.5)
Day and night, through the body, senses, mind, intellect, and sensations, they bind themselves to successive births and likewise to deaths. (13.6)
"Being afflicted" means [afflicted] by those various afflictions born of union and separation;
[he is so called] because their transgressions have been extinguished by the stream of his arising compassion. (13.7)
"By me, living beings are beheld, freed from suffering through my grace;
this is called 'favor' (anugraha), also known by the name 'descent of power' (śaktipāta).
At that time, while being observed by me, they attain the equilibrium of karma."
That shall be the final body of living beings as perceived by me. (13.9)
For I alone know that moment of the descent of power;
it is not brought about by human effort, nor by any other cause.
I look upon someone at some time solely by my own will;
from that moment on, that person’s inner self becomes perfectly pure. || 13.11 ||
Having attained equilibrium of the karmas and taking refuge in pure actions,
he is endowed with the knowledge of Vedānta and devoted to Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
By carrying forth true devotion toward Viṣṇu through the correct knowledge of the Sāttvata doctrine,
the yogi, after a long time, has shaken off the accumulation of afflictions.
Having shaken off various bonds and shining forth here and there, one attains the supreme Brahman, whose nature is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. (13.44)
This, however, is my fifth power, consisting of grace;
indeed, my own freedom (svācchandyam) alone is the cause for acts such as concealment.
"O Śakra, understand this: henceforth, you must not question me further.
Śakra said: "Homage to the one whose abode is the lotus! Homage to the refuge of Nārāyaṇa! (13–16)
Homage to her who is eternally faultless, the ocean of auspicious qualities! The great darkness within me has been washed away by the mass of the nectar of your speech. (13–17)
"I desire to hear further about the supreme form of the power of consciousness. Śrī said:
Nārāyaṇa alone is the god, the supreme self, the eternal.
He is the eternal treasury of knowledge, power, sovereignty, valor, strength, and vigor; he is without beginning and is indefinable in terms of space, time, and essential nature. (13–19)
I am his supreme goddess, radiant with the majesty of the six qualities; I am the eternal power named Ahaṃtā, the accomplisher of all tasks. (13.20)
Consciousness alone is my own nature, utterly pure and full of absolute freedom;
all the accomplishments of all living beings depend upon me.
Upon the wall of my own self, I manifest the entire universe by my own will;
these worlds flash forth within me like birds upon the surface of water. (13.22)
Out of my own free will, I descend as the one who performs the fivefold act; when I thus descend, I am indeed called the power of consciousness (cicchakti). || 13.23 ||
This contraction of mine is that which destroys the pure and free consciousness;
yet even within this [contraction], the world shines forth like mountains within the interior of a mirror. (13.24)
Like a diamond-jewel, this [Self] shines forth clearly at all times;
that which is its property, consciousness, is as stainless as the radiance of the sun. (13.25)
In that same way, this living being (jīva) vibrates by its own accord according to its corresponding form;
this living being also perpetually performs the five functions.
The activity that occurs toward blue, yellow, and so forth—[or, as in some versions: "toward the blue, yellow, etc., on the wall"]—is called "emission" (sṛṣṭi) by the wise.
That attachment which exists toward that object is proclaimed as "stasis" (sthiti).
The withdrawal from an object already grasped due to the desire to grasp another is declared as *saṃhṛti* (withdrawal) by those learned in the treatises on the principles (*tattva*). (13.28)
The obscuration of those latent impressions (vāsanās) is grace (anugraha), which is their dissolution;
this [consciousness], whose nature is to devour the object of perception, is always a consumer like fire. (13.29)
This individual soul (jīva) always nourishes my fuel by means of its own measure;
however, my true nature, which is beyond ignorance, was previously explained to you by me. (13.30)
When he abandons contraction through union with Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), then, shining forth, he is liberated from all bonds on every side. (13.31)
Through the union of knowledge and action, one is always all-knowing and all-doing; being free from limitation due to the absence of contraction, one becomes fit for my own state of being.
As long as this [Self] is not beheld by me through compassion, so long does it perceive the universe through its instruments with contracted knowledge. (13.33)
Having perceived objects with the eye and having conceptualized them thus with the mind, one determines them through the intellect alone, following self-identification and egoism. (13.34)

Now, during wakefulness—or rather, as at the end of wakefulness—in a dream, it moves by means of the internal organs; but having abandoned those in deep sleep, it abides in its own essential nature. (13.35)
These three states are innate and do not belong to the living being alone;
even the fourth state arises in the living being when he is established in samādhi. (13.36)
That too does not belong to him; rather, this is the abiding state of a pure being, which is without fluctuation and untouched by all ordinary qualities.
The nature of the individual soul (jīva), however, is composed of consciousness, unconditioned, and indestructible;
yet even though it is of such a nature, it is veiled by beginningless ignorance (avidyā). || 13.38 ||
"Therefore, he does not see me, who am so clearly visible and have become his very self.
Śakra said: "O Goddess, how can you be so clearly visible while remaining beyond all measure? (13.39)
"Even the Vedāntas do not know you in this manner, O Lotus-born One.
Śrī said: "But know me, O Śakra, to be directly perceptible to all embodied beings."
Having become composed in mind, listen to this my teaching.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Nature of the Jīva," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (Or: in the *Śrīpāñcarātra*, the illumination of the types of jīvas. 13.
Chapter Fourteen.
Root Text—Śrī said: [B, E: Śrī said]—
The Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is the very nature of knowledge, undivided by space, time, and other such factors; he is the Supreme Brahman, devoid of qualities and stainless. (14.1)
Bliss is eternally of one form, yet it possesses the sixfold attributes (ṣāḍguṇya), being undecaying and immortal; I am its supreme power, the eternal and constant egoity (ahaṃtā). 14.2
This power of my activity, characterized by the desire to emit (sisṛkṣā),
exists in portions of ten million, ten billion, a hundred trillion, a quadrillion, and a quintillion. (14.3)

I, having attained a twofold division through my own freedom, create [the world] by means of the states of the object of thought and the non-conscious; between these two, the power of consciousness is the conscious one.
Consciousness itself, which is my very self, has attained the state of both the cognizer and the cognized;
for consciousness alone is my form, transparent and overflowing with absolute freedom.
Through its union, however, it assumes a state of solidification, like sugarcane juice.
Therefore, when that object of cognition is examined, it will attain the nature of consciousness; it does not abandon its status as consciousness. || 14.6 ||

For just as fuel licked by fire becomes of the same nature as that fire, so too the object of consciousness (cetya), when thoroughly consumed by consciousness (cit), attains the state of being composed of consciousness (cinmayatā). || 14.7 ||
The undivided nature of consciousness— whether in blue, yellow, pleasure, or pain—
is differentiated by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) through the acquisition of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
For even conceptual construction is, in its very essence, my own form.
It is created solely out of its own freedom;
by means of it, the object of thought is conceptualized through the distinction between internal and external. (14.9)
Neither outside nor indeed within, that supreme form of mine is of the nature of consciousness; it is not divided by itself into the forms of the object of knowledge and the knower. || 14.10 ||

That form which is unassailed by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), which is not tormented by words, and which does not wither under limiting conditions (*upādhi*)—that very form has attained the state of being an object of cognition (*cetyatā*). When one dwells with a mind from which conceptual construction has been cast far away, [that is the state]. (14)
Then, by abiding in the middle way, one perceives the object of thought as consciousness itself.
Just as form situated in the eye perceives its own form externally, so too form situated in cognition perceives its own form within the object of knowledge. 14.13
Just as wood permeated by fire is perceived as having that [fire’s] form, so too the object of cognition permeated by consciousness is perceived as being of the nature of consciousness. 14–14.

When the object of knowledge, having been brought to the state of being known, is determined by the knower, then that "I," consisting of consciousness, becomes directly perceived and clearly manifest. (14–15)

For the state of "I-ness" (ahantā) itself is the nature of consciousness, a specific characteristic distinct from the object of knowledge; and that "I-ness" is indeed myself. Therefore, I am everywhere composed of pure consciousness.
I am the hand to support those who are sinking in the ocean of consciousness, where all objects of thought have merged into a single unity upon the island of the sevenfold *daṃpada*. (14–17)

Those whose entire latent impressions have been washed away by the flow of the nectar of the middle state perceive me alone within themselves—the consciousness that devours the flood of all objects of thought. (14–18)

(46) O people, it was through ignorance alone—just as I previously willed—that you imagined the state of being the knower and the known within my own mind, which is of a single uniform nature. (14–19)
By my very nature, I am neither quiescent, nor emergent, nor even intermediate;
such is the case for those who possess discernment of me, even while awake in the light of consciousness.
By means of a mind that is waveless and free from the sense of division,
I am known; yet, when being conceptualized, even though I am directly perceived,
I am forgotten.
Just as an object standing before one does not appear to a mind longing for something else, even so, I do not appear to those who are possessed by latent impressions (vāsanā). || 14.22 ||
Just as one who desires to know restrains the mental modifications with his mind and perceives the object directly, so too should he perceive me, the pure consciousness. (14.23)
My body, which is always unobstructed and luminous alone,
is directly perceived even at times when there is no movement of objects for those of pure self (or those who have realized the Self). 14.24
Just as a cloth that is white by nature, when dyed with some color, does not resort to another color again without first regaining its own original hue. (14.25)
If one who perceives blue and so forth in this manner does not find rest within me—the pure conscious self in the midst of the yellow—how indeed could he know that yellow? (14.26)
In that very way, while uttering the speech, how could one proceed from one phoneme to the next if one does not rest within me, the pure conscious self? (14.27)

Thus, though pure and independent, when she is colored by a particular form, I alone revolve in the center—pure indeed—as there is neither the abandonment of that nor the transition to another. (14.28)
By the cessation of movement through the right and left channels, resting in the middle channel,
the state that consumes fire and moon illuminates my state.
Not relying on the object of meditation through the intellect, and not touching any external object, that which one experiences within—that is my undisturbed form. (14.30)
But that which persists correctly in both light and darkness, in existence as well as in non-existence—that stainless body of mine shines forth. (14.31)
For one whose desire for sense objects has ceased and whose soul is radiant with devotion to me,
that internal, supportless "I-ness" (ahantva) is my very body.

For those who practice that very [discipline], the nature of the "I" (aham-rūpa), which transcends the body, vital breath, and so forth, remains for the discerning ones through absorption in Me (mad-bhāva). (14.33)
Just as light is manifested by the sun but not produced [by it], so too the nature of consciousness is manifested by objective states but is never produced. (14.34)
Just as the sun rises in the expanse of the sky without [physical] objects,
so too does my own form shine forth by itself, even without objects of cognition.
Just as a gem such as crystal, because its nature is absolutely transparent, does not appear in its own form when colored by things such as *japa* flowers. (14.36)
Furthermore, though I am pure, I am not perceived by ordinary people because of the objects of thought magnified by my own volition; yet, for all that, it is not that I do not exist. (14.37)

Just as the state of gold, though distinct from earrings and the like, cannot be pointed out [as separate], yet it certainly exists; so too, although it cannot be specifically designated, it truly exists. (14.38)
Thus, my state, which consists of pure consciousness, is eternal, pure, undivided by pleasure, pain, and the like, and is to be known through self-awareness. (14.39)
Likewise, there is a commonality of the act of knowing (*jānāti*) with respect to the knower, the knowledge, and the object of knowledge;
this very commonality of mine is not differentiated by the meaning of the suffixes [of the case endings]. (14.40)
Place, time, action, and form are well-known causes of differentiation;
how could there be any differentiation for that consciousness which differentiates them? (14.41)

For that time which is the differentiation of the object of thought, consisting of the triad of the past and so forth—that too is dissolved in the great ocean of consciousness and becomes identical with it. (14.42)
For when the past and the future are excluded from me while I am present, then this very state of being present would not exist at all. (14.43)
I am the support of all things without exception, yet I am never supported by anything;
since even space is conceived as a support, no such support exists for me. (14.44)
There is no state whatsoever for me in which consciousness does not exist; therefore, they worship me as the one, dense mass of consciousness, manifesting in all forms. (14.45)
Time, place, as well as form, action, the agent, the object, the instrument, the recipient, and that which results from them as the fruit—[all these arise from the mind]. (14.46)
The object of enjoyment and the enjoyer—all that is dissolved within the self of consciousness (saṃvidātman).
So too are the gods, the Daityas, the Nāgas, the Gandharvas, and the hosts of Rākṣasas. (14.47)
The eight classes [of beings] are the Vidyādharas, Piśācas, and Bhūtas;
and humans are manifold in nature, differentiated by caste, occupation, and so forth. (14.48)
Furthermore, there are domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and likewise other stationary beings whose nature consists of base conduct. (14.49)
The worlds situated in heaven and those situated in hell, as well as the fourteen worlds, the rivers, the continents, and the oceans— indeed, the entire succession of cosmic eggs.
High and low principles, various collections of sounds, that which is known as the object of enjoyment, the instruments of enjoyment, and the place of enjoyment. (14.51)
The sheaths, as well as those born from the sheaths—these consist of both conscious and unconscious natures;
the states composed of pure and impure elements constitute the fourfold purpose of the Person (puruṣārtha). || 14.52 ||
Everything is bound by the primary constituents (prakṛti) and likewise measured by time;
thus, this entire reality consists of the nature of both existence and non-existence. (14.53)
That which consists of the non-self and that which consists of the self are dissolved and remain within me;
for I am always, in every way, composed of pure, autonomous consciousness. (14.54)
By the wise one, she who consists of bliss and is peaceful should be perceived in every state of being; thus am I established, though designated by the name "concealment. (14.55)
Bound by Śakti, the power of consciousness does not perceive Me at all by itself;
but when it becomes weary of that state, it perceives Me through the drop of My grace.
Then, having propitiated me through various means, the individual soul— known as the power of consciousness—
diminishes all afflictions and shakes off the dust of latent impressions. || 14.57 ||
Having attained the true essence of knowledge and having his bonds destroyed through yoga,
he attains me alone— Lakṣmī, who consists of supreme bliss.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Nature of Lakṣmī," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, which is the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. || 14 ||
Fifteenth Chapter. Root Text—
Śakra:
Salutations to you, O Padmasambhūtā; salutations to you, O wearer of the lotus garland;
salutations to the dweller in the lotus, the housewife of Govinda. 15.1
Salutations to you, O Goddess whose playful tresses are fashioned from the filaments of the lotus;
O Omniscient One, who dwells within all beings and is the witness of all. (15.2)
All that has emerged from the lotus of your mouth has been understood by me;
it was created by you, protected by you, and it shall return to dissolution in you alone. (15.3)
The knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—these three are of Your own nature;
by worshipping You alone, living beings cross the ocean of worldly existence. (15.4)
"O Goddess, such things as these have been understood by me in their true essence;
yet, O Lotus-born One, a curiosity arises within me today. (15.5)
By what means are you to be propitiated, O Lotus-seated One?
For that which is the supreme human goal is the attainment of your favor. (15.6)
What would be the means for your pleasure? Of what nature and of what kind is it traditionally taught to be?
Tell me all of this; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One! (15.7)
Śrī said:
The Supreme Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, is the nature of the fourfold Self;
it is everything, transcending all, abiding within all beings, and free from all affliction. (15.8)
Vāsudeva is the Supreme Brahman, the great essence consisting of Nārāyaṇa (the refuge of men); I am His supreme power, composed of the consciousness of ego and bliss.
I exist both distinct and non-distinct from Him, like moonlight from the cool-rayed moon.
We two are that one single reality, yet we abide having become twofold.
[Through the knowledge of whom a yogi may attain me, the Brahman Nārāyaṇa.]
Through knowledge; there is no other path for the wise to reach this state than through discernment. 15.11
And that knowledge arises from discrimination; it is pure in every respect, free from blemish, has Vāsudeva as its sole object, and is the cause of non-rebirth. (15.12)
When that knowledge has arisen, they enter into me immediately thereafter;
with various means, I am pleased with those living beings of pure soul. (15.13)
I shall manifest that knowledge which reveals the light of the Self;
and those four means of mine increase my delight. (15.14)
Note 6:

Liberation (mokṣa) is the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha). Devotion to you is its means. As they say: "Indeed, there is no higher good than the grace of the beloved of the mind of the lotus-eyed one."
"Among men, this is only conceivable within the paths of saṃsāra, the imperishable, and Vaiṣṇava.

8. The essential definition (svarūpalakṣaṇa), which is established by such scriptural passages as "Truth, Knowledge," etc., is expressed by the word "Being" (sat) and so forth. Because He is the material cause of all and the Self of all, He is called "All" (sarva). Nevertheless...
He states that [it] is distinct from all other things by saying "supreme over all.
9. "Consisting of Nārāyaṇa" (*nārāyaṇamaya*): here the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in its own sense (denoting identity).
10. Śrī is merely a particular state (*avasthābheda*) of Brahman itself, just like the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
Disagreeing with the opinion of some, he says "bhinna" (distinct). 11—The *yati* is one whose self is restrained; here, the member of the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśramī*) is not intended.
12—Discernment (*viveka*) is the knowledge that Brahman is distinct from everything else.
14—Those known as Action, Knowledge, Devotion, and Renunciation (p.
49). Root-text: Śakra [B: omits six lines from here].
O Blessed One, O lotus-eyed beloved seated upon the lotus!
What are those means? And what are the four means? Show them to me, O Lotus-born One.
Śrī said:
O Śakra, listen to the four means that increase my pleasure, by which I shall attain supreme and enduring satisfaction. (15–16)
Action prescribed by one's own birth, as well as Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and the renunciation of everything—these have been declared by the wise to be the means [to liberation]. (15–17)
Vedic action, which pertains to one's own caste and stage of life, consists of the obligatory and occasional types; it is threefold and endowed with four characteristics. (15–18)
Action accomplished without being struck by desire is that means for the former [liberation];
therein, the wise man should practice the fourfold renunciation. (15–19)
Or in the deity mentioned in the mantra, or in the primordial nature, or in the senses,
or in the Supreme God of gods, Vāsudeva Janārdana.
First, there is the renunciation of agency and the renunciation of the fruits of actions; indeed, the renunciation of all actions is offered unto Janārdana, the God of gods. (15–21)
Acting thus according to the scriptures, performing the obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to worship me, that man constantly gratifies me. (15.22)
Thus has this been declared to you in brief, as demonstrated by the Śruti and Smṛti.
Now hear the second means, the knowledge of Sāṃkhya. (15–23)
Indeed, three types of Sāṃkhya are to be understood as demonstrated in the Sāṃkhya scriptures:
the first is worldly calculation (laukikī saṃkhyā), and the second consists of analytical reflection (carcanātmikā). || 15-24 ||
But that intellect which is correct is recited as the third;
the collection of these three forms of reasoning is what is recited as Sāṃkhya. || 15-25 ||
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well; ego, the Great One (mahat), and likewise primordial nature (prakṛti) as the supreme. || 15-26 ||
These are the eight primary natures (prakṛtis); hear this explanation of them.
Nature is said to be threefold: Māyā, Sūti, and that consisting of the Guṇas. || 15-27 ||
Note: Four yogas are intended here.
The four characteristics will be explained in the twentieth verse.

There is a threefold division based on the distinctions between obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) acts. Regarding optional acts, he states the distinction with the words "without desire" (*akāma*). Optional acts are those performed with a desire for specific results, such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and others; these are said to be "overpowered by desire."
Those actions performed solely for the sake of pleasing the Lord, without desire, are "unassailed by desire" (*akāmahata*).

By this, the performance of even those rites that are normally "desire-driven" (*kāmya*) without desire is permitted; however, this applies to those who are devoted to other means [of attainment]. But as for those established in the yoga of renunciation (*nyāsa-yoga*):

It should be understood that the established conclusion is that rites performed for the sake of desire must be abandoned in every respect, even in their essential nature, and not merely practiced without desire;
20— for those seeking liberation, the renunciation of actions into the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva alone [is required].
This must be performed. However, it should be understood that the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) upon the deity of the mantra and so forth pertains to one who seeks enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*).

21—The Blessed Lord Himself, through me—who am of the single flavor of being His subordinate—and by means of my own instruments, causes this action, which is His own subordinate, to be performed by Himself for the sole purpose of His own worship.
This is the intended manner of connection.
24—An exposition of all three of these knowledges will be provided right here.
25—The number of knowledges has been stated previously; their collection [is what follows].

This is called Sāṃkhya; this very same thing is called Jñānayoga. In this verse, worldly enumeration—that which has the world as its object—is described; the subsequent verses provide an exposition of this.

27. Māyā, Prasūti, and Traiguṇya are the divisions of Prakṛti. Although Prakṛti is indeed subtle, it is nevertheless designated in this way because it exists within that very [Prakṛti] in three forms: subtle, subtler, and most subtle.
Rooted in the fundamental [reality],
unattached and non-attached, free from the waves of duality, and imperishable— the supreme subtlety of insentient things is sung as *māyā*. (15.28)
The slight swelling of that [Prakṛti] is proclaimed as its "procreation" (prasūti);
the manifestation of the three qualities in a state of equilibrium is the supreme Prakṛti. (15.29)
The Unmanifest, the Imperishable, the Source, Ignorance, the Three Qualities, Stability, Māyā, and Self-nature—these and other such terms are synonyms expressing the same meaning. (15.30)
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are considered the three qualities (guṇas). Among them, sattva is to be known as light, consisting of happiness, and unshakable. (15.31)
That function is called illumination (prakāśa), consisting of the apprehension of consciousness;
and rajas should also be known as light, having the nature of suffering and being restless. (15.32)
That which is called *pravṛtti* is its activity, the cause of vibration, and imperishable.
That which is called *tamas* is to be known as heavy, consisting of delusion, and immobile. (15.33)
That which is called restraint (niyama) is the practice of remaining in that [state] at certain times, characterized by inducing sleep;
such a thing does not exist on earth, nor in heaven, nor in the sky, O Vāsava. (15.34)
That which is liberated from these three qualities born of nature is the true being (bhūta).
These qualities, having presided over the mind, likewise reside in the senses. (15.35)
Pleasure, pain, and likewise delusion, which reside in the objects of the senses, are produced;
having attained the state of body and senses, the *guṇas* perform actions.
Thus, he whose discernment is constant attains the transcendence of the qualities. || 15.36 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Methods of Means," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. 15.
Note (30):
Enumerating the synonyms for *prakṛti* along with its intermediate subdivisions, they are *avyakta* and so forth.
In the Upaniṣad it is said: "The unmanifest (*avyakta*) dissolves into the imperishable (*akṣara*); the imperishable dissolves into darkness (*tamas*); darkness [dissolves into the Imperishable]."
The conventional usage of these three terms—“becoming one with the Supreme Self,” “caitanya,” and “jñāna”—is as follows:
32. *Unmeṣa* means the emergence of consciousness (*caitanya*) or knowledge (*jñāna*), that is to say, the faculty of grasping the true nature of reality.
Chapter Fifteen: Niyama and Bandha.
Chapter Sixteen.
O Śakra, listen attentively to my explanation of the Great Root-Śrī.
For that which is the first manifestation of the imbalance of the qualities (guṇas).
That which is called Mahat also has three manifestations proclaimed:
the Sāttvika is said to be the intellect (buddhi), while the Rājasa is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa).
Time has been described as *tāmasa*; hear now this explanation of them:
intellect (*buddhi*) is the faculty of determination, and vital breath (*prāṇa*) is that of exertion. (16.3)
Time is the cause of transformation, which consists of the process of reckoning.
From the Great One (mahat), undergoing modification, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) was born.
And that too should be known as threefold, arising from the inequality of the qualities (guṇas).
From the tamasic [ego], however, arises the radiant group of subtle elements (tanmātras), beginning with space. || 16-5 ||

From that which is predominant in *sattva* is born the great group of the faculties of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), and from that which is *rājasa* is born the group of the faculties of action (*karmendriya*); the group consisting of both arises from both.
"This is the path of reality: that [the world] has arisen from both.
Herein, there is but one primordial nature (prakṛti), which is the root and eternal. (16.7)
The other seven, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), consist of both cause and effect; from the subtle elements (tanmātras) arise the specific elements (viśeṣas), such as space and the rest.
The two groups of five—the organs of cognition and the organs of action—and the mind itself:
these sixteen are to be understood by the wise as mere modifications. (16.9)
These twenty-four principles have been declared to you;
whatever further distinction exists here, and of whatever nature it may be, has also been explained.
All of that was previously told to you, O slayer of Vṛtra;
it is endowed with twenty-three of its own specific modifications.
Note 1:
By this, it is stated that the designation "Prakṛti" applies to the state of equilibrium of the three qualities (guṇas), whereas the designation "Mahat" applies to the state of their disequilibrium.
3—The tamasic nature of time (*kāla*) is stated here. According to the Upaniṣadic method, they maintain that time is indeed non-material (*aprākṛta*).

The view of many Pāñcarātrikas is that these [elements] are purely *sāttvika*. It is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "The ten deities are the *vaikārika* [evolutes], and the eleventh is the mind.
(7) This refers to the *tattvapaddhati* (the sequence of principles); the meaning is the sequence of the insentient (*acit*) principles. Thus, here is the classification of the principle (*tattva*).
Non-consciousness (acittattva) and consciousness (cittattva) are of two kinds. Therein, non-consciousness is twenty-fourfold:
the three—primordial nature (prakṛti), the great principle (mahat), and ego (ahaṃkāra); the five subtle elements (tanmātra); the five gross elements (mahābhūta);
and the eleven organs (indriya). Consciousness is twofold: the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). Altogether...
There are twenty-six principles. (p.
52) Root [verse]: O Lord of the Gods, this unmanifested *prakṛti* has been described to you.
This very [nature] consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, and is eternally characterized by productivity.
That indestructible power of consciousness (cicchakti) is to be known as distinct; it is called the individual soul (jīva) by the virtuous who are experts in the scriptures of reality. 16.13
This is pure by its own nature, devoid of transformation; it is immutable, a mass of consciousness, eternal, infinite, and without transition. (16.14)
These two—prakṛti and puruṣa—are by their very nature unattached, yet they remain as if their essences were attached; indeed, they are greater than even the great elements.
Both are graspable by means of a mark, and both are likewise eternally without marks; in this way, a wise person should infer their similarity and other such qualities.
O Śakra, understand from me the difference between these two:
Prakṛti is eternally composed of the three guṇas and is constantly subject to transformation. (16–17)
It is devoid of discernment, impure, always equal toward all living beings, insentient, and the object that causes pleasure, pain, and delusion. (16–18)
The Puruṣa is eternally neutral, active yet undisturbed;
he is the witness, the vision, and the seer—pure, infinite, and the essence of the qualities (guṇas). (16–19)
This is the difference between these two; now hear of their natures: that which is eternal, devoid of conceptual constructions such as "existent" or "non-existent," and so forth. (16–20)
I am Nārāyaṇī, the power of Viṣṇu, eternally risen, ever-blissful, whose form consists of the six perfections in their fullness; I am Śrī, the inseparable consort. (16–21)
For these two proceed from me and shall return to dissolution in me alone.
Thus, having expanded through various states of being,
I, who am established in Nārāyaṇa, shall emerge once more from him.

That which is the all-pervading Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, free from ailment—the state known as tranquility (śāntatā)—that am I, the mother of all that is tranquil. (18–19)
That slight exertion of mine which arose, known as the desire to create—that tranquil unfolding is called the differentiation of word and meaning. (18–20)
The emergence of meaning everywhere is traditionally held to be preceded by the emergence of the word;
for that "grossness" of the word consists in its nature as the manifestation of both meaning and sound. (18–21)
The unfolding of consciousness is known as sound (śabda), and the unfolding of sound is said to be the object (artha).
The emergence of sound is the first manifestation of power (śakti) from the tranquil Self.
That is renowned as *nāda*, which at that time is smooth in its expressibility;
together with *nāda*, that *śakti* is celebrated as "subtle" (*sūkṣmā*). || 18-23 ||
That second unfolding which is beyond the Nāda and arises from Śakti is called Bindu; here it remains as the smooth, indistinct object of expression. (18–24)
That state of mine is called Paśyantī; it is divine and of great exaltation.
Beyond that is the third unfolding, which arises from Śakti.
That middle state there brings about the latent impression (saṃskāra) of the connection;
at that time, the distinction between the signified and the signifier consists of that very latent impression. (18-26)
But the fourth unfolding of power, which is beyond the Madhyamā, is the state known as Vaikharī, in which phonemes and sentences arise clearly. (18.27)
I possess a power whose nature is action, which follows after the form of consciousness; it animates the succession of the unfolding of power beginning with *nāda* and the rest.
Then there are the forms Śāntarūpā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and likewise Vaikharī;
these four forms I shall describe as the fourfold object of speech (vācya) created by myself.
Vāsudeva and the others are to be understood as subtle, while Śānta and the others correspond to them in sequence;
I am to be known as the single-footed one, whose nature is light and bliss. (18.30)
Furthermore, she is remembered as two-footed through the distinction between the signified and the signifier;
and I am four-footed through the distinctions of the sibilants, semivowels, vowels, and stops. (18–31)
Through the division of the eight groups, it is known as the eight-padded *sāha*;
when joined with another form consisting of unvoiced consonants, it is known as the nine-padded. (18.32)
I am the divine one-footed supreme [state], consisting of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman);
furthermore, I exist as two-footed through the nature of sound and phonemes. (18.33)
Carving out all things—substances, classes, qualities, and actions—and expressing them in four ways, I am declared by the wise to be "four-footed" (catuṣpadī). (18.34)
Note 17:
"The state of being inwardly reflected upon" (*pratyagavamarśitā*) means being accessible through the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*).

21: The established doctrine of the system (*tāntrika-siddhānta*) is that the word arises first, and immediately thereafter its meaning. Even in the Śruti, in the passage "Let me manifest name and form," it should be understood that the manifestation of name is mentioned first, followed by the manifestation of form.

23. Thus, *śabdabrahman*, *parāvāk*, and *nāda* are synonyms. 24. That which follows *nāda* is the unfolding of power (*śaktyunmeṣa*), which is called *bindu* and also *paśyantī*. 25. Following *bindu*, the unfolding of power is named *madhyamā*.

31. *Śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha* are the sibilants (*ūṣman*). *Ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* are the semivowels (*antaḥstha*). The vowels (*ac*) are the sounds (*svara*). From *ka* to *ma* (inclusive) are the stops (*sparśa*). 32. There are eight groups: the group of vowels, the five groups beginning with *ka* and ending with *pa*, the group of sibilants, and the group of semivowels. And the voiceless [consonants] are: the *yamas*, the *jihvāmūlīya*, the *upadhmānīya*, and the *visarga*.

33. In another way, they are described as being "one" and so forth: they are of one form in the nature of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*); they are of two forms in the nature of sound and phoneme (*dhvani-varṇa*).

34. *Takṣatī*, "carving" or "shaping," means making thin or attenuating. She carves away all water—that is, the cause of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) consisting of attachment to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*). A specific form of satisfaction known as "water" (*salila*) is well-known in the Sāṃkhya tradition. Regarding this: "Gaurī has uttered [her voice], carving the waters; she is one-footed, two-footed, and four-footed.
Endowed with the two states of name and being, I am remembered as eight-footed. Abiding in both the non-conceptual and the conceptual, I am remembered as nine-footed. (18.35) *p. 63*
In the supreme sky, I am indeed the divine one, garlanded with infinite syllables;
I am the primordial I-consciousness, expanded to such an extent that it is all-pervasive.
She should be known as the mother of mantras, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation;
from me alone, the ocean of consciousness, surge forth the waves of mantras. (18.37)
Depending upon me, they revolve; again and again they go to their setting within me—those whose bodies are sound, beautiful with a mass of consciousness and bliss. (18.38)
For the phonemes, words, and sentences—along with their contexts and chapters—are composed of *mantras*, which are full of potency, bestow fruits, and consist of the nature of *manas*. (18.39)

Chapters, sections, creations, as well as breath-pauses (ucchvāsas), chapters (paṭalas) and so forth, divisions (avacchedas)—[ḍ: subdivisions (vyavacchedas)]—and questions, sections, and recitations (anuvākas). || 18-40 ||
The Maṇḍalas and the Kāṇḍas, the various Saṃhitās, the Ṛks, the Yajus, the Sāmans, and the Sūktas together with the Khilas. (18.41)
Words consisting of scriptures and tantras, as well as external and internal traditions, and those various languages—these are remembered as both manifest and unmanifest sounds. (18.42)
O Śakra, know that this form of mantra belongs to those who know my true nature;
the distinction between the mantra and the mantra-practitioner is established by the degree of their meditative cultivation.
The sound that has been mastered through yoga with the thought, "This protects me," and which always keeps its intention hidden, protects the knower of mantra from fear. (18.44)

That mantra, when recollected, is the expansion of the ego through the sequential stages born of sound; for it is connected to pure consciousness and arises from the fullness of the Great Ego (pūrṇāhaṃtā). || 18.45 ||
All mantras belong to me for those who know their origin and dissolution;
they are mine or belong to others according to the gradations of one's meditative realization (bhāvanā).
My mantras, which follow the nature [of the self], shall be preeminent;
they enter into Brahman, whose essence consists of existence and non-existence, by their own inherent power. (18.47)
Mantras such as the *tārikā* and *uttārikā*, which are inherent by their very nature, spontaneously attain that state which transcends worldly existence. (18.48)

Those such as Tāraprāsādaka and others should be known as bestowers of liberation, for they resort to a state of being that is either superior in disposition or equanimous toward worldly existence. (18.49)
Mantras such as the Tārikās and others should be known as bestowers of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
some enter into the very state of being, while others go toward worldly existence itself.

Bestowing both enjoyment and liberation, those two function according to their respective dispositions; such is the nature proclaimed for those who follow the path of *prakṛti*. By the power of intention (*abhisaṃdhi*), they extend everything within those two states. (18–51)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Mantras," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Note:

This verse echoes the Śruti: "She who has become eight-footed, nine-footed, and thousand-syllabled in the highest heaven" (Ṛgveda 1.164.41). She is four-footed, possessing four forms by way of words denoting substance, genus, quality, and action.
35. Since each of these is again twofold by way of word and meaning, she is eight-fold when taken together.

36. And this arrangement exists only in the ordinary world (*prākṛtaloka*); however, in the extraordinary world (*aprākṛtaloka*), it consists of infinite syllables. 38. They evolve and transform. Here, the "evolution" (*vivarta*) defined by others is not intended; for it has been stated that "the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) are subject to transformation," and thus sound is a transformation of the three qualities (*triguṇa*).
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter.
The nineteenth chapter. Śrī said:
"I am the primordial, full egoity of Hari, characterized by the desire to create."
I am declared to be the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti) whose nature is emanation.
O delighter of the gods, my ten and five states are equal;
my eternal nature is consciousness, self-realized and unsurpassed. (19.2)
The principle of speech (vāktattva), whose essence is the letter A, is the source of all verbal expression;
that very same principle, in the form of bliss, is held to be the second vowel.
The third is the nature of Will (icchā), the fourth is the nature of Īśāna;
the fifth is Expansion (unmeṣa), and the sixth is said to be the form of the Radiant Power (ūrjatā).
That which is the middle group of four is the transformation of [the powers] Will and the rest;
from the union with Anuttara and Will, that which is called the letter E is born. (19.5)
Through union with that very bliss, she is proclaimed as the womb of the universe;
through the yoga of the unsurpassed emergence, the name "O" is born. (19.6)
From the very union with that which is unsurpassed (anuttara), there arises the "newly born" (sadyojāta);
from this unsurpassed state emerge these expansions that depend upon the object of knowledge. (19.7)
The thirteen [powers], beginning with Ānanda, possess such-and-such manifestations;
these thirteen manifestations have resorted to the state of being reduced to pure consciousness. (19.8)
But that fifteenth vowel is the unsurpassed subtle state;
these fifteen states are the pulsations and efforts of emission. (19.9)
Thus, with fifteen limbs complete,
the divine power consisting of creation makes every effort toward each task in its desire to emit.
From her, as she emits, the twenty-five principles arise—beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Earth, and emerging from the letters Ka through Ma. (19.11)
From the manifestation of each respective syllable, each respective principle (tattva) emerges;
the group of four, consisting of the letters from *ya* to *va*, is proclaimed as the form of concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
Since they sustain the Person within, they are known as *dhāraṇās*.
The syllable *ka* is of the nature of slight activity (*kalā*), while the syllable *ya* is designated as wind (*vāta*). (19–13)
Vidyā, whose nature is limited knowledge, is the letter *repha*, known as fire;
Māyā, whose nature is paralysis and delusion, is the letter *la*, considered to be earth. (19–14)

Note 1: In the state of desiring to create (*sisṛkṣāvasthā*), she is celebrated by the name *Ahaṃtā* (I-ness); in the state of creation (*sṛṣṭyavasthā*), she is celebrated by the name *Parā Śakti* (the Supreme Power).

2: Regarding "ten," etc., it should be understood that there are fifteen states (*daśā*) beginning with the vowel *a* and ending with the nasal bindu (*m*). It should be understood that the visarga is not included among these states because it is the source-material (*prakṛti*) of the states.
5. "The group of four" means the forms of the vowels *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*; therefore, they have not been mentioned separately.
6. The source of the world (*jagadyoni*) is the vowel *ai*. 7. Sadyojāta is the vowel *au*.
8. "Remaining as sensation" (*vedanaśeṣitām*) means remaining in the form of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpeṇa*); this connects with the subsequent phrase "its subtle state" (*asya sūkṣmadaśām*).

9. The "subtle state" (*sūkṣmadaśā*) is the *bindu*. And that becomes the fifteenth when counting starting from the letter *a*. 10. "By the desire to emit" (*sisṛkṣayā*) is the instrumental case used in the sense of cause (*hetau*).

11. *Me* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that functions as a substitute for the fifth case ending (*pañcamī-vibhakti*), meaning "from me. It connects with the word *samudgatāḥ*. The sequence from *ka* to *ma* follows a non-sequential order (*vyutkrama*). 12. Regarding *dhāraṇā*: it is so named because it sustains (*dhāraṇāt*) a person who is descending from the supreme state (*paradaśā*) to the lower state (*aparadaśā*). (p. 65) Root-text—
The letter *va* is the power of passion (*rāgaśakti*), whose nature is attachment and whose essence is Varuṇa;
it always sustains the individual soul in the midst of the states of the supreme and the non-supreme.
These four dhāraṇās should be known by those skilled in the principles;
indeed, from 'śa' to 'kṣa', the pure fivefold Brahman is to be understood.
O Lord of the Thirty-three, the letters śa, ṣa, sa, and ha are to be known as Aniruddha and the others;
they constitute that wonderful form of mine, agitated at the beginning of creation, which brings forth the world. (19.17)
That great power is the agitator, whose nature is *kṣa* and who is known by the name Satī;
she is the five divine powers beginning with Earth and ending with Space. (19–18)
These divine powers, named after my own sattvas, consist of the fivefold group beginning with Power (Bala);
they are the embodiments of my wisdom, arisen from me, and are the Śādi-śaktis.
That which was previously called Visarga, possessing fifteen limbs, am I—the Śakti consisting of Soma, crowded with ten thousand rays. (19–20)
Contraction and expansion—those two alone are proclaimed as such;
that which is the final of the limbs was described by me as the fifteenth.
Know that the sun is truly the consumer of the morality of grasping;
O Purandara, these two, the sun and the moon, are the bindu and the sarga.
There should be seven rays for each of these two deities;
fourteen vowels remain, and one should arrange them into seven pairs.
O Purandara, among those seven pairs, the first seven are my rays, known as the "consumers," which have the form of the sun and belong to me who am called the "enjoyer. (19–24)
The seven rays in the northern pair are cool and refreshing;
they are my portions, nourishing and of the nature of the moon, known as the objects of enjoyment. (19–25)
Illumination, sharpness, pervasion, grasping, casting, movement in battle, and digestion—these rays originating from the sun were previously described. (19–26)
Fluidity, the state of coolness, tranquility, luster, clarity, the essence of rasa, and bliss—these are the seven lunar rays. || 19-27 ||
Resplendent with these rays consisting of Agni and Soma, she, as the qualifying attribute, takes hold of that male who is in the form of the Bindu. (19-28)
Surpassing the form of the moon, adorned with the mandala of the tip of power, the Great Emanation, the Great Bliss, proceeds as the essence of the final vowel. (19–29)
As that [power] proceeds, the pentad of Brahmā arises—beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, O Lord of the Gods, distinguished by the unfolding of Śakti. (19–30)
