Note 12: The sequence of correspondence is as follows: the letter Śa consists of Aniruddha. 17: He states that the letter Kṣa has the nature of Satya by saying "kṣobhikā."
18. *Balādi* means power (*bala*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), vigor (*vīrya*), capacity (*śakti*), and splendor (*tejas*).

21. *Bindu* is contraction; *visarga* is expansion. Regarding "the last," it means *bindu*. 22. *Bhoktāram* means the one who withdraws (*saṃhāraka*). *Bindu* is the sun; *visarga* is the moon—this is the meaning.
24. "The seven preceding" means the seven vowels: a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, and o. 25. "The seven following" means the seven vowels: ā, ī, ū, ṝ, ḹ, ai, and au.

26. He explains that the seven [vowels] beginning with *a* and ending with *o*, situated in pairs, consist of the rays of the sun and describes their qualities, starting with "Āloka" and so forth. Thus it is said in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*: "Āloka, Tīkṣṇatva, Vyāpti, Grahaṇa, Kṣepaṇa, Iraṇa, Pāka, and Prāpti—these eight are established in the solar portion (*sūryabhāga*) respectively within these short vowels beginning with *a*. (6.13) In this context, the number eight is stated by including the *anusvāra* as well. Root-text: "The syllable *kṣa* itself has arisen as the Great Turbulence (*mahākṣobha*), known by the name Satya."
He who was born as Saṃkarṣaṇa became known by the name Vāsudeva. || 19.31 ||
Pradyumna is to be known by the name Śākha, and Aniruddha likewise by the name Śākhi;
these five supreme powers (śaktis) consist of the essence of the five Brahmans. || 19-32 ||
Those manifestations, non-different from me, are the causes of the world's origin;
they are my powers, like the flames of a great fire, belonging to me, Brahman. (19.33)
O Purandara, four dhāraṇās have arisen, beginning with Vādya and ending with Yānta; these are proclaimed as the states beginning with Turya and ending with Jāgrat. || 19-34 ||
These sustain the male within the midst of two sets of ten;
this is what is called the "brahman-daśā," as well as that which is natural (*prākṛtī*) and elemental (*bhautikī*).
Between those two, that which is called *makāra* (the letter *m*) is the middle state arising from the fourfold set of concentrations (*dhāraṇā*);
it is said that the person (*puruṣa*), who possesses the distinctions of waking and so forth, is sustained by that. (19.36)

If it were not maintained by those [causes], it would fall into one of two states: either that of Brahman or that of the material world; otherwise, there would be no cycle of existence (saṃsṛti) at all. (19.37)
For this purpose, O Dhāraṇā, you have emerged from me by my command.
Thereafter, the Person (puruṣa), designated as the enjoyer (bhoktṛ), resides within the four sets of ten. (19.38)
"From me was born 'Ma'—thus [is he] fit for both enjoyment and liberation—for the sake of producing enjoyments for this Puruṣa, O Vāsava. (19.39)

From me, there arose by itself that which is insentient, supreme, subtle, the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), non-manifest, known as the nature of the womb (yoni), and designated as *bhaga*. (19.40)
Note 27:

Thus, he describes the lunar nature and the qualities of the subsequent vowels with the words beginning "dravatā" (liquidity). And in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*: "Liquidity, coldness, satisfaction, luster, clarity, fluidity, taste, and bliss—these eight are considered the lunar [qualities]. (6.15). Here, by joining the *visarga*, the number eight is to be understood. Note 31:
He states the names of the five Brahmans who preside over the letters from *kṣa* to *śa* with the words beginning "satya" (truth).
32. "Consisting of Brahman" means composed of Brahman.

33. "Of me, who am Brahman": this means of me, who am non-different from Brahman. 35. "In the middle": this means between the states of the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā). Regarding "beginning with *bha*": they should be understood as the presiding deities over the elements starting from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and ending with earth, corresponding to the letters beginning with *bha* and ending with *ka*.

38. The *dhāraṇās* are called "intermediate" (*antaḥsthā*). They are so designated because they abide in the midst of the states of Brahman and Prakṛti. In the *Ahirbudhnya*, however, another etymological derivation is stated: "They are called 'intermediate' because they lie within the Intermediate Person (*antaḥsthapuruṣa*). 39. By the phrase "From me (*mattaḥ*) was born 'ma' (*maḥ*)," the intended etymology of the word *ma* as denoting the individual soul (*jīva*) is expressed. Furthermore, its derivation from the root *man* is also mentioned elsewhere.

40. *Acaitanya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; its meaning is "insentient. It has been stated elsewhere: "It is insentient, for the sake of another, eternal, and constantly undergoing transformation. *Anulbaṇam* means "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). Its names are also "the womb" (*yoni*) and "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). *Bha* means "by virtue of being denoted by the syllable *bha*. (p.

67) For the sake of accomplishing the objects of enjoyment, the experience thereof, and so forth, [it belongs to] the wise one (*vipaścit*) who experiences [them]—or, according to some, the unwise one (*avipaścit*).
O Purandara, from the entire collection of phonemes beginning with 'ba' and ending with 'ka'.
From me, twenty-three manifest entities were born in succession;
likewise, the creation of intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and mind (manas) arose from the triad beginning with sound (śabda).
The emergence of the pentad beginning with the ear occurs within the letters from *n* to *d*;
the emergence of the pentad beginning with speech (*vāk*) occurs within the letters from *ṇ* to *ṭ*. (19.43)
The five subtle elements, beginning with sound and ending with the ether (vyoman), were born from the letters beginning with *i* and ending with *ña*.
The gross elements, beginning with space (*viyat*) and ending with earth, were born from the letters beginning with *ṅa* and ending with *ka*.
Cognition arises in the form of sound, and from that, sound [arises] in the form of meaning;
know, however, that cognition is my very nature, for all this manifestation proceeds from me.
O Lord of Gods, listen as I describe to you this middle path (madhyamā rīti) of the phonemic route (varṇādhvan), beginning from the first and ending with the last. (19.46)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Castes," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Note:
41. In accordance with the sequence of the manifestation of the principles (*tattva*), the letters have been indicated in reverse order, beginning with *ba* and *dya*.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter.
The twentieth chapter.
Śakra said: Salutations to the one who possesses the power to create, protect, and destroy all things.
Salutations to you, who are the very nature of Hari, O embodiment of knowledge! 20-1.
O Padme, through your grace I have heard this supreme secret;
you should now further explain to me the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) exactly as it is.
Śrī said:
Listen, O bull among the gods, to the primordial method of the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan),
by the thorough knowledge of which the practitioner attains my own nature.
That which is the supreme Brahman, free from the known and the knower, imperishable, whose nature is light that never sets, non-different from all, is the state denoted by the word "I. (20.4)

That which is called "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) is that power, non-different from Him, eternally manifest, whose nature is light that never sets, and which is devoid of the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower. (20.5)
I am the essence of light and bliss, having attained a state of universal equanimity;
yet, though remaining as a mere infinitesimal fraction of a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part, I am stirred into motion.
Indeed, by means of my own power, in the form of the Śabdabrahman, I arise from the Supreme Lord myself for the liberation of all living beings. (20.7)
Know that to be the unmanifest syllable, like an indistinct sound from a lute string; it becomes manifold for the sake of its persistence through the nature of separate phonemes.

This [Self], whose nature is the subtle phoneme (sūkṣmavarṇa), assumes the form of a continuous stream [of consciousness] for the discerning one who is established in Me and liberated from the sheaths of the five paths.
Through the grace of the Supreme Self, he attains the state of direct experience;
for the collection of my fourfold nature is indeed to be known as being of that very essence. (20-10)
Through the yoga of origin and dissolution, it is characterized by light, form, and sound;
it begins with the letter *sa* and ends with the letter *ha*. || 20.11 ||
The letter *ha* is at the end of the twelve in the manifestation of the fourfold self;
the letter *a*, however, is at the point of dissolution, and both of these are equal at the end of the twelve.
In this variegated collection of manifestations, rest, emergence, pervasion, and manifestation are to be known through knowledge and meditative absorption as originating from Vāsudeva. (20.13)

Note: 9. The five paths (adhvan) are the path of worlds (bhuvana), the path of words (pada), the path of mantras, the path of principles (tattva), and the path of limited powers (kalā). The five sheaths (kośa) are known as Māyā, the matrix of manifestation (prasūti), primordial nature (prakṛti), the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and the individual body (jīvadeha).

10. The fourfold nature (cāturātmya) consists of Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and the others. This exists in the form of that [divine essence] and in the form of the phonemes (varṇa); this will be explained immediately hereafter.

11. In the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), it is characterized by sound (*dhvani*); in the stage of dissolution (*apyayakrama*), which is the supreme form, it is characterized by consciousness (*citi*). When counting from the letter *a* up to the letter *sa*, there are forty-eight phonemes (*varṇa*). Namely: sixteen vowels (*svara*), twenty-five consonants (*sparśa*), four semivowels (*antaḥstha*), and three sibilants (*ūṣman*) excluding the letter *ha*. The same applies when counting from the letter *ha* up to the long vowel *ā*.

12. Regarding the manifestation (*prabhava*) of the fourfold selves, Vāsudeva and the others, the letter *ha* becomes the end of the twelve; at dissolution (*apyaya*), however, it is the letter *a*. This is the meaning: when the previously mentioned forty-eight syllables are divided twelvefold, four syllables result for each division. These are presided over in sequence by the four [Vyuhas], Vāsudeva and the rest. At the end of the twelfth part, *ha* occurs at manifestation and *a* at dissolution.

13. Vāsudeva and the others, established in their respective divisions, should be known as having the nature of repose (*viśrāma*), emergence (*udaya*), pervasion (*vyāpti*), and manifestation (*vyakti*) respectively. (p.
69) Root-text:
Here, indeed, each form (*mūrti*) above [the preceding one] should be understood in this very same way.
In brief, it is joined with the tetrad preceded by rest. || 20-14 ||
One should contemplate the Lord Vāsudeva as the eternal resting place;
the lotus-eyed one, the primordial deity, the eternal, who is the syllable *A*. (20.15)
For indeed, the principles (tattvas) beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa come to rest here in dissolution;
therefore, one should meditate upon the form and emergence of the god Saṃkarṣaṇa.
For that All-Self has arisen first as the self-existent creator of all; one should contemplate that Lord Pradyumna, who is pervading, as the syllable *i*. (20.17)
By him, whose nature is the action of the three Vedas, the world is obtained in its manifold variety;
one should meditate upon that Aniruddha, who is the letter *Ī* in the form of manifestation.
For here all powers, such as the creation of the world and so forth, are manifested;
indeed, they are situated exactly like this, arranged like a staff (daṇḍavat). (20.19)
Up to the letter *sa*, my fourfold nature is endowed with four forms;
during the contemplation of manifestation, one should remember the letter *ha* at the end of the twelve.
One should contemplate the letter *ha* as Vāsudeva, the state of rest;
one should likewise remember the letter *sa* as Saṃkarṣaṇa, the emergence at the time of dissolution.
In this manner, according to its aspects, one should contemplate the divine fourfold nature;
there are twelve meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās), each characterized by the internal self.
Having ascended that which serves as a staircase, one should enter the supreme city from the *dvādaśānta*;
this is shown to be the first method of the path of phonemes.
The subtle [speech] consists of those four aspects; it is of the nature of light, composed of mind, and supreme.
The intermediate [speech] has already been described; hear from me its specific distinction. (20–24)
The four *dhāraṇās* previously mentioned, which have my own nature, belong to Nīrur̤ha, who is designated by the syllable *va*; his power is known as Rāga.
Māyā is Mahālakṣmī, whose other name is Lakārā;
she who is known by the designation of the letter Ra is Vidyā, and she is remembered as Mahāvāṇī. (20–26)
Vātasaṃjñā, Mahākālī, and Kriyāśakti, who performs the sacrifice; the three forms beginning with Brahmā; and those wives beginning with Trayī—[these are the deities]. (20–27)
That entire subtle object of knowledge is situated in the first part of the letter *a*;
in the middle part, the eternal Puruṣa, the enjoyer, is established. (20–28)
Every transmigrating person abides in the final portion [of the phoneme].
This middle method of the path of phonemes has been shown to you. (20–29)
Now, O slayer of Bala, I shall describe the final mode (rīti).
Vaikharī is the final mode, which distinguishes effort and place of articulation.
When articulated by those with distinct speech, she certainly becomes manifest;
she is the guide to the various true paths for living beings bound within bodies. (20.31)
This Mātṛkā is born, nourished by the power (śakti) of Viṣṇu;
therein, fifty powers are proclaimed to be equal to Viṣṇu himself. (20–32)
Vāsudeva and the other vyuhas, numbering twelve— Keśava and the rest— preside over whichever *mātṛkā* consisting of the garland of phonemes they may be.
The gods presiding over the vowels are their powers; hear these from me:
Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā are declared to be the powers of the Vyūhas. (20.34)
Śrī, Vāgīśvarī, Kānti, Kriyā, Śānti, Vibhūti, Icchā, Prīti, Rati, Māyā, Dhī, and Mahimā. (20–35)
These powers of Keśava and the others are indeed these powers of the vowels; listen as I declare the deities presiding over the consonants beginning with 'ka'. (20–36)
The Viṣṇus named Padmanābha and others are the presiding deities of the letters beginning with *ka*.
They are Padmanābha, Dhruva, Ananta, Śaktīśa, and Madhusūdana. (20–37)
Note: 15. He clarifies that very point with the words beginning "rest" (viśrāmam).
20. Regarding the phrase "up to the letter *sa*": the meaning is "as far as the letter *sa*."
21. He states the placement of the fourfold self within the sequence of the letters: "the letter *ha*," etc.
22. "Up to the letter *ā*" means up to the limit of the letter *ā*.
37. The various manifestations (vibhava-bheda), such as those named Padma and others, were already recited in the eleventh chapter and should be understood [there]. (p.
70) Root-text: The presiding deity of the Mūlavidyā is Kapila, Viśvarūpa, and Vihangama.
Kroḍātman (or Dharmātman), Vaḍavāmukha, Dharma, and likewise Vāgīśvara. || 20-38 ||
The Lord reclining upon the single ocean, the Tortoise who supports the netherworld (pātāla),
the Boar, the Man-lion, and likewise the one who recovered the nectar of immortality.
The Lord of Śrī, possessing a divine body, the beloved soul, the bearer of nectar;
the conqueror of Rāhu, the slayer of Kālanemi, the great one who carried away the Pārijāta tree.
Then there was the Lord of the World, the peaceful-souled Dattātreya, the great master;
thereafter came the Blessed One who sleeps upon the banyan tree, whose body is like a single horn.
The god Vāmanadeha, the all-pervading Trivikrama,
as well as Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and likewise Kṛṣṇa.
Rāma, wielding a flaming axe; another Rāma, the wielder of the bow;
the Lord Kalki, the knower of the Vedas; and the Lord who reclines upon the netherworld (Pātāla). (20.43)
Among these last four, the four deities beginning with Rāma reside; they likewise reside in the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya sounds. (20.44)
Dhī, Tārā, Vāruṇī, Śakti, Padmā, and likewise Vidyā;
Saṃkhyā, Viśvā, Khagā, Bhūḥ, Gauḥ, Lakṣmī, and likewise Vāgīśvarī. (20–45)
Amṛtā, Dharaṇī, Chāyā, Nārasiṃhī, and likewise Sudhā;
Śrī, Kīrti, Viśvakāmā, Mā, Satyā, Kānti, and Saroruhā. (20.46)
Māyā, Padmāsanā, Kharvā, Vikrānti born of a man, Nārāyaṇī, Hariprīti, Gāndhārī, and likewise Kāśyapī. || 20-47 ||
Vaidehī, Vedavidyā, Padminī, and Nāgaśāyinī (or Padmavāsinī)—these goddesses, who are my own portions, are to be known as the Kādi-Śaktis. || 20-48 ||
And this [Mātṛkā] is presided over by the deities who provide the means for worldly existence,
such as Śrīkaṇṭha, Ānanda, Sūkṣma, and others, along with the powers (śaktis) beginning with Lambodarī.
And by the Vināyakas, the Durgās, the Kṣetrapālas, and likewise the Mātṛs; as well as by those established in the Samaya, by the Buddhists, the Ārhats, and others.
Just as hungry children attend upon their mother, so do all the gods attend upon the Goddess Mātṛkā. || 20-51 ||
For this is the womb of mantras and the birthplace of vidyās;
it is the site of the production of both the principles (tattvas) and their corresponding knowledges.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Mātṛkās," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Note: 44. *Raṅga* is nasal. The *yamās* are specific phonemes well-known in the *Prātiśākhyas*. Thus ends the twentieth chapter.
The Twenty-First Chapter.
Śakra said:
O Goddess whose form is the manifestation of word and meaning, who revolves through the six paths!
Salutations to you, O beloved of Hari, who are known as the awakening to that which has transcended the temporal paths.
O Goddess, the phonemes have been revealed to me exactly as they are, along with all their causal principles;
now you should explain to me the path of mantra according to its true nature.
Śrī said:
"The Supreme Lord is indeed one alone—the illustrious Puruṣottama, the divine ocean of the six attributes, the soul of all, whose face is turned in every direction. (21.3)
I am his supreme power, the ego, the inseparable Śrī;
the support of all, possessing all powers, all-knowing, and facing every direction. (21.4)
The universe shines within me like objects on the surface of a mirror;
consciousness alone is my true nature, characterized by stainless bliss. (21.5)
Subject to my own will, revolving within a portion of the Awakener,
and becoming composed of the Śabdabrahman, I manifest myself through the path of the Kalās.
The arts (kalās), beginning with knowledge (jñāna) and so forth, are declared to be the six attributes of the Supreme Lord.
Through their combination in groups of three and two, they evolve according to the path of the principles (tattvas).
O best of gods, Saṃkarṣaṇa and the other deities are the principles (tattvas); they further evolve through the intermingling of the castes by way of the path of mantras.
Listen as I describe the manifestation of that path of mantra:
this is an evolution of the Śabdabrahman, crowded with ten thousand rays.
The characteristic of the mind consists of six qualities, and its division is fourfold:
in some cases it is the seed (bīja), in some cases the mass (piṇḍa), in some cases the name (saṃjñā), and in some cases the word (pada). || 21-10 ||

The fourth state (turya), deep sleep (suṣupti), dream (svapna), and waking (jāgrat)—along with their seeds and so forth—correspond respectively to a single vowel, two vowels, or a pair consisting of a vowel and a consonant. (21–11)
O Lord of the Wise, the seed-syllable (bīja) should be understood as having many vowels;
in between [the consonants], there are *harayaḥ* (the letters *ha*, *ra*, *ya*), and sometimes a cluster (*piṇḍa*) joined with a vowel. || 21-12 ||
The naming of each respective object of expression is the designation joined with "namaḥ" and the "praṇava";
it is characterized by the connection of action and agent, as well as praise and address. (21.13)
The mantra is said to be the essence of the state, endowed with various superknowledges (*abhijñā*);
this fourfold mantra is complete within the self of the deity. (21.14)
Note: 1.
Regarding "the six paths" (ṣaḍadhva): the six paths are known as phoneme (varṇa), energy (kalā), principle (tattva), mantra, word (pada), and world (bhuvana).
2. Regarding "all" (sarva): this means both words and their referents.

6. "Dependent on desire" means according to one's own will (*svacchanda*). "Manifestation" (*vivarta*) means transformation (*pariṇāma*). "By the path of *kalā*" means by that which consists of qualities such as knowledge (*jñāna*).
7. "By the separation of the triad and the dyad" means by the conjunction of the three pairs.

11. The seed-syllables (*bīja*), clusters (*piṇḍa*), named words (*saṃjñāpada*), and mantras should be understood as being respectively associated with the four states beginning with the fourth (*turya*) and ending with the waking state (*jāgrat*).

12. "The *hari*s situated in the middle" means the consonants (*vyañjana*) within the *piṇḍamantra*; he states an exception to this with the words "in some cases. 13. He describes the nature of the *padamantra* with the words "action," etc.; "awakening" (*saṃbodha*) means the vocative case. 14. "Higher knowledge" (*abhijñā*) means a name (*saṃjñā*).
O Lord of the Thirty-three, that [Mūlavidyā], when connected with the fourfold [set], bestows the desired accomplishment and the state of the field and the knower of the field for mantras. (21.15)
Having understood the mantras according to their true nature, the wise one should employ them.
Śakra said:
"O Lotus-born One, tell me the true essence of the fields (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) in relation to the mantras. (21.16)
Having understood this, they do not become deluded and shall attain perfection before long.
Śrī said:
"The seed belongs to those who possess seeds; the life-force is proclaimed as the remaining field. (21.17)
For those without seeds, the primordial life-force (jīva) remains as the field;
and for the seeds and the physical bodies, that which is called the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is said to remain.
Furthermore, the remaining field (kṣetra) is indicated when [the letter] 'a' is absent;
moreover, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is indicated in the vowel alone. (21.19)
The first *mātrā* would be the individual soul (*jīva*), and the second and subsequent ones would be the body (or, according to variant B, the Manu).
In the single *mātrā*, however, there would be the individual soul, characterized by the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

That which is being uttered is the field (kṣetra); moreover, in the soundless syllable (piṇḍaka), the first is designated as the living soul (jīva), while the remainder is called the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
This true nature of the field and the knower of the field has been fully demonstrated to you—
at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end, or in all three, or in any one of them.
The aggregate of these, or else their seed-syllables, are those mantras that are effective at all times.
In the absence of specific seed-syllables for the mantras, one should take the first letter as the seed-syllable.
Subsequently, the entire mantra is said to be joined with the *anusvāra*.
Mantras cause a person who is colored by passion to sport. (21–24)

In the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) belonging to Prakṛti, which consists of fourteen divisions; and in the path of states (*padādhvan*) belonging to Prakṛti, beginning with deep sleep (*suṣupti*), excluding the fourth state (*turya*). (21–25)
Having rescued from the path of the worlds a person who stands within the vision of the Teacher and whose senses are restrained, the mantras— possessing faces gracious with serenity— deliver him.

And producing detachment at every step regarding the path of words, they gradually lead him through the stages of the principles (*tattva*), the powers (*kalā*), the phonemes (*varṇa*), and the words (*pada*). (21–27)
Having reached the palace of the mantra, with all bonds shaken off, he enters that eternal Brahman known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. (21.28)
Śakra:
O Goddess, what is the teacher like, and what is his disciple like?
Among mantras, which mantra is capable of leading to supreme attainment? (21.29)
How should he be instructed? Tell me this; homage be to you! Śrī said:
A Brāhmaṇa endowed with all the auspicious marks, who has mastered the Vedas... [21.30]
Note: 15. That deity.
17. For mantras possessing seed-syllables, the "seed" (bīja) refers to the seed-syllable (bījākṣara), which means the life-force (jīva).

18. *Ādi* means the first letter; that is to say, the letter *a*. 19. The phrase "again, when devoid of the letter *a*" connects with what follows. *Svaraḥ* means any vowel whatsoever. The phrase "and in a solitary vowel" also connects with what follows.
20. *Saṃskāra* means the intermediate speech (*madhyamā vāk*). In this regard, the twenty-sixth verse of the eighteenth chapter should be noted.
21. "Being uttered" means *vaikharī* speech.

23. Where there is no seed-syllable (*bīja*) in a mantra, the meaning is that the first syllable joined with the anusvāra is the seed-mantra; for example, in "gaṇapataye namaḥ," the seed-mantra is *gaṃ*. (p. 73) Root-text:

Devoted to the six duties, tranquil, engaged in the five times, and pure; one who understands the meaning of the Pañcarātra, observant of silence, and has exerted effort in the syllables of the mantra.
Neither fat nor thin, neither short nor one-eyed, nor indeed afflicted by disease;
neither blind, nor deaf, nor dull-witted, nor bald, nor lame. (21.32)
Neither deficient in limb nor having an extra limb, neither afflicted with leprosy nor hypocritical;
neither prone to anger nor having diseased skin, nor one whose consciousness is destroyed by greed. (21.33)
One should avoid one who is of low birth, of evil conduct, deceitful, and crooked;
but one should accept one endowed with compassion, self-restraint, and tranquility, who possesses firm devotion and is intent on ritual practice.

One who is truthful in speech and endowed with virtuous conduct, skilled in the arts of drawing lines, having conquered the senses, well-contented, and whose mind is filled with compassion. || 21-35 ||
One should know a Vaiṣṇava preceptor as one who is endowed with noble characteristics, upright, possessing a beautiful smile,
and thus filled with a multitude of virtues.
And such a disciple should be known as one endowed with all the required characteristics: patient, virtuous, highly intelligent, and free from anger and greed. (21.37)

One who is constantly devoted to bathing and worship, intent on serving his guru, faithful toward Brahmins, the sacrificial fire, the gods, and the ancestors, and habituated to performing libations (tarpaṇa).
One who is of noble birth, as well as wise, always devoted to the meaning of the scriptures—
whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra— who is intent upon the Blessed Lord.
A disciple endowed with such characteristics and possessed of sincerity, or a woman who is virtuous, discerning, and endowed with the performance of her caste-duties—[should be accepted]. (21.40)
One should know that she who is devoted to her husband and considers no other man as her lord should be given to him with his consent.
An ācārya who is absorbed in the Blessed One should, having examined such a disciple according to the prescribed rules and with the vision of a guru, cause him to understand the mantras. || 21-41 ||
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Guru and the Disciple," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra.
Note:
41. By this, the eligibility of women and Śūdras for receiving Tantric mantras is also established. However, regarding the Tārā [mantra], the specific details should be understood from other texts.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter.
The twenty-second chapter.
Śakra said:
O Goddess, who are without beginning or end, omniscient, and beloved of Hari!
How indeed should one cause the mantras to be known, and what is their form like?
Are these [virtues] of equal importance, or is there a distinction of seniority and juniority?
Having asked this, please tell me; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One. (22.2)
Śrī said: Listen to everything in its entirety from me, O Pākaśāsana,
as to how I am the form of the mantra and how I make them understand.
The Supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, possessing the six divine attributes, stainless and radiant,
unconditioned by space or time, formless, and incomparable.
That Brahman, which is the self-realization of one's own nature, devoid of qualities, without beginning or end, divine, and great, is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa—expressed as "I" alone. (22.5)
The divine essence of consciousness and bliss is indivisible, undecaying, and immortal;
it is devoid of the state of becoming, free from the distinction between the grasped and the grasper [or: abandoned by the grasper].
That Supreme Brahman is motionless; I am its state of motionlessness.
At times, that Supreme Brahman exists through the condition of becoming.
Sometimes, by her own will, she unfolds while not abandoning her essential nature;
I am that "I-consciousness" (ahaṃtā) whose essence is the state of "I," who is to be fully worshipped by the Supreme Self.
O Lord, I have arisen by Your will alone, just as the sun rises;
having gathered all necessary provisions, I abide by Your will alone, as if they were created by myself.
Having brought forth what was inscribed upon my own wall—[reading: *vilikhantīdaṃ* instead of *nītaṃ*]—I manifest through the six paths:
that consisting of phonemes (*vārṇa*), that consisting of kalās, that consisting of principles (*tāttvika*), and likewise that consisting of mantras (*māntrika*).
The six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) are proclaimed as the *pādika* and the *bhauvana*;
and that which is supreme, called the "I-sense" (*ahaṃtā*), whose nature is consciousness (*saṃvit*) and free from affliction. || 22-11 ||
The first unfolding of that [reality] is proclaimed as the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan);
its manifestation has already been shown to you previously, O Pākaśāsana. (22.12)
That very same great form of mine, consisting of pure consciousness,
unfolds as the path through knowledge and the rest, which have the nature of *kalā*.
The qualities of the supreme self— namely, the digits beginning with knowledge (jñāna)—
have already been described by you in detail, as many as they are and of whatever nature they may be.
Depending upon the two time-periods (past and future), that form of mine, consisting of consciousness,
exists by way of the path of reality in the form of Vāsudeva and others.
Note:
3. "I make known" (jñāpayāmi) means that I cause [you] to understand by way of being the Teacher. 4. "Incomparable" (anūpamam) means "without comparison" (anupamam).
5. *Nirguṇa* means devoid of the natural qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and the rest.

6. Regarding the phrase *anunmiṣat* and so forth: the meaning is that in the state of supreme tranquility (*śāntaparāvasthā*), there is an absence of the manifestation (*unmeṣa*) of existence in the form of becoming. The same should be understood for the phrase *grāhya* and so forth.
8. *Unmiṣati* means it shines forth. Regarding the phrase *ajahat* and so forth: the meaning is not relinquishing its innate state of changelessness (*nirvikāratva*).
9. From Vivasvat, meaning from the Lord who consists of splendor.
15. The two paths, meaning the path of the castes (varṇādhvan) and the path of the phases (kalādhvan).
Mūla—

The cosmic arrays (vyūhas), the manifestations (vibhavas), and whatever else consists of the Lord—this is proclaimed as the unfolding of the path of reality (tattvādhvan) from the Supreme Self. (22.16)
Taking up the two preceding paths, that very form of mine, consisting of consciousness,
perpetually unfolds through the supreme path of Mantra.
For the sake of delivering living beings submerged in the ocean of existence, for the enjoyment of those dwelling in worldly life, and for the generation of dispassion; (22.18)

For the sake of accomplishing propitiation, for the sake of success, and for the purpose of mental focalization, the path of mantra is supremely exalted, characterized by my own nature of consciousness. (22.19)
This [mantra] attains the state of being an image of Vāsudeva and the other deities;
all mantras are of the nature of consciousness, omnipresent, and accomplishers of all things. (22.20)
These [mantras] protect the reciter and, according to the scriptures, provide concealment;
for they bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation from the Lord of Gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
O Blessed One, my mantras are to be understood as stainless forms:
the fourfold states consisting of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turya). || 22-22 ||
The nature of the path of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) is the waking state, which proceeds through the external sense organs;
this occurs when the power of the external senses has been overcome by *tamas*. (22–23)
That modification of the internal organ which remains as a residual impression (saṃskāra) is to be known as dream; in the absence of that [modification], there is the state of deep sleep.
When the activity of the external and internal organs has ceased for the wise man who is not overcome by darkness and is established in purity, [he attains the state of Brahman]. (22–25)
The continuum of the pure being’s clarity is designated as the fourth state.
Thus, these fourfold paths have been described in this work titled *Pada*.

Excluding the fourth state (turya), [the soul] resorts to impure states such as deep sleep (suṣupti) and so forth. The sequence of worlds (bhuvanapaddhati) is said to extend from Māyā down to the earth (kṣiti). || 22–27 ||
That path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) should be known as impure and defiled by the mire of impurity;
those mantras constantly cause a man who is dominated by passion to sport [within it].
While he was being deluded by the display of various nets of sensory enjoyments, he was properly beheld with a compassionate gaze by the Guru, who looked upon him with mercy. (22.29)
They carry them across, engendering detachment at every step; then, they gradually lead them along paths consisting of purity. (22–30)
Such great-souled mantras, supremely purifying, lead one who is proficient in the Śabdabrahman to the highest glory. (22–31)
They are to be known as threefold: the inferior, the middling, and the superior—those who have attained the form of deities through the requisites of worldly existence. (22-32)
Mantras that grant finite fruits should be known as inferior by the wise;
for mantras are the very forms of the powerful deities together with their Śaktis.
Note:
16. "The other" means other arrays (*vyūha*) and other manifestations (*vibhava*).
18. He states the purpose of the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*) with the words beginning "for the sake of deliverance" (*uttāraṇāya*).

19. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of providing a mental object": the meaning is that by displaying forms with beautiful substrates, it provides a meditative object for the minds of yogins. This has been explained in detail in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*. 20. Now, he describes the greatness of the mantra under discussion, beginning with the words "mantrāḥ" (the mantras). 21. By way of describing its greatness, he states the etymological meaning of the word "mantra" with the words "and because they protect" (*trāyaṇāt*). The sense is that [the word] is derived from the roots *man* and *trai*. He gives another derivation with the words "protected" (*gupta*). The root is *matri*, meaning "to speak secretly."
23. He defines the state of dream with the words beginning "bāhya" (external), etc.
24. "In the absence of that" means in the absence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
27. He defines the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) with the words beginning "māyādi" (beginning with Māyā).
30—The meaning is: at every step, beginning with the waking state (*jāgrat*).
31—The meaning is: within the *śabdabrahman*, that is, within the mantras.
32—Regarding "the supreme" (*pare*): the meaning is "the highest. "Instruments of existence" (*bhavopakaraṇāni*) means those things that serve as instruments for creation (*sarga*).
Those who plunge into Brahman, which consists of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, should be known as the middle mantras, the supreme forms of the cosmic array (vyūha). (22.34)
Those mantras established through existence and non-existence are the most excellent of the excellent;
thus should the priority and posteriority among them be understood by those skilled in mantras.
Those established in the Pañcarātra are the highest; those consisting of the Trayī (the three Vedas) are middling;
and those established in other tantras are to be known as inferior by one who possesses the eye of the scriptures. (22–36)

Mantras possessing all their constituent parts (kalāṅga) are to be known as supreme; those with other [missing] parts are remembered as middling; and those lacking parts (anaṅga) are inferior. Listen further, O Lord of the Gods. (22–37)

Those mantras joined with seed-syllables (*bīja*), clusters (*piṇḍa*), and so forth, are proclaimed as supreme; those mantras that have a seed-syllable at the beginning or at the end are designated as middling. (22–38)
Mantras that lack the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and other such elements are to be known as those designated as inferior.
Having thus understood the various types of mantras, the teacher, whose eye is the scripture, should, when requested, instruct the disciples regarding the mantras according to their true nature.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Mantras of the Six Paths," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Note 36:

"Established in the Pañcarātra" means that they are considered supreme because they are devoted to the description of the Bhāgavatas, who are the most excellent Sāttvika portion [of devotees] and have no other purpose. "Consisting of the Trayī" means that they are considered middling because they concern the realm of the three guṇas.
37: "Kalās" refers to knowledge and the other [perfections].
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter.
The twenty-third chapter:
Śrī.
That which is the all-pervading, supreme, and great Brahman is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
I am indeed Nārāyaṇī, His supreme power of egoity (ahaṃtā).
For the sake of favoring the worlds, I have assumed the role of a teacher;
in the form of Saṃkarṣaṇa, I illuminate the scripture.
And again, abiding in the form of the Guru and endowed with perfect realization,
she [should look upon him] with her own gaze consisting of Śakti, filled with compassion and mantra.
Having become a guru, I protect the disciples who approach me;
therefore, that teacher should always be known by the disciples as being identical with my own self. (23–4)
One should instruct the disciple in the mantras; listen attentively to how that is done:
first, in a place that is pure, level, smooth, and free from defects of the ground. || 23-5 ||
In a place rich with colors corresponding to the [appropriate] castes, smeared with cow-dung, perfumed, free from thorns, and adorned with fragrant flowers and other offerings. || 23-6 ||

Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and anointed it with sandalwood paste and other unguents, one should place a vessel made of fine clay and filled solely with auspicious flowers. || 23-7 ||
One should worship with one's own mantra, beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Then, it should be recited together with the *vyāhṛtis*, preceded by the *praṇava*.
Then, having spread earth upon the ground, scented with perfumes and incense,
it should be made either square or circular, measuring two cubits or even one cubit.
Having made the seat of the Mātṛkās perfectly level, one should spread it out;
she who is the single Goddess residing in the divided classes [of consonants], consisting of fifteen syllables.
She is the manifest mother of mantras and my very body composed of sound;
the practitioner of mantra should spread her out either in the form of a lotus or in the form of a wheel.
In the Pauruṣa [cakra], one should follow the wheel-form and the lotus-born Lakṣmī;
the power consisting of Agni and Soma is called Visṛṣṭi, which is sixteenfold [the Vidyā known as Sṛṣṭi is sixteenfold]. || 23-12 ||
One should write that which is called "Svara" (the vowels) on the leaf or the spoke situated in the eastern direction.
As for the five groups beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma', they consist of the elements starting from Earth and ending with Puruṣa. (23–13)
One should draw that [mandala] like a leaf of a tree, beginning from Fire (Agni) and ending with Wind (Vāyu);
within it is the form of the internal dhāraṇā, consisting of the four letters beginning with Ya and ending with Va.

Commentary: 5—The defects of the ground (*bhūdoṣa*) consist of contact with hair, nails, and bones, as well as salinity (*ūṣaratva*) and so forth. 6—"Corresponding to the [caste] colors" (*varṇānurūpa*), etc.: this means possessing white and other colors in accordance with the castes (*varṇa*) such as the Brāhmaṇa. As it is stated in the *Paramasaṃhitā*: "The ground of a Brāhmaṇa is white; that of a Kṣatriya should be ruddy; that of a Vaiśya is yellow in color; and that of a Śūdra is declared to be black" (7.5). "Piercing objects" (*śalya*) refers to thorns and the like.
7—By "alone" (*kevalaiḥ*), it is meant "loose," that is, unstrung.
8—By "the former" (*pūrvayā*), it is meant "by means of utterance" (*vyāhṛtya*).
10—"Of divided classes" (*bhinnavargā*) means "divided by way of the *ka*-class and so forth."
13. The letter *ka* is Earth; the letter *ma* is the Person (*pumān*).
On page 78: The wise one should write the leaf or the spoke rising from the root as before.
The fivefold Brahman that has been described begins with the letter Śa and ends with the fourth vowel (Ū). || 23-15 ||
One should write [the syllables] situated in the ten directions upon a lotus or even a leaf;
that which is called Sound is the Supreme Brahman, consisting of light and free from affliction.
One should meditate on the form of light at the periphery of the wheel and the lotus, using those syllables known as the *tattvas*, beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. (23.17)
There, the wise one should worship me in my form as the *tattva*, according to each individual's nature;
then, in the center of its pericarp, he should contemplate the mantra-mātṛkā.
I bow to the Goddess who is without beginning or end, the Great One, the Supreme Person;
the Goddess who holds the noose and the goad, the Lotus-Born One adorned with a garland of lotuses.
She is serene, possessing the luster of the interior of a lotus, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds,
her limbs fashioned with perfect color and adorned with ornaments of hue.
One should know that the Śabdabrahman is the body and should remember the Praṇava as the head;
one should know "a" and "ā" as the two eyebrows, and "i" and "ī" as the two eyes.
*u* and *ū* are the two ears; *ṛ* and *ṝ* are the two nostrils;
*e* and *ai* are to be known as the two lips; and *o* and *au* are the two rows of teeth. (23–22)
One should contemplate the letter *aṃ* as the tongue, the letters *ka* and *ca* groups as the hands,
the *ṭa* and *ta* groups as the feet, and the wise man should contemplate the letters *pa* and *pha* as the sides.
One should contemplate the syllable *maṃ* as the region behind and the region in front;
one should know that *ya* and *ra* are the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and heat (*uṣman*), and one should contemplate *laṃ* as the necklace (*hāra*).
One should remember the letter *va* as the waist-thread (*kaṭisūtra*), and *śa* and *ṣa* as the two earrings;
one should know the letter *sa* as the heart, and one should remember *ha* as residing within the heart.

One should know the spreading radiance to be the syllable *kṣa*, blazing like lightning. One should know the stage located at the tip of the nose; one should remember that which is called Yama in the heart.
One should know that the jihvāmūlīya occurs immediately at the root of the tongue; likewise, one should know that the upadhmānīya occurs at the lips in due order. (23–27)
She wears a forest garland made of auspicious lotuses consisting of the elements of fire and moon, which hangs from her neck down to her feet.

The wise one should contemplate the crown of the Supreme Lord, which shines with the luster of ten million fires, moons, and suns, adorned with shimmering jewels, and marked by the syllable *Ha*. (23–29)

Having thus recollected that goddess Mātṛkā, the mother of mantras, one should worship her with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and so forth, [reciting]: "Oṃ, salutations to the Mother of Mantras. (23–30)
"Accept this arghya," saying thus, one should offer the articles of enjoyment in this sequence;
then, with palms joined in reverence and body bowed low, one should prostrate on the ground with the eight limbs.
O Goddess who dwells in the lotus, whose abode is the lotus, who are the lotus itself, beloved of the lotus-eyed one; O Sovereign Mother of all mantras, the support established by all principles!
"Reveal to me your supreme, divine form, which consists of Lakṣmī.
Having thus prayed with a disciplined mind, the practitioner himself shall become identical with Lakṣmī. (23–33)
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the Mātṛkā, being himself composed of the true Mātṛkā,
he should extract the desired mantra and then instruct it to the disciple.

Mantras consisting of seed-syllables (*bīja*) and clusters (*piṇḍa*) have attained the state of being the most excellent among mantras; therein, O Lord of the Gods, the seed-syllables are even more excellent than the clusters. (23–35)
Note:
19. *Puruṣottamī* is the feminine form of *puruṣottama*. 22. This means the two other phonemes, *ḷ* and *ḹ*. Because these two are neuter, they are not referred to by name.
26. A nasalized vowel [is used] for the stage.
34. "The Mother" (mātṛkā), etc. (p. 79). Root-text:
O Vāsava, among the seeds there are seven that are like jewels:
the first seed is Tāraka, and the second is known as Tārikā. (23–36)
Equal in splendor to those two is the third, Anutārikā;
but the fourth is called the supreme seed, the source of the universe.
The fifth seed-syllable is that of Prādyumna; the sixth is considered to be that of Sarasvatī; and the seventh is proclaimed to consist of Mahālakṣmī. (23–38)
The gross, subtle, and supreme [aspects] have been proclaimed for each one individually;
O Śakra, being attentive, listen to the seed-syllables in their proper sequence.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Mātṛkās," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
36. The sequence for extracting the mantras of Tārā and others will be explained in the following chapter.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter.
[Now begins] the twenty-fourth chapter.
Śrī said:
The Supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the incomparable supreme light—Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is Brahman, free from defect and stainless. (24.1)
Pervading all this universe as one, there exists the supreme, great Light;
"I am I" is the supreme egoity of that Brahman, the Supreme Self. (24.2)
Arising by her own will for the benefit of all living beings,
she becomes composed of the Śabdabrahman, having the Mātṛkā-mantra as her very form.
I am the form of the mantra, imitating each respective object of expression;
first, in the form of the *tāra*, one should extract it just as I am.
First, taking hold of the *dhruva*, one should then extract the *karṇa*;
afterwards, one should extract the *nābhi* and join these three together as one.
This syllable "Om," which has arisen as the first *tāraka* of Brahman,
should subsequently be adorned with the *bindu*, and after that with the *nāda*.
One should meditate with a continuous sound, like an unbroken stream of oil;
this is that Vaiṣṇava form, the three-syllabled eternal Brahman.
Aniruddha is the letter *a* here; Pradyumna is the fifth vowel (*u*);
Saṃkarṣaṇa is the letter *m*; and Vāsudeva is the nasal dot (*bindu*). (24.8)
O Lord of the Gods, there is no division of the four [states] within that sound (nāda);
that which is the supreme limit of sound is I-consciousness (ahaṃtā), the Supreme Goddess.
That power is supreme and subtle, called the sky at the end of sound (*nādānta*);
consisting of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), subtle, and all-pervading, she is I. (24.10)
When the resonance has come to rest, that light which clearly manifests by itself is the supreme Brahman, known by the names Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
Thus has been described to you this supreme, personal abode of Viṣṇu;
now listen to the true nature of that which is its peaceful form.
Having first taken up the emission, one should join it with the Sun at the end;
when the supreme proximity has arisen, that is the Great Splendor uttered as "Om."
This is that supreme abode, characterized by the withdrawal of power;
when remembered, it unfailingly reveals the supreme reality.

Note: 10. Regarding "nādānte" and so forth, the meaning is that [the Goddess] has the nature of the space (*gagana*) at the end of the previously mentioned *nāda*, which is the *daharākāśa* (the internal space). Since the Goddess has the nature of the *daharākāśa*, it is heard in scripture that the Supreme Brahman has its fixed abode therein: "Therein is the small space, free from sorrow; that which is within it is to be meditated upon. And in the *Śrīsāttvata*: "In the space at the conclusion of *nāda*, the infinite Lord is fully present" (2.69).

13. *Visṛṣṭi* means emission (*visarga*). The Sun is the syllable *aṃ*. When *aḥ* and *aṃ* stand together, by the rule *ato roḥ*, the *r* is replaced by *u*, followed by *guṇa* and *pūrvarūpa* sandhi, resulting in *oṃ*. 14. Because it consists of the conjunction of the *visarga* and the *bindu*, its meaning is that it characterizes both creation and dissolution. (p. 81) Root Text:
Having withdrawn the entire collection of all things arising from the pure and impure paths,
the Power, intent upon creation, [rests] in the eternal Sun, the Puruṣa.
Having brought about the process of reabsorption into that supreme form of the enjoyer,
she has emerged from that gross state consisting of fire and moon.
The Śakti, eternally resting upon the middle couple consisting of Bindu and Nāda,
rests upon the divine, subtle couple whose nature is peace.
It becomes established in the divine, all-pervading Supreme Self.
Its measures are declared by those who know the ritual procedure to be three and a half. (24.18)
There are three fires, three worlds, three Vedas,
three qualities, three deities, three manifestations, three social classes, and three vowels.
O Śakra, whatever triad exists within the world, that should be known as the primordial triad; the half-mora is the stainless one.
O Purandara, all sounds arise from the syllable *a*; from the syllable *u* come the three fires; and from the syllable *m* arise everything from earth up to primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
That half-measure consists of light; it is the supreme digit composed of consciousness.
It is formed by the vowels together with their bindus, situated at the beginning and end of the two groups of six vowels.
Furthermore, his limbs are fashioned with the six qualities beginning with knowledge (jñāna) as their limit:
at the navel, on the back, and likewise on the two arms, the two thighs, the two knees, and the feet. (24–23)
O Pākaśāsana, one should further assign the qualities preceded by the syllable *tāra*;
having thus assigned them, one should assign that mantra together with its limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*).
The Guru should contemplate Puruṣottama residing within his own self;
listen to me as I explain correctly how this occurs, preceded by the dissolution of the universe and its elements. (24–25)
The universe, which is the locus of the waking state, the impeller of all the senses, and the enjoyer of the five objects of the senses beginning with sound. (24–26)

One should contemplate that reality, which is of the nature of Aniruddha [and designated as Aniruddha], within the first syllable. Then, having dissolved that deity, together with his implements, into the letter *A*.
One should dissolve the syllable *a* into the radiant deity Pradyumna, who moves within the realm of dreams and impels the functions of the internal organs. (24–28)
One should dissolve that [universe], together with its implements, into the god Ukāra;
and Ukāra into Īśvara, who abides in the body of Saṃkarṣaṇa as Prājña.

Having dissolved that Lord of Gods— who is eternally situated in the state of deep sleep, the pervasive impeller of the vital breaths and so forth— into the half-mora established in the Fourth State (turya).
One should dissolve [the mind] into the god Vāsudeva, who consists of knowledge and bliss;
and that fourth state (turya) into the one beyond the fourth (turyātīta), whose essence is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Having dissolved his own divine Vaiṣṇava egoity, he should take refuge in that [state];
becoming absorbed in that, he then gradually reaches such a place of dissolution.
Note:
15. "In the Sun" means in the masculine form as the *bindu*. 20. "The first triad" means the triad beginning with the letter *a*. The half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) is the *bindu*.
21. The triad of splendors consists of the forms of the sun, the moon, and fire.

22. The supreme digit (*kalā*) is *nāda*. The first group of six vowels runs from *a* to *ū*; the final group of six vowels runs from *ḷ* to *au*. Among these, the even vowels are *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *ḹ*, *ai*, and *au*. With these, together with the *bindu*, one performs the ritual assignment of limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). The assignment of the secondary limbs (*upāṅganyāsa*), however, is performed with those same vowels accompanied by the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) and the words beginning with "knowledge" (*jñāna*). 26. "The universe" (*viśva*) refers to the names of the self situated in the state of waking.

27. Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, and the deities known as Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, Turya, and Turyātīta are the presiding deities of the waking state and the others. (p. 82) Root-text:
Then, having descended into the waking state, [the teacher] places the initiated disciple before him.
The true guru, having become one with the Self (manmaya), should himself personally teach the Tāra-mantra.

He should constantly bestow his own self as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru, along with the wealth [of the ritual], together with the limbs and sub-limbs, the sequence, the meditative absorption (samādhi), and in full detail. (24–34)
Then, having obtained permission, performing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa),
he should go to the bank of a great river or to a sanctuary of the Siddhas and others.
Or he may dwell in a forest of *pālāśa* trees, which is entirely pure and whose ground is not seen by others;
performing ablutions three times a day, remaining celibate, and having his senses subdued. (24–36)
Eating any one of these— milk, barley-gruel, or alms-food— only once a day,
he sat upon a heap of *kuśa* grass, clothed in *kāśa* grass and *kuśa* lotuses.
Clad in a black antelope skin, he should carry a staff made of *pālāśa* wood; with his mind fixed on Me and becoming absorbed in Me, he should proceed by the path instructed by his guru.
Constantly devoted to yoga and possessing the meditative absorption of right knowledge,
one who observes silence should recite the Tāra mantra ten hundred thousand times— the savior from the cycle of existence.
One should offer oblations ten times [the number of recitations] with *parṇa* leaves, fuel-sticks, or even clarified butter;
thus propitiated, I, the supreme Vaiṣṇava egoity, manifest myself to him. (24.40)
Then, in the mind of the practitioner that is thoroughly discerning of the real, that state of aesthetic integration known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa shines forth. (24.41)
Even while living, he becomes liberated and purifies the world with his very glance;
all mantras, whether worldly or Vedic, become perfected for him.
He becomes one who has bathed in all the Vedas, in all branches of knowledge,
in all established doctrines, and in all sacred fords.
Whatever applications there may be for all mantras—however many and of whatever kind—they are determined to be his applications as well, being just as numerous and of the same nature. (24.44)
Its three utterances (vyāhṛtis) have arisen from the three castes;
indeed, the Sāvitrī, the purifier of all, has arisen from its feet.
From her feet came the three Vedas, characterized as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman;
indeed, all this speech—both worldly and Vedic—is composed of these alone. (24.46)
Just as a great tree is contained within the seed of a banyan,
so too this entire universe consisting of speech is always situated within this [Self].
This is the primordial great seed, the supreme source of all sounds;
it is the Brahman of sound, the highest abode, the most pure, the greatest. (24.48)
Oṃkāra, Praṇava, Tāra, Haṃsa, Nārāyaṇa, Dhruva, Vedātmā, the source of all Vedas, Āditya, and the purifier of all. || 24-49 ||
The giver of liberation, the path to liberation, capable of sustaining all—such are the names [of this supreme sustainer] found by the wise in every scripture. (24–50)
Note:

32. *tanmayaḥ* means consisting of egoity (*ahaṃtāmayaḥ*). 33. He states the thought concerning the descent from the place of dissolution to the place of creation with the words "jāgarām" (the waking state).

35. *Puraścaraṇa* refers to the performance of recitation (*japa*), fire-oblations (*homa*), and so forth, to be carried out for the purpose of producing greater potency in a mantra received from a guru. That [practice] consists of five limbs. Thus it has been said: "Recitation, oblation, libation, ritual bathing, and the feeding of Brahmins—this five-limbed worship in this world is called *puraścaraṇa*. (24) 40. Regarding the phrase "one-tenth part" (*daśāṃśam*): the meaning is "one hundred thousand times" (*lakṣakṛtvaḥ*).

47. An illustration is given regarding how *tāra* (the syllable Om) is the embodiment of all speech—beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*). A *dhānā* is a minute seed. Here, the statement that the great tree exists in a subtle state within the seed follows the Sāṃkhya doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect in the cause (*satkāryavāda*). However, in the Upaniṣadic view, since the material cause (*upādāna*) of both the seed and the great tree is one, it is indeed *satkāryavāda*; yet there is a distinction in that the conventional relationship of cause and effect arises from a difference in states. (p. 83) Root-text: The great merits of the Great Soul, Oṃkāra, have been studied [or, according to Ā and Ṅ: recounted].
This is the refuge for those who lack knowledge; this alone is [the refuge] for those who possess it.
This [mantra], formed by the conjunction of the letters *ha* and *au*, is known as the *Prāsāda*; it is a boat for those seeking heaven and for those desiring to cross to the further shore. (24.52)
This is the *piṇḍa* (the condensed essence) of all principles (*tattvas*), being eternal and having become a single mass;
it consists of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the practice (*pratipatti*), the application (*viniyoga*), and the retention (*dhāraṇā*).
O Lord of the Suras, know that this [mantra] is like the seed of this temple;
this very mantra of its name is the great *manu* called *Haṃsa*. (24.54)
Know the enjoyer to be the first letter and the object of enjoyment to be the second;
the former consists of Nārāyaṇa, while the latter consists of Śrī.
Know these two letters to be the eternal embodiments of Agni and Soma;
between them, O Śakra, the nature of the Bindu is established. (24.56)
One should raise the phoneme of the enjoyer from the base to the top of the head;
one should emit the second phoneme, known as the "enjoyed," from the mouth. (24.57)
The entire creation was brought forth by him through the practice of the utterance of *haṃsa*;
this is proclaimed as the *ajapā*, the science beautiful in all its parts. (24.58)
In the eighty-eight crores and sixty-four million species of birth,
and within their various subdivisions, this mantra always recites itself spontaneously.
Along with the exhalation, the Vidyā arises, blazing within;
the states of rising and setting are equal to inhalation and exhalation.
Sixty breaths constitute one *prāṇa*, and six *prāṇas* are considered one *nāḍikā*.
Sixty *nāḍikās* make up one day and night; such is the progression of the movement of time. (24.61)
"O Lord of Gods, know that from the rising of the *haṃsa* there are twenty-one thousand and six hundred [breaths]; that many recitations (*japa*) have been performed. (24.62)
However, at the beginning of the day and other times, the wise person should form a mental resolve with the thought: "I shall perform this many recitations of the *japa*. (24–63)
One should place the five limbs; learn from me their form:
Sūrya and Soma, ending in the dative case, accompanied by "namaḥ" and "svāhā. (24.64)
The two [mantras] ending in *vauṣaṭ* and *huṃphaṭ* are stainless and without appearance;
the root mantra itself, ending in *phaṭ*, is the weapon (*astra*). These are its five limbs.
This very same mantra is known as the *paramātma-mantra* when it is inverted.
Having remembered the Śakti together with her equipment (*sasaṃbhārā*), one should unite her with the Sun, who is the enjoyer.
The remaining [portion] is to be contemplated as being like the *praṇava*; this is the rule for the *saṃjñā-mantra*.
In the *Pāñcarātrika* ritual procedure, it should consist of three parts: the *pada*, the *mantra*, and the *astra*. (24.67)
"Salutation to Viṣṇu," "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa," and first, "Salutation to the Blessed One Vāsudeva"—thus [one should recite]. (24.68)
Note:
55. "The first letter" means the letter *ha*. "The second" means the letter *sa*. 56. The two functions of the *bindu* are creation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).

57. Beginning from the seat of the *ādhāra* (the perineum) and moving upward to the crown of the head (*mūrdhan*), one should utter the syllable *ha*; one should emit the syllable *sa* through the mouth.
58. This is the name of the *haṃsa-mantra*: the *ajapā-mantra*. 62. The meaning is that when the *haṃsa-mantra* is recited even once, a total of 21,600 recitations have been performed.
63. "Thus, as many as" means "of such a number.
64. "The sun and moon" refers to the letters *ha* and *sa*.

66. "Inverted" means the mantra "so 'ham" (I am that). The meaning is that one should take the power (*śakti*) by means of the letter *sa* and join it with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in the letter *ha*.

67. Regarding the word "three": although four mantras will be mentioned, nevertheless, by taking a certain distinction among them, a separate designation of three is made. 68. He states the essential forms of the mantras: beginning with "to Viṣṇu" and so forth; at the beginning, "namo bhagavate," and at the end, "vāsudevāya. The meaning is that the mantra is "namo bhagavate vāsudevāya. (p. 84) Root text—
Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
Salutations be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Great Being, O Primordial One.
O Purandara, this fourth is proclaimed as the *pada-mantra* of the *praṇava*;
those who know the ancient tradition understand these mantras to be accompanied by the syllable *oṃ*. (24.70)

The arrangement of the limbs (aṅga) should be performed with syllables such as the *praṇava* (Oṃ), which are endowed with qualities such as knowledge and end with "namas"; likewise, the arrangement of the secondary limbs (*upāṅga*) should be done in the same manner. (24.71)
For a mantra that lacks syllables, the construction of an auxiliary limb (upāṅga) should be performed by means of its final syllable, joined with words expressing its respective qualities.

In the same way, for one of exceptionally radiant complexion, one should fashion the final subsidiary limb (upāṅga) together with its splendor by means of all the remaining [syllables], increased by twelve.
The Kevala, the Tāraka, and the four beginning with that—
these five all-pervading mantras are proclaimed in the Pāñcarātra.
There is nothing here that cannot be accomplished by these mantras of the Great-Souled Ones;
this five-stepped ladder leads to the ascent into the Supreme Brahman.
This divine Great Being is the fifth mantra, consisting of the nature of Man (Manmaya).
By properly relying upon her through worship, recitation, meditation, and so forth, one attains one's own Vaiṣṇava being and realizes the Supreme Brahman. || 24-76 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Savior" (or "The Savior"), in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.

Note: 72. Regarding "of that which has fewer syllables": this refers to the deficiency in syllables between the six-syllable and eight-syllable mantras; the meaning is that in such cases, the completion must be effected by means of the final syllable. 73. Regarding "of that which has expanded syllables": this means having an excess of syllables, as for example in the mantra *jitaṃ te*.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter.
The twenty-fifth chapter:
Śrī [Śrī said].
Thus, O Śakra, this detailed account of Tāraka has been told to you by me;
now hear the sequence of my Tārikā, who delivers one across the ocean of saṃsāra.
First, learn the technical designations for the sake of accomplishing the ritual procedures for the phonemes;
when these have been heard according to rule, the application of the mantras proceeds. (25.2)
The letter A is immeasurable and is remembered as the first pervader;
likewise, the letter Ā is the primordial deity, bliss, and is remembered as the protector. (25.3)
The letter *i*, known as Rāma, is proclaimed to be kindled and desired;
the letter *ī* is indeed the five dots (*pañcabindu*), Viṣṇu, Māyā, and Indra. (25.4)
The letter *u* is called Bhuvana, as well as Uddāma and Udaya;
the letter *ū* is Ūrja, Lokeśa, and indeed Prajñādhārā. (25.5)
Satya and Ṛtadhāman, and the letter Ṛ which is indeed the goad;
the letter Ṛ is called Viṣṭara, and it is also the flame and the spreading. (25–6)
The Lord is declared to be the soul of the *liṅga*; the syllable *ḷ* is remembered as the Savior (*tāraka*).
The syllable *ḹ* is Dīrghaghoṇa, Devadatta, as well as Sthira and Virāṭ. (25.7)
The triangle is known as Eka (the One), the source of the world, and formless;
it is sovereignty, the sustainer of yoga, and is remembered as Ai, Sa, and Airāvaṇa. || 25-8 ||
Okāra is Otadeha and Odana, the valiant; Aurva is called Bhūdhara, and Au is remembered as being of the nature of medicinal herbs. || 25.9 ||
The pervasive Aṃkāra is the Lord of Space (Vyomeśa), bestowing sovereignty over the three worlds; Visarga is known as the creator of emanation, while Hyakāra is the Supreme Lord.
Kamala and Karāla are the letter Ka, the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti);
Khakāra is Kharvadeha, the soul of the Vedas, the creator of the universe. || 25-11 ||
The letter *ga* is the destroyer of disease (*gadadhvaṃsī*), Govinda, and the wielder of the mace (*gadādhara*);
the letter *gha*, moreover, is the portion of Dharma, radiant and luminous. (25.12)
The letter *ṅa* is known as Ekadaṃṣṭra, the self of beings and the creator of beings; the letter *ca* is Cañcala, the wielder of the discus (*cakrī*), and he is called Candrāṃśu. (25.13)
The Lord of Desire, the destroyer of deceit (or strength), the letter *cha*, and indeed desire itself; the destroyer of birth, the unconquered, and the eternal letter *ja*. || 25-14 ||
The letter *jha* is known as *jhaṣa*; he is a singer of the Sāmans and a reciter of the Sāman hymns.
The letter *ña* is the Lord called Uttama, the upholder of the principles (*tattva*).
The letter *ṭa* is Candra, the delight that nourishes the universe; the letter *ṭha* is Dhārādharas, and Nemi is said to be Kaustubha. (25–16)
Daṇḍadhāra, Ḍakāra, Mausala, Akhaṇḍavikrama, Ḍhakāra, Viśvarūpa, Vṛṣakarmā, and Pratardana. (25–17)
The letter *ṇa* is proclaimed as the Teacher who bestows fearlessness, Vaikuṇṭha;
the letter *ta* is remembered as Tālalakṣman, Vairāja, and Sragdhara. (25.18)
Dhanvī and Bhuvanapāla are the letter *tha*, the obstructer of all; Dattāvakāśa and Damana are known as the letter *da*, the bestower of peace. (25.19)
The letter *dha* is proclaimed as the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the Sustainer, and Mādhava;
the letter *na* is declared to be Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and the Path. (25–20)
The letter *pa* is Padmanābha, the Purifier with a western face;
the letter *pha* is Phullanayana, the wielder of the plow, known as Śveta.
The letter *ba* is Vāmana, short, and he is said to have complete limbs;
the letter *bha* is known as Bhallātaka, which certainly bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*). (25–22)
The letter *ma* is proclaimed as the crusher, time, and the primary principle;
the letter *ya* is the fourfold course of existence, and it is called the subtle conch. (25.23)
The letter *ra* is the support of all worlds without exception, the fire that consumes time;
the letter *la* is known as Vibudha, the Lord of the Earth, the Sovereign of Puruṣa. (25.24)
The syllable *va* is known as Varāha, the support of nectar; the syllable *va* is remembered as Varuṇa; the syllable *śa* is proclaimed as Śaṅkara, the peaceful Puṇḍarīka.
Nṛsiṃha is the form of fire; likewise, the letter Ṣa is the Sun.
The letter Sa is proclaimed to be nectar, satisfaction, and the Moon. (25–26)
The letter *ha* is the sun and is proclaimed to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
The letter *kṣa* is Ananteśa, the end of the consonant classes, and likewise Garuḍa. (25–27)
These designations for all the phonemes have been proclaimed by me;
indeed, they should be described again according to the forward and reverse order of the phonemes.
O Śakra, whatever designation or number is common [to all], O Mahāmati, all these phonemes are portions of consciousness, possessing radiant forms. (25–29)
They are the cause of all mantras, augmented by the power of Lakṣmī;
these phonemes (varṇas), honored with their respective names, are praised, worshipped, and meditated upon with devotion. (25–30)
They bestow supreme prosperity and cultivate higher knowledge;
furthermore, they enter into a state of mutual interdependence within the arising of the mantra.
In this world of moving and unmoving beings, there is nothing that has not been permeated by these;
for although those supreme, divine forms of the mantras are eternal. (25–32)
Nevertheless, through such meditations on these syllables, mantras become fully empowered according to the teachings of the scriptures. (25–33)
In this way, O Mahāmati, objects of perception indeed become the basis for cognitions;
even though space is partless, a part is conceptually constructed by the cognition. (25.34)
For the sake of ease, a portion of the letters within the mantra is thus meditated upon;
having indeed performed the pervasive absorption (vyāpti) of the letters into the states of being, the worship of the letters is threefold.
One should extract the mantras from the lotus on the ground, or likewise from the body of the Goddess;
having taken up the Supreme Self, one should join it with the fire of time. (25–36)
One should employ this Māyā, endowed with the sovereignty of the three worlds, in this [mantra].
This is that supreme Vaiṣṇavī Śakti, the bestower of all desires. (25.37)
Existence is full, consisting of consciousness and bliss; it is my uninterrupted form.
This is that supreme consummation which is eternal for those who know Brahman. || 25-38 ||
Having reached this firm conclusion, those who know reality enter into the Brahman that consists of Me;
this very [truth] is contemplated in every scripture by the foremost among the knowers of reality. (25.39)
This other [aspect] is woven upon her; she is indeed the meaning of the word "world.
By means of her alone, I, the eternal one, am always enumerated by the Sāṃkhyas.

Note: 28. The meaning is that [the numbers are arranged] in ascending order for the name and in descending order for the number; it is well known that the movement of digits is from left to right. 36.

He extracts the *tārikā* mantra—beginning with "the Supreme Self" (*paramātmānaṃ*). The Supreme Self is the letter *ha*. The fire of time (*kālavahni*) is the letter *ra*. *Māyā* is the letter *ī*. The bestower of sovereignty over the three worlds is the *anusvāra*. Through the conjunction of these, *hrīṃ* is the *tārikā* mantra.
Root-text (p. 87):
By this very [power], I am concentrated by those established in concentration through that concentration;
by this very [power], I am designated by the Śaivas as the final of the thirty-six [principles]. (25.41)

In the same way, I am the Great Queen; by this very [power], I am the supreme Trayī (the Threefold Veda) within the collection of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and within the solar mandala that is to be meditated upon.
The experts in Lokāyata philosophy determine that a young woman, endowed with beauty and lovely in all her limbs, is the [ultimate goal]. (25.43)
By those who know the doctrine of momentary destruction, the intellect is considered to be without an object;
and by the Ārhatas, I am always proclaimed by this very name, Yakṣī.
She is the supreme savior-power (tārikā-śakti), the savior (tāriṇī) whose form is that of the Savior (Tārikā);
she is Lakṣmī, Padmā, Mahālakṣmī, Tārā, Gaurī, and Nirañjanā.
Hṛllekhā, who resides in the Supreme Self, is the power Bhuvaneśvarī;
she is the power of consciousness (cicchakti), whose nature is peace (śānti), the resonant one (ghoṣaṇī), and born from resonance (ghoṣa). || 25-46 ||
"Kāmadhenu, Mahādhenū, Jagadyoni, Vibhāvarī—such are the names [of the Goddess] proclaimed by the learned in scripture after scripture. (25.47)
The etymologies of *tārikā* have been explained by scholars in each Veda;
one should know that *anutārikā* is another form of this very [goddess]. (25.48)
One should establish Śānta in the place of the former, the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
The rest is the same; for this is my other body that leads others across.
And in her, who is like a *tārikā*, a great majesty is to be recognized;
these two supreme, divine powers, O Purandara, are my own bodies. (25.50)
Whatever is to be accomplished or achieved by her must be done otherwise;
for these two proceed in a sequence of prior and posterior through their mutual desire.
And for the practitioners who are correctly accomplishing their desired goal. || 25-51 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Tārā and Anutārā," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.

Note: 49. Śāntaḥ śakāraḥ (The letter śa is peaceful). "The rest is the same" means it is the same as the *tārikā*. The meaning is that *rīṃ* should be joined [to it]. *Śrīṃ* is the *anutārikā* mantra.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter.
The twenty-sixth chapter. Śakra said:
O Supreme Brahman, O Supreme Abode, O You who dwell in the lotus and wear a garland of lotuses!
Salutations to you, O lotus-born one, O lotus-like one, O housewife of Govinda!
"O Goddess, these two eternal bodies of yours have been described. Is there some distinction between these two in terms of their subtle form? [26-2]
Śrī said:

In the beginning, there was one supreme reality consisting of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, in whom the six divine attributes were perfectly quiescent, and who was a dense mass of pure and autonomous consciousness. (26.3)
I am His supreme power, following Him in all states; I am that supreme, divine Goddess, known by the names of the gross, the subtle, and the transcendent.
O Purandara, these two powers of mine, Tārikā and Anutārikā, both of them fulfill all desires.
Both these divine doctrines are considered supreme and ultimate;
both are regarded as the final resting places, and both are beloved by Viṣṇu. (26.6)
Having reflected upon both of these, they then go to the supreme goal;
now listen as I declare to you that which is the supreme, subtle reality.
From that comes the Supreme Brahman, from that the Peaceful, and from that the Sound (nāda); such is the sequence.
Pervading everywhere, I am she who exists in the form of both closing and opening the eyes.
The first is that supreme Brahman, subtle and possessing latent power;
having established himself there, the Tāra extends his far-reaching course.
This unfolding of the Lord Brahmā, the Supreme Self, which consists of the states of "being" (bhava) and "becoming" (bhāva), is that in which Tārikā is established. (26.10)
The descent of Brahmā, which is peaceful in form and characterized by the desire to create, rests upon that [power] called Śāntā, which abounds in the state of being (bhāva). || 26.11 ||
But the second is the descent known as Śakti, which is a powerful state;
there, O Vāsava, the seed-syllables beginning with Vāgbhava reside.
Thus has this subtle distinction between these two been explained to you;
now listen as I declare the seed-syllables beginning with Vāgbhava.
One should extract the syllable *ai* (aiśvarya), which is endowed with the sovereignty over the three worlds;
this seed-syllable, known as *vāgbhava*, is declared to be the source of the universe. (26.14)
This is that very Kuṇḍalinī power, within which the universe is coiled;
understand how it exists in the form of the power of sound (śabdaśakti). || 26-15 ||
This Māyā is the supreme power, the stainless source of the universe;
for she is the glory of the Immeasurable, the wife of the Householder. (26.16)
One should first join the vowel *i* to this [letter] with a subtle eye;
in this way, whatever is desired, whatever substance, and whatever [is required], that is established therein. (26–17)

Note: 14. He states the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable with the words beginning "trailokya" and so forth. *Aiśvarya* is the syllable *ai*. When this is joined with the *anusvāra*, the seed-mantra *aiṃ* is formed. Its nature as the womb of the universe will be explained immediately hereafter. 15. The intended etymological derivation (*yogavyutpatti*) of the word *kuṇḍalinī* is that "in her the universe is coiled" (*kuṇḍalitam*).

16–18. He explains that the vowel *ai* consists of a combination of four phonemes: "ī is Māyā," etc. The sense is that by joining the phoneme *i*, called *Iṣṭā*, which precedes this [Māyā]; then the phoneme *ā*, called *Ānanda*, which precedes that; and then the phoneme *a*, called *Aprameya*, which precedes that—when the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) is performed, the form *ai* arises.
