Root Text: One should first contemplate the Ānanda of this [syllable] with the subtle eye.
Then, one should first apply the immeasurable [object] with the subtle eye [or: with subtle vision]. (26.18)
This power, the womb of the universe, radiant with the sovereignty over the three worlds, arises from the Supreme Self, which is immeasurable, without beginning or end, and all-pervading. (26.19)
Gopanī is the power of all beings, replete with bliss;
she is endowed with the forms of will, knowledge, and action, which arise from the syllable *I*.

"The Goddess who bestows sovereignty over the three worlds, the consort of Viṣṇu, the mother of the universe"—thus one should meditate upon the lotus-born [Goddess] as the seed of the womb of the world. (26–21)
In the world, *rati* is designated as play (*krīḍā*), and for me, play is action (*kriyā*). Fuel, illumination, knowledge, and desire are indicated by the letter *i*. (26–22)
The three worlds are indeed the *triloka*; these are the living beings (*jīva*) who exist in a threefold manner. By bestowing sovereignty upon them, she is called *Trailokyaiśvaryadāmbikā*. (26–23)
Having expanded the worlds through the path of the universe by means of the immeasurable and so forth,
[he dissolves them] once again into that very Supreme Self, the Lord of Space.
Thus, my arising and setting are established as being beyond [the world].
Such is this Great Vidyā, the womb of the universe and the progenitor of speech. (26.25)
The fifth is Kāmasū, also known by the name Kāmabījā;
she is Prādyumnī, the supreme Śakti—learn from me her form. (26–26)
That which is declared to be the western face among the principles of the qualities (guṇatattva) is the Madhyama;
it is characterized by the coloring of both sattva and tamas through slight experience (bhoga).
That supreme primordial nature (prakṛti), known as Kā, ordaining the arrangement of the world,
prepares itself for creation through its union with the Lord of Puruṣa.
Māyā, who manifests the three forms known as the Unmanifest, Puruṣa, and Īśa— that Goddess Śrī, moreover, is established in Vyomeśa.
Thus have the form and power of that seed of desire been shown;
now listen as I declare the sixth *vidyā*, that of Sarasvatī. (26–30)
For I am the support of wisdom, O Śakra, the birthplace of supreme knowledge;
as such, I am the mother of wisdom, endowed with the arising of Viṣṇu.
One should join Ānanda before her with a subtle vision;
first, one should meditate upon the Immeasurable with a subtle vision. (26–32)
I am that immeasurable, arisen, auspicious one consisting of great bliss;
I am the foundation of wisdom, established once more within the Mistress of Space.

Commentary on verses 22–24: He explains the meaning of the long *ī* contained within the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*) as "pleasure" (*rati*). *Rati* is the letter *ī*; fuel and so forth are its meanings. He etymologizes "bestower of sovereignty over the three worlds" (*trailokyeśvaryadā*) as "the three worlds" (*trailokya*). "The living beings are threefold" means bound, liberated, and eternal. "In the Lord of Space" (*vyomeśe*) refers to the *bindu*. Verses 28–29: Taking the letter *ka*, which is *prakṛti*, one should join with it the Lord of Puruṣa, which is the letter *la*; Māyā, which is the letter *ī*; and the Lord of Space, which is the *bindu*. Thus, *klīṃ* is the seed-syllable of Kāma.

30–34. He states the seed-syllable of Sarasvatī with the verse beginning "the sixth," and so forth. The support of wisdom is the vowel *ū*. Prior to that is the arising, which is the vowel *u*. Prior to that is bliss, which is the vowel *ā*. Prior to that is the immeasurable, which is the vowel *a*. At the end is the Lord of Space (*vyomeśa*), the bindu. Again, there is the visarga. Through the conjunction of these, *auḥ* arises. He explains the meaning of the individual components with the verse beginning "arisen from the immeasurable," and so forth. (p. 90) Root-text: She has come to the Supreme Lord for the sake of union with the emission once again.
The sixth science has been extracted by you both in its words and in its meaning.
This triad of seed-syllables is declared to be the Vidyā known as Tripurā;
for whether through inversion or in direct order, it bestows identity with the Self (or even the attainment of the Self). || 26–35 ||
This Vidyā is declared to be the fulfiller of desires when accomplished through recitation, fire-oblations, and other rites.
Through the combination of consonants and vowels—[namely, the consonants followed by the vowels and so forth]—they know that it has many divisions [or, according to C: many parts]. (26–36)
Having both analyzed and synthesized the causes of the four aims of human life,
this seventh Vidyā is Mahālakṣmī, the accomplisher of all things.
Taking up the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti), one should join it there with the sun;
having joined it through churning, one should then unite it with the fire of time (kālavahni).
One should adorn the *piṇḍa* with *māyā* and, at the end, bring in the pervasive one (*vyāpin*).
O Purandara, this seed-syllable of Mahālakṣmī has been explained to you. (26–39)
For, by my own splendor, I draw forth the state of manifestation,
having assumed the primary role as the one who manifests the three forms.

"Having emanated every state of existence, [the practitioner] is established in the Lord of Space (Vyomeśa). This is the seed-syllable to be contemplated by the practitioner while reciting it. (26.41)
Thus, these rays are to be known as belonging to the Vidyā whose form is Tārikā;
[the rays] beginning with Anutārā are the Vidyās—this is the essence of Tārikā. (26.42)
One who worships this Tārikā vidyā according to the prescribed rule attains inexhaustible enjoyments in this world and the next. || 26-43 ||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Seven Vidyās," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra (or, according to A: in the Śrīpañcarātra).

Commentary (Ṭippaṇī) on verses 38–39: He describes the extraction of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Mahālakṣmī with the words beginning "parām" and so forth. Taking the *prakṛti*, which is the letter *ka*; by that, one should join the *bhāskara*, which is the letter *ṣa*; the *mardana*, which is the letter *ma*; the *kālavahni*, which is the letter *ra*; the *māyā*, which is the letter *ī*; and the *vyāpin*, which is the nasal dot (*bindu*). Thus, the mantra is *kṣmrīṃ*. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*: "The *grāsa* [letter], *nabhas* [letter], joined with *dāhavahni* and *sva* is the mantra of Kaulinī. In this context, *grāsa* is the letter *kṣa*; *nabhas* is the letter *ma*; *dāhavahni* is the letter *ra*; and *sva* is the letter *ī* along with the *bindu*.
43. The seven Vidyās are: Tāra, Tārikā, Anutārikā, Vāgbhava, Kāmabīja, Sārasvatībīja, and Mahālakṣmībīja.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter.
[Now begins] the twenty-seventh chapter.
Root-text:
Śakra said:
"Obeisance to you, O Lord of the World, beloved of the Lotus-eyed One."
O Sovereign of the entire world without exception, O Omniscient One, O You who exist in all things! || 27-1 ||
I have correctly heard this supreme truth of the sciences;
you should further explain to me the ritual procedure for the Tārikā.
Śrī said:
The primordial, singular, supreme Brahman, omniscient and consisting of existence and consciousness, is the divine splendor of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, manifested through His own power. (27-3)
I am that supreme, eternal power called Ahaṃtā; possessing its attributes, I am constant and stainless like the radiance of the sun. (27.4)
O son of Āditi, those five functions are always performed by me alone,
who am of the nature of His unfolding.
O Purandara, my supreme divine power is eternally conjoined with my own nature; she is Hṛllekhā, the supreme Vidyā, whose very form is mine. (27–6)
With a mind that is constantly attentive, full of faith, surrendered, and having approached me, receive from me this commentary upon it. (27.7)
They declare that Self which is supreme over all that moves and stands,
the cause of the origin, maintenance, and destruction [of the world], known by the name of the Sun.
Know that the first phoneme, the syllable *ha*, is the eternal, primordial Puruṣottama, who is the constant impeller known as Prāṇa. || 27-9 ||
That which is His first unfolding, which embraces the three worlds, is the support of all realms, blazing in form, and immeasurable by anything else. (27.10)
Know that the letter *repha* (ra) is the supreme, eternal form of light; it is indeed the full unfolding of consciousness, pervading every state of existence.
He sustains the five functions characterized by emission (sṛṣṭi) and so forth, while bearing the *bindu*,
and he is the form of wondrous knowledge within the continuous flow of the opening and closing of the eyes.
Bearing the forms of will, knowledge, and action, and transcending the expansion of sequence, this is the eternal state of the pair whose forms are *i* and *ī*. (27.13)
Thus, I am the pervasive arising whose nature is supreme expansion; consisting of will, knowledge, and action, I perform the fivefold activity of the All-pervasive Lord.
Consisting of various wonders, a mass of consciousness, and the very form of bliss, she is to be known as abiding in the Supreme Self, all-pervading, and the beloved of Viṣṇu. (27.15)
Having performed her entire duty, she who bestows sovereignty over the three worlds [merged] once again into that very god, the Lord of Space, the Supreme Self.
Note:
6. *Hṛllekhā* is the mantra *hrīṃ*, also known by the name *tārikā*, as specified in the twenty-fifth chapter. Its actual form will also be indicated immediately below (p. 92). Root Text:
Having taken up all the requisites, I abide as the partless one;
those who know reality declare that her forms here are fivefold. (27.17)
O Lord of Gods, listen as I describe those forms:
this form which is proclaimed as one is that which extends to the end of Vyomeśa. (27.18)
Some desire the Supreme Lord beyond Vyomeśa;
others, however, having set aside Vyomeśa, assign Pradhāna [as the highest]. (27.19)
Some wise ones desire the Bindu and the Nāda, and at the end of those, that which is like the Praṇava; others declare that at the very end there is only the one Pradhāna.
Others among the Vaidikas maintain that she is the creator at the end;
thus the wise know these five forms of Tārikā. (27–21)
O Lord of the Suras, such forms as these belong to Śāntasthā;
likewise, they exist at the end of Pradhāna, at the end of Visṛṣṭi, and similarly at the end of Vyomeśa.
Within these four forms— beginning with Vyomeśa and ending with the emission (visṛṣṭi)—
there is the supreme accomplishment pertaining to this world, and that which pertains to the hereafter is the highest.
At the end of the primary *bindu* and *nāda*, there is only the glory of liberation (*mokṣaśrī*);
having thus contemplated the supreme state of the *Tārikā*. (27–24)
The teacher should impart the knowledge whose nature is the Supreme Brahman to a disciple of virtuous conduct who seeks the welfare of his guru and brahman.
Having first performed the placement of the hands and limbs upon oneself,
and then having performed it upon the body of the disciple, one should thereafter impart the mantra.
One should first place the supreme mantra within the heart of the disciple with devotion;
then, one should again place that most excellent mantra within one's own heart.
A discerning disciple, having received the Vidyā from the Ācārya, should perform all of this preceded by initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration (abhiṣeka). (27–28)
Having given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) one's own self, one's own wealth, or even all of it, half, or a portion—whatever by which the preceptor is satisfied. || 27–29 ||
And while Vedic tradition and worldly custom are firmly established,
one should remain vigilant toward good conduct, toward teachers, elders, and Brahmins.
Constantly practicing non-malice toward the fourfold collection of living beings, always endowed with his own virtues, he is a follower of the characteristics of the Dharma. || 27-31 ||
Refined by pure purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), he performed the rituals for the gods, the ancestors, and guests;
he studied the divine scriptures as well as the Vedic *Nigamas*.
With a mind free from greed, moving through the various philosophical systems and taking from here and there only as much knowledge as is necessary for his purpose. (27.33)

Without finding fault with the scriptures, proceeding in accordance with the means of valid cognition, and performing his daily rites according to rule, he realized the meaning of the scriptures through the sequential performance of actions. (27–34)
Day and night, beginning with the day and ending with the night, he should constantly make them fruitful by performing the sequences of actions as they are enjoined. (27–35)
Always delighting in the five times (pañcakāla), devoted to the five sacrifices (pañcayajña), he was adorned with self-restraint and charity, as well as truthfulness and non-violence. || 27-36 ||
Having diligently accomplished this vidyā according to the prescribed sequence, one should remain constantly endowed with a serene mind, intent upon both one's own welfare and the welfare of others.
Desiring only supreme prosperity, one should avoid misfortune;
one should purify all beings through thought, sight, and speech. (27.38)
Note:
18. "Up to Vyomeśa" means up to the Bindu (the nasal dot). 19. The Supreme Lord is the Visarga; the primary [syllable] is the letter Ma.
21. Visarga is the creator of emanation.
22. He describes the gradation of the fruits of these mantras with the words "at the end of Pradhāna," etc. (p. 93). Root-text:
Cultivating the four goddesses who clarify the mind—loving-kindness and the others—one who seeks peace should be devoted to the sacrifice of recitation. || 27-39 ||
Remaining vigilant and established in his own duty, even if negligence occurs through fate,
he should properly perform the penance appropriate for each specific instance.
Through deed, mind, and speech, I have constantly sought refuge in Janārdana, the God of gods, and in me, who am devoted to his dharma.
Having beheld the Supreme Person and the Woman, and remembering me,
one should constantly honor a married couple and never cause the bond of matrimony to fail.
Whether residing in sound or manifesting as meaning, know that the various forms of masculinity and femininity are of that same nature; remember Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. (27.43)
Having seen me—excellent, endowed with virtues, and radiant with beauty and youth—with a mind free from desire, he thought only of me. (27.44)
He was always patient toward women, never speaking anything unpleasant, avoiding transgression, and not even considering what had already occurred. || 27-45 ||
Purifying the transgression being committed by women with purificatory rites—even toward a woman who is humpbacked, deformed, or in any state whatsoever—[he should act]. (27.46)
Moving about without censuring women, acting agreeably to them in accordance with the scriptures— a man of such conduct and virtuous behavior is freed from all taint.
My devotee, who acts for my pleasure, who worships me, and who is intent upon me,
attains the supreme abode— that highest step of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O Śakra, the supreme state of Tārikā has been described to you; as have those of other vidyās as well. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Illumination of Right Conduct," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Note:
44. Regarding "by one who is not greedy": the meaning is "by one who is free from excessive attachment. 45. "Transgression" means negligence.
46. Regarding the word *pāvanaiḥ*: it means by means of purificatory rites (*śuddhikarmabhiḥ*). *Vyatikrama* means negligence (*pramāda*).
49. Regarding the word *tārikāyāḥ*: it means that which has the alternative name *hṛllekhā*. Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter.
The twenty-eighth chapter.
Śakra said:
"Salutations to you, O abode of Kamalā; salutations to you, who dwell within the three Vedas."
By your grace, the mantra has been heard according to the rules through meditative concentration.
You should now explain the entire path of practice, the true nature of reality as it exists, and the daily conduct for day and night.
Śrī said:
"Nārāyaṇa alone is glorious, beginningless, lotus-eyed, and a vast ocean of knowledge, sovereignty, great power, valor, and splendor. (28.3)
He is the self of all beings, the Haṃsa, Nārāyaṇa, the Subduer [Hari]. I am his singular power, possessing the same attributes as he.
I, repeatedly bringing about states of being such as creation and the rest,
when propitiated, deliver everyone from the ocean of worldly existence.
Satisfied by righteousness, I bestow various enjoyments; my body, beginning with sentient beings, is established in the supreme state of the True Dharma. (28.6)
This dharma consists of conduct; conduct is its defining characteristic.
I shall proclaim that conduct which is observed by the virtuous. (28.7)
Having abandoned the sleep born of yoga and having arisen during the latter part of the night,
one should take refuge in Hari, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Lord of Śrī, who is the protector.
O Lord of the Gods, the nature of surrender has already been described to you;
listen further as I shall explain how it may become firm within you.
Having sipped water and become purified, and having remembered the weapon-mantra which has the form of fire, he enters it; then, having emerged, he becomes sanctified by the splendor of that weapon.
One should employ that surrender (prapatti), endowed with its five constituent limbs:
hostility having been abandoned and favor having been resorted to; || 28-11 ||
By me, toward all beings, according to my ability and according to my understanding—as one who is lazy, of little power, and lacking full knowledge—[this has been done] exactly as it is. (28.12)
Those means being employed would not at all be my deliverers;
therefore, I am miserable, wretched, untainted, and destitute of anything. (28.13)
Hṛṣīkeśa, together with Lakṣmī, who is the embodiment of compassion, is celebrated as the protector of all beings in all the Siddhāntas and in the Vedānta as well. (28.14)
Whatever I possess that is difficult to relinquish— my sons, wife, ritual acts, and so forth—
all of it is completely entrusted by me at your feet, O Lord of Śrī.

Note: 6. Regarding "various" (*vividhān*): the meaning is that she bestows not only those things that grant liberation (*apavarga*), but also incidental enjoyments pertaining to this world and the next. The term *saddharmapareṣu saṃsthānaṃ yasyāḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

8. Regarding "consisting of yoga" (*yogamayīm*): among the religious duties such as *abhigamana* and so forth, the fifth duty called "yoga" is to be practiced starting from the night of the previous day until the *brāhma-muhūrta* of the following day.

14. "Great trust" (*mahāviśvāsa*) is intended here; [it applies] to all established doctrines (*sarvasiddhānta*), to all divine scriptures (*divyaśāstra*), and to the Vedānta Upaniṣads. 15. By the words "whatever belongs to me," etc., he speaks of the entrusting of both self and what belongs to the self (*ātmātmīyanikṣepa*). "By the self" means "together with the self.
(p. 95) Root-text:
"O Lord of Gods, O Protector, O Consort of Lakṣmī, be my refuge! For one who has thus sought refuge even once, no other duty is required. (28.16)
For a person who has abandoned both the higher and lower means and is abiding in the middle, another means is sought due to the weakness of his intellect. (28.17)
Henceforth, learn from me as I describe the conduct of the virtuous:
one should rise with the aspiration for the arising of happiness for all living beings. (18)
May all beings abide on the pure path of goodness;
may they ever worship the Lord of Śrī and enter the supreme state. (28.19)
Having thus properly offered blessings for the welfare of all beings with both mind and speech,
he, being learned, performed the purification of his body according to the prescriptions of the Dharmaśāstras.
Having performed purification according to the rules, he should chew the tooth-stick;
then, having sipped water according to the prescribed rite with purifiers enjoined by the scriptures. || 28.21 ||
Having performed the ritual ablution, one should worship the twilight (saṃdhyā), the purifier of the three worlds;
she is my own threefold power, manifesting in the forms of the sun, the moon, and fire. (28.22)
For the purification of all beings, the Goddess Sandhyā proceeds;
having approached the Sun, who dwells within as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
One should properly perform the fire-ritual and then carry out the act of taking up [the materials];
however, if one possesses wealth, a wise person should not perform the taking up. || 28.24 ||
There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, the performance of work, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous. (28.25)
Having performed the threefold bath according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures,
and having then performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should carry out the subsequent sacrifice.
One should worship me, Viṣṇu, or both of us, according to the scriptures, with enjoyments produced by oneself, increased, obtained, or likewise acquired from disciples and others. (28.27)
In the afternoon, the wise practitioner should properly perform the private recitation (svādhyāya) according to the eightfold ritual procedure, concluding with the secondary sacrifice (anuyāga).
One should study the divine scriptures and the Vedic collections;
one should thoroughly practice all the established doctrines for the sake of self-realization.
Note:
16. He states the prayer for protection with the words beginning "śaraṇam" (refuge).

17. For one who abides in the middle [path], there is no other duty to be performed; this connects with what was stated previously. Regarding the phrase "due to weakness of intellect" (*buddhidaurbalyāt*): the sense is that engaging in difficult action without considering one's own capacity is indeed prompted by a deficiency of intellect. Here, the "other means" refers to *bhaktiyoga*. One should not think that this constitutes a censure of *bhaktiyoga*, nor that *bhaktiyoga* is inherently contradictory to the nature of one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). No discerning person would say that the statement, "A man’s desire to grasp the orb of the moon arises from weakness of intellect," censures the lunar orb itself. Furthermore, it would contradict the teaching that devotion is an alternative means, as seen in the words, "O high-minded one, either through supreme devotion or through surrender" (*bhaktyā paramayā vāpi prapattyā vā mahāmate*). If it is argued that for an incapable seeker of liberation, it is contradictory to their nature, there is no disagreement on this point.

23. *Vivasvantam* means "possessing distinguished radiance"; this is an epithet of Puruṣottama. *Antaḥstham* means "situated within," referring to Him who dwells inside the solar orb. The intended meditation (*dhyāna*) here is as described in such passages as: "Situated in the center of the solar orb, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns. 24. *Upādāna* refers to the acquisition of materials suitable for the worship of the Blessed One. For one who is destitute, this consists of accepting unasked-for rice and other provisions offered by excellent devotees who are devoted to the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) and the five daily observances (*pañcakāla*). For one who is wealthy, however, it consists of the gathering of fruits, flowers, *tulasī*, and other such items required for that purpose.

28. The eightfold sacrifice (*aṣṭāṅgayajana*) is as follows, according to the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*: the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), the sacrifice of enjoyment (*bhogayāga*), the sacrifice of honey and so forth (*madhvādiyāga*), the sacrifice of food (*annayāga*), the formal transmission (*saṃpradāna*), the satiation of the fire (*vahnisaṃtarpaṇa*), the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyāga*), and the subsequent sacrifice (*anuyāga*) (22.75–80).

29. Regarding the phrase "the established doctrines" (*siddhāntān*): it means the various divisions of the established doctrines, such as the scriptures of the Mantra school and others. (p. 96) [Root Text]
With a mind free from greed and devoid of passion and hatred, one should not, either in thought or in speech, revile scriptures of any kind, whether high or low. (28–30)
One should take only so much as is necessary for one's own purpose; for all the scriptures expound everything solely for the welfare of all living beings. (28–31)
Having reached each respective state, they extend that which is beneficial—at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end of all the scriptures. (28–32)
The glorious Nārāyaṇa was proclaimed by that very ordinance;
and I too am Nārāyaṇa, omniscient and all-seeing. (28–33)
Knowing the causes and resembling a physician, I manifest myself in the forms of various gurus and others, and thus promulgate those various scriptures in their respective ways.
According to one's specific qualification, the authoritative means of knowledge are likewise [determined];
there is no scripture whatsoever that is to be rejected absolutely under any circumstances. (28–35)
In every situation, that which is beneficial is easily found, whether it be small or great;
therefore, one should not harbor malice, but should resort to whatever is necessary for one's purpose.
One should never enter there for the *samaya* nor undergo initiation (*dīkṣā*) at all;
thereafter, one should perform the evening twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) when the sun is half-set.
Having performed the duties pertaining to the sacred fire, he should then indeed practice yoga in a well-secluded, pure, thornless, and delightful place. (28–38)

On a seat strewn with soft coverings, topped with cloth, deerskin, and kusha grass, and purified both inside and out, one who has been cleansed by the restraints (yama) and other practices [should sit]. || 28-39 ||
Having assumed a posture— either the lotus (padma), the cross-legged (svastika),
or whichever one the intellect finds pleasing— one should remain there, pressing upon the pathways of the channels (nāḍīs).

Having conquered the village of the breath and subdued the senses through withdrawal (pratyāhāra), and having exerted himself in the meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās), he, being well-composed, should meditate upon me. (28.41)
[It is] incomparable, indescribable, non-conceptual, and stainless;
it is the fortune easily accessible everywhere, having attained the state of being the object of all cognition. || 28-42 ||

Or else, the yogi [should visualize] the supreme Padmā, who possesses form, who bestows boons and fearlessness, who resembles the interior of a lotus, who holds a lotus in her hand, and who is endowed with auspicious marks. (28.43)

Or else, [one should meditate upon] the Goddess, who consists of consciousness and bliss, seated on the lap of Nārāyaṇa and having attained a state of aesthetic union (sāmarasya), and likewise the Lord of Śrī in that same manner. (28–44)
O Lord of the Gods, you should know that those paths of yoga are manifold;
among them, you should adhere to that single dharma in which you possess devotion and faith.
Having generated correct contemplation, one should rely upon meditative concentration;
that wherein the triad of the meditator, the meditation, and the object of meditation dissolves. (28.46)
At that time, I alone shone as the eternal, perfect I-consciousness,
once I had attained oneness within me, the great ocean of consciousness.
Nothing else shines forth; at that time, I alone am the supreme.
When weary from yoga, one should perform recitation (japa); when weary from that, one should practice yoga. (48)
I quickly become pleased with that wise person who is devoted to the practice of recitation and yoga;
having thus spent the first watch of the night in recitation, yoga, and so forth. (28–49)
Remaining established in yoga, he should sleep for two watches (six hours) after that;
then, having risen during the latter part of the night, he should practice what was previously described.
Thus, O slayer of Bala, that which is called the mixed duty has been declared to you;
one should pass the five times without flaw through the performance of the rites for the Blessed One.
Commentary:

33. Intending to show that all scriptures have the welfare of living beings as their goal by means of revealing the supreme reality (*paratattva*) and teaching its propitiation, the author says "the illustrious one" (*śrīmān*).
46. The highest limit of yoga is stated by the words beginning with "meditated upon" (*dhyāta*). "Wherein" (*yatra*) means in that state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

47. When the state of oneness (*aikadhya*)—that is, a single nature (*ekabhāva*)—has been attained by the yogin, nothing else whatsoever manifests; rather, "I alone am the light," is the connection with what follows. 49.
He explains *yoganidrā* (the sleep of yoga) with the words "having thus brought [the mind]... 50.

What is called "yoga" is the contemplation of the multitude of attributes of the Supreme Self, preceded by the surrender of the individual self (*ātman*) into the Supreme Self. The meaning is that while performing that very [contemplation], one experiences sleep.

51. "Mixed" (*vyāmiśrā*) means worship of the Blessed One accompanied by a manifold collection of ritual acts. "Without gaps" (*acchidrān*) means free from those gaps (*chidra*) as described in the *Garuḍapurāṇa* (Pūrvakhaṇḍa 222–22): "That moment or even that instant during which Vāsudeva is not meditated upon is a loss, a great gap, a delusion, and a derangement.
(p. 97) The root-text states:
"The initiated one, who knows the five times (*pañcakāla*), is devoted to the mantra of Lakṣmī."
There is no difference whatsoever between these two at the point of culmination, O slayer of Bala.
Both of these are considered devoted; they enter into me at the dissolution of the body.
One who bears the discus and the lotus shall eternally be devoted to Lakṣmī.
He should be devoted to his own wife and should always remain a celibate student;
he should constantly practice my mantra, with his mind fixed on me and intent upon me alone. (28.54)
One should contemplate all sounds, whether high or low, as being of that same nature;
for one who knows the division between fire and moon, and understands the distinction between action and its manifestation.
He is the knower of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme according to reality;
he knows the tantras of the limbs and sub-limbs, and he is an expert in the rules for the various types of mudrās.

Skilled in internal sacrifice, external sacrifice, recitation, and fire-oblation; knowing the various types of preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa); and understanding the reality of the means for attaining supernatural powers (siddhi).
He is one who knows the formation of names and forms, who understands the methods for accomplishing them,
who knows the reality of the substratum of the body, and who is an expert in the principles of yoga.

A man of this kind—one who knows the meaning of the scriptures, is steadfast and discerning, non-violent, and established in self-restraint and charity—should worship me for the sake of prosperity. (28.59)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Right Conduct," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter.
Chapter twenty-nine: Śakra—
Salutations to the illustrious Śrīvatsabhāminī, the variegated wall for the manifestation of the six paths—both pure and impure—and the pacifier of the torments of worldly existence. (29.1)
O Lotus-born One, tell me truly the division of Agni and Soma, as well as the rules for the manifestation of ritual actions, for the sake of the *tārikā* of the Vidyā. (29-2)
Śrī said:
That which is the all-pervading Supreme Brahman, which is indeed the power Nārāyaṇī—through transformation, I become that very one in the form of the Praṇava. (29.3)
O delighter of the gods, listen to me regarding the division of Agni and Soma within the Tārikā, and the ritual procedure for the manifestation of the elements exactly as it is. (29.4)
The supreme unfolding of Viṣṇu, primordial and consisting of the six qualities, is I; I am that power of yours who was described previously as having gathered all necessary provisions.
Since I have created the entire universe, my form manifests in two ways as I strive for its protection: through the mouth of sovereign power and through the mouth of splendor. (29.6)
The sixfold policy itself is my form; it is considered by some to have its face as splendor.
The sixfold policy itself is my form, facing toward supreme sovereignty.
That form which has light as its face is called the power of action (kriyāśakti);
that very power is called fire because it burns away all afflictions.
The form manifest as sovereignty is called Bhūti and Lakṣmī;
that power, abounding in sovereignty, is my body consisting of the moon.
The power of fire, consisting of action, dries up all defects;
the other prosperity, which nourishes the world, is here called Soma.
These [forms] of mine are born from my manifestation (vyūha) and consist of will, knowledge, and action;
I am that Supreme Goddess, the Manifesting One (vyūhinī), whose body is the sixfold attributes (ṣāḍguṇya). || 29-11 ||

That power of mine known as Action (kriyā), which is radiant with the brilliance of the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), had three manifestations (vyūha): the powers of the Sun, the Moon, and Fire. || 29-12 ||
Among them, the first is supreme, divine, and radiant, known as the power (śakti) called Sūryā;
performing the tasks of the world, she revolves incessantly. (29–13)
O Lord of the Gods, know that this [power] called Sūryā has three forms: the internal (adhyātma), the celestial (adhidaiva), and likewise the elemental (ādhibhautika). 29.14.
Abiding within the self, known as Sūryā, she moves along the path of Piṅgalā;
through her light, the power of the Sun (Sūryaśakti) situated in the objective world proceeds. || 29-15 ||
That other power which is of a divine nature is situated in the solar orb;
those rays which are proclaimed to be situated in the solar orb [are it]. (29.16)
Know those blazing rays, O Lord of Gods, whose nature is heat, to be the *ṛc*s;
know those splendors situated within them to be the *sāman*s for me. (29.17)
Note:
6. "By means of the mouth" (mukhena) means primarily.

16. In order to state that the deity residing within the solar orb possesses the nature of the three Vedas, his nature as the *Ṛgveda* is first described in the second half of the verse, beginning with "sūrya... and so forth.

17. He states its nature as the *Yajus* in the verse beginning with "Antaḥsthā. By this, the Taittirīya Śruti—"The sun indeed is this [disc]; it shines as this orb; therein are those *Ṛks*; that is the orb of the *Ṛks*"—is further corroborated. And it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa (2.11.11): Root Text:
The supreme power (*parā śakti*) who resides within, having assumed a human form...
Know that to be the divine, delightful Person, consisting of the Yajurveda. || 29-18 ||
[He meditates on] the glorious Lord, who bears the conch and discus, whose four arms are full and noble, whose face is serene, who is seated upon a lotus, and whose eyes are like lotuses. (29.19)
O Lord of the Gods, the ten-hotṛ is said to be within the head of this Puruṣa,
and the four-hotṛ is his feet and hands.
O Lord of the Gods, hair, flesh, bone, marrow, and blood are the Pañcahotṛ;
the two breasts, the testicles, virility, and the Apāna are the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ. (29.21)
The seven vital breaths located in the head are declared to be his seven *hotṛ* priests;
his splendors are the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and his joints are remembered as the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*).
The channels (nāḍīs) are his wives of the gods; the heart and mind are those of the Hotṛ priests; consciousness is the Pauruṣa Sūkta, and power is said to be the Śrī Sūkta. || 29-23 ||
The syllable Oṃ, the Praṇava, the Tāra, and the eternal secret name;
the Rudra-śukra Yajus verses, as well as the Sāmans—these are his gross names.
A person who practices the divine Manu consisting of the Yajurveda is liberated even from the sins of incantations and malevolent spells. (29.25)
Thus the supreme power, consisting of the three Vedas, shines in the sky under the name of the Sun;
this supreme power is celebrated in its threefold form by the designation "Sūrya. (29–26)
The mother of the Vedas, named Sāvitrī, revolves;
she is supported by the three syllables of the *praṇava*, and possesses the three channels of *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*. (29.27)

With the wind of the first letter as her breath and the *śiras* mantra fashioned as her crest-jewel, she has the letters beginning with Earth and ending with Puruṣa as her form, consisting of light and bliss. (29–28)
Having arisen from Brahman, she is established again in Brahman;
she is the mother of the Vedas and the supreme mother of the phonemes.

Note: 20. For this Person situated within, the Daśahotṛ becomes the head. By the terms "Daśahotṛ" and so forth, the mantras bearing those respective names are intended. The mantra beginning with "cittiḥ sruc" (consciousness is the ladle) is the Daśahotṛ, found in the first section of the third book of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka. The mantra beginning with "pṛthivī hotā" (the earth is the Hotṛ), recited in the second section of that same work, is the Caturhotṛ. [In the compound] "pāda-pāṇī," the singular form is used as a collective.
21. The Pañcahotṛ [formula] is recited in the third Anuvāka, beginning with *agnir hotā*. The Ṣaḍḍhotṛ [formula] is recited in the fourth Anuvāka, beginning with *sūryaṃ te cakṣuḥ*.

22. The Saptahotṛ [formula] is recited in the fifth Anuvāka, beginning with *mahāhavir hotā*. The Dakṣiṇās are recited in the tenth Anuvāka, beginning with *devasya tvā*. The Saṃbhāras are recited in the eighth Anuvāka, beginning with *agnir yajurbhiḥ*.

23. The *devapatnyaḥ* (wives of the gods) are those recited in the ninth anuvāka, beginning with *senendrasya*. The *hotṛhṛdayam* (the heart of the Hotṛ priest) is that recited in the eleventh anuvāka, beginning with *suvarṇaṃ dharmam*. The mantras of the *puruṣasūkta* and *śrīsūkta* are well known. 24. The *rudriyāḥ* are those recited beginning with *namaste rudra manyave*. Likewise, the *śukriyāḥ* are also specific types of mantras. In this regard, the fifty-eighth and fifty-ninth chapters of the *ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā* should be consulted.

25. "Consisting of the Yajus" refers to the Sāvitrī. It follows after the Anuvyāhṛtis and the Vyāhṛtis. The phrase "practicing this" is to be construed with what precedes. 26. Regarding "the Trayī": the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) should be kept in mind, which states, "The Sun moves along, not devoid of the three Vedas.

28. Regarding "beginning with that": the meaning is the phonemes beginning with *tat*. "The Head" refers to the Gāyatrī-Śiras mantra. Regarding "earth and so forth": the phonemes beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*.
(100) Through the root-mantra and by way of both direct and reverse order, she is declared to be the lunar and the fiery [nature].
She is this divine Sāvitrī, whose body is the sun, the digit consisting of my own self. (29–30)
That which is called Gāyatrī protects the one who sings it from great fear;
having taken up the life-force produced by cattle, rivers, and living beings.
Furthermore, she releases [the water] held for nine months by her rays into the clouds.
Thus has been described the power consisting of the sun; now hear about the supreme power consisting of fire. (29–32)
O Śakra, this power of mine consisting of fire is also threefold:
one has celestial substances as its fuel, while another has the earth as its fuel upon the ground.
Likewise, within the stomach, the power consisting of fire is threefold after it has consumed the fuel;
this very power, comprising all the gods, is called the mouth of the gods.

Praised by those established in the three aims of life (trivarga), this very [verse] is called Triṣṭubh by the wise; it carries men who are devoted to its own recitation across all difficulties. (29–35)
The other [power] consists of Soma, and that too is said to be threefold:
one exists in the sky as the solar disc, while another exists in the form of medicinal herbs.
Moving within living beings as the singular essence of immortality, she who is praised by the *anuṣṭubh* meters is declared to be this very *Anuṣṭubh*. (29–37)
That knowledge which destroys death is called Mṛtyuñjayā;
O Purandara, it consists of the forms of the Sun, the Moon, and Fire. (29–38)
Manifested from the sun as the preparer of the oblation (haviskṛt), she consists of the oblation and takes the form of Soma;
likewise, under the name of Agni, she consumes the oblation through her nature as the fire and the mouth of the Brahmin.
By means of these three, the entire system of the world functions day and night;
thus, that Vyūhinī, whose nature is action, is endowed with a triple array.
My power, supremely profound, has emerged from the mouth of my splendor;
it blazes like the combined radiance of ten million, a hundred thousand, and a billion suns, moons, and fires.
The discus named Sudarśana becomes the shatterer of enemies;
it is the supreme, most blazing weapon, known as the Āgneya, belonging to Viṣṇu. || 29-42 ||
That supreme form, which is the very nature of the self, is the vitalizing force of the vital breaths and so forth;
from it all weapons and all powers arise. (29.43)
The instrument (karaṇa) is that which is most effective in Hari’s performance of the fivefold act;
there is no such act of the high-souled Viṣṇu that could exist without it.
In the creation [of the world], she proceeds as the very nature of volition and so forth;
likewise, in protection and in withdrawal, she assumes a body consisting of the discus.
Born from my own portion, the Vaiṣṇavī power of action (kriyāśakti) is indeed to be known as Parāgneyī;
she stands pervading the entire universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, in six ways.
In that regard, O Vāsava, first hear about the wheel consisting of phonemes:
the pair of Tārikā and Tāraka situated on the axle, belonging to the Supreme Lord.
At the navel is the form of the sun, moon, and fire, resting upon the syllable *svāra*, consisting of sixteen spokes (*dviraṣṭaka*).
The letters from *ka* to *bha* occupy the eighteen spokes (*triraṣṭāra*), while those from *ma* to *ha* reside on the rim (*nemigam*).
The rim (pradhi) consists of the fire at the end; it is the final phoneme, resembling a mass.
This divine wheel of phonemes revolves by way of the path of phonemes. (29–49)
Note: 31. Regarding "having taken": here the Vedic scripture should be recalled, which states, "By those [rays] with which the sun shines, Parjanya rains.
33. It should be understood that lightning is celestial and has water as its fuel; terrestrial fire has wood and the like as its fuel; and that which resides in the stomach is digestive (kauṣṭhī).

36. Even the moon-natured [energy] is threefold: in the sky as the nature of the disc (bimba), on the earth as the nature of medicinal herbs (oṣadhi), and within the bodies of living beings as the nature of the *iḍā* [channel].
46. "Sixfold" means by way of the wheels (cakras) known as *kalā*, *tattva*, *varṇa*, *pada*, *mantra*, and *bhuvana*.
47. The *tārikā* is the *hrīṃ* mantra; the *tāraka* is the *praṇava* (Oṃ).
48. *Svāra* is a collection of vowels. "Twice eight" means sixteen. "Three times eight-spoked" refers to that which has the form of twenty-four spokes. (p.
101) O Śakra, this is the root *kalācakra*, whose axle is gnosis (*jñāna*) and whose hub is power (*śakti*).
By means of the three qualities beginning with power—namely, sovereignty, energy, and strength—the rim and so forth are formed.
The reality (tattva), however, is the axle of Vāsudeva; the hub is the radiant Saṃkarṣaṇa;
likewise, O Śakra, Pradyumna is the spokes, and Aniruddha is the form of the rim.

The wheel of the [mantra] syllables is established by means of the axle, the hub, and the rim, beginning with the fourth [syllable], and by means of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and clusters (*piṇḍa*) known as words (*pada*). || 29-52 ||
The unmanifest, whose eyes are Time, contains within its womb the cage of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest;
it is a sphere consisting of the transformations of the mind, the senses of hearing and so forth, and their respective objects. (29.53)
Bearing in her hands the final wheel, the world-system extending as far as the Lokāloka mountain, she has assumed a human form consisting of six wheels.
Sudarśana is the power of action (kriyā-śakti), belonging to Viṣṇu, situated in the center of the discus.
Listen now to its fourfold nature: as seed-syllable (bīja), as aggregate (piṇḍa), as word (pada), and as name (saṃjñā). (29–55)
Having first taken the *soma*, one should join it with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) at the end;
then, having taken the nectar (*amṛta*), one should join it with the fire of time (*kālapāvaka*).
One should place the fire within that [mandala], with the Māyā-bīja pervading it at the end;
this is the Saurdaśana seed-syllable, manifested from my power of action (kriyā-śakti).
This divine seed-syllable, consisting of seven phonemes, bestows great supernatural power (*maharddhi*);
it is itself the great *piṇḍa*, free from the pervasive influence of *māyā*. (29–58)
Having the appearance of ten thousand suns at the end of time, with the roar of a vajra-cloud, this great mass of five colors is difficult for even gods and dānavas to withstand. (29.59)
But by one who is pure, it should be remembered once—that which is difficult for those with uncontrolled senses to remember.
Having remembered it for the sake of peace, my seed-syllables beginning with the *tārikā* should be remembered. (29.60)
That syllable situated in the upper portion of the *piṇḍa*, known as Kālānala,
by it the lords of the Daityas and the worlds themselves are consumed at the end of the age.
The fire is kindled by the fire abiding within the second power;
the vital breath, filled with the radiance of nectar, animates that power. (29.62)
Thus, O bull among gods, the nature of the *piṇḍa* has been told to you;
the *piṇḍa* is fashioned by the five pervasive [syllables], fixed within at every interval. (29–63)
Beginning with the *dhruva* [syllable] and ending with the armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*), it attains the status of a name-mantra (*saṃjñāmantra*).
One should join the two pervaders (*vyāpaka*) at the end of the two clusters (*piṇḍa*) of Soma and Sūrya.
One should indeed bring forth a single pervader before the peak of Soma and Agni;
likewise, the two [pervaders] are traditionally taught for the first and last syllables of the final [group].
He is the armor, the vital breath, victory, and the sky; he is the crusher of wicked afflictions.
He who is Saṃkarṣaṇa is the dissolution at the end of the eon, pervading all things.
That *phaṭ*-sound, and at its end, joy which brings about pacification;
thus is the mantra known as both gentle and fiery, consisting of the drawing out of the *piṇḍa*. (29–67)

Note: 56–57. *Soma* is the letter *sa*; *prāṇa* is the letter *ha*; *amṛta* is the letter *sa*; *kālapāvaka* is the letter *rā*; *anala* is the letter *ra*; *māyā* and *vyāpin* are the letter *īṃ*. Thus, *sahasrāra īṃ* is the seed-mantra (*bījamantra*). 58. "Consisting of seven syllables" means it is composed of the seven syllables in the form of *soma*, *prāṇa*, *amṛta*, *kālapāvaka*, *anala*, *māyā*, and *vyāpin*. "Devoid of *māyā* and *vyāpin*" means it is without the letter *īṃ*. Thus, *sahasrāra* is the aggregate-mantra (*piṇḍamantra*).
60. "Smarye" means that which is to be remembered.
64. He clarifies what was previously stated with the words "the two pervaders.
66. "Varma" means armor. The "huṃ-mantra" is the space between the vital breath (prāṇa) and the victory (ujjaya).
67. *Vikarṣa* is the continuous thread (*anusyūti*). (p.

102) This powerful *Manu* of the Sudarśana [discus], possessing its own phonemes and limbs, is the means for attaining enjoyments belonging to the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms. (29-68)
O Purandara, this Manu is a wish-fulfilling tree for those who depend upon him;
he has arisen from Nārāyaṇa for the eternal welfare of the world.

O slayer of Vṛtra, the division between Agni and Soma has been described by you, as well as the distinction between action and its manifestation, and the differentiation of the power of action. (29.70)
And the power of the energy of action [is manifested] through the distinctions of seed-syllables (*bīja*), clusters (*piṇḍa*), and so forth.
Furthermore, O Śakra, hear of such vast supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) belonging to the energy of action.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Division of Fire and Moon," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.

Note: 68. Regarding "with their own syllables" (*svavarṇaiḥ*): the meaning is that one should perform the assignment of the six limbs, beginning with the heart, using those six syllables of the previously mentioned six-syllable mantra. He describes the majesty of the mantra with the words beginning "divya" (divine).
69. In the phrase "for the welfare of the world" (*jagaddhite*), the locative case is used in the sense of a cause; thus, it means "for the sake of the welfare of the world."
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter.
The thirtieth chapter: Śrī.
O Śakra, this power (śakti) consisting of action has been described to you by me. I have explained to you its pervasiveness as it is differentiated into the sun, the moon, and fire. (30.1)
I have also told you of Vyūhinī by the name of Bījapiṇḍā; O Śakra, learn from me her nature as a word-mantra.
The first *piṇḍa* is the conjunction of the *ajita*, *anala*, and *sarga* syllables;
the second *piṇḍa* is the union of the *kamala*, *anala*, and *sarga* syllables. (30.3)
The third *piṇḍa* is said to be the conjunction with Śvetā and the others who bestow delight;
the fourth *piṇḍa* is that which pervades the solar energies, and by means of that, it is situated in the center.
Then, the beloved of Agni [the syllable *hrūm*] offers three weapons to Kālacakra; preceded by *tāraka*, this wheel is the sovereign mantra of the state (*pada*). (30.5)
O Vāsava, indeed there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by this mantra;
one who applies their mind to it shall never suffer defeat.
O Vāsava, I shall further explain the entire power of that supreme Manu, Tṛyugārṇa, whom I previously described to you.
Meditating on the wheel of nameless form, radiant with the majesty of the six qualities, and reciting the mantra with its seed-syllable, one is liberated from bondage. (30.8)
The body of my power of action (kriyāśakti) is the Great Mantra (mahāmanu), consisting of six syllables; it is established at the end of the Atharvaveda and is augmented by the [Śrī]cakra. || 30.9 ||
One should meditate upon the supreme Sudarśana discus, composed of the six paths and full of splendor, radiant with its parts clearly distinguished as the spokes, the nave, and so forth.
One should contemplate the syllables of the mantra, beginning with *amṛta*, upon the parts of the wheel:
on the hub (*akṣa*), the nave (*nābhi*), the spokes (*ara*), the rim (*nemi*), the felly (*pradhita*), and the teeth (*danta*). (30.11)
In the Sudarśana [chariot], the rim is composed of the principles beginning with *prakṛti* and ending with the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*); *māyā*, procreation, and the three *guṇas* are the felly.
The mantras consist of a thousand spokes arranged at the end of the path;
the end of the spoke stands on the path of the cosmic array (vyūha), and there the nave consists of the kalās.
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) indeed extends as far as the senses; in its midst I am the Supreme Power (parāśakti).
Within me is the Supreme Brahman, which is devoid of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper.

Commentary: 3. Ajita is the letter *ja*; Anala is the letter *ra*; Sarga is the *visarga*. [Thus: *jraḥ*. Kamala is the letter *ka*; [thus: *kraḥ*. 4. Śveta is the letter *pha*; Āhlādī is the letter *ṭa*. [Thus: *phaṭ*. Sūrya is the letter *ha*; Ūrja is the letter *u*; Vyāpī is the *bindu*. [Thus: *huṃ*.

5. In the middle are three *phaṭ* mantras; then *svāhā*. *Oṃ jraḥ kraḥ phaṭ huṃ phaṭ 3 kālacakrāya svāhā*. 7. The six-syllable mantra consisting of the three ages (*triyuga*) is: *sahasrāra huṃ phaṭ*. 9. Regarding "Atharva": here, the statements from verses 21–24 in the twentieth chapter of the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā* are to be consulted.
11. *Amṛta* is the letter *sa*. By the phrase "beginning with *prakṛti*" and so forth, the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) is indicated.
13. He speaks of the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*) with the words "the mantras.
(p. 104) [This is] the root [text].
In the center, one should contemplate the Tāra; outside of that, one should remember the Tārikā;
outside of that, the Kriyā-bīja; and outside of that, the first syllable. (30.15)
Thus, the four seed-syllables should be known to be in the hollow of the sense-organs in sequence;
however, the sun and the others are in the navel, heart, and so forth, according to the direction previously stated. (30.16)
That which is of the nature of the short form possesses a thousandfold lineage,
differentiated by the pairs of the Sun, Time, and Fire, beginning with the immeasurable.
And by joining pairs of Amṛta and Anala, as many and of such a kind,
one should pierce the letters beginning with Ka by means of the vowels consisting of Agni and Soma.
Excluding the sun, moon, and wind, and thirty-one [others],
there are exactly one thousand minus eight syllables that exist directly.

Then, the eight seed-syllables beginning with *tāra* (oṃ) should be joined with the short vowels; they are situated in the directions starting from the northeast (īśa) and ending at the southeast (vahni) and northwest (vāyu). || 30–20 ||
Having offered the pair of threads and the *cārī*, one should divide the ground into four parts;
one should make fifty spokes for each level.
There should be a thousand spokes; upon them, one should place a thousand syllables from the east (prāk) to the moon (soma), and then indeed upon the diagonal threads.
One should place the four goddesses who abide in the path of mantra, possessing the qualities of fire, in sequence:
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā.
The mantra-deities stationed upon the lines from Agni to Īśāna fill the spokes;
that rim of the Sudarśana remains thus established.
O Vāsava, all weapons are situated within the hub of the wheel;
O Purandara, they are the initiators of all weapons that proceed from the front.
One should meditate on both sides equally upon those who turn back with their heads marked by weapons, with palms joined in reverence, yet still arrogant.
In the Nemi-kṣetra, Mahālakṣmī is situated in the eastern direction;
in the south is Mahāmāyā, and in the west is Sarasvatī. (30.27)
In the northern direction, she who is the destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura is to be known;
outside of that, all around, are the gods, the threefold forms beginning with Brahmā.
Beyond that are the incarnations joined with the powers beginning with Turyā;
then follows the twenty-fourfold [principles] starting from Prakṛti and ending with Viśeṣa. (30.29)
In the eastern sector, the assembly of deities of the principles (tattva) stands in their proper sequence;
in the middle [sector], the gods who are the instruments of worldly existence (bhava) are firmly established.
The worlds beginning with Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Suvar, situated separately in their final portions along with the various cosmic realms (bhuvanas), are firmly rooted within the interior of the Brahmāṇḍa.
All the mountains, such as Meru and others; likewise the rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and others;
the oceans, such as the Ocean of Milk and others; and the islands known by names such as Jambū and others. (30–32)

All the hosts of celestial beings dwelling in palaces, as well as the planets beginning with the Sun, the lunar mansions, the stars, the constellations, and likewise the bhūtas, pretas, and so forth. || 30–33 ||
O Purandara, those thirty-three crores of gods who have taken refuge in its rim are like bees [gathering] honey.
Note:
17. "Sūrya," etc., means by means of *hraṃ*, *hrāṃ*, and so forth.
18. "Amṛta," etc., means by means of *sraṃ*, *srāṃ*, and so forth.
19. "Sūrya," etc., means excluding the letters *ha*, *sa*, and *ya*. Regarding "reduced by eight": 31 × 16 × 2 = 992 syllables are to be known. 20.

When the eight seed-syllables (*bīja*) are added to the previously mentioned 992 syllables, there are one thousand syllables. However, in the *Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā*, the state of having one thousand syllables is described in another manner (23.82, 83).
21. *Cārī* is a horizontal movement; multiplied by five, it is fifty, [which amounts to] 250.

23. *Vartinyaḥ* means those who abide (*vartinīḥ*). This connects with the following term, "the mantra-deities. 29. *Turyādi* means the states known as waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turya*). *Avatārāḥ* refers to the emanations (*vyūhāḥ*).
34. *Tisraḥ* and so forth; the meaning is thirty-three. *Saraghāḥ* are honey-bees. *Sāragham* is honey.
O Lord of the Gods, there are twenty thousand [units] at the base, on both the front and the side.
The fires revolve, acting as both initiators and terminators. || 30-35 ||
There, the fires that set things in motion, possessing the brilliance of a thousand fires of cosmic destruction and filled with flickering, blazing flames, consume the Daityas and Dānavas. (30–36)
The steadfast ones, tranquil and profound, serene and of brilliant splendor,
turn me away from my desires and pacify those impulses that lead to worldly engagement.
At the end of the Sudarśana-mantra is that most terrible plough-weapon (lāṅgalāstra) born from Saṃkarṣaṇa, which effects the destruction of all things.
For one situated transversely at the edge of the rim, those arising from its eastern half are initiators,
while those arising from the portion above that are terminators.
These [two] are of the nature of Agni and Soma, acting as the impellers and the restrainers;
the lineage of missiles arises from that which arises from Agni and Soma. (30–40)
Listen to the two tens of thousands of forms of the fires of various natures,
by remembering which a person may cross over the terrible ocean of calamity.

This *piṇḍa*, the support of all worlds without exception, possessing the vital essence (*ūrjabindu*) of the four states of existence, is the savior; it is said to be the body of the fires from the beginning up to the station of Vāyu. (30–42)
The *piṇḍa* [mantra] of Nivartaka and the others—preceded by the *Tāra*, consisting of Amṛta, Ādhāra, Vahni, Ūrja, and Bindu—is declared to be their divine body. (30.43)
Having divided the rim (pradhi) tenfold according to the forms of time, person, the unmanifest, and the manifest, preceded by their respective forms and colors.

In the sequence beginning with the eastern quarter and so forth, by means of the eight seed-syllable leaders starting with *ka*, preceded by the vowels and ending with the final vowels, and multiplied by twelve (the sun and fire), [the directions are established]. || 30-45 ||

One should write the *pravartaka* (initiating) body ending with *namaḥ* joined with those [syllables] in groups of four; likewise, one should write the *nivartaka* (concluding) body with groups of four consisting of *amṛta* (the nectar-syllables) and *agni* (the fire-syllables).
One should recollect the seven terrible and seven peaceful flames of each individual fire,
beginning from the start with the seven pairs and so forth, sequentially interspersed with the vowels.
Born from the pair of the Sun and Fire, arisen from the pair of Nectar and Fire;
the end of the consonant classes, the Pradhāna, and likewise Vāmana, the bestower of success.
Śveta, Tattvadhāra, Jhaṣa, and Śāśvata; Chāndaspati, as well as Cakrin—these are the letters beginning with *ka* together with the nasal bindu. (30–49)
The four forms of Īśvara, situated at the center of the navel and within the thread, are established;
in the spokes all around are stationed the gods beginning with Keśava.

Those beginning with Padmanābha and ending with Dāmodara are to be meditated upon with their respective marks, such as the lotus and others; all of them are situated on the spokes and the rim of the wheel. (30–51)
All the gods were endowed with their respective powers;
in the eastern quarter was the goddess Kamalā, and in the south was the radiant Kīrti.
Jayā is in the western quarter, and likewise Māyā is in the northern quarter;
each is surrounded by a retinue of śaktis numbering in the tens of millions.
They constantly preside over the thousand-spoked Sudarśana, the wheel of time which is without beginning or end; its splendor is thus proclaimed.
Note: 38. The *lāṅgalāstra* has the mantra *phaṭ*.
41. The word division is *dve ayute*; the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) is archaic (*ārṣa*).

42. The syllable *repha* is the support of all worlds without exception; the syllable *ya* is the four states of existence; the syllable *ū* is vigor. 43. The syllable *va* is the support of nectar. 48. The pair of Sun and Fire is *hra*; the pair of Nectar and Fire is *sra*. The final letter of the consonant classes is *ha*; the primary [syllable] is *ma*; the bestower of success is *bha*; the dwarf is *ba*.

49. *Śveta* is the letter *pha*; *Tattvadhara* is the letter *ña*; *Jhaṣa* is the letter *jha*; *Śāśvata* is the letter *ja*; *Chandapati* is the letter *cha*; *Cakrī* is the letter *ca*; *Kāla* is the letter *ma*. 52. The *Śaktis*, such as Lakṣmī, Kīrti, and others, are mentioned in this very twentieth chapter (p.
It is fashioned with five distinct divisions, designated as the year, the seasons, the months, the half-months, and the days and nights, and bounded by the axle, the nave, the spokes, and the rim.

The five [elements] beginning with the male [principle], along with another five, are sustained by the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra), which possesses a thousand spokes and is adorned with a rim, spokes, and a hub. (30.56)
And the six paths—consisting of phonemes, principles (*tattva*), categories (*kalā*), and so forth—are maintained [or exist];
this body, which consists of all principles, is the Vaiṣṇava Puruṣottama. (30.57)
This supreme [body] is mounted upon a machine; it is held steady and made to revolve by the thousand-spoked wheel with its rim, which is situated at the bulb of the navel.
By this wheel, which consists of various mantras and is firmly established within him, the Rākṣasas, Daityas, and Dānavas are slain.
This thousand-spoked [wheel], when practiced incessantly by men, destroys enemies immediately upon being merely remembered. (30.60)
One should destroy in an instant all the defects consisting of afflictions, karma, and latent impressions—the fourfold set comprising the seed, the mass, the designation, and the form. (30.61)
This thousand-spoked wheel, devoid of beginning or end,
nourishes this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings by pervading it with the sun, the moon, and fire.
The first form is that of Agni; it is the divine power called Kriyā.
In the form of the thousand-spoked wheel, it creates, protects, and destroys.
O Lord of the Gods, this ritual procedure has indeed been declared by you through the arrays of the Sun, Moon, and Fire;
now listen further to it from me.
Thus has been described the array (vyūha) which takes the form of the sun, the moon, and fire;
now learn from me this very same array as the power of action (kriyāśakti).
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Power of Action," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Note: 55. *Vibhakti* means division (*vibhāga*).
56. Five times five is twenty-five. Beginning with the Puruṣa and ending with the Earth, these are the deities of the letters beginning with *ma* and ending with *ka*.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter. The thirty-first chapter:
Śrī.
That power of action, which was manifested as abiding in the splendor of the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya), assumes a human form by resorting to a fiery nature. || 31-1 ||
Interwoven with all missiles and weapons, rooted in the sun, moon, and fire, it is the great one named Sudarśana, adorned with various forms. || 31-2 ||
Situated in its center is the power of action (kriyāśakti), which has assumed a human form;
it exists through its own gentle and fiery nature according to the arrangement of the respective times.
The fourfold designator of that [reality] has been shown previously;
among these, the mantra consisting of names is by far the most powerful. (31.4)
O Śakra, listen as I explain this to you:
that power whose essence is Soma is the first unfolding (unmeṣa) of Hara.
I am the primordial power, Śrī; she is established in the first syllable.
She is nectar, the embodiment of satisfaction, the essence of the moon, and the sovereign of all. (31.6)
One should perform the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), with the digit of the moon situated at the beginning of creation;
the mantras beginning with the head-lotus are joined with the Supreme Lord. (31.7)
By means of this emission (sṛti), one should effect both satisfaction and complete perfection;
for this is the eternal power of life (jīvaśakti) conjoined with the creative force (sṛṣṭikṛt). || 31-8 ||
Endowed with the sovereignty of the three worlds, situated in the imperishable wind-dwelling,
she should be visualized in the form of a star upon the head of the enemy for the sake of achieving his destruction.
From this Śakti, who is embraced by the immeasurable and who delights in the nature of Agni and Soma, has arisen this radiant Puruṣasūkta.
Sages know that there are thousands of such hymns;
this very mantra, which is ever-nourished by me as I take pleasure in Agni.
There is nothing in the three worlds that cannot be accomplished by this [Goddess], who partakes in various effects and possesses the triad of powers inherent in each respective phoneme. (31.12)
Note:
1. The meaning is that it exists primarily as *tejas* (splendor) even within the context of the six political expedients (*ṣāḍguṇya*).

2. The density of all weapons and missiles (*śastrāstra*) in the *Sudarśana* is stated in the twentieth chapter of the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*. The statement regarding its being rooted in the Sun, Moon, and Fire is made with reference to the nature of the syllables [of the mantra] beginning with "sahasrāra."
3. With reference to the activity consisting of protecting devotees and disciplining the wicked, there is the statement regarding its nature as both gentle (saumya) and fiery (āgneya).
4. There is a fourfold division according to the forms of seed-syllables (bīja), clusters (piṇḍa), names (saṃjñā), and words (pada).

6. The first syllable is the letter *sa*. By the words beginning with "immortal" (*amṛta*), he states its nature as being composed of nectar and so forth; both satisfaction (*tṛpti*) and the moon (*soma*) also follow the letter *sa*.

10. "Of her" (*asyāḥ*) means of her who consists of the first syllable. The meaning is that from the letter *sa* the Puruṣa-sūkta emerged. Thus, the Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā states: "O Sage, from the first syllable of her the Puruṣa-sūkta arose; the one called Śrī-sūkta was produced from the second syllable" (18.33).
Root-text: She gives birth to all powers and subsequently authorizes them.
Furthermore, it is recorded in the Smṛti that "she withdraws these again. || 31-13 ||
Presiding over his own unfolding manifestation, that eternal Lord of Weapons, the sovereign of power, has arisen as the Supreme Self for the sake of the world. (31.14)
And the Sun, having attained the state of the enjoyer and sustaining life, is desired as the vital breath (prāṇa);
endowed with the sovereignty over the three worlds, he reveals the Self.
Yogins investigate that [Self] which resides in the center of the heart-lotus;
for one who meditates correctly, it is to be pierced by the force of the arrow of concentration. (31.16)
Because he leads the vital breaths (prāṇas) to their highest excellence, he is designated by the word "Prāṇa.
Enveloped by the lunar orb, he is all-pervasive and possesses immeasurable magnitude.
Meditated upon as situated at the root of the tongue, he restrains the activity of speech;
meditated upon as situated in the circle of *am*, he indeed flows with nectar.
When meditated upon, he renders even the worlds free from poison;
for it is well said that the Goddess of Fortune has emerged from this very one embraced by Rāma.
The sages know a thousand such hymns as these,
[to be recited] by one who experiences the respective times and who partakes in the threefold power of the respective castes.
There is nothing in the three worlds that cannot be accomplished by this;
it destroys the entire world and leads one to the stainless state. (31.21)
"It causes one to abandon all affliction; it is reached by those who contemplate yoga"—thus is it described by the wise who abide in its etymological definition. (31.22)
That very power of the Supreme Self, which is the support of all worlds without exception and is made manifest through volition, is recognized [as such]. (31.23)
Everything in it moves, and everything is always supported by all [beings];
this very earth, established upon a pillar, is bound by the flow [of consciousness]. (31.24)
"Saha" means strength; therein it delights, and that [strength] becomes a thousandfold.
It is called "sahasrati" because it would become a thousand from my own nature as Agni and Soma. (31.25)
That power of mine consists of Agni and Soma; it performs all actions.
Kindled by firm resolve, it is a formidable mass of splendors.
Having attained the state of fire, she has become the conflagration of time;
thus becoming solitary (kevalī), she blazes with incessant rising.
She, who is the Supreme Lord and the cause of supreme wonder,
is indeed the Great Power called 'Ra', my primordial power known as Kriyā.
Note:
12. The triad of powers refers to the powers of the Sun, Moon, and Fire.
14. Hetideva is Sudarśana.
15. The letter *ha* is the sun; it is also the vital breath (*prāṇa*). 16. Regarding the phrase "of the liberated," and so forth: the meaning is "with extreme velocity.
17. The *anusvāra* is the pervasive one (*vyāpin*).

18. "At the root of the tongue" refers to the location of the throat. The "circle of *a*" (*aṃ-maṇḍala*) is the anusvāra. 19. "Embraced by Rāma" means accompanied by the letter *i*. 21. By the words "is struck," etc., the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the letter *ha* is performed. With reference to the meaning of the verbal root *han*, which signifies both "to strike" and "to go," he says "he causes to go."

23. The letter *repha* is the support of all worlds without exception. 24. He provides the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word *srā*: "it moves" (*sarati*). The meaning is that it goes; or, it is moved, it is traversed, it is reached. From movement (*sṛtyāḥ*), there is "stopping" (*stambhe*), which means in a state of immobility. The meaning is that, having been turned back from movement, it is restrained by being made rigid.

25. He provides an alternative etymology and explanation for the collective term *sahasra* with the words beginning "saha" (*saha...*). From the word *saha*, which signifies strength (*bala*), when the syllable *ra*—derived from the verbal root *ram*—is joined above it, the form *sahasra* is produced.

26. He provides the etymology of the syllable *ra* with the words beginning "agni" (*agnī...* etc.). It refers to the state of being a fire of time (*kālapāvakatā*) in the form of the letter *repha*. The word *kevalī* is an adjective qualifying *śakti*. (p. 109) Root Text:
An infinity of thousands is called an *arānantya*;
O Purandara, the essential nature of both armor (*varma*) and weapons (*astra*) has thus been shown to you. (31.29)
The eternal *praṇava* has already been described as its beginning;
thus indeed is this great mantra, the essence arisen from the *Śabdabrahman*.
The great power of the Atharvan is the beloved, vast body of the power of action (kriyāśakti).
Indeed, known as the Atharva, it is the essence of the three Vedas, a great scripture consisting of five sections.
By means of this mantra, one is brought forth, just as a tree is produced from its essence;
those who know the rules for its limbs declare that it has six limbs.

One should also construct the Gāyatrī, known as the "Wheel," and the enclosure wall designated as "Fire," [which arises] from the protection, the elevation of Varuṇa, the rising sun, and likewise from the nectar.
"Ūrdhvaṃ cakrāya ca svāhā"—from the heart up to the crest-lock (śikhā), and from the word "sūryajvālā" upwards, [this is] from the Sudarśana [mantra] joined with "mahā". (31–34)
"Ūrdhvaṃ cakrāya ca svāhā"—this is the ritual procedure beginning with the armor (varman) and ending with the weapon (astra).
At its conclusion is "namaścakrāya"; we know that this consists of four yugas. (31–35)
At the end of the thousand flames is the nine-syllable mantra beginning with *dhīmahi*;
in the center of the wheel is the eight-syllable mantra beginning with *tannaḥ pracodayāt*. (31–36)
Having formed the fist and extending the index finger, with the index finger positioned as if threatening,
one should whirl it around while meditating on the fire situated within the enclosure wall.
With the palms facing each other, right over left, the tips of the little fingers and thumbs are joined, and the remaining [fingers] are likewise extended long. || 31-38 ||
One should thus rotate it all around; this is declared to be the Cakra-mudrā.
The Aṅga-mudrās will now be described; listen to the mantra for the absorption of Śakti.
The purifier mounted upon fire, extending even to the left and beyond the Praṇava;
thus [is praised] the King of Discuses, Mahāsudarśana, the great traveler.

Then, after reciting "astagatate" (O you who have gone to the setting), "sarvaduṣṭabhayaṃkara" (O terrifier of all evil ones), and "chindhi chindhi" (cut, cut), one should subsequently proclaim "bhindhi bhindhi" (split, split). || 31-41 ||
One should then recite twice: "Tear asunder! Devour the mantras of others!
Devour! Devour! One should then utter twice: "Consume the spirits! Terrify them! (31–42).
The armor, the weapon, the fire, and the wife [of Śiva] constitute the mantra for swallowing the Śakti;
having himself become Sudarśana, he should recite this mantra. (31–43)
One should mentally suck the power from the mouth, heart, and other limbs of the Supreme;
O Purandara, hear now the meditation upon the six-syllabled mantra. (31–44)
Note: 29. He provides another etymological derivation with the words beginning "saṃkhyā" (number). The compound means "that whose spokes are infinite thousands. 30. *Dhruva* refers to the *praṇava*.
31. *Pañcaparva* means the five sections consisting of the *nakṣatra-vidhāna*, *vidhi-vidhāna*, *saṃhitā*, *śānti*, and *kalpa*.

32. It means having grown like a tree by means of the essence of the earth (*bhūsāra*). The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) refer to the six limbs beginning with the heart. 33. *Gopana* is the letter *ā*; *varuṇa* is the letter *va*; *udaya* is the letter *u*; *amṛta* is the letter *sa*. The mantra is *vāṃ suṃ*.

34. "Hṛdādi" refers to the forms of the heart, head, and crest (śikhā). Regarding "mahāyukta," it is intended to mean "to Mahāsudarśana. 35. "Varmādyah" refers to the armor, eyes, and weapons. "Caturyugaḥ" refers to the eight-syllable mantra: *namaścakrāya vidmahe*.

36. "We meditate upon the one with a thousand flames; may that Discus inspire us"—this is the mantra. 40–43. "The Purifier," etc. *Oṃ praṃ*, O Great Sudarśana, King of Discuses, great traveler, who causes all evil beings to tremble with fear when you have arrived! *Chindhi chindhi* (cut, cut), *bhindhi bhindhi* (split, split), *vidāraya vidāraya* (tear asunder, tear asunder)! Devour the mantras of others, *grasa grasa* (swallow, swallow), *bhakṣaya bhakṣaya* (consume, consume)! Terrify the spirits, *trāsaya trāsaya*! After this, one should join the armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*) and the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), and at the end, append the word *svāhā*. This is the mantra for devouring power (*śaktigrāsa-mantra*). (p. 110) Root [text].
With his limbs marked by the mudrās of the wheels, he stands within a rampart of fire—
a great thousand-spoked wheel, fierce with a mass of ten-thousand fires.

One should meditate upon the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all affliction, who abides within the senses, and who is the manifestation of my power, appearing as the deluded state consisting of the six paths. (31–46)
One should meditate upon Īśāna in the form of a discus, resembling saffron in color, wearing divine yellow garments, and adorned with ornaments of pearls. (31.47)
One should meditate upon him with eight arms during a flood of great calamities—
standing in a most beautiful manner, with one knee raised, and wielding many weapons.
In the four right hands, there is a discus, a pestle, a fierce goad, and a lotus; then, in the four left arms: || 31-49 ||
Holding in his divine right hands a conch, an arrow, a bow, a noose, and a heavy mace, his face was radiant with fangs.
Then one should meditate upon the god Sudarśana, who has tawny eyes, is adorned with tawny hair, is encircled by garlands of flames, and possesses sixteen arms. (31–51)
When an insult from others has been received for which there is no remedy,
and even when one's own position is untenable, having nevertheless conquered the enemies— || 31.52 ||
When great danger has arisen from thieves, tigers, elephants, and the like,
one should visualize the Lord standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, facing the direction of the enemy host.
It was adorned with uplifted, muscular arms exerting themselves in the effort of abandonment,
and with a spear, a flaming sword, and a fire of a hundred rays.
Then, with his right lower hands, he holds in sequence a goad, a staff, a spear of blazing luster, an axe, and a discus.
With the conch and the preeminent bow, then with the noose and the plow,
with the thunderbolt, the mace-weapon, the club, and then from the trident.
It was filled with blazing weapons held aloft or directed downwards,
and agitated by the tumultuous roar of the terrible flames of fire spat from his fangs.
It was strewn with intertwined skulls and adorned with a divine garland of forest flowers;
the lords of the Daityas and Dānavas fled in terror from its horrific, loud laughter.
In that fire, thick with the fat of Daityas burning amidst a mass of flames,
a dwelling place for tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of fires of blazing splendor.
In times of great danger, a person should meditate upon the Lord as the supreme wheel-bearer (Cakrin) within the wheel consisting of the six paths (adhvaṣaṭka). || 31.60 ||
Commentary:
