45–51. He describes the meditation on Sudarśana with the words "having performed the *aṅganyāsa*. This means having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs. The *cakramudrā* is explained in this very chapter, in verse thirty-eight, and the "enclosure of fire" (*vahniprākāra*) is explained in verse thirty-seven. The description of Sudarśana begins with the words "in the thousand-spoked [wheel]," and so forth. He introduces the meditation on the Supreme Self in the form of the wheel within the center of the wheel with the words "situated in the axle," and so forth. He describes the weapons held in the right hand with the words "the discus," and so forth. He describes the weapons held in the left hand with the words "the conch," and so forth; "right" here means capable or effective. The detailed meditation on the eight-armed Sudarśana should be understood as it is set forth in the forty-fourth chapter of the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*. By the phrase "with upraised knee," the intended meaning is the combat-ready posture known as *pratyālīḍha*.

53–60. The stance known as *pratyālīḍha* was previously indicated by the phrase "with the knee raised. Regarding the weapons in the sixteen arms, he describes those of the eight right arms with the words beginning with "with the spear" (*śaktyā*), and those of the eight left arms with the words beginning with "with the conch" (*śaṅkhena*). The phrase "consisting of the interwoven principles" (*saṃsyūtatattvayā*) means "composed of the twenty-four principles"; this is a description of the nature of the forest garland (*vanamālā*). For this very reason, it is also conventionally referred to as the "garland of elements" (*bhūtamālā*). The "six paths" (*adhvaṣaṭka*) refers to the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvā*) and so forth.
Root Text: Having meditated thus, one should again meditate upon the four-armed Sudarśana.
Otherwise, there would be no peace at all, nor would there be the sword, the fire, or the splendor of Hari.
Meditation on the Puruṣa is said to be divided into the categories of the terrible (ghora) and the peaceful (śānta), and so forth.
Thus, O tiger among gods, I have explained that meditation to you; now hear from me another form of meditation.
Whatever modes of human effort have been described in this meditation,
one should recollect all of them as being composed of myself alone, for the sake of swift accomplishment.
O Śakra, this most wonderful secret has been proclaimed to you;
O bull among the gods, hear yet another secret from me.
That power of mine which was formerly proclaimed as the Āgneyī, shining with the brilliance of ten million billion suns and resembling ten million billion fires; || 31-65 ||
My body, consisting of vibration, shines with the luster of ten million billion moons;
it is the nectar, the Supreme Self, and the support of all worlds. (31.66)
Abiding as the nature of the five points (bindus) and touching the all-pervading Supreme,
she arises from the Supreme Lord for the welfare of all beings.
One should conceive of that power as the axle, its radiance as the navel-mandala,
the six mantras as the spokes, and the letters together with the Sun and Uddāma along with the bindu.
One should meditate on the two well-established [wheels] situated at the rim, while the remainder is the circle of the hub (pradhimaṇḍala).
One should meditate on oneself in the center as the Māyā of both the individual self (sva) and the supreme self (paramātman).
The yogi, devoted to meditation, should constantly meditate in this way, casting off all worldly attachment while remaining situated between the sun and the fire. 31.70
Having completely shaken off all worldly defects without exception and having attained supreme devotion unto me, he attains me alone at the end.
Standing between the Supreme Self and the Immortal,
the wise man should constantly recite [the mantra] with his mind and remember the nourishment of the nectar.
For he is being bathed with nectar flowing from the cavity of the Śakti,
and his defects are consumed by the brilliance of the fire as he is vitalized by the Prāṇa.
Having attained mastery through the practice of the five drops (pañcabindu), he is established in supreme sovereignty;
through the yoga of continuous practice, he is self-controlled and has conquered his senses.
Having abandoned all affliction and having assumed my own form,
the yogi, born proud, becomes entirely self-controlled through his practice.
Having become the supreme Lord, abiding as the embodiment of all-pervasiveness,
one attains Me alone, My own abode, through My grace.
That which is action is called consciousness (cit), and that which is consciousness is supreme action (kriyā).
These three, together with supreme bliss (paramānanda), are proclaimed to be these [four]. || 31.77 ||
The supreme Śakti is indivisible, one, and consists of consciousness, action, and bliss; she is the Vaiṣṇavī, the supreme I-consciousness, and that "I" which fulfills all purposes.
Note: 61. Through meditation on this [mantra], the pacification of all calamities (*ariṣṭa*) is described in the forty-seventh chapter of the *Ahibudhnya-saṃhitā* and should be consulted there.

66. [The mantra consists of] the power of vibration (*spandamayī*) and the power of action (*kriyāmayī*). "Amṛta" (nectar) is the letter *sa*. The Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the letter *ha*. The support of all worlds (*aśeṣabhuvanādhṛti*) is the letter *ra*.
67. The "five dots" (pañcabindu) is the vowel *ī*; the "pervasive" (vyāpī) is the *anusvāra*. 68.
By "six spokes," the six-spoked wheel (*ṣaḍaracakra*) is intended; "Sūryoddāma" is *hu*. 69. "The remainder" means *phaṭ*.
73. By the vital breath (*prāṇa*), [there is] the letter *ha*; the fire (*anala*) is the letter *ra*.
77. He states that the activity of its own nature consists of consciousness, bliss, and form, saying "iti. (p. 112) Root-text:
By my own free will, my creative resolve unfolds in this twofold manner:
one is the power called Action (kriyā), and the other is the Great Manifestation (mahābhūti). || 31.79 ||
O Śakra, I, the Supreme Goddess, abide generally within these two;
thus has this entire power of yours, in the form of action, been demonstrated.
Perceive the Tārikā according to her gross, subtle, and supreme aspects;
she is one whose creative activity is closed yet whose nature is manifest sovereignty.
My subtle form consists of the sixfold qualities; that prosperity is called Tārikā. Listen to me as I describe its gross and other forms exactly as they are.
O Lord of Gods, these [teachings] being spoken, listen with an attentive mind. || 31-82 ||
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Illumination of Sudarśana," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*.
Note: 79. "In two ways" means by way of the distinction between the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) and the power of manifestation (*bhūti-śakti*).

81. He introduces the description of the power of manifestation, which is the subject matter of the immediately following chapter, with the words "with eyes closed," etc. The meaning is that within the form of the power of manifestation, the power of action remains as if closed. "Clearly" means that sovereignty becomes manifest.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter.
The thirty-second chapter: The Root Text.
Śrī said:

"This which is indeed the supreme knowledge, the Tarikā who delivers one across [the ocean of existence]—listen now to her threefold form: the gross (sthūla), the subtle (sūkṣma), and the supreme (para). (32-1)
The body consisting of five colors and four colors is gross in nature;
my supreme form, composed of Viṣṇu, which is known as subtle, consists of three colors. || 32-2 ||
These three states of mine are each indeed threefold;
however, that which is the supreme state within the gross is based upon the Supreme Self.
This [nature], which is the support of the entire world, the pervasive refuge of Viṣṇu, and consists of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed—learn from me its form. (32.4)
By that which is the support and abode of all worlds without exception, whose birth pervades [all],
and which, beginning with the Supreme Self (paramātman), has reached the surface of the forehead.
Having assumed the form of Viṣṇu, she establishes herself once again in her own [form];
the beloved of Hari shines with the sound that is the cause of liberation.
Bearing with her intellect the entire world, including the enjoyer and the enjoyed,
the Goddess rests upon the all-pervading Supreme Self.
For that duration, she remained as Viṣṇu’s form, the gross, supreme state—
the power (śakti) that performs the fivefold cosmic acts and is augmented by the three kinds of sovereignty.
Sustaining the Lord, who possesses the splendor of the surging ocean,
this subtle movement is considered by me to have resorted to a state of fire.
Having then performed the creation and other acts,
the Goddess, who causes all wonders and is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and end [of the world], remained established in the supreme void.
Resorting to the Sun and impelling Viṣṇu for the maintenance of the world,
she is massive with the fiery splendors of the fire of time, consisting of gross elements, and wondrous.
The three gross courses of mine have been described, O Vāsava;
now hear, O slayer of Vṛtra, of the three subtle courses.
Note: 1. "Vidyā" means the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*). By the term "bhavatāriṇī," he states that the name *Tārikā* is etymologically appropriate.

2. Regarding "hrīṃ": by adding the resonance (*nāda*) heard above the *bindu*, like the sound of a bell, it possesses five phonemes; setting that aside, its four-phoneme nature is to be established. "Trivarṇā" means having the form of *ī*. He states its supreme form (*pararūpa*) as "consisting of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇumayī*), meaning it has the form of the solitary letter *ī*.

3. "Each one is threefold" means that there is a threefold division: in the gross form (*sthūla-rūpa*), there are the gross, subtle, and supreme forms; in the subtle form (*sūkṣma-rūpa*), there are the gross, subtle, and supreme forms; and in the supreme form (*para-rūpa*) as well, there are the gross, subtle, and supreme forms. Regarding the supreme form within the gross, he says "in the gross, however": the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the letter *ha*; the support of all worlds is the letter *ra*; Viṣṇu is the letter *ī*; and the pervasive one is the *anusvāra*. Thus, taken together, it becomes *hrīṃ*. 5. For the phrase "having reached the surface of the forehead," the word "by its form" (*rūpeṇa*) is to be supplied.
6. By the word "having entered" (ākramya), the non-manifestation of the Vaiṣṇava form is intended.

8. Regarding the phrase "by that [form]": the meaning is "in the form of the enjoyer and the enjoyed. Then, regarding the gross [state], he states the subtle [state] with the words beginning "fivefold activity" (pañcakṛtya) and so on. The fivefold activities are creation and the others. 10. Regarding the gross [state], he states the gross form with the words "creation and so forth" (sṛṣṭyādikam). [The passage begins] with "all wonders" (sarvāścarya) and so on. It should be understood that previously, in the context of the subtle, the volition for the creation of the world was mentioned; here, however, its actual creation is described.
This subtle Root, the Supreme Goddess, is indeed the reckoning of non-time;
resting upon the all-pervading Supreme Self, she exists eternally. (32.13)
The pure category and likewise the impure—this twofold creation is said to be the object of emanation.
The gross [creation] is situated in that which is other than the pure, while the subtle is established in the pure.
One should correctly perceive all three of these states as being like that of the gross [body].
O Śakra, behold now the form of that which is my supreme body.
All-pervading, divine, partless, and stainless, she is the supreme power (parā śakti) consisting of myself (manmayī), who is designated by the name Viṣṇu. (32.16)
This indeed is that Vaiṣṇava essence; this is considered by Hari to be the true "I-ness" (ahaṃtā).
This is the final state of the yogins; this is the goal of those whose nature is Sāṃkhya.
Such is that supreme form; such is that supreme goal.
She is the primordial power Kuṇḍalinī, the female bee who bestows yoga. (32.18)
For she is unstruck, soundless, and boundless; she has arisen from the river [of speech].
She is the Śabdabrahman, as well as Śakti, the supreme Mātṛkā-yoni. (32.19)
Gāyatrī, Kalā, Gaurī, the goddess Śacī, Sarasvatī, Vṛṣākapāyī, Satyā, Prāṇapatnī, and Yaśasvinī. || 32-20 ||
She is the consort of Indra, the great cow, Aditi, the delighter of the gods;
she is the goddess who is the mother of the Rudras and likewise the benefactress of the Vasus.
The sister of the Ādityas, the navel, the sustainer of immortality, the supreme; Iḍā, delight, she of lovely form, the great nourisher, most exalted. (32.22)
She is the Earth, she is Renown, she is the Triple Veda, she is the Cow fond of living beings;
she is Power, she is Primordial Nature, the Great Queen who yields the milk of abundance.
Tārā, Sītā, as well as Śrī, Kāmavatsā, Priyavratā, Taruṇī, Varārohā, Nīrūpā, and Rūpaśālinī. || 32-24 ||
Ambikā, Sundarī, Jyeṣṭhā, Vāmā, Ghorā, Manomayī, Siddhā, Siddhāntikā, Yogā, Yoginī, and Yogabhāvinī. || 32-25 ||
Such names as these have been declared in various scriptures by the wise who have reached the further shore of established doctrine—the secrets of Śakti. (32.26)
This very supreme, divine Śakti exists in three forms;
this triad is demonstrated through the states of gross, subtle, and supreme. || 32-27 ||
Its essential nature has been declared as follows, and it exists in three ways:
in the form of the "unmeasurable" (aprameya) and so forth. Listen now to this explanation of it. (32.28)
When that supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva—the imperishable, wherein all distinctions have been withdrawn—is alone, then it is indeed one. (32.29)
Then, by the name "Immeasurable," that deity is meditated upon by yogis;
whether as the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader, or as the process of creation and the created. (32.30)
Note:

13. He states the common nature of the subtle form with the words "akāla" (timeless). By this, it is intended that the previously mentioned gross form is subject to being consumed by time (*kālakālyatva*).
14. He states another distinction with the word "śuddha" (pure).

15. Regarding the threefold subtle form under discussion, he extends by analogy the previously mentioned gross movement with the words "the three," etc. The only distinction is this: the previously mentioned gross movement has impure objects as its domain, whereas this one has pure objects as its domain.

16. Next, he describes the common form of the supreme [movement] with the words "pervading all," etc. 17. "Of those who possess Sāṃkhya" means of those who possess knowledge such as the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.
18. He states her different names, beginning with "śakti" and so forth.
19. Nada means nāda. 28. "Ī" means the vowel *ī*.

29. He states the supreme form of Parā as the "sixfold attributes" (*ṣāḍguṇya*). Regarding the word "withdrawn" (*saṃhṛta*): "differentiation" (*bheda*) refers to the manifold world (*prapañca*). This expression is used because, during the reabsorption (*pratisaṃcara*), the entire manifold world is dissolved into Brahman. Regarding "only one": the meaning is that Brahman, characterized by the subtle state of both the conscious and the unconscious, became the single reality (*tattva*). Root Text: At that time, there exists no other object of knowledge for Him whatsoever.
Then it is as if empty of all forms, as if entirely fallen asleep. || 32-31 ||
The sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) is Brahman; therein this [power] is established under the name of Viṣṇu.
It has the form of a waveless ocean, being the state of both power and the possessor of power.
Then, when the flawless Brahman known as Vāsudeva unfolds by its own volition, that is called the first [manifestation]. (32–33)
For when Brahman manifests through the path known as pure and impure,
it is then called Māyā, which has the nature of the volition of Brahman.
He remains within her womb as everything from Saṃkarṣaṇa down to the earth;
yet when the Supreme Brahman, having accomplished his own will, becomes distinct once more— || 32–35 ||
Divided into the pervaded and the pervader, it exists as accompanied by a second; at that time, O Goddess, it consists of five bindus and performs the fivefold cosmic act.
Thus, the threefold path has been declared to you as my own body;
dividing itself into form after form, it pierces through each respective element and syllable.
Having been led to the state of denoting this or that [object], the body of the world, by its own will, abides as its very self within those various principles (tattvas). || 32–38 ||
That portion of mine which is subtle in form, hidden like fire within wood,
having assumed those various forms, is the eternal one called Sevanī.
Through the coloring of various castes, the body of each individual person is itself [divine];
therein, that portion which is of the nature of the Supreme Self exists as the presiding deity.
The Vaiṣṇava [power], being of the nature of Śakti, remains restraining me;
this very imperishable Goddess assumes the state of denoting each respective [object]. (32–41)
The Yoginī Parameśvarī is the support of all worlds without exception;
she alone, as the essence of the phonemes (tattvavarṇa), has attained the sovereignty over the three worlds.
Each respective gross element reveals my eternal power (śakti) through the designation of its particular state,
when that state is seen as being governed by it.
This very Goddess Īśvarā abides as a twofold power (śakti);
that which was previously shown to you as the fivefold Brahman, beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *śa*.
In her essential form as *kṣa* (or *kṛśi*, etc.), she has attained the bestowal of sovereignty over the three worlds;
she is established in two ways: both in her essential nature and in her restrictive function. (32–45)
The tetrad of dhāraṇās, beginning with *yā* and ending with *yām*, has been proclaimed;
therein, abiding in the subtle and supreme state, this [practice] is twofold as before. (32–46)

Note: 31. *Prameyatva* means being an object of valid cognition (*pramā-viṣayatva*). "As if empty" (*śūnyam iva*) means it is like a non-entity because all activity has ceased; the word "as if" (*iva*) is used to refute the reality called "emptiness" (*śūnya*) which is asserted by outsiders. 32. Now, he describes the subtle form of the Supreme (*parā*) with the words "power" (*śakti*), etc. The phrase "when" (*yadā*), which occurs later in the sentence, should be understood here at the beginning. The connection with what follows is: "when there is the manifest movement—that is, the comprehension—of power and the possessor of power."
33. "The first" means "volition" (saṃkalpa); this is the ellipsis. 34. The meaning is that "this is the supreme power" (parā śakti).
35. He states the gross form of the supreme [power] as "Saṃkarṣaṇa."
36. Pañcabindu is the vowel *ī*.
37. Trayī means that which is threefold by way of its gross, subtle, and supreme forms.
39. Sevanī refers to the specific configuration of articulatory organs, such as the tongue and other places, which is necessary for the utterance of phonemes.
40. Regarding the phrase "which part": its connection is with the word "this [is] hers" (*asya seyam*) found in the immediately following verse.
43. "Even every gross reality becomes eternal through my power. By this, the refutation of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) is intended.
44. "Attached" (*saktā*): the meaning is "endowed with attachment. He explains that very point with the words beginning with "kṣādi" (*kṣādīti*).
45. "In two ways" means that she exists in a twofold manner, demonstrating both the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the regulation (*niyamana*) of all [the elements].
46. The meaning is that the fourfold group ending with *vādi* is said to be the fourfold group of concentrations (*dhāraṇā*). (p. 116) Root-text—
This letter *ma* is said to have three states and to denote consciousness;
therein, it is twofold in two ways within the two stages of the subtle (*sūkṣma*) and the supreme (*parā*). || 32-47 ||
That which is born of Māyā and consists of the three qualities (guṇas) is called Bhārūṇa; there too, as before, the Goddess named Ī resides within two of the ten [digits]. (32–48)
Regarding the three forms of intellect, ego, and mind, such as those beginning with *bāda*, this Goddess is likewise twofold within each of these two groups, as previously described. (32.49)
In each of the two groups of channels, as well as in the two groups of sense organs, this [power] abides in two ways within the ten subtle and supreme [elements]. || 32-50 ||
In the fivefold manifestations (*vibhūti*), both the gross and the subtle in nature—namely, *ñādika* and *ṅādika*—the Goddess resides in the two [groups] as before. (32–51)
On the path consisting of both the pure and the impure, this Power herself, through seventy distinct divisions, assumes many forms like a dancer. (32.52)
Having meditated upon this Supreme Goddess, who has attained such vast extension, one goes to the supreme, eternal abode of Viṣṇu. || 32-53 ||
Wherever this [power] has gone, whether on the pure or the impure path,
it remains there without ever abandoning its connection to Viṣṇu.
Combined with one, two, three, and so forth, she is colored by vowels and consonants;
situated within the classes of the pure and impure paths, she is brought forth through various divisions.

Furthermore, for this very [energy] which is devoid of the stain of the matted locks (jaṭoparāga), those who contemplate reality should know that there is a threefold division according to its gross and other forms. (32.56)
She is the creator of emanation, conjoined with the gross and the subtle; she is conjoined with Vyomeśa;
she is the stainless, supreme "I," and thus truly full of passion.
This supreme consort of Viṣṇu is unshakable like the flame of a lamp;
she remains perfectly motionless within all the foundational lotuses.
From the region of the navel up to the head, this single [channel] follows the path to Brahman;
it is radiant, blazing, purifying, and glorious. (32.59)
Having emerged from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and reached the Great Lotus,
she is woven like warp and woof upon the path of supreme bliss.
Having dissolved the mortal form, one should inundate the person with the nectar,
together with the mantras consisting of Viṣṇu, along with the mantras that are composed of me.
"Indeed, she is my [goddess] whose glory is truly undiminished; for she is the supreme reckoning (saṃkhyā).
And those non-dual mantras of that Sāṃkhya bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation through their recitation. (32.62)
Note:
47. *Tryavastha* itself is *traiyavastha*. 49. *Bādika* refers to the *baphapāḥ*.
50. The *tavarga* [group of dental consonants] begins with *n*; the *ṭavarga* [group of retroflex consonants] begins with *ṇ*. 51.
The meaning is that the fivefold *cavarga* and the fivefold *kavarga* are said to have the nature of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the gross elements (*sthūlabhūta*).

52. Regarding the phrase "seventy": since there are thirty-five divisions each for the pure (*śuddha*) and impure (*aśuddha*) paths, there are seventy divisions in total. *Ī* refers to *Śakti*; it means the power in the form of the vowel *ī*.

56. *Jaṭā*: this means [consonants] beginning with *ja* and *ṭa*. This is an illustration; it also includes the coloring by other phonemes (*varṇa*). 57. He states the divisions of the form of *ī*, such as "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth. "Creator of creation" (*sṛṣṭikṛt*) is the *visarga*. "Lord of space" (*vyomeśa*) is the *anusvāra*.
59. *Basti* is the region below the navel.
60. *Otaprota* means "pervading all. 61. *Mārtyava* refers to that which belongs to death; the meaning is "subject to the nature of mortality.
62. *Anūnaśrīḥ* (500): the meaning is "those who possess the form of consciousness, numbering two hundred and fifty."
p. 117) Root:
These very [energies] are proclaimed to be the droplets of that Supreme [Power], just as light, having pervaded its mass of rays, remains as luminosity itself. (32.63)
For just as stability pervades all earthly entities, remaining present within them in various manifestations and forms, and existing through various arrangements and structures; || 32-64 ||
Pervading equally all external and internal existence consisting of sound,
the illustrious Goddess, the consort of Viṣṇu, remains thus established.
O Śakra, this distinction between the gross, the subtle, and so forth has been shown by me as it truly is;
now hear from me the limbs and other components of the Tārikā.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Gross and Other [Levels]," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra (or the Śrīpañcarātra).
Note:
63. *Tejastva* is luminosity.
65. The grammatical connection is that the goddess, whose form is *ī*, is situated there.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter.
The thirty-third chapter:
Śrī [C: Śrī said].
Listen, O child Sureśāna, to my [explanation] of the limbs and sub-limbs of the mantra, consisting of various mantras, for the sake of the *tārikā* of the Vidyā. (33-1)
Gopana, Pañcabindu, Ūrja, Airāvaṇa, and Aurva—these five are each accompanied by Vyāpin. (33-2)
Having placed this group of five *piṇḍas* above the fire of the vital breath (*prāṇānala*), one should contemplate this seed-syllable of the limbs (*aṅgabīja*) from the heart up to the eyes. (33-3)
[In place of these and the following two lines, B. reads:
"One should place the word *paraṃ* with the two seed-syllables of *praṇava*, and the word *jñānāya*;
likewise, *hṛdayāya namaḥ*—this is the eleven-syllable mantra."]
After the seed-syllable of the heart (*hṛdbīja*), the word *jñānāya* should be joined, followed by *hṛdayāya namaḥ*; this mantra bestows the power of concentration (*dhāraṇā*). || 33-4 ||
This eleven-syllable mantra begins with the Praṇava and ends with "namaḥ.
However, for the sake of attaining sovereignty, one should place the word [denoting the deity] between the two seed-syllables of the Praṇava.
And likewise, "śirase svāhā"—this indeed consists of eleven syllables.
One should then place the word "śaktaye" preceded by the two seed-syllables of the Praṇava (oṃ). || 33-6 ||
"Śikhāyai vauṣaṭ"—this ten-syllable mantra is indeed the Śikha;
one should place the word "balāya" between the two seed-syllables of the Praṇava. (33–7)
The mantra for the armor is "kavacāya hūṃ," which consists of ten syllables;
one should further assign the word "tejase" preceded by the two seed-syllables of the Praṇava (oṃ).
With "vauṣaṭ" for the two eyes, this is the ten-syllable eye-mantra;
one should then install the Supreme Lord situated above the fire of the vital breath.
Therefore, preceded by the *praṇava*, one should assign the word for *vīrya* and then *astrāya phaṭ*; this mantra consists of ten syllables. (33–10)
This group of six limbs has been declared; now hear the triad of subsidiary limbs.
At the end of the *tārikā*, one should sequentially assign the sixfold word as before.
One should place [the mantras] in sequence from Jñāna up to Tejas, and at the end of that, the words "for the belly," "for the back," and "for the two arms. (33.12)

Note: 2. Gopana is the letter Ā; Pañcabindu is the letter Ī; Ūrja is the letter Ū; Airāvaṇa is the letter AI; Aurva is the letter AU; Vyāpin is the Anusvāra (Ṃ). 3. Prāṇa is the letter Ha; Anala is the letter Ra. The "five clusters" (piṇḍapañcaka) refers to the fivefold mantra: HRĀṂ, HRĪṂ, HRŪṂ, HRAIṂ, HRAUṂ. "Hṛdādi" means the heart, head, crest, armor, and eyes.

4. He indicates the mantra beginning with *hṛt* and so forth: *oṃ hrāṃ jñānāya hṛdayāya namaḥ*. 5–10. *oṃ hrīṃ aiśvaryāya śirase svāhā*. *oṃ hrūṃ śaktaye śikhāyai vauṣaṭ*. *oṃ hraiṃ balāya kavacāya huṃ*. *oṃ hrauṃ tejase netrābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ*. *oṃ hraḥ vīryāya astrāya ca phaṭ*.
11, 12. *oṃ hrīṃ jñānāya udarāya namaḥ*. *oṃ hrīṃ śaktaye pṛṣṭhāya namaḥ*. *oṃ hrīṃ balāya bāhubhyāṃ namaḥ*.

p. 119) "To the root [limbs], to the thighs, then to the knees, and to the feet"—in this sequence, the word "namaḥ" (homage) should be applied thereafter; this is the rule for the secondary limbs (upāṅgas). || 33-13 ||
Thus, the twelve mantras of the primary and secondary limbs have been proclaimed;
now listen as I speak the armor-mantras and the ornament-mantras.
Then the Kaustubha gem, merged with space, is the Supreme Self;
it is further pervaded by fire above and below, and is also endowed with the upward energy (ūrja).
The creator of the universe is joined with [the letter] *sa*; the Kaustubha jewel is joined with the pervasive (*vyāpin*);
thereafter is the salutation (*namaskṛti*), and after that, to the Self of Light (*prabhātman*).
Then, "Kaustubhāya Svāhā"—this sixteen-syllable mantra, beginning with the Praṇava, is the Kaustubha mantra that accomplishes all rites. (33-17)
One should first extract *tāra* (the syllable Om); then one should extract *dhareśa* (the Lord of the Earth).
Below that, one should place the one known as *tṛpti* (Satisfaction), and below that, one should set down *varāha*.

One should subsequently adorn it with *māyā* and then mark it with the pervasive [syllable]. This aggregate of phonemes consists of five aspects; after that follows the salutation (*namaskāra*). (33.19)
Then one should utter the word *sthalajalodbhūtabhūṣitapada*, followed by *vanamāle* and then *svāhā*; this mantra accomplishes all objectives. (33.20)
This great mantra, consisting of nineteen syllables and composed of a forest garland (vanamālā),
should have the syllable 'vāmana' extracted at the end of the word 'tāraka'.
Having applied satisfaction beneath that, one should adorn it with the Arising (Udaya);
the four-syllable Piṇḍa, marked by the Pervasive (Vyāpin), is most wonderful. (33.22)
After that, "namaskāraḥ," then "śrīnivāsapadam," then "padmāya" and "vahnijāyā" (svāhā); this is the twelve-syllable (or thirteen-syllable) Pādma mantra. || 33-23 ||
First, one should take Vaikuṇṭha and place the letter *ra* above it;
thereafter, one should mark it with Ānanda and then with Vyāpin.
One should place the *kāṣṭhakāṣṭha* footstep and thereafter the pair of rims (*nemi*).
"Svāhā to the excellent noose" (varapāśāya vai svāhā); indeed, this is the King of Nooses preceded by the *praṇava*. (33-25)
This fifteen-syllable mantra brings swift accomplishment for those possessed of desire;
it is joined at the end with the Praṇava, and the one named Virāṭ is conjoined with Vyāpin upon the head. (33-26)
The two [syllables] are to be joined together as a single unit: the letter *ra*, the lotus, and the goad;
this third syllable is conjoined with the Pervasive One (*vyāpin*) at its head. (33.27)
The word *pada* is for the sharp-nosed one (*niśitaghoṇāya*) and for the goad (*aṅkuśāya*); [this is] the beloved of Śikhin.
This fifteen-syllable mantra, known as Aṅkuśa, bestows swift accomplishment. (33.28)
This pentad has been declared for the ornaments and the weapon-mantras;
now hear, O Purandara, the form of the mantras for the support and the seat. (33.29)
Without the *tārikā*, completion does not occur at all;
the vital breath (*prāṇa*), situated between two fires, is possessed of *māyā* and endowed with the *bindu*. (33–30)
Then, beginning with the Praṇava (Om) and ending with "namaḥ" for Ādhāraśakti, this nine-syllabled mantra of Ādhāraśakti should be known. (33–31)
Situated between the two analas, ending with the bindu and joined with ūrja;
then, preceded by the Praṇava and ending with "namas," [the mantra] is for Kālāgnikūrma. (33–32)
Commentary: 13. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the thighs for sovereignty (aiśvarya). Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the knees for valor (vīrya). Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the feet for splendor (tejas).
15–17. Oṃ ṭhaṃ rhrūḥ ṭhaṃ, svāhā to the Kaustubha gem, the soul of light (prabhātman).
18–20. Oṃ lsvīṃ namaḥ sthalajalodbhūtabhūṣite vanamāle svāhā.
21–23. Oṃ bsuṃ namaḥ śrīnivāsapadmāya svāhā. [The compound *tryadhikā daśākṣarā yasya* is a *bahuvrīhi*, meaning "that which has thirteen syllables.
24, 25. Oṃ rṇāṃ kastha kastha ṭhaṭha varapāśāya svāhā.

26–28. Oṃ ḷṛṃ rkṛṃ, svāhā to Niśitaghoṇa, the goad. 29–31. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti. 32. "Situated between two fires"—the word *prāṇa* is to be supplied here. Oṃ rhrūṃ, obeisance to Kālāgnikūrma.
p. 120) This ten-syllabled root-mantra (mūla-mantra) of Kālāgnikūrma is to be known;
it marks the vital breath (prāṇa) with concealment and is joined with the pervasive [power] at the crown of the head. || 33-33 ||
Having extracted [the mantra] ending with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), followed by "Anantāya namaḥ," this eight-syllabled mantra of the Nāga king is proclaimed. (33–34)
Having condensed the fourfold— the lotus, the form of fire, the Pradhāna, and the Lord of Puruṣas— along with that which pervades the Gopanī, || 33–35 ||
After "vasudhāyai namaḥ," this mantra beginning with the Praṇava (oṃ) is to be known as that for Viśvaṃbharā; it is conceived as the support. (33–36)

One should extract the syllable *amṛta* (am) and the two syllables of *varuṇa* (va-ra), joined together as a single cluster (*piṇḍīkṛta*), combined with the pervasive *gopana* (ga), at the end of the *praṇava* (oṃ). (33–37)
Then, "Kṣīrārṇavāya namaḥ"—this is the nine-syllabled mantra;
it is pure, joined with the *udaya* and the *vyāpin*, and ends with the *praṇava*.
"Salutation to the foundational lotus; this [mantra] for the lotus consists of ten syllables.
Thus, the sixfold mantra of the six supports has been proclaimed. (33–39)
O Purandara, O Vāsava, listen to the ritual procedure for the mantras known as Ādhāra and Īśa: Dharta, Ajita, Amṛtādhāra, and Vibudha. (33–40)
Having extracted these four castes,
the best of practitioners should then place upon them four other castes, beginning with Satya.
O Vāsava, these four seed-syllables, beginning with the *praṇava*, bestow sovereignty over the three worlds; they belong to the sixteen-fold self, beginning with Dharma.
Dharma and the rest, adharma and the rest, mṛga and the rest, and kṛta and the rest—
these four groups of four are established [or conventionally recognized] in the world.
One should arrange sixteen designations in groups of four;
these sixteen mantras are traditionally taught as beginning with the seed-syllable and ending with "namaḥ."
One should place this short [syllable], together with the *udaya* and *amṛta*, above the *praṇava*.
"Salutation to the Unmanifest Lotus"—this is the mantra known as the Unmanifest Lotus (*avyaktapadmaka*). (33–45)

For each of the positions of the Sun, Moon, and Fire, as well as for the mandala, the mantra consists of the syllable *Oṃ* at the beginning and the word "namas" at the end; these are the mantras for the three mandalas.
Commentary—33, 34. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta. 35, 36. Oṃ kṣmlāṃ, obeisance to Vasudhā.
37. Oṃ svāṃ, obeisance to the Ocean of Milk. 38. Oṃ puṃ, obeisance to the Support-Lotus (Ādhārapadma).

40–43. Dhartā is the letter *dha*; Ajita is the letter *ja*; Amṛtādhāra is the letter *va*; Vibudha is the letter *la*; Satya is the letter *ṛ*. Oṃ dhṛṃ, oṃ dhṝṃ, oṃ dhḷṃ, oṃ dhḹṃ—these are, in sequence, the seed-mantras of the Lords of the Supports known as Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya.

*Oṃ jṛṃ*, *oṃ jṝṃ*, *oṃ jḷṃ*, *oṃ jḹṃ*—these are, in order, the seed-mantras of the Lords of the Supports (Ādhāreśa) known as Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, and Anaiśvarya. *Oṃ vṛṃ*, *oṃ vṝṃ*, *oṃ v-ḷṃ*, *oṃ v-ḹṃ*—these are the seed-mantras of the Lords of the Supports known as Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan. *Oṃ l-ṛṃ*, *oṃ l-ḹṃ*, *oṃ l-ḷṃ*, *oṃ l-ḹṃ*—these are the seed-mantras of the Lords of the Supports known as Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali.

44. Now, the name-mantras of the sixteen qualities beginning with Dharma are stated starting with the word "catuḥ": *Oṃ dhṛṃ dharmāya namaḥ*; *Oṃ dhṝṃ jñānāya namaḥ*; and so on, they are to be understood in this sequence.
45. The short *ba* syllable: Oṃ bsuṃ, homage to the unmanifest lotus (*avyaktapadma*).

46. Oṃ, homage to the solar mandala (*sūryamaṇḍala*). Oṃ, homage to the lunar mandala (*indumaṇḍala*). Oṃ, homage to the fire mandala (*agnimaṇḍala*). These are the mantras for the three mandalas. (p. 121) Root [text]:
The word "soma," which refers to the inner self (pratyagātman) and possesses the quality of emanation, is proclaimed as this three-syllabled mantra known as *cidbhāsanā*. || 33-47 ||
Thus, twenty-one mantras known as the "seats" have been declared;
this collection of mantras, ending with the worship of the seats (pīṭha-pūjā), has been proclaimed by me.
Now listen to this supreme secret, the ultimate mystery:
the collection of mantras beginning with Kṣetreśa, which is capable of crushing all obstacles.
Then, having condensed Garuḍa, Kāla, and Anala into a single form, one should mark [the deity] with the Savyāpini Ādideva, saying: "Obeisance indeed to Kṣetrapāla. (33-50)
This nine-syllable mantra of Kṣetreśa begins with the Praṇava;
for Śrī, the Tārā follows after, while the Tāraka comes at the beginning followed by "namaḥ. (33–51)
The six-syllable mantra of Śrī; now hear of Caṇḍa and the others. The syllable *tāra* (Oṃ), together with the flickering fire (*cañcalānala*) and alone, should be placed at the beginning.
"Caṇḍāya namaḥ"—this seven-syllabled mantra is the most excellent;
it should be preceded by the *pavitra*, the fire (*analas*), and the *tāra* (Oṃ), or by the *tāra* alone at the beginning. (33–53)
The mantra is "Salutation to Pracaṇḍa. This Pracaṇḍa consists of four yugas; it is preceded by the eternal fire (Śāśvatānala), the Tāra (Oṃ), and the Kevala (Namaḥ). || 33-54 ||
"Jayāya namaḥ"—thus is the description of Jaya by the best of sages;
it is joined with Varāha and Anala, and likewise the pure Tāra (Om) is placed at the beginning. (33–55)
Salutation to Vijaya; he is this Vijaya, the four-yuga one.
He is Govinda, possessed of fire, the master of illusion (māyī), the all-pervading, who reaches the end of the Praṇava.
"Salutation to Gaṅgā"—thus is the description of Gaṅgā by the best of sages; she is equanimous, accompanied by fire, subtle, all-pervading, and culminates in the Praṇava. (33–57)
Salutation to Yamunā; and he who is born of Yamunā is Caturyuga.
Śaṅkara, together with Anala and Urja, is the all-pervading one who reaches the end of the Praṇava.
And then: "Salutation to Śaṅkhanidhi"—this is that nine-syllabled mantra, which is purifying, accompanied by fire (Ra), joined with the moon (Sa), pervasive, and ending with the Praṇava (Oṃ). (33–59)
Then, "Salutation to Padmanidhi"—this is the nine-syllable mantra.
This is the tenfold set of mantras, beginning with Kṣetreśa and ending with Padmanidhi. (33–60)
Now listen to the established doctrine beginning with Gaṇeśa and the collection of mantras:
Govinda, joined with the pervasive *ūrja* syllable, ending with the *praṇava*. (33–61)
Then Govinda, Vaikuṇṭha, Pavitra, Sragdhara, as well as Jagadyoni, Gata, Śaṅkha, Nara, Kāla, and Visargavat. (33–62)

This nine-syllable mantra is indeed proclaimed as belonging to Gaṇapati; one should join Govinda with the six [syllables] beginning with the pair [of consonants], starting with 'ga' and so forth. (33–63)
The ritual assignment of its limbs (aṅgakalpti) should be joined with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and so forth;
it is conjoined with fire at the beginning and end, and endowed with the pervasive *māyā*.
Note:
47. "I am that" (ahaṃ saḥ) is the mantra for the manifestation of consciousness (cidbhāsana).

48. Regarding the number twenty-one: it should be understood that there are sixteen mantras for the lords of the foundations (ādhāra), one mantra for the unmanifest lotus (avyaktapadma), three mantras for the mandalas, and one mantra for the manifestation of consciousness.
50. Oṃ kṣmrāṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla. 51. Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Śrī. 52. Oṃ croṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍa.
53. Oṃ proṃ, homage to Pracaṇḍa.
54. Oṃ jroṃ, homage to Jaya. 55. Oṃ vroṃ, homage to Vijaya.
56. Oṃ grīṃ, obeisance to Gaṅgā. 57. Oṃ yrīṃ, obeisance to Yamunā. 58. Oṃ śrūṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkhanidhi.
59. Oṃ prūṃ, obeisance to Padmanidhi.

61–62. “Gaṇeśa and so forth” means the mantras beginning with Gaṇeśa and ending with Ādisiddha. Oṃ gūṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. 63. Oṃ gāṃ, obeisance to the heart; thus it should be understood for the others as well.
64–68. Oṃ kṣrīṃ hrīṃ syrāṃ stryāṃ a-kṣa (the letters from *a* to *kṣa*) vāgīśvaryai namaḥ. (p.
122) One should meditate on the root [mantra] Garuḍa at the end of the *tāraka*, and at the end of that, the *tārikā*.
One should contemplate Soma, enriched by the deities beginning with Repha and Śaṅkha, and endowed with the pervasive one (Vyāpin). || 33-65 ||
O slayer of Bala, one should remember this fourth seed-syllable, which is enriched by the Vairāja, Anala, and Śaṅkha, and joined with Gopana and Vyāpin.
O Śakra, one should remember the fifth [letter], which is of the color of the moon and supremely wonderful,
beginning with the immeasurable primordial deity and extending as far as the color of Garuḍa.
Having recited according to the text, then "Salutation to Vāgīśvarī.
This great mantra of sixty-one syllables is known as the mantra of Vāgīśvarī. (33–68)

The wise practitioner should correctly perform the arrangement of the limbs, joined with the internal seed-syllable, using the fourth seed-syllable which is distinguished by its concealment and other qualities.

One should place the *praṇava* and *namaḥ* at the beginning and end of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) which has been differentiated by means of concealment (*gopana*) and so forth; thereafter, one should fashion the *jāti*.
The three *praṇavas* joined with the pervasive [syllable], followed by *sa-udaya-gaḥ*, and then "namo gurave"—this is renowned for the worship of the Guru. (33.71)
At the end of the triad of *praṇavas*, joined with the *pavitra* and the *vyāpin*, [the mantra] "Salutation to the Supreme Guru" is proclaimed as the Guru of Gurus. (33-72)
At the end of the three *praṇavas*, the syllable *paḥ* joined with bliss, followed by "to the Parameṣṭhin" and then "namas"—this is the mantra of the Guru of the Guru of Gurus. (33–73)
One should place the five *tāras*, which are the source of delight, in the ether above the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
and one should place the two *kālānalas* below that, above the Lord of All Worlds.
Having formed a single mass (piṇḍa) from the syllables uttered in their proper sequence, one then says "svadhā" to the ancestors and "namaḥ. This is the king of mantras for the assembly of ancestors.
Ṣaṭtārā, Ādideva, then Vyomavān, then he alone;
Rāmavān, Damana, then from the Siddhas, and then obeisance. (33-76)
This mantra belongs to those who are perfected from the beginning, whose selves are permeated by the Blessed One;
it is capable of crushing obstacles and [attaining] the final goals of the lords of the field and others.
The mantrin should worship even before the time of formal propitiation. Now, O Vāsava, listen to the characteristics of the mantras of Lokeśvara. (33–78)

Having condensed the vital breath (prāṇa), the Lord of the Earth (dhareśa), and bliss (ānanda) as they abide in their sequential order, and having placed them together with space (vyoman) at the crown of the head, one should then offer salutation to Indra. || 33-79 ||
This mantra has been declared as belonging to Indra; now learn from me those beginning with Pāvaka.
One should form the *piṇḍa* by means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), fire (*anala*), bliss (*ānanda*), and the pervasive one (*vyāpin*).
And with the deities Prāṇa, Kāla, and the others, as well as Vyāpin, one should offer the piṇḍa, saying "Obeisance to Agni" and likewise "Obeisance to Yama. (33-81)
That pervasive Lord Nara is the Piṇḍa; salutation to Nirṛti.
This is the mantra of the Lord of Yātudhānas; now learn that of the Lord of Waters.
The wise one should concentrate upon Prāṇa, Varuṇa, Ānanda, and Vyāpin as a single mass;
"Salutation to Varuṇa" is this supreme mantra of Varuṇa. (33–83)
The wise one should concentrate upon the subtle vital breath (prāṇa), as well as bliss and the all-pervading [self]. "Obeisance to Vāyu"—this is the supreme mantra of the Vāyava-tattva. (33–84)

Note: 69. *Oṃ syrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* and so forth are the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*). "Jāti" is said to be the limb. 71–73. *Oṃ oṃ oṃ guṃ gurave namaḥ*. *Oṃ oṃ oṃ paṃ paramagurave namaḥ*. *Oṃ oṃ oṃ pāṃ parameṣṭhine namaḥ*.
74, 75. Oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ ṭ-hmrūṃ svadhā to the ancestors (pitṛ), obeisance! 76, 77. Oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ āṃ to the primordial perfected ones (ādisiddha), obeisance! 79. Oṃ hlāṃ to Indra, obeisance!
80, 81. Oṃ hrāṃ, homage to Agni. Oṃ hmāṃ, homage to Yama. 82. Oṃ nḷṃ, homage to Nirṛti.
83. Oṃ hvāṃ, homage to Varuṇa.
84. Āṃ hyāṃ, salutation to Vāyu. (p.
123) One should merge the Root-mantra with Gharma, Aṃśu, Varuṇa, and Ānanda, together with Vyāpin.
"Salutation to Soma"—thus is the Saumya Mantra proclaimed. || 33-85 ||
One should then sequentially condense Sūrya, Ūrja, Vyoman, and Cakrin;
thereafter, "Obeisance to Īśāna" is the supreme mantra of Īśāna.
One should sequentially merge Prāṇa, Vaikuṇṭha, and Ānanda with Vyāpin;
thereafter, "Salutation to Ananta"—this is the mantra of the King of Serpents (Nāgarāja).
One should sequentially merge Prāṇa, Kharva, and Ānanda with Vyāpin. "Salutation to Brahman" (brahmaṇe namaḥ) is the supreme mantra of Brahman. (33-88)
The *praṇava* comes first for all [mantras]; now hear [the sequence] of the weapons:
Anala, Janmahantṛ, Pradhāna, Anala, and Urjaka.
One should form the *saṃjñā* with the *sarga*; "Namaḥ" is the king of vajra-mantras.
Having removed the *ūrja*, that position is adorned with *māyā*. (33.90)
That very mass is the notion and the name; this mantra is Śakti, Time of unbroken stride, the Lord of the World, the Supreme Lord. (33.91)
Then, having condensed the mantra, this is the name-mantra: *namo daṇḍamanu*.
It is the Supreme Lord, the Master of the World, Time, who brings nourishment to the universe.
Then, having condensed them, this is the mantra of the name "Namaḥ Khaḍga":
the Moon, Śānta, Ādi-deva, and Sṛṣṭikṛt—these are the condensed [mantras]. (33.93)
"Salutation to Pāśa"—this is the wonderful mantra of the noose (pāśamantra).
These [syllables], namely Ajita, Varuṇa, Ānanda, Sṛṣṭikṛt, and Piṇḍita, are thus combined. (33–94)
"Salutation to the Banner"—thus is the banner-mantra proclaimed.
One should merge the unrestrained fires of the Supreme Self with those associated with the act of creation.
Salutations to Musala; this Mausala is the supreme Manu.
He is Anala, the destroyer of birth, and Udaya, endowed with the power of creation. || 33-96 ||
Then, having condensed [the essence], this mantra of the trident (śūla-manu) is: *Namaḥ*, joined with *Karāla* mounted upon fire (*anala*), followed by *odana* and *sṛṣṭikṛt*. (33.97)
Then, having condensed them, this very Saṃjñā uttered the names: "Salutation to Sīra, to Varuṇa, to Nara, and to Gopana joined with Sṛṣṭikṛt."
Then, having condensed [the preceding], this is the mantra for the lotus named Saṃjñā;
for all [of these], the Praṇava comes first. Now hear the mantra of Viṣvaksena.
One should sequentially merge Anala, Prāṇa, and Lokeśa with Vyāpin;
likewise, one should sequentially merge Varuṇa and Bhūdhara with Vyāpin.
This *piṇḍa* [mantra] bestows knowledge; thereafter follows the king of mantras of Viṣṇuvakṣeṇa.
This mantra, beginning with the *praṇava*, is declared to be the accomplisher of all aims. (33.101)
But that which was previously devoid of energy, by means of that very [energy] joined with bliss and so forth,
there shall be the formation of its limbs, endowed with the birth-signs (jāti-mudrā).
Commentary—85. Oṃ dhvāṃ, salutation to Soma.
86. Oṃ hcūṃ, salutation to Īśāna.
87. Oṃ hṇāṃ, homage to Ananta. 88. Oṃ hravāṃ, homage to Brahmā.
89. Oṃ rjmrūḥ, homage to the Thunderbolt (Kuliśa).
90. Oṃ jmrīḥ, obeisance to Śakti.
91. Oṃ ḍmūḥ, obeisance to Daṇḍa. 92. Oṃ ṭmrūḥ, obeisance to Khaḍga.
93. Oṃ ṭśāḥ, homage to the noose (pāśa). 94. Oṃ jvāḥ, homage to the banner (dhvaja). 95. Oṃ hrūḥ, homage to the pestle (musala).
96. Oṃ rjuḥ, homage to Śūla.
97. Oṃ kroḥ, homage to Sīra. 98. Oṃ vnāḥ, homage to Padma.
100. Oṃ rhūṃ vauṃ, obeisance to Jñānadā (the Bestower of Knowledge).
102. Oṃ rhrāṃ, obeisance to the Heart, and so forth. (p. 124) Root [Mantra]:
One should gradually merge Soma, Varuṇa, and Īkāra with Vyāpin; "Salutation to Surabhī"—this is the mantra preceded by the Tāra (Om). (33.103)
The mantra of Surabhī is declared to serve the purpose of fulfilling all enjoyments;
at the end of the two *praṇavas*, one should extract the two *tārikās*.
Thereafter, by my grace, Paramadhāmā remains here;
and when one is intent upon spiritual application (*abhiyoga*), she likewise descends into this world.
In this context, the triad consisting of the word *abhimata*, the word *siddhide*, and then within the body of the mantra, the syllable *tāra* (om), *tārā*, and *namo namaḥ*. (33.106)
The forty-five-syllable mantra is for the purpose of invocation;
it consists of the Praṇava, the Tārikā, the three vital breaths (prāṇas), and then the three Vyāpina mantras. (33–107)
After reciting the three *tārikās*, one should utter the word "idam" three times;
then "gṛhāṇa" followed by the wife of Vahni (svāhā)—this is the mantra for the offering of enjoyment.
First, one should extract the syllable Oṃ; then Viṣṇu conjoined with Vyoma (Ha);
thereafter, one should extract Tārikā (Hrīṃ), and again Viṣṇu in that same manner.
Then [one should utter] the *prāṇa* joined with *vyoman* and endowed with the name *soma*; then the *praṇava* directed toward the Supreme Lord who is beyond the beyond. 33-110.
The *tārikā* and the word "namaḥ" at the end constitute this mantra for propitiation: first the *praṇava*, then the *tārikā*, and then the word "bhagavatī. (33.111)
"O you whose form is the mantra, may I then attain my own state; that duality—having uttered 'forgive me' twice, [reciting] 'Tārā, Tārā, salutations, salutations'. (33.112)
"Vaisarjana-manu" and "so'yam"—these are the leaders of mantras, O tiger among gods; they have been declared as the removers of all sins and impurities. (33.113)
And these should never be given to those who are not devotees, nor to those of cruel deeds, nor to atheists, nor to the wicked, nor to rogues who delight in deception. (33.114)
Especially for my devotees, the faithful, those who practice faith and self-restraint, those intent on my lineage (or my ritual action), and those who have been consecrated.
This should be spoken to Vaiṣṇavas who have approached [the teaching] in truth and who rely upon firm faith; however, it is not to be spoken to others.
He who speaks otherwise than the truth out of delusion, greed, desire,
ignorance, or childishness, goes to many hells in succession.
Therefore, having observed all the aforementioned collection of qualities, one should explain [the doctrine] to the seeker in accordance with the Dharma and according to the proper method.
Commentary: 103. *Oṃ svīṃ surabhyai namaḥ*.
104–106. *Oṃ oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ paramadhāmāvasthite madanugrahābhiyogodyate ihāvatarehābhimatasiddhide mantraśarīre oṃ hrīṃ namo namaḥ*. This is the invocation mantra (*āvāhanamantra*).

107, 108. *Oṃ hnīṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ hnīṃ hnīṃ hnīṃ, accept this, this, this, this *arghya*, svāhā*, and so forth. 109, 110. *Oṃ īṃ hrīṃ īṃ, O Supreme Goddess who transcends the *haṃsa*, be gracious; oṃ hnīṃ, obeisance*. This is the mantra for propitiation (*prasādana*). 111, 112. *Oṃ hrīṃ, O Blessed One, embodiment of the mantra, take your own place, take your own place; forgive me, forgive me; oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance, obeisance*. This is the mantra for dismissal (*visarjana*).
(125) Root-text: He who speaks unrighteously, or he who asks unrighteously—both of them go to a terrible hell for an inexhaustible time. (33.119)
O Vāsava, even if one were to give away the earth filled with jewels, it should certainly not be given to one who is not devoted, nor to one whose character has not been tested. (33.120)
"Thus, O Śakra, your devotion toward me is exceedingly great;
and because you have approached me here in truth, I am well pleased."
The treasury of mantras for the primary and secondary limbs (aṅga-upāṅga) and so forth has been revealed;
now listen to me as I speak of the treasury of mudrās.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Mantras of the Limbs and Sub-limbs," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Note:
119. In this regard, the statement of Manu should be kept in mind: "He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—one of these two dies, or incurs enmity" (2.111).
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter.
Chapter Thirty-four:
Śrī said: O Vāsava, I shall now proclaim the treasury of mudrās for the treasury of mantras.
By the mere knowledge of which, the most exalted accomplishment of mantra is attained. || 34-1 ||

The mantra-practitioner should indeed bind the mudrā at the time of bathing within the water, at the time of performing the self-assignment (nyāsa), at the end of the worship, and during the ritual procedure for the maṇḍala. || 34-2 ||
In the case of image worship, in the placement of mantras, in the arghya vessels, in the ritual feeding,
at the conclusion of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and when the mantra is situated within [the heart], || 34-3 ||
For the destruction of those who cause harm and for the pacification of all obstacles, one should place both hands facing forward, well-joined and fully extended. (34-4)
Facing each other, with the middle fingers joined and the others extended, they are formed by the group of arms directed toward one another.
Renowned as Mahāśrī, she bestows all auspicious fortune;
she is the liberator from all defects and the grantor of swift accomplishment. (34.6)
For a being who has become inert, there is indeed the awakening characterized by the emergence of sensation;
[this is indicated by] the left hand being extended upward with the fingers spread apart and held aloft. (34–7)
The fingers should be made with their tips slightly contracted; the thumb should be like a bridge, joined facing them among the fingers, with the middle finger [held] between them.
One should bind the Śakti-mudrā, which bestows happiness, facing the heart.
O highly fortunate one, these mudrās are worshipped by the assembly of yogins. (34.9)
But for her who abides in the supreme subtle state and bestows love upon me, behold the Yonimudrā of me who abide in the gross state. (34.10)
Having placed the two hands facing each other, well-joined and well-stretched out,
the two ring fingers are indeed reversed at the middle and at the base on the back.

Having placed [the hands] at the bases of the two index fingers, one should conceal them with those two; the tips of the two middle fingers and the tips of the remaining two [middle fingers], along with the pair of little fingers, are positioned in front.
With the backs of the hands joined together, the middle of the palms should be raised;
one should place the tips of both thumbs upon the first joints of the two middle fingers.
This mudrā, known as the Great Source (Mahāyoni), brings all under control;
this mudrā of mine has been demonstrated in three ways for each of the three types.
The mudrā known as Sūkṣmā is the power (śakti); its modification is described therein:
starting from the forefinger, each finger is joined one by one with the thumb like a bridge. (34–15)
O Purandara, these four mudrās are to be known by placing them upon the fingers; they belong to my Śaktis, Lakṣmī and the others.
Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā—these indeed are the divine powers (śaktis) of Umā;
with the right hand, one should form the fist-gesture (muṣṭibandha). || 34-17 ||
O best of gods, having placed the left thumb raised within [the palm] and facing the heart, this is the Hārda-mudrā, which increases the intellect. (34.18)
One should extend all the fingers and touch them with the thumb;
this shall be the Śairasī mudrā, which brings about the presence of the mantra. || 34-19 ||
Forming a fist with the index finger extended upward is known as the *śikhā-mudrā*; it strikes fear into all malevolent beings. (34.20)
One should always display this [mandala] for the destruction of root-faults and obstacles;
therefore, at the outset, one should diligently display it within the sacrificial chamber. (34.21)
When joined with the mantra, it effects the destruction of all obstacles;
the branches of both hands should be positioned facing each other.
When the two [hands] are joined at the middle starting from the wrist-binding, this becomes the Vārmāṇī mudrā; with it, one should touch both shoulders. (34.23)
It is indestructible by the assembly of the wicked, by spirits, vetālas, or yogins;
and at the time of performing the rite, this [mudrā] must be firmly bound by the mantra-practitioner with great effort.
The fingers of the two hands are interlaced and closed, with the backs of the hands facing outward;
the two index fingers are joined at their tips, forming an elevated hollow between them.
With the two thumbs joined at their bases and crossed with one another, this is the Cākṣuṣī mudrā; it should be bound near the eyes.
One should snap the threatening gesture with the thumb in the ten directions;
then, with both hands, one should gaze swiftly with the eyes.
This is renowned as the Astra-mudrā, the terrifier of the enemies of the gods;
it is designated as the mudrā of the limbs (aṅga-mudrās), the sixfold mudrā that accomplishes all goals.
Now, observe these mudrās for the three pairs of Upāṅgas:
one should join all four fingers situated on the right side together. (34.29)
One should likewise place the thumb across the base of those [fingers];
this is the mudrā for the secondary limbs (upāṅgas), and with it, one should touch each respective station.
Now, observe the mudrās for the ornaments and the mantras:
the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger are held in the center of the hand like a fist. (34–31)
Then, with both hands behind, the wise one should join the two fists together;
having extended the pair of index fingers, he should then join them at the tips.
Having reversed the tips of the thumbs and placed them between the two index fingers, this is the mudrā named Kaustubhī; now hear of this Mālā-mudrā.
Rotating from the neck down to the feet and up to one's own shoulders with both index fingers,
one should perform this auspicious gesture representing the forest garland (vanamālā) all at once.
One should interlace the eight fingers, excluding the thumbs, with their tips joined together; one should let the two arms hang down—this is the *vanamālikā* (garland) mudrā.
With the two thumbs joined at the sides and the fingers remaining spaced apart—
this is the Pāṅkeruhī mudrā, which increases nourishment and good fortune.
With the right hand turned upward, one should join the tips of the thumb and the little finger like a bridge; the remaining three fingers should be closely pressed together like a triple creeper.
This mudrā, with the fingers formed in the shape of contracted hoods, is the noose (pāśa). First, one should form two fists with the thumbs placed on the back of the hands. (34–38)
One should place the left hand facing downwards, and likewise the right hand upon its back;
this mudrā, originating from the tortoise and fire, belongs to the Śakti beginning with Ādhāra.
Of the left hand turned downwards, having bent both the ring finger and the index finger, one should place them well-positioned upon the back of the middle finger.
One should make the middle finger straight and facing downward;
then, one should firmly extend the little finger and the thumb.
This is the Anantāsana-mudrā; just as this Ananta has arisen, so too is this proclaimed as the foremost among all āsana-mudrās. (34–42)
The supreme power is undivided, designated as both the support and the supported;
it is the Kūrma-mudrā, and its unfolding is the Ananta-mudrā (or Nāmikā-ananta), whose essence is sound.
This should be constantly cultivated in this manner during the practice of sitting:
one should clasp both hands together in front with the two fists joined. (34–44)

(128) With the three fingers starting from the base, one should join the two thumbs and the two index fingers; having brought them together at their tips, one should then join that pair once more. (34–45)
This is that earth-mudrā, which sustains all beings;
the wrists are joined together, with the tips of the nails of both hands touching.
The ritual actions are performed with the fingers interlaced, facing one another;
one should move them rapidly between the tips of the thumbs, which are held without support.
One should make the middle of the two hands like a deep cavity resembling a hollow;
this is the Padmī mudrā of the Ocean of Milk, as previously shown.
Having first kept the two hands unjoined, one should then join them: the mouth to the mouth, and likewise the two index fingers and the two middle fingers in succession. (34–49)
Then, after that, one should place the face [of the hand] against the face [of the other], and the pair of thumbs against the tips of those respective little fingers.
This set of four mudrās corresponds to the fourfold [set] beginning with Dharma; likewise, there is a set of four mudrās for the fourfold [sets] beginning with Adharma. (34–51)
The *mudrā* of the lotus situated above that is the previously mentioned *pādmī*:
it consists of the joining of the index finger and the thumb of the right hand. (34–52)
Having performed that binding, one should then gradually expand it,
and once again make the collection of branches individually supine.
This is the mudrā of the three abodes; now hear that which pertains to the manifestation of consciousness:
one should make the two hands clearly extended in the form of a *añjali*.
This supreme mudrā, consisting of pure being (*śuddhasattva*), is the seal of the manifestation of consciousness;
thus, among the thirty-two mudrās, it is the destroyer of all defects. (34–55)
O Śakra, the ornaments, weapons, postures, and so forth have been shown to you;
now hear the ten mudrās of Kṣetreśvara and the others. (34–56)
Having grasped the collection of fingers with both hands,
one should press them together forcefully while keeping the two thumbs raised.
O Purandara, this is the mudrā of Kṣetrapāla, which destroys all that is evil; it is formed by placing both hands palms-upward and close together.
Having placed the entire group of fingers bent and positioned at the middle,
one should cause the two thumbs, having been brought down, to gradually attain clarity.
This mudrā of the seed-syllable Śrī has first been described to you;
having raised the index finger from the left hand, which is born from the seed-syllable Caṇḍa.
One should display that very same [mudrā] from the right hand for Pracaṇḍa;
having raised the middle finger from the left hand, that is the [mudrā] of Jaya.
It is proclaimed that [the mudrā] of the seed-syllable named Vijaya comes from the right;
know that the Gāṅga [mudrā] is formed by placing the ring finger from the left as before.
O Indra, the mudrā of the seed-syllable of Āmuṇa is said to begin with the right [hand];
the mudrā of Śaṅkhanidhi is said to be the little finger of the left hand.
Likewise, from the right hand of Padmanidhi,
that little finger [is to be grasped] with the right hand in a fist together with the thumb.
One should press the ring finger and the little finger of the left hand;
then, the middle finger should be applied to the back of those fingers whose tips have been exerted with effort.
And just as it appears with the form of a hanging hand, [one should hold] the little finger of the left hand not too close to the fist. (34.66)
One should contemplate it as having fangs with the side of the right thumb;
the left thumb and the other [the right forefinger] should be slightly oblique and clearly extended. (34.67)
Just as those two auspicious [tusks] are seen, resembling the ears of an elephant—this is the seal of Gaṇeśvara, which brings about the destruction of all obstacles. (34.68)
First, having joined the wrists of both hands together,
the pair of middle fingers should be raised from their tips so that they meet at the front.
Likewise, the pair of ring fingers and the pair of little fingers [should be joined];
having doubled the thumbs, one should bend them downward.
p. 129) At the root, one should slowly touch each of the palms of both hands; likewise, one should clearly and very widely separate the two thumbs. (34–71)
With both little fingers held level on the ground—
this is the Vāgīśvarī mudrā, which bestows the power of speech.
Having joined the two hands together in front and extended them, they should be applied to the forehead while the head is bowed down. (34.73)
This mudrā, which clarifies the mind, belongs to the triad beginning with the Guru;
it is formed by extending the right hand and then [arranging] the group of fingers.
Having slightly contracted the joined thumb and then fully extended it,
one should then gradually and slightly turn it sideways and subsequently face it downwards.
This mudrā is remembered as that which brings eternal satisfaction to the host of ancestors;
it always brings greater pleasure to the ancestors than a thousand śrāddha rites. (34.76)
It should always be made beautiful through effort during the worship of the ancestors;
one should place both palms turned upward at the region of the navel.
This is the mudrā of the assembly of the Siddhas:
the right hand is placed behind the left, well-touched, while one's own [other] hand is turned away. (34.78)
One should form the left hand turned away and hanging down;
these two mudrās, granting boons and fearlessness, are known as those of the World-Protectors.

With each individual mantra, one should sequentially display the [deities] beginning with Vajra, joined with their respective weapons, together with the previously mentioned Śaktis known as Astras. || 34-80 ||
Now, regarding the weapons of the World Protectors (lokapāla) when worshipped here in sequence:
the three fingers beginning with the little finger of the left hand are placed in the middle of one's own palm. (34–81)
Of those [fingers], from the thumb, the index finger should be raised at the back;
it is placed in the region of the bridge of the nose, and then with the right hand— (34.82).
Having formed a fist with only three fingers as before,
one should double the index finger and join it to the tip of the thumb.
The right arm raised like that wielded for the hurling of a discus—
this is the mudrā of Viṣvaksena, which severs all bonds.
One should slightly contract the right hand and bring it toward the heart;
with the two thumbs separated and clearly visible, this is known as the mudrā for invocation.
Both hands, with fingers slightly spread, should be shaped like the edge of a sword; having formed the thumbs like a staff, one should gradually perform the fist-binding.
One should perform [this] with the little fingers and so forth; this is the mudrā for dismissal.
Having made the two hands open and well-joined, with palms facing downwards... (34.87)
Likewise, having joined the two little fingers and the two thumbs so that they are well-joined,
one should place the pair of middle fingers against the backs of each other's hands.
Having inserted the pair of ring fingers and likewise the pair of index fingers,
this mudrā named Kāmadhenu fulfills all desires.
O Vāsava, know that the application of mudrās is of two kinds:
the internal, which is the form of consciousness itself, and the external, which is born of speech, action, and mind. (34.90)
Whoever, knowing the ritual procedure, binds the mudrā according to this method,
by him all this is sealed for the sake of achieving the state beyond rebirth.
Thus, O Purandara, the entire host of mudrās has been taught to you.
Now, for the sake of the section on propitiation, hear the supreme procedure for bathing.
Misfortune (alakṣmī) takes possession of one who is possessed of internal and external impurities;
for the purpose of warding it off, bathing is prescribed in all cases. (34.93)
Furthermore, that bath is threefold, according to the sequence of water, mantra, and recollection; O Puruhūta, this is remembered as being a hundred times superior in each successive stage.

The bath performed at sacred fords such as Puṣkara is considered to be of the nature of water; however, the bath prescribed by the scriptures of the Blessed One is a hundred times more meritorious than that.
Therefore, the power of mantra arising from the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the limbs of the body is a hundred times greater than that;
and supreme meditation, consisting of pure consciousness, is a hundred times greater than that.
p. 130) At the beginning, in the root [text], one should perform the water-bath according to the general rule; afterwards, according to the specific rule. Now, this is the specific rule: || 34-97 ||
Having first bathed with clay and water, one should afterwards apply fragrant unguents and the like;
that constitutes a bath which destroys impurity, and one should perform it along with breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform the filling with the *tārā* mantra twelve times;
one should hold it with sixteen repetitions, and then release it again with twelve.
By means of the sequences of exhalation through the left and right nostrils,
he destroys the impurities previously accumulated within the channels of the vital breath.

Then, having become composed of reality, one should purify the impure aggregate of elements— which consists of the six sheaths and is devoid of essence— by means of the power of meditative concentration (dhāraṇā).

All the principles (tattvas), beginning with earth, [which are the causes], each in its own cause—[one should] lead them to their dissolution in due order by means of concentrations (dhāraṇās), ending with the unmanifest (avyakta). || 34.102 ||
Then, one should merge oneself into me like milk into milk;
having subsequently become composed of Lakṣmī, one becomes identical with Nārāyaṇa.
Having attained the bond of concentration with a mind of pure essence,
that state which consists of the nature of the Supreme Self is considered the supreme power.
Remaining in that very state, one should burn one's own body with the fire of concentration (dhāraṇā)—
the mass of radiance of the flame of consciousness, which is the abode of sparks of light.
Then, one should meditate on a blazing mass [of light] falling upon the head;
thereafter, the true essence (sattva) residing within becomes tranquil, while rajas and tamas are reduced to ashes.
Having dispelled the ashes consisting of rajas and tamas by means of the wind of awakening,
[one emerges] from the great ocean of consciousness-bliss, which is a mine of qualities free from waves.
One should visualize the nectar-water spreading forth along the path of emanation;
by that, one should bring that internal essence, once nourished, to the state of a body.
That pure [soul] assumes a physical body through the process of creation;
this is called internal purity. Now, hear about external purity.
One should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) using the limbs according to the sequence to be described;
when external purification has thus been achieved, one should then perform the ritual bath (snāna).
Holding a portion of earth consecrated by mantras in his hand,
he should place it three times upon the tips of his left hand— at the root, the middle, and the tip.

First, one should perform the purification of the sacred site (*tīrtha*) by means of the nature of the power of consciousness (*bodhaśakti*). That sacred site is said to be threefold, consisting of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme self.
In its gross form, it satisfies the entire gross world;
but through its subtle essence consisting of *sattva*, it satisfies the ancestors along with the gods.
One should lead [the disciple] toward the state of fitness for my ritual action by means of the supreme form of bliss;
therefore, purification must first be performed personally at a sacred site (tīrtha) according to the vision of the scriptures.

Having drawn forth the Vaiṣṇava essence of the sacred sites by means of the retention of knowledge (jñāna-dhāraṇā), and having brought it into dissolution within me, who am the power, in the great abode of consciousness and bliss; || 34-115 ||
Having burned the gross [body] with the fire of knowledge, one should fill it with the bliss of Brahman;
then, having projected the Vaiṣṇava essence into the sacred ford by means of the power of knowledge.

The wise one should sequentially recollect the weapon mantra (*astra*), the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), and the limb mantras (*aṅgamantra*) upon the portions of earth in the first, middle, and final sections respectively.
One should cast the weapon-mantra in the ten directions for the pacification of all obstacles;
one should cast a portion accompanied by the root mantra into the middle of the sacred water (tīrtha).
By that, may there be the immediate presence of me, whose form is the mantra;
with that portion of earth which is the mantra of the limbs, one should smear the limbs.
Having entered into the midst of the water, one should indeed dive and emerge again;
then, with both hands, one should first sprinkle upon the head the water over which the Astra-mantra has been recited.
The second [offering] is with the root mantra (mūlamantra), and the third with the limb mantras (aṅgamantra).
Then, having reached the bank and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) properly, one should proceed.
One should perform the ritual bath with mantras according to the rules through the rite of nyāsa;
thereafter, one should perform the bath of meditation (dhyānasnāna) with a mind that is fully attentive.
Having meditated upon the supreme Lakṣmīdhara, the lotus-eyed one who resides at the root of the sky,
one should recollect the stream born from the water of his feet as it falls upon one's head. (34.123)
With that [water], one who is composed should flood the entire body, both internally and externally,
either one by one, or in pairs, or even in threes.
According to one's ability and at the appropriate time, one should perform the threefold bath;
[one should worship] the gods who consist of me with their names, preceded by the syllable *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.
Then, having gratified the sages, one should gratify the ancestors at the conclusion of the *svadhā* offering.
Having thus performed the bath, one should then [worship] the Lord of Mantras situated at the sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
Then, having drawn [the weapon] with the *pūka* [mudrā], one should remember it within the heart;
and having mentally drawn back the weapon that was previously stationed in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

Having taken up the ritual implements for the sacrifice, one should proceed to the sacrificial hall—whether it be self-established, composed by a seer, or prepared by perfected beings (siddhas). (34.128)

Or else, a celestial chariot (vimāna) according to the Pāñcarātra tradition, complete with all auspicious characteristics, fashioned by humans or conceived within the minds of those whose inner selves are purified by me.
A beautiful lotus pond shore, a secluded and enchanting place, or a solitary garden adorned with sacred trees. || 34-130 ||
Or a delightful sandy bank, spread out upon the sand, free from wind, untouched by the spray of water, and devoid of nearby defects. (34.131)
Or rather, wherever the mind finds pleasure, there one should go by the power of the mind—to the supreme mantra abiding in the center of the heart, whose form is awakened bliss. (34.132)
Not looking toward any direction, observing silence, and restraining his breath, he should reach a favorable position there and exhale through the tip of the nose.

Having performed the placement of the mantra of the Self (ātman), the Supreme Self (paramātman), and the form of blazing fire, as well as the external weapon-mantra, one should strike the earth with the foot.
Meditating upon me alone as the Supreme Goddess, whose nature is mantra,
one should go to a secluded place and assume a comfortable posture.
On darbha grass, a hide, a cloth, or on a plank made of sacrificial wood,
having saluted Hari, me, and the lineage of gurus with devotion alone— || 34.136 ||
Having received their mental command, bowing his head to them,
he should perform all mental rites through the meditative absorption of gnosis.
Whatever action is performed with knowledge through the meditative absorption on Brahman,
that becomes composed of pure being (*śuddhasattvamaya*), imperishable, and eternal.
Since the defects characterized by passion (rājas) and darkness (tāmasa) depend upon external objects, their purification must therefore be accomplished through action, mind, and speech. (34.139)
Therefore, having firmly established that pure knowledge which arises from consciousness, which is entirely free from defects and permeated by meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), || 34.140 ||
"One should indeed perform actions that are ultimately real through the cultivation of knowledge.
Thus, O Lord of the Gods, the procedure for bathing has been correctly proclaimed to you;
hereafter, I shall describe to you the placement [of mantras] on the limbs and so forth, as well as the [proper] location.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Rules for Bathing," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Chapter Thirty-Five:
Śrī says— Listen to the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) for the sake of accomplishing the internal sacrifice and other rites.
O Śakra, listen with an attentive mind as it is being told by me.

The purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is said here to be the mental transformation into the nature of *man* (consciousness) of the primary elements, beginning with earth and ending with *ka*, as well as those beginning with *ka* and ending with *bha*. (35.2)

Regarding the eightfold nature consisting of earth and the rest up to primordial matter (prakṛti), the wise know that it possesses two forms through the distinction between the gross and the subtle. (35-3)

That which exists as the configuration within the range of the eye is described as gross form (*sthūlarūpa*); that wherein the nature of a cause resides is called a subtle element (*tanmātra*). (35.4)
This reality consists of sixteen principles divided into gross and subtle;
one should assign the objects, the senses, and their functions to their respective places therein.

The triad beginning with the nose and so forth, the triad beginning with the anus and the generative organ, and the triad beginning with smell and so forth— one should bring these three groups to quiescence in their respective order of reversal within the series of subtle elements, earth, and the rest.
Just as waves in the ocean subside due to the wind,
so do the surges of the sense objects and the senses subside within the great ocean of the primary elements.
In the same way, the wise person should bring that [mind] to its cessation through well-applied intelligence;
one should likewise bring both the mind and the conceit of "I" (abhimāna) to rest within the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). || 35-8 ||
