One should suppress the vital breath, the mental resolve, and the intellect within the principle of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*); one should then lead the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—into primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
That which is the unmanifest cause consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) of the great principle (mahat) and the rest—
namely, the triad of qualities, the productive power, and Māyā— that is indeed threefold.
Thus, these ten primal natures (prakṛtis) are to be known by those who know reality;
furthermore, through the distinction between gross and subtle, they are traditionally reckoned as twenty.

For the gross primordial natures (prakṛtis), these ten mantras are traditionally taught: they begin with the Tārikā and the Dhruva, end with "huṃ phaṭ," and are designated by their respective names. (35.12)
Commentary:

1. *Bhūtaśuddhi* (Purification of the Elements) is the purification of the elements constituting the practitioner’s natural body, which consist primarily of flesh, fat, and bone. This is for the purpose of attaining fitness for the worship of the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*). As for its method: having first contemplated the dissolution of those natural elements into their respective causes and offered them to the Blessed Lord, one then meditates on the persistence of the body commenced by them, preceded by the manifestation of non-natural elements consisting of the Blessed Lord from His presence. This *bhūtaśuddhi* is seen to be propounded in the various *tantras* by all Tantric practitioners according to their respective traditions.
2. Regarding "beginning with *ka* and ending with *bha*": by the letter *ka*, the earth (*pṛthivī*) is grasped, and by the letter *bha*, primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

7. He states the previously mentioned dissolution (*laya*) by way of illustration: "the waves," etc. 10. Regarding "the three qualities" (*traiguṇya*): the Upaniṣadic usage for these, in their respective order, is "Pradhāna," "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*), and "Tamas."

12. Regarding "those respective designations": first the *praṇava* (Oṃ), then the *tārikā* (Hrīṃ), then the designation of the element, then *huṃ phaṭ*. Thus, the mantra is: Oṃ Hrīṃ Pṛthivyai Huṃ Phaṭ. However, in the Jayākhyasaṃhitā (10.15), other mantras are prescribed in place of the *tārikā*:
"Having recollected the root [syllables]—flesh (*māṃsa*), fat (*medas*), and likewise taste (*rasa*)—and the three syllables of space (*vyomākṣara*). [C: and again the syllable of space]. Page 133.
Beyond that, there are two others, adorned with bindu and nāda. || 35-13 ||
Of the ten subtle forms, those nine beginning with Śakti are traditionally taught;
they are the powers known as "Supreme" (parā) which constitute the living principle within bodies. (35.14)
Thereafter, one should meditate upon these—Śakti and the others—conjoined with Māyā and Vyoman;
likewise, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti.
Śāntyatītābhimānā, Prāṇā, Guṇavatī, Guṇasūkṣmā, and Nirguṇā—these are recorded as their names in sequence. (35.16)
Having joined together the fire, Viṣṇu, and half-moon within that group of ten seed-syllables,
one should know these mantras as belonging to the presiding deities.

The glory of fragrance, the glory of taste, the glory of form preceded by touch, the glory of sound, the glory of self-conceit, and the glory of the vital breath preceded by the qualities. || 35.18 ||
In the same way, there are also presiding powers within my group of ten, known by the names Guṇasūkṣmā and Māyāśrī.
Having thus understood the preparatory ritual (parikara), one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
First, one should perform the purification of the place (sthānaśuddhi); listen now to how that is done.
Having meditated upon me, who possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns at the time of universal dissolution and resembles smokeless embers,
one shall consume the earth with the fire issuing from my mouth.
Then, one should sprinkle with water produced from the mouth, which has the luster of ten thousand moons;
in this way, the purification of the site is accomplished. Now, listen to the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having drawn the earth— square, level, yellow, and marked with the vajra—
with the mantra from within the body, one should cause it, while remaining in its own place, to undergo dissolution.

Then, having dissolved that [scent] into its own seed-syllable within the mere scent, one should dissolve that [seed-syllable] into myself, who have become the locus of empowerment, and cast me into the external water. (35.24)
By means of the mantra, one should lead that deity— which resembles the half-moon and is marked with a lotus—
to dissolution in its own place within the mere essence (rasa) by means of its own mantra.
Having established that [deity] with the mantra, one should cause it to dissolve into me;
then, one should cast me into the external fire—this is the sequence for the Āmāya rite.
A wise person should not perceive anything as manifold anywhere, for it is all dissolved within my power;
just as one might pour clarified butter into milk that has been produced by churning.
Clarified butter exists elsewhere than in milk, and that milk also exists elsewhere than in clarified butter;
in this way, the wise man should contemplate the powers presiding over the primary material cause (prakṛti).
Thus, one should meditate upon me as that supreme power, endowed with the nine powers,
whose nature extends to the end of the qualityless state, and who acts as the substratum of Māyā.
Having led the tenth [power] beyond that, he established the eleventh power,
which consists of great agitation, is the embodiment of prosperity, and takes the form of the manifestation of the cosmic array (vyūha).
Note:
15. He states the names of the life-forces (*jīvaśakti*) beginning with "Nivṛtti," etc.
17. Regarding "Vahni," etc.: the meaning is that one should join this syllable *rīṃ*.
18. *Gandhaśrī* and so forth are the names of the powers (*śakti*).
20. Regarding the word "previously" (*pura*): it means prior to the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
22. He describes the reanimation of the place thus consumed by fire with the words beginning with "Soma."

23. Regarding "by means of the mantra": here, the mantra *ślāṃ* is stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* (10.17). 26. Regarding "by means of the mantra": the mantra *ṣvāṃ* is stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*. "Up to *āmāya*" means up to the end of *māyā*. 27. Regarding "not one": the grammatical connection is that one would not perceive dissolution (*laya*) as being of a single kind everywhere. He states this very point by way of an illustration with the words "just as," etc. "Arising from its churning" is an adjective qualifying the clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*).
Having brought that eleventh stage, which is the twelfth stage consisting of the Supreme Self—
indescribable and incomparable— one should cast that twelfth stage into me. (35.31)
Thus, having raised that supreme power, which consists of all things and is twelvefold,
up to the end of the *dvādaśānta*, one should meditate upon it within me, who am composed of phonemes.

Resplendent with the brilliance of ten million fires, moons, and suns, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides, my subtle body consists of the phonemes and has the form of a continuous stream. 35–33.
For the benefit of all living beings, she who is composed of every kind of spiritual provision arose long ago from Viṣṇu, radiant like lightning from a cloud.
Śakra said:
"In which locations within this body should the dissolution be performed in sequence? And what are the forms of the elements, beginning with earth, within the lotus? Please tell me. (35–35)
Śrī said:
The place of earth is remembered as extending from the knees; that of water is up to the waist; the place of fire is up to the navel; and the place of air is at the heart. (35–36)

The abode of the ego (ahaṃkāra) extends from the ears up to the sky and down to the navel; the abode of the Great One (mahat) extends from the eyebrows up to space; and that which is beyond space is remembered as the Supreme.
Then, at the tip of the span-measure (prādeśa), four finger-breadths from the top of the head, is the location of Prakṛti; the remainder consists of the sixteen fingers. (35–38)
On the eleventh day of the two six-fold [periods], the abode of the glory of the syllable of reality (tattva) is a great square mandala,
the earthly form marked with a vajra.
That which resembles a half-moon, is white, and bears the mark of a lotus is known as the element of water;
that which is triangular, bears the mark of a svastika, and is red is said to be the element of fire. (35–40)
Smoke-colored, joined with six dots, and circular is said to be the wind element;
likewise, the space element is like the color of collyrium, known as the supreme, consisting of a mere disc.
Thus, when the summary of reality has been made, [the breath] which has arisen from the cavity of the heart, supported by the rope of knowledge, and following the middle channel (suṣumnā)— 35–42.
Having raised [the breath] upward as far as the knees by means of a series of steps of power (śakti),
one should cast it into me, who abide in the center, within the row of the *dvādaśānta*.
And at its end is a great lotus endowed with a thousand petals,
possessing the brilliance of ten million suns and the radiance of ten million times ten thousand moons.
Abiding within the union of Agni and Soma, my supreme body consists of great bliss; it is composed of pure consciousness and is beyond all comparison or description. 35–45.
Note: 32. Regarding "dvādaśānte": The traditional convention is that the place twelve finger-breadths above the head and above *māyā* is called *dvādaśānta*.
33. He specifies the body consisting of phonemes (*varṇamayīṃ tanuṃ*) with the words "fire," etc. Regarding "dhārāsaṃtāne": the meaning is "in the form of a continuous stream of nectar."

38. He states that the location of *prakṛti* is in space with the words "from there" (*tataḥ*). It is situated four finger-breadths above the head; this is the station of *prakṛti*. From there, sixteen finger-breadths further up is the station of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).

39. Eleven finger-breadths above that is the station of *māyā*. Twelve finger-breadths above that is the station of the Sound-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*); such is the distinction. This very point is called the "End of the Twelve" (*dvādaśānta*). 41. Regarding the phrase "mere image" (*bimbamātra*): it means that for *pradhāna* and the others, there is only their mere image, not their phonemes or other qualities.

43. "He should cast it into me": when there arises the possibility of imagining the burning of the living being (*jīva*) residing within the body upon the contemplation of the burning of the body, the casting of that *jīva* into the Goddess is stated in order to prevent this.
44. "At its end" means at the *dvādaśānta*. "The great lotus"—the word "exists" is to be supplied. (p. 135) Root-text:
From this [state], the excellent river Jīvānanda flows forth in part;
having brought this self-bliss, it leads one to the state consisting of great bliss.
Then, one should burn from all sides that mass, which resembles a heap of salt, with great, high-velocity flames consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmaya*) issuing from one's own mouth. (35–47)
The sixth [syllable] is Sarasaka, joined with a bindu and known as Dāhapāvaka;
it should be recognized by one with the eye of the scriptures as being situated between Tārikā and Nati. || 35-48 ||
Then, one should flood [the body] with nectars arising from my mouth which consists of the essence of Soma;
for the subtle Moon, together with the ether, is traditionally taught to be that which nourishes the physical body (piṇḍa). (35–49)
By me, desiring to create, consciousness—embraced by the vital breath—is raised up;
one should remember those powers of memory (smṛti) impelled [by it], which abide within me as consisting of phonemes.

Then, one should sequentially recollect that [universe], beginning with Māyā and extending down to the earth (kṣiti), was fashioned by those powers (śaktis) through the process of impulsion (codanā) and the gateway (dvāra).
Then, having thus produced the great *piṇḍa* consisting of pure *lakṣmī*, which is radiant with the organs and the marks, and from which the *piṇḍa* arises— || 35–52 ||
Then, by means of the previously mentioned path, one should bring the heart and the individual soul (jīva) [into the body].
The three syllables, formed into a single mass, are Fire, Moon, and the Moonlight.
The *jīvamantṛa* is declared to be situated between the *tārikā* and the *natimadhya*;
having thus purified one's own form, one should perform the ritual placement (*mantranyāsa*) of the mantra. (35–54)
For the sake of authorization in worship, for the delight of the worshippers, for the destruction of Daityas and other obstacles, and for the sake of victory; || 35-55 ||
The practitioner of mantra should contemplate five times that plank or similar object which was previously placed upon the ground, each with its own respective mantra.

One should meditate upon Garuḍa situated there— in the forms of the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), the tortoise (Kūrma), the earth (Urvī), the ocean of milk (Dugdhābdhi), and the lotus (Ambuja)— established as the essence of the seed-syllable Kharva (the syllable *haṃ*).
Having sat there and meditated upon his own form as the Lord of Lakṣmī,
he should bind the directions with the Astra-mantra, repeating this process again and again.
Having fashioned a rampart resembling a net of arrows outside the seat, one should enclose that place, together with its rampart, with the armor-mantra. || 35-59 ||
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in such a way that it remains invisible to those staying in the sky;
having first performed the placement on the hands, one should then perform the placement on the body.
One should place the *tārikā* on the thumb, and its powers (*śaktis*) on the fingers:
one should place Lakṣmī on the index finger, and then Kīrti on the middle finger. (35–61)
Note:
46. *asyāḥ* means "of this" [my] body (*tanvāḥ*).

47. When the *jīva* has been led out from the body and brought to the *dvādaśānta*, the contemplation of the burning of the body is described by the words beginning with "tataḥ" (thereupon). The phrase "resembling a heap of salt" (*lavaṇakūṭābham*) is a designation for the body whose *jīva* has been removed.

48. The mantra for the fire that burns [impurities] is stated: *hrīṃ rthūṃ namaḥ*. 49. Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the attainment of a non-material body, he says: "consisting of Soma. In this regard, the mantra is *ṭyaṃ*; however, in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, it is stated as *vsam* (10.78). 51. That which is the extremely subtle state of *māyā* as the primary principle (*pradhāna*), which the followers of the Upaniṣads call *tamas*.
53. Regarding the *jīvamant*ra, he says "become a single mass" (*piṇḍabhūtā*). [The syllable] *rṭsa* is thus produced. It is stated in exactly the same way in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*. 57.
"The seed-syllable *kharva*" means that which has the form of *kha*. 58.
"One's own form" (*svarūpa*) means "consisting of one's own self" (*svātmaka*), according to the principle stated as "they understand it as the Self."

59. With the *astra* [mantra], that is, with the *astra-mantra*, for the sake of valor, using the mantra "phaṭ"; likewise with the *kavaca* [mantra], that is, with the *kavaca-mantra*, for the sake of strength, using the mantra "huṃ. (p. 136) One should then place the *mūla* [mantra] on the ring finger (*anāmikā*) and the *jayā* and *māyā* [mantras] on the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*).
The sequence of those [mantras] consists of the perception of "sat" (being) and "tāra" (the Savior), which is extremely subtle. || 35-62 ||
Then, having sequentially assigned the five limbs, beginning with the heart, to the little finger and the other fingers, one should contemplate the eye within the [corresponding] limbs.

One should place the Kaustubha gem on the right surface and the forest garland (vanamālā) on the other; likewise, one should place a lotus in the middle of the right side and also on the left surface.
One should place the goad on the right and likewise the noose on the palm of the left;
by this procedure, one should first perform the placement of the hands.
Now, listen to how one should perform the ritual placement of the body (vigrahanyāsa), from the head down to the feet, and from the feet back up to the head.
Then he should place Tāraka and Tārikā— both of whom resemble moonlight—
upon his left shoulder, and Lakṣmī and Kīrti upon his right.
One should place Jayā in the right hand and Māyā in the left hand;
the heart-mantra between the eyebrows and the head-mantra on the crown of the head.
Having placed the *śikhā* at the location of the crest-lock and the *kavaca* on the two shoulders, one should then place the *netra* on the two eyes and the *astra* on the palms of both hands.

The best of those who know the mantras should correctly place the secondary limbs (upāṅgas) at the navel, the back, both hands, the thighs, the knees, and the feet, and [place] the three ages (triyuga).
Placing the Kaustubha gem upon his chest and the forest garland around his neck,
and resting his two hands upon lotuses, he should repeat the mantra in two ways.
Then, one should place the noose in the left hand and the goad in the right hand;
the gross and subtle Tārikā should be placed at the two feet and in the joints.
She is indeed the leader of the mantras, residing at the *brahmarandhra* at the end; with each placement (*nyāsa*), one should contemplate the mantra which resembles moonlight and sunlight. (35.73)
The practitioner should mentally visualize the mudrās in each respective place; he should contemplate that everything is pervaded by Tārikā, the supreme goddess. (35–74)
Having arranged all the mantras everywhere, as if they were submerged in water;
when the connection of the mantras following their various paths has been thus established— (35–75)
Just as the waters in the ocean become one, a single form is produced;
when the ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed in this manner, the practitioner of mantra becomes manifest as Lakṣmī herself.
By relying on the power born of meditative absorption, one shall partake in all authoritative capacities;
and for the meditator, the manifestation of all spiritual accomplishments arises. (35.77)
With his limbs thus placed, he may remain fearless even in a region crowded with the wicked;
he shall conquer untimely deaths and all calamitous afflictions.
Having duly placed the limbs [of the mantra] upon himself according to the ritual and the scripture with a focused mind,
the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon me, the Supreme Goddess, as that very body composed of mantra.
"I am that Blessed Lord Viṣṇu; I am the eternal Lakṣmī"—the yogi who possesses such a realization is never born again. (35.80)
Thus, O Śakra, this purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) has been described to you exactly as it is.
Now I shall speak of the internal sacrifice (antaryāga); listen to that according to its true nature.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Purification of the Elements," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra.
Note: 62. Regarding "satāra" and so forth: the meaning is that it is performed in the manner of "oṃ hrīṃ lakṣmyai tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ" and so on.
64. Now, the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa): by means of the verse beginning with "kaustubhaṃ," etc.; "madhyataḥ" means in the center of the palm.
66. He describes the placement of the deities upon the body (*dehanyāsa*) from the head down to the feet, and from the feet up to the head, beginning with the words "From the head" (*āmūrdhna*).
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter;
[now begins] the thirty-sixth chapter.
Śrī said:
O Śakra, that which consists of the bliss of Brahman and is worshipped within the heart with ultimate enjoyments—this is known as the internal sacrifice (antaryāga). (36-1)
Having assumed either the lotus posture, the svastika posture, or the yoni posture,
one should meditate upon the Śakti in the form of the Ādhāra between the navel and the genitals.
Above that [is] the Goddess, who cannot be established by anything else, formless, and consisting of light; and above her, the stainless Kālakūrma, whose body is radiant.
The supreme deity has the form of a tortoise and bears the conch, the discus, and the mace;
and above him is the lord of serpents, whose face resembles the full moon. (36–4)
One should bow to him who is higher than the highest, who is endowed with a thousand hoods, whose eyes roll with intoxication, and who holds a discus and a plow in his hands.
Above that, he beheld the goddess Vasudhā, resembling powdered saffron,
her body variegated with gold and jewels, and her face and eyes serene.
One should meditate on her with palms joined at the level of the head, recollecting the All-pervading Lord,
situated within the field divided into four parts between the navel and the genitals.
In this manner, one should contemplate these deities, beginning with the Power of the Support (Ādhāraśakti).
At the navel, one should meditate upon the Ocean of Milk, whose form is as white as a jasmine flower or the moon. (36.8)
One should meditate upon him who is radiant with rays from his eyes, whose face resembles the full moon, whose form is profound, who possesses form yet is formless.
Then one should meditate upon the lotus arisen from the interior of the Ocean of Milk,
having the appearance of a tranquil fire and the splendor of the rising sun.
With a protruding belly, laughing, possessing white teeth and a beautiful face,
he has two arms and is constantly surrounded by various auspicious six-legged insects.
Endowed with a thousand petals, surrounded by a thousand rays, and resembling a thousand beams of light—one should place the seat upon its back. (36-12)
One should meditate upon these as the feet of the seat, located in the cardinal directions starting from the southeast, in this sequence: Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya.
All these have the forms of men; they are white and lion-faced.
Possessing great energy and great heroism, they are intent upon upholding me. || 36-14 ||
The opposites of dharma and the other [qualities] are to be known as situated in the directions starting from the east; likewise, adharma, ignorance, non-detachment, and lack of mastery. (36.15)
These, having the form of men and resembling the bandhūka flower,
are located between the eastern and northeastern directions, that is, in the interval between the east and the southeast.
Note: 2. The location of the *ādhāra-śakti* is stated by the words "the navel," and so forth.
3. Regarding the phrase "above that": the meaning is the upper portion of the *ādhāra-śakti*.
4. "Of him" means upon the tortoise.
6. "Above that" means above the throne of the lord of nāgas.
7. "Recalling" means meditating.
12. "On its back" means on the back of the lotus. "One should place" means one should meditate upon that which has been placed.

13. The legs of the seat—namely Dharma, Jñāna, and so forth—are to be known as being in the intermediate directions, beginning with the southeast (āgneyī). 15. Their opposites—namely Adharma, Ajñāna, and so forth—are in the cardinal directions, beginning with the east (prācī).

p. 138) At the base, between Yātavī and Vāruṇī, and within the intermediate direction of the weapon of Paśi, there is a tetrad beginning with the Ṛgveda; it is yellow and has the form of a horse and a man. (36-17)
Between the directions of Īśāna and Soma, between the directions of Vahni and Antaka, between the directions of Rākṣasa and Antaka, and between the directions of Vāyu and Soma. (36–18)
The series of Yugas beginning with Kṛta is dark, having the form of a bull and a man;
all of these have four arms, and likewise, they hold a pedestal with two [hands].
With two hands joined in añjali, they bow to her as she sits upon her seat;
one should contemplate above them a supreme pedestal consisting of pure intelligence.
One should visualize an unmanifest white lotus above that with eight petals;
and above that, a solar disc possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Above that is the lunar disc, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons;
above that is the disc of fire, possessing a radiance of ten billion fires.
One should contemplate these qualities—tamas, rajas, and sattva—in their respective order;
for the Praṇava and the bow, the names corresponding to those [qualities] are placed in the middle. (36.23)

The groups of mantras are known to extend from the principle of intellect (buddhi) up to the principle of pure being (sattva). Thereafter, one should offer the seat of consciousness (cidāsana), which has the nature of supreme egoity (parāhaṃtā).
When the space from the navel to the heart is divided into five parts,
one should arrange the sequence beginning with the oceans and ending with the seats using four of those parts.
By the fifth [syllable] alone, one should conceive of the lotus seat and so forth;
the elements, however, are placed upon the Support-Energy (ādhāraśakti), and the group of subtle elements (tanmātraka) upon the Tortoise (kūrma).
One should meditate on speech and the other [organs] in Ananta; likewise, the five beginning with hearing on the earth; the mind in the Ocean of Milk; and then the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) in the lotus.
Twice eight [sixteen] are the primary qualities (dharmas) and so forth; the seat is also said to be the intellect (dhī).
Above that is the unmanifest (avyakta), and there stands a pure lotus.
For the qualities beginning with darkness (tamas) have been declared to consist of the three lotuses;
some say this [time] consists of the triad beginning with the unmanifest (bhūtādi).
Some have declared that the person is the seat of consciousness called Ananta; others describe Garuḍa as being above the seat of consciousness. (36–30)

O Lord of the Gods, the wise declare that mantra to be the ninth, consisting of *kha*, *ra*, *va*, *vi*, *o*, *m*, *a*, *n*, *vi*, *taṃ*, followed by *kha*, *ga*, *ā*, *na*, *na*, *ma*, *yo*, *yu*, *taṃ*. (36–31)
When the seat has been prepared in this manner through various mantras in due order,
one should [worship] the god Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe, Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all affliction.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Self, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
four-armed, clad in yellow garments, with eyes resembling the white lotus.
One should recollect the arisen God from the vibration of one's own power;
understand from me further how that which is to be properly meditated upon is exactly as it is. (36.34)

Note: 17. The direction of Nirṛti is the southwest. Pāśin is Varuṇa. 20. Regarding "by two": the word "arms" (*bhujābhyām*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding "with joined palms" (*añjalibaddhābhyām*): the meaning is "with [hands] in the *añjali* gesture."

23. One should know that the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire consist respectively of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*. The mantras are "Oṃ, salutation to the orb of the sun," and so forth. 25. Having divided the portion from the navel up to the heart into five parts, one should first meditate upon the seat beginning with the Ocean of Milk within the first four parts.

26. In the fifth part, however, one should meditate upon the unmanifest lotus (*avyaktapadma*). Regarding the location of the constituent elements in the aforementioned places, he says "the elements" (*bhūtāni*); this means the five gross elements.
28. *Avadātam* means a white lotus, that is, an unmanifest lotus (*avyaktapadma*).
29. This refers to the unmanifest lotus (*avyaktapadma*). In the *Pārameśvara-tantra* (5.14), it is designated as the "Wheel of Time" (*kālacakra*).
31. *Kham*: Homage to the one with the face of a bird (*khagānana*).
33. Here, the scriptural statement, "His eyes are like a lotus with petals as yellow as a monkey's bottom," serves as an elaboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the meaning.
Root Text:
Having properly applied the mantras to his limbs (or all his limbs), and having well-prepared the internal seat;
Having displayed all the mudrās, he should recollect the majesty of the mantra.
The Supreme Brahman, the supreme abode situated beyond darkness,
is that splendor Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa existing in the state of both the possessor of power and power itself.
He is everything, transcending all, abiding in all, and the sustainer of all;
he is a mass of consciousness and bliss, whose form is the nectar of the six perfections in their fullness.

As the inner self of all entities— whether they be of the nature of consciousness or matter, existence or non-existence, and so forth— it is the locus for each respective expression of the "I-consciousness" (ahaṃkāra).
By means of some cause that is inconceivable and beyond questioning,
it exists in two ways through the relationship between the possessor of power and the power itself.
That which is expressed by the duality of the word and its cognition as "I" shall become Nārāyaṇa; and that which is his supreme egoity (ahaṃtā) [is likewise he].
That Lakṣmī, who possesses those attributes, is Śakti; she is of the nature of existence.
She alone is the performer of all actions, and that very Śakti expands the universe.
Having taken recourse to the Possessor of Power (Śaktimān), just as moonlight rests upon the cold-rayed moon,
she indeed formerly desired to expand herself in the form of the Śabdabrahman.
Then, having expanded herself, she extends [herself] by way of the objects of meaning;
that which was previously composed of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman) is what first arises as Name.
Free from blemish, consisting of the path of the arts (kalā), it is experienced by those established in yoga as the nature of the Self;
that which consists of the sequence of the stream of phonemes is called the Path of Phonemes (varṇamārga). || 36–44 ||
Having presided over the path of the *kalās*, he then rises again by way of the path of mantras,
taking with him the entire wheel of Vaiṣṇava power (*śakti*).
The supreme light, characterized by bliss, which is both other than the self and the self itself, has been described to you previously in its threefold form. (36–46)
That very supreme form then proceeds by way of a subtle path in the form of the expansion of mantra; and that shall be shown to you.
That subtle [body] further exists in three ways through a gross path;
and that which is the gross body is the one distinguished by its limbs and minor members.
This is the form of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, augmented by the six divine qualities;
herein, indeed, the entire universe of sentient and insentient beings is to be contemplated.
The bestowing of various sovereign powers and the presiding over them—this indeed is the Vaiṣṇava form of the mantra, which should be understood by the wise. (36–50)
That power of his which performs those various functions is I, the Lotus-born;
for that which is the consciousness of the mantra, they declare to be the Person (Puruṣa).
The capacity for the production of fruit is called the natural form (*prakṛti-rūpa*); that which is firm resolve is the quality (*guṇa*) belonging to the Great One (*mahat*). (36–52)
Note:
37. The meaning is that he possesses all forms because he is the inner self of all and the controller of all.
38. That very point is expressed by the phrase beginning with "as the inner self," and so forth.

42. By stating that the Goddess’s agency in the cosmic process (*jagadvyāpārakartṛtva*) exists only by depending upon the Lord and not independently, it is shown that there is no inconsistency in the Lord’s unique defining characteristic (*asādhāraṇalakṣaṇa*), namely His being the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe. It is thus stated that the Lord is the instigating agent (*prayojakakartā*) and the Goddess is the executed agent (*prayojyakartrī*). By this, there is no room for the suspicion that this Pāñcarātra doctrine enters into the fold of the Śākta school. 44. "The path of *kalā*" consists of the qualities such as the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and so forth. "Stream" (*dhārā*) means a continuous flow; this is the indication of the "path of phonemes" (*varṇādhvan*). 45. The "wheel of powers" (*śakticakra*) consists of Lakṣmī and the others.

49. Here, however, the meaning is "in the gross form consisting of mantra. 50. With the words beginning with "tattad" (that and that), he describes the abiding of all the principles (*tattva*) within the mantra-form. 52. Of the "Great" (*mahat*), that is, of the principle of the Great (*mahattattva*).
The sense of "I" in the root-mantras is the quality of egoism (ahaṃkāra);
the mental form of the mantras is the cause of sensory cognition. (36.53)
That which is the nature of sound within the mantra should be known as abiding in the ether;
trembling upon the immersion into the mantra is said to be the form of air. (36–54)
The state of being a light-maker in meditation is that which consists of the mantra and the nature of fire;
that which is satisfaction in the true essence of the mantra should be understood as being in water.
For whatever state resides in the mantra is said to be the earthly quality;
thus the practitioner of mantra should clearly recollect this all-pervading extension of the mantra-nature. (36–56)
Soon, through the power of the mantra and by that very disposition, he is born;
thus, through the power of consciousness, the pervasive energy of the Tārikā [arises]. (36–57)
One should first perceive the throbbing [consciousness] within the cave of the heart-lotus, in the previously mentioned manifestation of consciousness, like a flash of lightning in the sky. (58)
While the form of Tārikā is vibrating within the Śabdabrahman, one should recollect the eternal, divine couple; understand this correctly as it is. (36–59)
One should remember the flawless Nārāyaṇa, whose form consists of the rays of the sun and fire, seated upon the throne of consciousness, with eyes as broad as lotuses.
Clad in yellow garments, with noble limbs, adorned with a girdle and anklets,
and radiant with necklaces, earrings, armlets, a crown, and bracelets.
Or he may have a splendor conforming to the age (yuga), or resemble a blue garment;
he is the god who holds the conch and the discus, bestowing the boons of granting wishes and fearlessness.
Like a gem filled with its own radiance, like the ocean in its profundity,
like the sun in its brilliance, and like the moon in its moonlight.
Having first meditated upon Hṛṣīkeśa, whose lotus-face is serene,
one should worship Puruṣottama with the eighteen offerings.
Then, O Vāsava, [one should worship] with the Puruṣasūkta, the Praṇava,
and likewise with those consisting of twelve, six, four, three, and two syllables, as well as with the "jitaṃ te" mantra.
Then, having worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should meditate on Lakṣmī as pervading all limbs;
having worshipped her with a mind of absorption, one should then invoke Lakṣmī.
Then, one should worship her as she sits on the left lap of the Lord who bears the Śārṅga bow,
with various enjoyments as prescribed by the scriptures in the proper manner.
Śakra said: O beloved of the gods, O goddess of gods, salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one!
Tell me the ritual procedure for the Puruṣasūkta and for the Tārā-mantras and others.
Śrī said: "The one god Nārāyaṇa is glorious and lotus-eyed;
I alone am the supreme Śakti of Hari, the accomplisher of all his tasks. (36.69)
We two, the lords of all, are seated in the supreme ether for the welfare of all beings,
and are always served by the wise.
A certain resolve arose in the hearts of those two:
"Let a means be sought for the deliverance of living beings."
Note:
57. "By that state" (tena bhāvena) means by those respective attributes (tattaddharmeṇa).
58. "As previously stated" (pūrvokta) means as stated on the occasion of the exposition of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) and so forth.
59. By this, it is stated that the Tārikā is of the nature of Śabdabrahman (the Absolute as Sound).
60. To describe the mental worship of the Supreme Person named Nārāyaṇa, he states his form with the words beginning with "sūrya" and so forth.

65. Regarding "dviṣaḍ" and so forth: the meaning is by means of mantras consisting of six, eight, and twelve syllables; and by the mantra in the form of the verse beginning with "jitaṃ te puṇḍarīkākṣa" (Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one), and so forth.
p. 141) Root-text:
The great ocean of the Śabdabrahman is the splendor produced by us two;
from that ocean, as it was being churned, the nectar of the two hymns emerged. (36.72)
The hymn of Puruṣa and the hymn of Hari, as well as my own hymn,
are mutually infused with power and adorned by one another’s syllables.
The hymn to Puruṣa is held to have Nārāyaṇa as its seer and is unmanifest;
other hymns are said to have Madhucchandas as their seer, such as that which is called the Śrīsūkta. (36–74)
The five mantras beginning with the Praṇava have been correctly demonstrated previously;
now hear, in brief, the sequence for their worship.
Eighteen verses have been proclaimed in the Puruṣa-sūkta, the most excellent of hymns;
by means of those [verses] preceded by the Praṇava, one obtains eighteen supreme enjoyments.
One should perform the rites beginning with invocation; these are recorded as eighteen:
invocation, the seat, the offering of water (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and likewise water for sipping (ācamana).
Bathing, clothing, along with an upper garment and a sacred thread; perfume, flowers, a lamp, incense, and the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka). || 36-78 ||
The offering of sweet betel-leaves with a moon, a handful of flowers at the feet, the gift of self-offering, and the contemplation of one’s desired abode. (36–79)
Endowed with all auspicious marks, consisting of the support of all things, supreme, eternal, and complete with the six divine qualities— that is the radiant form of Viṣṇu.
This very form is called the "mantric form" (māntrī mūrtiḥ), because by means of mantras whose essence is consciousness,
the practitioner of mantra causes the deity to accept that [form] through his own splendor.
This is called "invocation" (āvāhana) by those who have reached the further shore of mantra-knowledge;
for Hari, by his very nature, effects well-being for all that is conscious and unconscious. (36.82)
That which presides over the entire universe is the seat; following that is the ritual action.
My power consists of bliss, by which the God is nourished. (36.83)
That very [power] takes the form of the arghya, ācamanīya, and so forth; thus one should contemplate the arghya and other offerings.
All the worlds and all living beings are dependent upon it [as its support]. (36–84)
By the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), it is illuminated that both [the Lord and the devotee] share in the remainder of that [offering], which is the joy of both.
Having divided my own form into six parts, I satisfy the Eternal One. (36.85)

By means of the five objects of experience, beginning with sound, as well as through internal conceit, and by enjoyments such as those pertaining to this visible world whose true nature has been fully entered into; (36-86)
One should propitiate the Lord of the World with a mind full of vigilance;
those for whom pleasure is produced by the mere sight [of him] are considered *sāṃdṛṣṭika* (those who find joy in the present). || 36-87 ||
Note:
73. "My *sūkta*" means the *Śrīsūkta*.
74. "Nārāyaṇa" means that Nārāyaṇa is the *ṛṣi* of the *Puruṣasūkta*. "Madārṣakam" means that Śrī Rāma is the *ṛṣi*.
75. "The five" means Tārā, Anutārā, Ṣaḍakṣarā, Aṣṭākṣarā, and Dvādaśākṣarā.
79. "Prāpaṇa" refers to food offerings such as rice and the like; "indu" refers to camphor. 82.
"Āvāhayati" means she causes [the deity] to accept the mantra-body; this is the etymological meaning.

84. "She herself" means that she is indeed the power consisting of bliss (*ānandamayī śakti*). This is because it is stated that all worlds have her as their material cause, based on the scriptural declaration: "In the beginning, he created the waters alone, which are of the nature of water, being the transformations of water. "Dependent upon her" means those who sustain life by means of water. The statement regarding their dependence on her is made because living beings (*jīva*) are not themselves transformations of water.

85. The meaning is: "I myself, in the form of sound and so forth, worship the Blessed Lord. 87. He describes the enjoyments (*bhoga*), divided into four types—visual, gustatory, tactile, and mental—beginning with the words "by sight alone," and so forth.
The primary auspicious signs are those characterized by a preponderance of form, such as lamps, boats, and the like;
these are the enjoyments that constantly bring about welfare, for they satisfy one with their essences. (36.88)

Those waters for drinking, rinsing the mouth, and so forth, which are conducive to consumption, pleasant, delightful, and soft to the touch—those which satisfy the Unborn (Aja) with their tactile sensations; 36-89.
Those enjoyments consisting of touch should be preceded by water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and a seat;
some of those consisting of touch are fragrances, while others are edible.
The winds and other elements are established in their respective orders; the last [elements] possess the fragrance of what is produced by ripening.
Indeed, those enjoyments consisting of sound—such as hymns of praise, instrumental music, and songs—are of the nature of sound.
Those who offer their palms joined in supplication out of wretchedness and so forth are known as those possessed of pride (ābhimānika).
Thus, by means of these four kinds of offerings, according to the path seen in the scriptures, || 36-92 ||
One should gratify Puruṣottama with Ṛg-verses preceded by the Praṇava;
at the end of the mantra, there is the assignment of enjoyments, and immediately thereafter, satisfaction. (36.93)
Having uttered the syllable *oṃ* and performed worship, and having recited the five [mantras] beginning with the *praṇava*,
I invoke Lakṣmīśa, the imperishable Supreme Self.
May the divine Lord of the World, the Supreme Person Nārāyaṇa, together with Śrī, assume this form out of a desire to show me favor. (36.95)

Having thus brought [the deity] down from the flowers held in his joined palms into his own form, and having prostrated and asked about his welcome, he should ask for forgiveness with this thought: || 36-96 ||
Having prostrated before the Blessed One, I thereafter honor him with a seat;
having spoken the mantras and uttered them, one should then indicate this by saying "this" three times. || 36-97 ||
Afterwards, having specified the name, one should then express the wish for favor;
thereafter, one should say, "May the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva be pleased. (36.98)
One should pour out the *arghya* upon the altar; this is the sequence for the ritual of enjoyment (*bhoga*).
One should prescribe the seat, the *arghya*, and so forth among the objects of enjoyment according to their respective characteristics (*liṅga*). (36–99)
One should perform the invocation with the first [verse] and the offering of a seat with the second;
the *arghya* water, drawn up together with flowers, should be offered upon the head with the third.
Water for the feet (pādya) should be offered with the fourth [mantra], water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) with the fifth;
the ritual bath (snāna) should be performed with the sixth, and the lower garment (paridhānaka) with the seventh.
On the eighth day, the upper garment; on the ninth, the application of fragrant unguents;
on the tenth, garlands and ornaments; and on the eleventh, the lamp.
On the twelfth day, fragrant incense; on the [next] day, the supreme honey-mixture (madhuparka);
on the fourteenth day, the offering of food (prāpaṇa); and on the fifteenth day, the anointing (anuvāsana).
With the sixteenth [verse], however, there is salutation; with the seventeenth, the offering of a handful of flowers (kusumāñjali);
and with the eighteenth, the presentation of the rite of propitiation.
One should provide water for bathing, garments, and lamps, as well as the act of offering water for sipping (ācamana).
First, the honoring (arhaṇa) should be performed by means of the gift of honey-mixture (madhuparka) and food. || 36.105 ||
After the libation and the sipping of water, one should perform [the rite] with two *praṇavas*.
Thus, in the case of bathing and other such activities, according to the requirements of place, time, and so forth.
The practitioner should perform the conduct like that of a king with the respective mantra;
there are three triads: resolve, offering, and gratification.
Note:

94. "The five beginning with the *praṇava*" means the mantras consisting of the *tāra*, the *anutāra*, the six-syllabled, the eight-syllabled, and the twelve-syllabled [mantras]. 96. "In one's own form" means in a form imagined by oneself.
98. *Sanāma* means preceded by the designation of the names of the objects of enjoyment, in the manner of "this is this, this is the water for washing the feet," and so forth.
100. He states the application (*viniyoga*) of the verses of the *Puruṣasūkta* in the offering of enjoyments with the words beginning "by the first [verse]," etc.
103. *Anuvāsana* refers to fragrant betel leaves and the like, which are to be given after the meal.
105. *Arhaṇa* is the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*āpośana*).
(p. 143) One should perform the root [mantra] in all enjoyments, taking into account the place, time, and other relevant factors.
Being composed, having joined his palms in *añjali*, he then said: "O Blessed One! (36-108)
Having said, "I shall honor [you] with a seat," one should then offer the seat;
having recited the mantra, one should point it out, saying, "This is the seat. (36.109)
Saying, "Oṃ, may the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva be pleased," and taking the water for the *arghya* and other offerings, he should place it in the presence of the deity.
With these [waters] for the arghya, and likewise with these for the pādya, with these for the ācamanīya, and also with these for the arhaṇīya. || 36-111 ||

With words such as "these waters are for satiation" and "these are for bathing," one should express the intention of pleasure; and with words such as "these are for the arghya offering," one should express the intention of satisfaction. (36.112)
The formula to be recited at the time of offering should correspond to the gender [of the recipient]; this is the sequence.
Furthermore, the preparation of the *arghya* and other offerings will be prescribed later in the context of the external sacrifice.
Thus, with the six [offerings] beginning with the garland, one should worship Janārdana,
the God of gods, with five, four, three, or even two [of them].
Or, having propitiated [the deity] alone according to the requirements of place and time,
one should meditate upon Janārdana, the God of gods, as being worshipped by me alone.
Like the ocean at the rising of the moon, she was fully developed in all her limbs;
she was forever destined to be indescribable, incomparable, and infinite.
Like fragrance residing in a flower or light residing in a lamp, I am inseparable from the Supreme Person; it is impossible to extract me from him, for I am non-different from him.
Meditating according to the rule, the mantra-practitioner should worship me through the yoga of dissolution;
having sought the procedure for the *tārikā*, he should worship me as that *tārikā*.
Then, the wise one, having mentally visualized [the goddess] emerging from Puruṣottama by His will, like lightning flashing forth from a cloud, || 36.119 ||
One should contemplate me seated on the left lap of the God of Gods, knowing our two natures to be unified and perfectly cool. (36.120)
One should take refuge in Janārdana with the two verses beginning with "hiraṇya," and one should console her with the following two verses: "Console me, who am as yet not separated from you. (36.121)
And with the fifth [syllable], one should enter while contemplating her with a clear mind, having understood the actual power of the Tārikā as previously described. (36.122)
O Lord of the Gods, the mantra known as "invocation" (āvāhana), when accompanied by its corresponding mudrā, should be recited mentally while performing inhalation (pūraka).
Then the God shall carry me upon his lap, the lap of the Supreme Self—
me, whose face is ever serene and who am marked by all auspicious characteristics.
Resembling the interior of a lotus, lovely, with dark and long eyes,
and adorned with shimmering bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and earrings.
She has a deep navel, her slender waist is adorned with three folds, and she possesses breasts that are very firm, hard, high, full, rounded, and dense. || 36.126 ||
Her mass of hair was overspread by a swarm of moving bees, her bimba-like lower lip was slightly reddened, and her teeth were like bamboo seeds and pearls. (36.127)
She wore a shining forehead ornament upon her brow shaped like a half-moon;
she was endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed dark, curly hair. || 36.128 ||
Bestowing boons, with hands holding a lotus, adorned with a garland of lotuses, she is embraced by Viṣṇu’s left arm, her lotus-hand resting upon his shoulder. (36.129)
Note:
111. In the passage beginning with "ābhirarghyābhiḥ" (with these waters of honor), the substantive "adbhiḥ" (with waters) is to be supplied from the subsequent sentence.
114. The meaning is "with the six," namely: the garland, the lamp, the incense, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), the food offering (prāpaṇa), and the anointing (anuvāsana).
116. "Anaupamyām" means incomparable (*anupamā*). "Aupamyam" is simply "comparison" (*upamā*); the suffix *pyañ* is used here in the sense of the base word itself.
117. "Viniṣkraṣṭum" means to cause to emerge or to draw out. 120. "Aikadhyam" means being of one kind or uniformity.
121. "With two *ṛc*s" means with the two verses beginning "hiraṇyavarṇām" and "tāṃ ma āvaha. 127. "Dvijāḥ" refers to the teeth.
128. "Lalāṭikā" refers to a forehead mark (*tilaka*); the suffix *-kan* is used here in the sense of an ornament.
(144) According to the Root [Tantra]:
"She carries a divine cluster of blossoms with her left arm;
she may have hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, or she may hold a noose and a goad. (36.130)
Having meditated upon me, who am seated in the half-svastika posture and adorned with a shimmering crown, one should bring face-to-face that eternal form which is the embodiment of the mantra.
Furthermore, with all the mantras beginning with the root mantra as before,
one should perform the deposition upon the body (*dehanyāsa*) upon me, omitting the deposition upon the hands (*karanyāsa*).

Then, with a truly respectful mind, one should offer flowers, the water of honor (arghya), as well as a lamp, incense, garlands, ointments, water for the feet (pādya), and water for sipping (ācamana).
Then one should perform prostration with the eight limbs, offer mental shouts of "Victory!",
and display those mudrās which were previously shown.
Welcome to you, O lotus-eyed one; take up residence with me, O lotus-born goddess.
Accept this mental worship, which is contemplated according to its true meaning.
Having then obtained permission from me, one should perform the mental sacrifice with pure,
ultimate enjoyments produced by mere resolve.

One who is well-versed [in the teachings] should worship me perpetually through the external ritual procedure to be described hereafter, with enjoyments such as those pertaining to touch and so forth. (36.137)

Having performed the ritual up to the point of the final attainment, he should then remember his Guru—the agent of the rite—whether he be living or deceased; thereafter, he should offer everything to him.

The knower of mantras should distribute his wealth according to the portion for guests, whether for those still living or for those who have passed away, with a mind focused solely on the purpose [of the rite]. (36.139)
One should remember all the attendants who will be described in detail,
as being dissolved within me, their cause, like seeds within a tree.
One should worship by means of the application of the respective mantra through the process of dissolution;
one should perform the auspicious oblation in the kitchen, which bestows the fortune of liberation. (36.141)

Having churned the fire-drill of meditation within the triangular fire composed of the three qualities, situated in the center of the support of the three qualities, and having brought down the fire of consciousness; || 36-142 ||

Having consecrated [the fire] with the ritual purifications (saṃskāras) according to the wisdom to be described, the wise one [should offer oblations] into the Vaiṣṇava Jātavedas (sacrificial fire) which has entered the locus of the three characteristics.

Having taken the sacrificial oblation of Brahman that has flowed forth from the space at the end of the sound (nāda) through the Tārikā, one should then enter by means of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Then, having gone to the fire-chamber and prepared clarified butter according to the scriptures,
one should perform the entire ritual action with that ghee according to the prescribed rule.

Then, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, the wise one should, with devotion and the mindset to be described hereafter, mentally renounce that ritual action along with its underlying intention within me.
Whatever sequence has been prescribed for the external [practice], all of that should be performed here in the mental [practice] with focused attention, using materials consisting of myself. (36.147)
This mental sacrifice (mānasayāga), which pacifies all calamities and bestows all fruits, has been described; it should be performed until the fall of the body. (36.148)
Then, having diligently transformed all substances into the nature of mind,
one should perform the external ritual for the sake of pacifying the latent impressions arising from external objects.
Thus, O Śakra, has my internal sacrifice been described to you;
now listen to me regarding the true nature of the external sacrifice.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Internal Sacrifice," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra [Śrīpañcarātra].
Note:

131. *Svastika* is a particular type of posture (*āsana*). 143. Regarding the term "by means of purificatory rites" (*saṃskāraiḥ*): it means by way of the process of making [the disciple] a Vaiṣṇava (*vaiṣṇavīkaraṇa*).

148. Regarding the phrase "until the fall of the body": by this it is stated that for the *paramaikāntin* (the single-minded devotee) who is devoted to the five-fold daily duties (*pāñcakālika-dharma*), the worship of the Lord must necessarily be performed for each person and every day; this constitutes the obligatory duty (*nitya-karma*).
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter.
[Now begins] the thirty-seventh chapter.
Śrī said:

"If I am worshipped with substances situated outside the sacrificial altar and other locations, perceived through meditation on me and serving as objects of enjoyment, that is traditionally known as the external sacrifice (bahir-yāga). (37-1)
Impression (vāsanā) is said to be of two kinds, arising from external and internal causes;
the mental sacrifice (mānasa-yāga), which is supreme, dispels all those that are internal. (37-2)
For the sake of purifying external dispositions, the external sacrifice is prescribed;
having established oneself upon ground prepared according to the scriptures, within that decorated pavilion.
Then, having established an altar endowed with all excellent qualities in the place of Brahmā,
it should be measured at eight cubits, or half of that, or even half of that again.
One should stretch a perfectly white thread from end to end across the middle of the altar;
on both sides of that [thread], as well as in the middle and at the two half-middles.
Having made three marks, one should drive five stakes:
three in the middle of the two outermost [marks], and two there in the middle of the two penultimate [marks].
One should cause a peg to be placed at the point where the middle of the cord is reached;
then, having fastened two loops, one should bring them together at the central mark.
Having established the two marks on the right and on the left,
one should fix two threads at the center and bring the middle of the thread together.
And at the location above the mark, one should gradually place a gnomon (śaṅku) there where the middle of the thread reaches on both the right and left sides.
Having fixed one cord at the eastern point and the other to the south,
one should then form a clockwise corner at the central mark of these two.
One should likewise perform the rite for the northeast corner (Aiśa), and then, having released [the cord], proceed further toward the north;
in this same manner, one should do so for the west and south, as well as for the west and north.
Having released the two cords in sequence, one should likewise form the other two corners;
then, for the sake of clearly delineating that field, one should stretch threads in the four directions.
In the field divided into sixteen parts, one should fashion a nine-petalled lotus by means of four central squares and the regions starting from the east.
Listen now as to how the middle lotus should be made with eight petals:
one should divide the field into four parts, excluding the eighth [segment] on the outside.
The pericarp, the filaments, the junction of the petals, and the node are, in sequence, each measuring one part; one part is left out, and outside of that is the space (vyoma).
Upon that [lotus], one should cast eight threads situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
furthermore, one should likewise cast eight more threads within the intervals between those threads.
Note: 1.
"By those perceived through meditation on me" means by those conceived as my own self. "Having become objects of enjoyment" means having become instruments of enjoyment.
3. "Āśaya" means latent impression (*vāsanā*). "In the place of Brahman" means in that which has been permeated by the meditation on Brahman.
13. "Divided among the devotees" is the meaning. (p. 146) Root-text:
By means of the thread situated at the joint of the lotus, one [draws] the eight petals in the sequence of the directions.
The innate, well-defined lines are known as the groups of celestial lines. || 37-17 ||
In this very same manner, there should be eight other lotuses;
thus is the delightful, preeminent city, characterized by nine lotuses.
It should be provided with an outer gate and endowed with the beauty of the corners and other features;
it should be made with four colors for the purpose of distinguishing the pericarp and other parts.

On a bed of flowers, or on a well-washed cloth, or one that has been fumigated, or on a new garment scented with perfumes, or on a consecrated altar smeared with cow-dung, [he should perform the rite].

The practitioner, for the sake of the ritual, should visualize a nine-petaled lotus; and following the path of meditation, he should fashion an image according to the teachings of the scriptures. (37.21)
In a firm vessel made of gold, silver, or copper, free from cracks and the like, one should worship—[or invoke]—within a full jar filled with curd, milk, or water. (37-22)
Having visualized a new lotus upon a surface covered with excellent sprouts and provided with cloth, silk, and so forth, the best of mantra-knowers should perform worship. (37.23)
In the jar, in the city, and likewise in the image, the mantra-practitioner should worship in sequence that which consists of all worlds, the supreme refuge of all the gods.
One should meditate upon the supreme city consisting of the support of all, which is a nine-petalled lotus;
then, one should worship it with the syllables of the *tārikā* and the word *namaḥ*, using the water for honor (*arghya*) and other offerings.
Then, there should be four vessels made of gold or other precious materials,
filled with pure water, perfumes, garlands, gems, medicinal herbs, and kuśa-grass water.
On the altar, one should place [the mantras] in the four corners of the image situated in front;
one should thus arrange them in this sequence, starting from the northwest (vāyavya) and ending with the southeast (vahni). || 37-27 ||

The practitioner of mantra, reciting these mantras, should prepare the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamanīya), the water for washing the feet (pādya), and the water for bathing (snānīya) in their proper sequence.
Thinking "I shall arrange the Tāra," the designations should be placed directly in the center;
and there, the arghya for the many objects should be prepared in a vessel in the middle.
White mustard seeds, sesame, dūrvā grass, barley, and white rice, combined with water, milk, and fruit, are declared to be the materials for the *arghya* offering. (37–30)
Having filled the vessel with the Tārikā, whose body is a mass of nectar,
one should contemplate the wheel of mantras within that state which is devoid of parts (niṣkala).
Having first worshipped the partless middle *arghya* with flowers and other offerings,
one should properly contemplate it as having the nature of both fire (*agni*) and moon (*soma*).
This is the first consecration; now attend to the second:
one should burn that [substance] with the fierce rays of the sun. (37.33)
One should then extinguish that which has been burnt with the rays of the cool full moon,
and fill it with the waves of the ocean of the nectar of Brahman-bliss.
Note:
19. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the pericarp, etc.," the filaments, the junctions of the petals, and the nodes are included.
20. Like a mandala, even a bed of flowers and the like should be accepted as a locus for worship.
26. He clarifies what was previously stated as "with the *arghya* and so forth" by saying "then" (*tataḥ*).

27. Regarding "one should place": the ellipsis is "as the vessels for the *arghya* and so forth. Regarding "in the [directions] beginning with Yāmya": the meaning is "in the corners starting from Nairṛtya and ending with Āgneya. 29. The intention is that it is done according to the sequence beginning with "Oṃ, I prepare the *arghya*. Regarding "having many purposes": its traditional renown is that "this water is for all purposes" (*sarvārtham*).

32. Having worshipped that which is to be worshipped; "to be meditated upon" means that which is to be contemplated. 33. "The second" refers to the form to be described, such as burning, flooding, and so forth. Regarding "one should burn": the traditional teaching (*saṃpradāya*) is that one should burn it after first drying it.
(p. 147) Root-text—
Having consecrated the principal [substances] with their respective mantras, beginning with the Tārikā,
one should then take water and place it into other vessels.
Alternatively, one may perform such a sequence of consecration for each individual vessel;
from this, one should effect the nourishment of the vessels and bring them joy. (37–36)
The wish-fulfilling cow, Saurabheyī, should be fashioned as a mudrā by means of her own mantra—
Surabhi, resembling the snowy mountain, established in the supportless state.
Having meditated upon it, one should display that mudrā which resembles her breasts, with both hands smeared with fragrance and with a mind full of attentiveness. (37–38)
Having sprinkled the mandala and the pavilion with water from the arghya vessel,
one should strike all the sacrificial materials without exception while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Afterwards, one should bathe [the deity] with the *mūla-mantra*; then all that shall turn into an object of enjoyment.
Then, having paid homage to Viṣṇu and the Lotus-born Goddess seated upon his lap—
One should worship with the root mantra using loose flowers and other offerings;
then, taking the vessel for the *arghya* water, one should present flowers, incense, and unguents.
In this same manner, one should offer the lamp and the food offering (naivedya),
and then perform the sacrifice at the gateway (dvārayāga) at the base of an Udumbara tree, situated in the middle of the outer door.
One should worship the Field Protector (Kṣetrapāla) who stands upon the ground, endowed with meditation and other [qualities],
resembling a dark blue cloud, holding a staff in his hand, and possessing a massive body.
Kṣetreśvara should always be meditated upon with the left hand forming a fist;
here, the mudrā should be displayed, and for others, the procedure follows this sequence.
One should worship Lakṣmī, who stands above the door and resides upon the udumbara tree,
holding a lotus in her hand and seated upon a lotus.
On the southern and northern branches and at the base [of the door] are Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa;
likewise, Jaya and Vijaya are on the outside and inside of the door.
All those beginning with Caṇḍa and ending with Vijaya should be known as four-armed;
they hold maces and discs, have conchs in their hands, and possess great strength. (37–47)

Indeed, they should be meditated upon as threatening those who are non-devotees and as being intent on destroying all defects; having thus worshipped them, these finger-rings (mudrikās) should be displayed. (37–48)
Then, between the two branches, one should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā on the left and right respectively. 37–49.
Holding with both hands a water-pot filled from a sacred bathing place,
she possesses the beauty of fresh youth, is white in form, and has a smiling face.
The Gaṅgā should be meditated upon as serene, with a face like the full moon;
the river Yamunā is likewise [to be visualized], resembling a dark blue cloud. (37.51)
By that same sequential method, one should worship with water for honoring, flowers, and other offerings the two lords of treasures named Śaṅkha and Padma, who stand inside the door.
Those two Lords of Treasures (Nidhīśau) are to be meditated upon as seated upon treasure-vessels;
they have stout bellies, tawny eyes, two arms, and are identical with the Blessed One.

Having thus performed the sacrifice at the door, one should then [offer] a flower facing [the deity] with the three fingers— the thumb, index finger, and middle finger— while reciting the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
Note:
35. "From that" (tataḥ) means from the vessel filled with consecrated water. 36. "To each one's own" (pratisvam) means for each individual vessel of the *arghya* offering and so forth.
39. "With the *astra*" means with the mantra: *oṃ vīryāyāstrāya phaṭ*. 40.
"With the root" means with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*).
41. "Worn" (*āmukta*) means not strung together, but sparse.

42. The word *udumbara* refers to the two pieces of wood placed above and below the door. 43. He describes the form of the Field Protector (*kṣetrapāla*) as "blue" and so forth. 45. The worship of Lakṣmī is prescribed "above the door."
46. *Śākhā*: a piece of wood forming the side of a door. 48. *Abhaktān*: those who are not devotees; the meaning is "those who are not devotees of the gods.
49. *Śākhādvayasya*: of the two side-panels, that is, of the two pieces of wood forming the sides of the door.
50. The forms of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā are described by the passage beginning with "with the two hands," etc. (p. 148).
Root Text:
Having taken [the water] and consecrated it, one should then visualize the Cakra above it.
It was sharp-edged, blazing in form, and raining down fire and thunderbolts.
One who destroys the web of obstacles should place [the hand] within the sacrificial hall;
then, one should properly position the right index finger facing upwards.
Having remembered [the goddess] who is conjoined with the *śikhā* mantra and possesses a radiance flashing like lightning, he should enter the sacrificial hall while whirling that [garland].
One should sprinkle one's own seat with water from the *arghya* vessel using the *astra-mantra*.
Upon that, one should worship the *mantric seat*, beginning with the *ādhāra-śakti*.
Wherever and whichever mudrā is to be displayed,
having sat down there, one should worship the Lord of Gods who resides in the heart.
One should cause that supreme splendor known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa,
which resides within the heart and constitutes an imperishable union of husband and wife, to pass before both eyes.
Having brought all that to the state of being that [deity], he should gaze with steady eyes upon the pavilion,
the altar, or wherever he desires to sacrifice.
One should worship the support and the seat with water for the guest (arghya), flowers, and other offerings;
thereafter, one should worship Dharma and the others, located in their respective directions.
Then, visualizing the lotus and sun-mandalas up to the seat of the deity through successive stages of yoga, one should worship them with flowers and other offerings.
To the right of the deity situated within the maṇḍala, upon the maṇḍala,
starting from the beginning of the Kṛta age and ending with the Vāyu and Īśa [corners], in successive order.
Having first divided the site into seven parts, one should worship Gaṇapati upon its pericarp,
seated on a lotus throne within the petals of that lotus.
And with his two upper arms, he holds a rosary and an axe;
while with his first two hands, he displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
However, having thus meditated upon the mudrā, with the hands granting boons and fearlessness, the form of the Vyākhyā-mudrā arises from the joining of the index finger and the thumb. || 37-67 ||
One should place the six limbs— plump, pot-bellied, stout, single-tusked, and elephant-faced— upon the filaments of the six petals of the lotus.
Having formed the mudrā, the wise one should worship it with flowers and other offerings using his own mantra;
thereafter, the wise one should worship the goddess Vāgīśvarī with his own mantra.
Seated upon a white lotus situated within the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire;
though entirely free from all limiting adjuncts, she has nevertheless assumed a formal manifestation.
[One should meditate upon] my own Śakti, who is directly composed of sound, arisen first [at the beginning], having two eyes, two arms, white in color, and holding a conch and a lotus. || 37-71 ||
Then [he saw] the Guru and his Guru, both possessing forms established in the world, wearing ornaments and garments resembling shimmering waves of nectar.
Afterwards, one should worship the Guru who is the Supreme Preceptor (Parameṣṭhin) in his world-established form;
then the group of ancestors is to be worshipped, for they are formless yet resemble the sacrificial cakes (piṇḍas).
Thereafter, one should worship those who are eternally perfected, who are intent on meditation upon the Blessed One,
who are tranquil, with eyes closed, possessing auspicious limbs, and preeminent in splendor.
Having obtained permission from them and having received their authorization in due order,
he should afterwards worship me, having invoked me as seated upon the lap of the God of Gods.
Listen, O Lord of the Gods, to each of those in whatever manner they occur.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the External Sacrifice," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the venerable Pāñcarātra.
Note:

60. *Yāpayet* means "should cause to pass" (i.e., spend). 75. *Anujñām prāpya* means "having obtained permission," that is, having kept in mind the permission received from the guru, the paramaguru, and so forth.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter.
The thirty-eighth chapter: Śrī.
The one god Nārāyaṇa is the embodiment of the six perfections in their fullness;
I am his supreme power, the single, eternal I-consciousness. (38.1)
For the sake of favoring practitioners, I have assumed a formal manifestation;
listen now to how I am to be worshipped while seated upon the lap of the God of Gods. 38-2.

Then, having obtained permission from Gaṇeśa and the other deities, one should invoke the Supreme Self residing within the heart, who has been worshipped through the internal sacrifice (antaryāga). || 38-3 ||
Having recited three times that *tāraka* which is full of the six qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*) and filled with power (*śakti*), one should then recite the *tārikā* three times. (38–4)
Then, uttering the masculine mantra, one should invoke the Supreme Person,
the lotus-eyed one, who has four stout and noble arms.
Uttering the supreme mantra very slowly with the *recaka* breath, one should draw it forth from the belly through the nostril by way of the path situated between the two, fire and moon. (38–6)
One should cause Lakṣmīśa, the abode of divine power, to descend from the unstruck (anāhata) state or from the foot, having attained equanimity in every respect. || 38-7 ||
One should remember the deity as having emerged like a mass of lightning from a cloud;
one should then place him, situated within the mental seat (bhāvāsana), in the midst of a handful of flowers.
Performing the four mudrās—namely, *saṃnidhi*, *saṃnirodha*, *saṃstambha*, and *sthāpana*—one should practice them correctly with the mind. (38–9)
Having placed the two palms together with the fingers facing upward, one should touch each respective little finger with the two thumbs; that is the *saṃnidhīkaraṇa* (invocation) mudrā.
Likewise, one should perform the wiping (*unmārjana*) between the two middle fingers;
at that time, both the stabilization (*saṃstambha*) and the restraint (*saṃnirodha*) are accomplished. (38.11)
Having formed two fists with the four fingers of both hands,
and having turned them sideways toward each other, one should place them upon the other two fists.
O Śakra, this placement of the two thumbs shall be thus; becoming such as this, one should recite the mantra beginning with Tārā. (38.13)
One should meditate on Hari as having arisen after the rites ending with the offering of water for the feet and the guest-offering (arghya).
Likewise, one should meditate upon Him during the offering of the bath, ornaments, garments, and garlands, as well as during the act of adorning Him.

In other cases, during rites of enjoyment (bhogayāga), one should, in accordance with each specific enjoyment, meditate upon [the deity] in its scripturally prescribed form, full of compassion and facing [the practitioner]. (38.15)
But when the body has been fashioned, he remains in that very form;
while enjoyments are being offered, there is that supreme power consisting of my own self. (38.16)
Note:
5. "The masculine mantra" means the *praṇava* (the syllable Om).
7. "Anāhata" refers to the twelve-petaled lotus situated in the heart.
9. The mudrās for *saṃnidhi* and the others will be explained immediately hereafter.

14. Regarding the word *kālam*: it means "at the time. The accusative case is used here to express continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). 15. Both *sānukampaṃ* and *susammukhaṃ* are adjectives qualifying Hari.
p. 150) Root-text:
One should meditate upon her as being actually present there, just as Hari receives [the offering] when summoned; then, one should offer a full añjali of flowers along with arghya. (38.17)
Having scattered [the flowers], one should worship in sequence with the two hands joined palm-downward upon the head, using the *tāra* (oṃ), the *tārā* (hrīḥ), both together, and the *namaḥ* (namas).

One should perform the rites, both in brief and in detail, at the appropriate time, using flowers, water-offerings, incense, and ointments, along with the root mantra and other mantras, in their proper sequence. || 38-19 ||
Thereafter, one should worship Śakti—who is complete with those limbs, formless, and incomparable—with Tārā; subsequently, one should worship the deities in their respective limbs.
One should worship the weapons, ornaments, powers, and so forth, each with its own respective mantra.
This sacrifice, known as *laya*, is great and bestows the accomplishment of all goals. (38.21)
Then, from the body of the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, which was fully endowed with power,
there emerged a single divine form consisting of all powers, supremely radiant.
The goddess who embodies the sixfold policy, who is indefinable and incomparable, who is in every way inseparable from Viṣṇu at all times and in all places. (38.23)
Out of compassion, for the sake of the practitioner, she herself has assumed a formal appearance;
yet, without ever abandoning that very form of the deity, she remains distinct from it.
Following the stated sequence, the wise practitioner should first invoke me with the mantra;
he should perform the entire procedure as prescribed for the rite of invocation. (38-25)
One should meditate upon me as Viṣṇu’s beloved, seated on his left lap;
and my form, which is to be meditated upon, has already been described previously. (38.26)
In that state, by means of the process of dissolution, one should sacrifice everything into me in due order;
then, one should remember that which has emerged from me, beginning with Śakti, in sequence.
Listen now to how one should place each individual [syllable] in its respective seat of enjoyment, just as one would [place] a mass of sparks from a brightly blazing flame. (38.28)
One should meditate upon the lotus-eyed Puruṣa seated on the conceptual throne in the center of the pericarp of the central lotus, and the lotus-born goddess seated upon his lap. (38.29)
One should meditate upon Lakṣmī, who has emerged from the body of Lakṣmī in the center of the pericarp of the eastern lotus; she has two arms, two eyes, and beautiful earrings. (38–39)
Wearing white garlands and garments, adorned with necklaces and armlets, endowed with all auspicious marks, and possessing full, elevated breasts. (38–39)
Her wide eyes were like blossomed blue lotuses, her face was graced with a beautiful smile,
and the rows of her curls were as lovely as swarms of hovering bees.
She had a tilaka-mark upon her forehead, lips as red as young shoots, and black, curly hair; her teeth were like bamboo and pearls. (38.33)
One should meditate upon her seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), with two hands holding a noose and a goad,
her form resembling the interior of a lotus, and facing toward both of us.
One should remember her situated in the center of the pericarp of the lotus on the right side,
equal to Lakṣmī in dress, ornaments, and so forth, or indeed white like a jasmine flower.
[They saw] Kīrti, who had emerged from my form, supreme and consisting entirely of glory,
seated upon the pericarp of the lotus situated behind us.
One should meditate upon Jayā, who is similar [to herself] and reddish, as having emerged from one's own form;
one should remember her situated within the center of the pericarp of the northern lotus.
One should visualize Māyā, who has emerged from my own form, as being of such a red hue;
her heart is in the lotus of the southeast, and her head is in the lotus of the southwest.
One should place the *śikhā* [mantra] on the lotus of Vāyu and the *varma* [mantra] on the lotus of Īśāna;
the *netra* [mantra] on the front petal of the central lotus, and the *astra* [mantra] in the corner.
One should contemplate the god Vāsudeva in front of the eye;
one should remember the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa on the petal in the middle of the southern direction.
Note:
