17. "Of the one summoned" (āhūtasya) means of the one who has been brought into presence. 19. "Smeared" (lepaḥ) refers to the anointing with sandalwood paste and the like.
20. *Anūpamām* means incomparable (*anupamām*).
Root-text: One should remember Pradyumna on the western petal of the central lotus.
Aniruddha is situated in the two pairs of corner petals located above. || 38-41 ||
One should visualize serpents showering nectar behind the weapon;
likewise, one should employ gulgulu (or guggulu), tagara, madana, and śalala.
One should place the four-armed makers of the nectar-pots, white as a conch or a jasmine flower, upon the petals of Lakṣmī’s lotus; one should place the Kaustubha gem everywhere.
In this manner, one should place the forest garland upon the petals of the heart-lotus;
one should place the ornament-lotus upon the petals of the fame-lotus.
One should thus place the armor upon the petals of the Jayā lotus, on the leaves of the Varma lotus,
and on the lotuses themselves, across the fourfold set of lotus petals.
One should place the supreme goad upon the petals of the lotus at the head; one should place Garuḍa, the best of winged creatures, at the front of the four gates. (38–46)
Or one should station the *nāgas* there at the front of their own respective gates;
on the ground of the eastern gate, one should place Balākikā, who holds a lotus in her hand.
Likewise, from the southern gate, one should likewise [worship] the white Vanamālikā, who has eyes like lotus petals, is serene, and is short in stature; she is blue in color.
In the middle of the western gate, one should visualize Vibhīṣikā of red color;
and in the middle of the northern gate, Śaṅkarī, who has the luster of honey.
From the eastern direction up to the northeast, at the outer entrance area,
one should visualize the eight world-protectors, Indra and the others, together with their vehicles.
Above that, one should meditate upon Nāgeśa and Brahmā;
and outside of that, one should meditate upon their weapons, such as the vajra and others.
One should meditate upon the Lord Viṣvaksena, who stands in the sky amidst the directions beginning with Somaśaṅkara (the northeast),
approaching from the midst of the firmament with his noble limbs.
Now, O Purandara, hear from me the meditation on those [deities] not yet mentioned:
[the one who is] of the nature of nectar, whose limbs are like clouds, and whose eyes are as long as lotuses.
One should meditate upon Vāsudeva, who holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus; who has the Śrīvatsa mark on his chest; who is clad in yellow garments; and who possesses four arms. (38–54)
One should meditate upon the supreme Saṃkarṣaṇa, who has the appearance of a mass of snow, wears blue garments, possesses four arms, and holds a plow and the Śārṅga bow.

One should meditate upon Pradyumna, the Lord, who is red in complexion and clad in red garments, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and who is capable of uplifting those submerged in distress. (38–56)
One should meditate upon Aniruddha, who bears the Śārṅga bow and arrows, bestows boons and fearlessness, is yellow in color, and is clad in pure white garments.
Holding a sword and a shield in their hands, and with their supreme hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
all these lotus-eyed men were seated.
Beholding the northeastern quarter, as well as myself and Viṣṇu the eternal,
elephants resembling the snowy mountains drenched us both with jars of nectar.
His body has the color of white blood, he wears white garments, and has four arms;
he is seated in the lotus posture and is marked by a lotus and a conch in his hands. || 38-60 ||
His hand is adorned with the heart-mudrā, while his left hand always bestows fearlessness;
he is richly endowed with white ornaments and garments, and his body is smeared with camphor.
The wise one should meditate upon the heart-mantra seated before us—
supreme, red like the bandhujīva flower, and bearing a lotus and a discus.
Dark as the soot of a crow's eye, bearing the lotus and the *kaumodakī* mace,
he is enriched by his own mudrā with his right hand and grants fearlessness with the other.
One should remember the Lord as our armor, seated facing us, smeared with musk and adorned with dark flowers and other ornaments. (38–64)
Note: 42. Gulgulvādayaḥ are names of the Nāgas.
55. Saunandaka is the mace of Kāmapāla.
63. "Śyāma" means dark like a crow, like a bee, or like soot; or alternatively, *kākāli* refers to a specific type of crow that is of an extremely black color. (p.
152) [The Lord] who resembles turmeric and is reddish, and who holds a mace and a lotus in sequence...
With his two front hands occupied with forming his own mudrā. || 38-65 ||

One should meditate upon the Weapon-mantra (Astra), which is richly adorned with golden garments and ornaments, possesses the prowess of the fire of universal destruction, and is seated facing both of us, exerting great effort.

Or the most excellent practitioner should visualize these [deities] as women—beginning with the Heart and the others—richly adorned with the aforementioned ornaments and attire, and anointed with perfumes suited to themselves. (38–67)
Thus has been described the auspicious meditation on the limbs [of the deity], which removes all sins;
one should meditate upon Kaustubha as having two arms and a splendor equal to a thousand suns.
Richly adorned with blazing garments and ornaments, he bears his own mudrā at his heart;
he wears a beautiful five-colored forest garland and possesses auspicious eyes.
One should meditate upon the serene one, resembling a mature woman, holding a lotus and a lotus-faced [image] in her two hands, and shining like the moon. (38-70)
Two-armed, with all limbs beautiful, holding a ring with both hands, dark like fresh dūrvā sprouts, the Lord of the Noose (Pāśeśa), who has the face of a serpent [or: who devours serpents].
Two-armed, holding his own supreme mudrā with the right hand and likewise the hand of boon-granting,
he is of terrifying form and inspires fear.
One should visualize him holding a sharp goad and a long nose, appearing fearsome;
with his right hand he displays the mudrā of the South, and with his left, the gesture of granting boons.
Those world-protectors were well-known by their dress, form, and ornaments; they bore weapons in human form marked with their respective insignia upon their heads. (38.74)
Viṣvaksena, bearing a conch and a discus, should be meditated upon as four-armed;
he is visibly equal to Viṣṇu, with his other two hands occupied in performing mudrās.
Then, one should meditate upon Garuḍa standing at the entrance, with terrifying eyes,
a red beak, a large nose, and the luster of molten gold.
"With broad fangs, a vulture-like face, and adorned with a circle of feathers"—
thus has the meditation on your retinue been described in brief.
Above our two gross forms, one should meditate upon the subtle Tārikā,
who bears the form of a divine couple— subtle, as if both visible and invisible, and sinless.

Above that, however, is the supreme Tārā, who consists of the fullness of the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), our divine and supreme union as husband and wife, belonging to the Pārameśvara state. || 38-79 ||
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides,
it eternally shines forth sound and meaning by its own splendor, ever-risen.
Within this, the entire wheel of mantras appears like a reflection;
thus, the supreme Tārīkā is extended through the forms of both direct and reverse order.
Having understood this through one's own being according to reality, one should perform worship as prescribed;
from the beginning, one should worship the two sinless ones, who are the abodes of all things, with a focused mind.
Then, with a web of enjoyments beginning with the *arghya* offering and ending with its presentation, the knower of mantras should worship the retinue, starting from Śakti and ending with Viṣvaksena.
First of all, O Śakra, this placement has been shown to you according to the sequence of the sacrifice of enjoyment (bhogayāga): Garuḍa, the Goddesses, and the four female gatekeepers.
Now learn from me what the enjoyments are, how many there are, and of what kind they are. || 38–84 ||
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the External Sacrifice," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Note:
69. Regarding "vanamālām" (the forest garland), the word "should meditate" (dhyāyet) is to be supplied.
72. "By the southern hand" means by the right hand.
74. The female gatekeepers, such as Balālikā and others, were mentioned previously in verses 47, 48, and 49.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter;
[now begins] the thirty-ninth chapter.
Śrī said: Listen, O Lord of the Gods, to those enjoyments by which I am satisfied when they are offered;
it is in these that my power remains extended for the enjoyment of what is to be enjoyed. (39.1)
In accordance with one's capacity, when those various objects of enjoyment are provided—
manifesting through diverse manifestations of divine power that have attained a state of solidity— (39-2)
That excellent seat, completely filled and worthy of the Lord, should be meditated upon in its entirety as being spread with a soft covering; this is the first [step]. (39-3)
Having first offered water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and water for sipping (ācamanīyaka),
one should thereafter offer oneself and one's possessions preceded by a prostration.

Having then requested permission, [he should provide] thereafter an unsurpassed seat for bathing, a footstool, and the water for the arghya offering; then follows the reception of the water for washing the feet.
Water for the feet, sandals, a bathing garment, a small cloth, a mirror, scented water, and water for washing the hands. (39-6)
A tooth-stick, water for rinsing the mouth and sipping, scented oil, and powder made from rice and wheat. (39.7)
Next, for the purpose of rubbing the body, [use a paste] mixed with turmeric powder and slightly infused with lotus; then, for the purpose of bathing, [use water] combined with *khalī*.
Warm water mixed with sandalwood and moon-mist (camphor) for the purpose of anointing;
likewise, cow's milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugarcane juice. (39–9)
Then follow water with fragrant myrobalans, thereafter water with *lodhra*,
water with red sandalwood, and the excellent water with turmeric.
Afterwards, [he should offer] the milk of granthiparṇī, then water infused with tagara,
and water containing priyaṅgu, jaṭilā, siddhārthaka, and all medicinal herbs.
Flowers, leaves, fruits, and water; likewise seeds and scented water; then gold, gems, river water, water from sacred fords (tīrtha), and pure water, respectively.

Note: 1. "She remains" (tiṣṭhate) means she remains manifesting her own intention; the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is used in the sense of manifestation. 3. Specific types of enjoyment are described by the words "soft" (*mṛdu*) and so forth. Regarding the worship of the Lord, there are six seats (*āsanas*), namely: the seat of mantra (*mantrāsana*), the seat of bathing (*snānāsana*), the seat of adornment (*alaṃkārāsana*), the seat of food (*bhojyāsana*), again the seat of mantra (*punar-mantrāsana*), and the cross-legged seat (*paryaṅkāsana*). Among these, the first, the seat of mantra, is described here.

4. He states the items to be offered upon that seat with the words beginning "arghyam" (the water of honor), etc. Regarding the manner of offering oneself and one's possessions, the *Pādma* (4.3.140) says: "I am your servant, O Lord of the World, together with my sons and dependents. Command me as your messenger; always employ me in what is beneficial for you to do. 5. Here, the second item is the bathing seat (*snānāsana*). The mantra for this is clarified by me in the *Sāttvata* (6.26): "O God, while you are intent on bathing, quickly provide this supreme, auspicious, and great bathing seat, complete with a footstool, out of a desire to show me favor."

6. *Mātrā* and *śālikā*: Here, the meaning of the term *mātrā* is a vessel filled with unhusked, white-colored *śāli* rice grains. Thus it is said in the *Pādmapurāṇa* (4.6.36): "with a measure (*mātrā*) of *śāli* rice. And this offering of *mātrā* is for the purpose of remedying any deficiencies that may have occurred during the course of the worship. 8. *Khali*: A solidified residue of fragrant oil, perfumed with musk and other scents.
9. *Candra*: Camphor (*ghanasāra*).
These waters, together with the root-bathing water, should be offered;
likewise, the *arghya* water from the *arghya* vessel should be offered at intervals between the various baths. (39.13)
One should offer a cleansing with water and flowers at intervals,
and fill [the vessel] with the water remaining from the bath, enriched with turmeric and *śāli* rice [or a turmeric knot].
Having taken the water-pot, adorned with garlands and other ornaments, in his hand,
he should then whirl the vessel containing white mustard seeds and incense over the head [of the disciple].
Then, one should cast it outside and give two well-washed lower garments—
one for removing water from the hair and the other for removing water from the body.
Then one should offer two beautiful, well-washed garments, one for the lower body and one for the upper body, purified by incense and perfumes, followed by an auspicious seat.
One should purify [the site] with full water-pots and meditate upon Hari as immersed in the sky;
thereafter, a seat adorned with ornaments and abundant with a soft cushion should be provided.
In that regard, everything such as the *arghya* and *pādya* offerings should be presented as before;
furthermore, there is the parting of the hair and its cleansing with a comb. (39–19)
Then those flowers for the head, followed by the arrangement of the topknot;
then the fragrant substances such as sandalwood, and the fan for the purpose of drying. || 39-20 ||
Extremely wonderful ornaments, such as crowns and others, should be offered, along with garlands of various forms composed of sattvic flowers. (39.21)
A handful of flowers was offered at his two feet, a wall was constructed with heaps of blossoms, and his eyes were anointed with collyrium cooled by fragrant substances. (39.22)
Likewise, there is the act of touching, as well as the tilaka mark on the forehead;
a polished, stainless mirror, and a thorough examination all around.
A lamp, incense, a vehicle, sentient and insentient beings, hymns of praise, auspicious songs, and the sight of dance and instrumental music. (39.24)
And there were measures filled with jewels, intended to fill the gaps in his enjoyments;
these various activities, worthy of a king of kings, were fashioned by his intellect.
For [the deity] seated upon the ornamented throne, these enjoyments indeed consist of myself;
then the seat for the meal should be offered, as well as the water for honor (arghya) and the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth.
One should worship with the madhuparka; understand it as it truly is:
the madhuparka consists of a mixture of milk, honey, and curd. (39.27)

Having placed the vessel filled with madhuparka before him, the offering for honoring (arhaṇa) and the libation for satisfaction (tarpaṇa) shall be performed separately from the arghya in two other vessels. (39.28)
First, there is worship with the *arhaṇa* offering, followed by the *madhuparka*;
then the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the substances fit for libation, and finally the purification (*niṣpuṃsana*) performed upon the hand.
Afterwards, water for sipping (ācamana) and a cow as the measure for the honey-mixture (madhuparka) should be provided;
one should then perform the sacrifice with the food-offering (annayajña), complete with its ancillaries, just like the madhuparka rite.
Note:
14. After the bath, the lustration (nīrājana) is described as "the remains of the bath" (snānaśiṣṭa). 15. "In the hand" means in the left hand; elsewhere, it refers to the right hand.
17. Bhadrāsana is the seat for bathing. 18. Khapluta is situated at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta). He speaks of the third, the seat of ornamentation, beginning with "alaṃkāra":
19. Kaṅkata is a comb for grooming the hair.
24. "Vehicles, whether animate or inanimate" refers to those made of gold and other materials, such as elephants and horses.
25. By the phrase "made of clay," the subject matter mentioned at the beginning of the chapter is recalled. Now, the fourth [category], the food and seating, is described.
27. He describes the *madhuparka* with the words "of milk... and so forth.

29. *Arhaṇa* is the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*āpośana*). *Tarpaṇa* is the water for drinking. *Niṣpuṃsana* is the wiping of the hands. 30. Furthermore, the taking of a cow as a measure [of honor] is here mentioned to prevent any deficiency in the intended offering of the *madhuparka*. (p. 155) Root Text:
Portions of cooked rice made from *śāli* rice should be offered for the sake of the *anna-yajña*;
likewise, betel-leaf with camphor should be offered as an after-treatment (*anuvāsana*). (39–41)
And then, for the sake of providing rest, a most wonderful celestial chariot (vimāna) should be offered there; everything, beginning with the respectful offering (arghya), should be given as before.
Thereafter, one should perform the recitation (japa), unobserved by other people, using an auspicious rosary that has been properly consecrated with mantras. (39–33)

The ordinary [count] is by means of the fingers; however, by means of the joints, it is increased by ten; and by means of a rosary of beads, it should be understood as being increased by one hundred and so forth. (39–40)
The vocal [recitation] is for the purpose of minor rites; the whispered [recitation] is for the rite of accomplishment;
the mental [recitation], consisting of meditation, bestows the fortune of liberation and grants all perfections. (39-35)
The rosary should be made in such a way that it is not visible to ordinary people;
beads the size of a bone are proclaimed to be the best. (39-36)
Those resembling the stones of the *dhātrī* fruit are proclaimed as middling; those with the appearance of jujube stones are inferior. The best consists of one hundred and eight. (39–37)
Half of that is declared the middling [size], and half of that again is remembered as the lowest.
[An image] made of gold is for the attainment of wealth, for nourishment, and for rites concerning the ancestors.
Silver and copper forms are for the sake of attaining wisdom and heroic power; tin is for the accomplishment of yakṣiṇīs; lead is for [the subjugation of] rākṣasas and piśācas. (39)
For the purpose of accomplishing the Vetāla, one should know that the rosary is made of brass or bell-metal; for the accomplishment of Nāgas and Pannagas, it is likewise understood. (39–40)
An iron [vessel] is for the purpose of minor tasks; a jewel made of metal is for the sake of longevity, health, and prosperity—indeed, every jewel is for the sake of increase. (39–41)
A crystal gem is said to lead to liberation and peace;
for good fortune, one made of coral should be used, while one made of pearl should be used for the sake of final release.
The gem born from the root of the *tulasī* plant leads to peace, liberation, and nourishment;
the *pādma* gem bestows all perfections (*siddhis*); and the *śaṅkha* gem is considered to grant prosperity. (39–43)
An excellent pearl gem bestows longevity, progeny, and fame;
one should take up one of these [gems] at an auspicious time when its qualities are preeminent.
Immediately thereafter, one should wash it with scented water while reciting the Astra-mantra;
then, having prepared a new, firm thread made of hemp, cotton, or wool, [one should proceed].
Having tripled the cord and made it fourfold as firmly as possible,
one should wash it with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra and then string the beads upon it.
Neither deficient nor excessive, equal, immovable, and joined at their intervals,
they are like a string threaded with gems of desired number between two ends.
One should fashion a *maṇi* [bead] from Meru; this is the procedure for the rosary (*akṣamālā*).
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the External Sacrifice," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Note:
31. Betel leaves and other items to be offered at the fifth seat, the Mantra-seat (mantrāsana). 32. Thereafter, the sixth is called the Paryanka-seat (paryaṅkāsana).
33. Among the implements for counting the number of recitations (*japa*), the rosary (*akṣamālā*) is recommended.
35. The specific types of recitation, such as the vocal (*vācika*) and others.
38. He describes the specific beads of the rosary with the words "made of gold," and so forth.
40. *Rīti* is a specific type of brass or bronze.
42. *Sautra* means made of thread.
47. *Meru* is a large, special bead located at the principal knot of a rosary (*japamālā*).
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter.
The fortieth chapter: Śakra said—
Salutations to you, O one born from water; salutations to you, O one born from a lotus. Please tell me the method for the consecration of the rosary, O Lotus-born One.
Śrī said: One should place the consecrated rosary in an auspicious vessel;
having worshipped it with water for the guest (arghya), flowers, and other offerings, one should perform its purification. (40.2)
Having incinerated it with the Astra-mantra and extinguished it with the Varma-mantra,
one should then nourish that garland with the Śrī-mantra, which consists of the supreme nectar, and contemplate it as such.
Four-armed, incomparable, consisting of the essence of the Mind, like another form of myself;
with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and with two hands joined in the añjali gesture. || 40-4 ||
One should meditate upon the Goddess who resides in the lotus of the Brahma-door, resembling a tuft of hair;
she is the supreme Vaiṣṇavī Śakti, consisting of the self (manmayī), and the destroyer of my [dualistic] delusion. (40–5)
Having contemplated her at the *dvādaśānta*, one should then meditate upon her in sequence within the heart-lotus;
she has risen again from the heart-lotus and emerged through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). (40–6)

One should contemplate that [deity] situated upon the garland, gradually manifesting, endowed with the sequence of limbs and minor limbs, and consisting of the gross, subtle, and supreme natures. (40.7)
O Lord of the Gods, one should meditate upon me there in the form of the Tārikā within that Śakti;
likewise, one should meditate upon the jewels, the thread, the rosary, and the Vaiṣṇavī residing within the rosary.

O Lord of the Gods, one should meditate upon all illusion as having been turned into a single ocean; having contemplated this rosary given by me and consecrated, [one should perform the recitation]. (40.9)
Thereafter, one should perform the recitation (japa) according to the previously stated procedure,
[contemplating] the supreme unmanifest, the subtle, and the gross Self itself.
One should contemplate this pentad as having the form of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa:
namely, the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), the fourth (turya), deep sleep (suṣupti), dreaming (svapna), and waking (jāgara).
Likewise, there are the five states, as well as their agents, instruments, and so forth;
likewise, the emergence of the agent, that which resides therein, and the external instrument. (40.12)

Likewise, one should contemplate every gross syllable of the mantra as being composed of that [light], situated in the center of the heart-lotus and emerging from the lotus-face of the Mantra-deity. (40.13)
One should remember the Vaiṣṇavī power consisting of sound, which pierces through my [the Guru's] ego;
one should meditate upon the Mātṛkā, the mother of mantras, as having emerged from her.
Then, one should contemplate the rosary as being composed of the Self and consisting of the mantra to be recited;
one should indeed contemplate the mantras there as flowers upon a creeper.
Visualizing the throbbing at the touch of the jewel and its dissolution upon its removal, the wise practitioner should perform the recitation of the Lord of Mantras. (40.16)
Recalling this sequence of the outward and inward movement of the manifestation of the luminous form within the heart, one should recite it once; that is equal to ten million recitations.

Note: 2. "Established" means created. 3. "Having extinguished" means having dried. "With Śrī" means with the Śrī-mantra. "One should visualize" means one should meditate upon it in the form that will be described hereafter.
5. The *brahmadvāra* is the channel known as the *brahmarandhra*. The *śikhā* is the crest of fire. 6. At the *dvādaśānta*, in the location twelve finger-breadths above the crown of the head.
(p. 157) The root—
Having completed the recitation according to the rules, one should consign the recitation performed to me;
one should contemplate that power, which resides within my mouth, in the form of the recitation. (40.18)
One should employ the ringing of the bell during the offering of the lamp, incense, and the arghya;
likewise, during the invocation, the arghya, the food offering (naivedya), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
And for the purpose of pleasing [the deity], the wise one should employ the ringing of the bell;
it should not be moved without worship, nor should one perform worship without moving it.
For those desiring the accomplishment of their goals both in this world and the next, she is indeed the power named Ghaṇṭā, the Mistress of Speech, Sarasvatī. (40.21)
All mantras reside in speech, and everything that is to be spoken resides within the mantras.
When this [speech] is set in motion, the mantras follow swiftly like calves.
Desiring [liberation], they approach that bell, the mother of mantras;
one should meditate upon the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), facing downwards, together with the families and non-families of the worlds.
Above that stalk, however, the wise one should visualize a circular lotus—
auspicious, white, with eight petals, and endowed with a pericarp and filaments.
In the center of that, one should meditate upon the Goddess endowed with eight arms;
with her four principal hands, she holds a noose, a conch, a lotus, and a goad.
Holding in her four right arms a rosary, a book of wisdom, the gesture of fearlessness, and likewise the gesture of granting boons.

Seated in the lotus posture, with eyes like lotuses, possessing a splendor equal to the interior of a lotus, wearing a garland of lotuses, and adorned with yellow and white garments and unguents. || 40-27 ||
While uttering the *tārikā* with a long vowel and in pairs, one should cause this goddess—who vomits forth a flood of mantras and is praised by Brahmā and the others—to move. (40.28)
By worshipping with this, the practitioner of mantra attains the perfection of mantra.
Then, having invited the gurus—whether they are identical with me (manmaya) or Vaiṣṇava— || 40-29 ||
While reciting my mantra, one should offer them half of the food portion;
then, one should properly [offer] the supreme [oblation] consisting of Agni and Soma, which has entered the fire. (40.30)
O Lord of the Gods, satisfy me; listen attentively as I explain how this is done.
Then, in the northern direction, either outside the temple or elsewhere.
On a portion of ground endowed with the auspicious marks, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) possessing symmetrical characteristics—
either square and level, or heart-shaped in the form of a lotus.
For a number of fifty oblations, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be twelve finger-breadths;
for one hundred and eight, it should be equal to a cubit (aratni); and for a thousand, it should be one cubit (hasta).

In a rite for ten thousand (ayuta), it should be two cubits; for a hundred thousand (lakṣa) oblations, four cubits; and for ten million (koṭi) oblations, it should be eight cubits; one should have it constructed according to the scriptures.
Alternatively, one may construct a triangular fire-pit for the oblation, provided with three tiers (mekhalā).
Having first raised [the altar] with the *tāra* mantra, one should sprinkle the ground three times with that same mantra.
One should properly perform the drying, burning, and flooding [of the elements] by means of the *tāra* (the syllable Om);
beginning from the *ādhāra-śakti* and extending up to the *bhāvāsana*, which is the object of worship. (40.36)
Therein, indeed, is the supreme power known as Nārāyaṇī, consisting of light, composed of the Self (manmaya), having the nature of nectar, and possessing a form that surpasses all else. || 40.37 ||

Having brought down from the lotus of the heart the eternal [Deity], who abides within the totality of all powers and resides within the interior of all things, by way of the path of emanation; 40-38.
Having descended from the heart-lotus in the form of the radiating *tārikā*,
one should cast it into the lotus within the center of the *kuṇḍa* by means of the exhaling breath (*recaka*).
Note: 30. The satiation of the fire is described by the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth.
33. The dimensions of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in accordance with the number of oblations (*homa*) are described by the passage beginning with "śatārdha" and so forth.
35. By that Tārā. 36. Bhāvāsana is as previously stated in the section on Ādhāraśakti (p. 158). Root—
Having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having displayed the lotus mudrā,
one should meditate upon the Śakti who is in her season, well-bathed, and dressed in new garments.
One should meditate on that very Śakti, who is the soul of all, as the lower fire-drill (adharāraṇi);
and one should meditate on Hari, who consists of all splendor, as the upper fire-drill (uttarāraṇi).
One should thoroughly churn with the *tārā* mantra and likewise with the *anutārā*;
having taken up the fire produced by the *tārā*, which arises from the *śakti*. (40–42)
Having grasped [the child] with his fingers, he should perform the consecration (saṃskāra) known as Vaiṣṇava;
and he should perform the tonsure (cūḍā), preceded by the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), using the Tārā mantra.
Then, having brought the fire near with the *tārayā* and *anutārayā* [mantras],
he [should offer oblations] to Jātavedas with the two goddesses, Svāhā and Svadhā.
One should perform the marriage ceremony with either the *tārā* or the *anutārā* [mudrā];
all rites such as the naming ceremony (*jātakarman*) and others should be performed while consisting of meditative visualization (*dhyānamaya*).
When fire has been produced from iron, stone, or gems for the sake of some specific purpose,
or even in an ordinary worldly fire, one should perform the sacraments beginning with the *niṣeka*.
Having placed [the offerings] in a vessel made of metal, earthenware, or a new one, the wise man should worship the Lord of Svāhā together with the Goddess using *tāra*. (40–47)
Having withdrawn [the breath] by means of *pūraṇa*, one should lead it to rest within one's own self;
then, through the power of bliss (*ānandaśakti*), one should gradually unite it with the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
Having again brought him down step by step along the path of emanation,
one should lead him to the earth situated within the lotus in the center of the sacrificial pit by means of the Tāra mantra.
One should worship Vahni with Svāhā, Īśāna with Svadhā, and Agnīṣoma with Maya; reciting the Tāraka mantra, one should offer three fuel-sticks (samidhs) one by one.
Thereafter, with offerings of rice, sesame, and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should then offer three oblations of clarified butter;
having first uttered the Tārikā, one should recite "awaken" twice.
Stationed there, the fire itself perceives the oblation exactly as it is offered;
the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) should be performed by one whose hands are moistened with water.
One should spread the darbha grass with *tāra* mantras, dividing it threefold and threefold in the four directions;
one should spread a heap of darbha grass on the northern side of the fire-pit.

One should cause all of these to be placed there: the vessels for the *praṇītā* and *prokṣaṇī* waters, the large and small ladles (*darvī* and *dhmā*), the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), and the two strainers (*pavitra*).
Having filled the *praṇītā* vessel with fragrant water and purified it three times with the two strainers (*pavitra*), one should meditate upon me, Śrī, by means of the *tārā* mantra. (40–55)
Having established the *prokṣaṇī* vessel to the north of the fire, one should fill it with water for prosperity;
then, having purified that water by straining it, one should sprinkle the sacrificial implements equally with it.
Having taken up the vessel for the clarified butter and having placed the clarified butter within it,
one should meditate upon that clarified butter as the Brahman arisen from the ocean of ghee, situated to the north of the fire.
Having kindled it with the *tāra* mantra and placed it at the tip of a blade of *darbha* grass,
and having kindled it again with that same mantra, one should perform the rite of circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
Having established that [mixture] behind the fire and purified it with the pair of pavitra-strainers,
one should cast that pair of pavitras into the fire while reciting the Tāra mantra.
One should enclose [the area] in the four directions with sacrificial boundary-sticks (paridhi).
Having placed two fuel-sticks (samit) in the center of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), positioned between the directions of Agni and Śarva.
Then, having placed the dry fuel consisting of fifteen pieces,
and having sprinkled water around the fire with the *tāra* mantra, one should heat the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
Having wiped [the ladle] with the *tāraka* [mantra], they should subsequently sprinkle [it] with that same *sruk*;
then, from the direction of Vāyu up to the direction of Agni, and extending as far as the direction of Śarva (the North-East), [they should proceed].
One should cause it to flow in a stream into the fire; one should offer oblations with the *sruva* ladle in the center, either one hundred and eight times, or half of that, or half of that again.
Note:
40. By the words beginning with "dhyāyet" (one should meditate), the transformation of the fire into a Vaiṣṇava form is described.

43. "Abhigūhya" means having covered or enclosed. The mention of "annaprāśana" (the first feeding of solid food) is also an elliptical expression that includes the *jātakarman* (birth rite) and *nāmakaraṇa* (name-giving ceremony).
(159) Reciting the Tārikā ending with "svāhā," one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the root-mantra using the *sruva* ladle;
thus this fire shall become fit for the sacrificial offerings of the Blessed One. (40.64)
Then the wise practitioner should first place seven fuel-sticks made of sacrificial wood derived from trees of the *brahma* and *kṣatra* classes, using the *tārikā* mantra. (40–65)
One should offer ten other fuel-sticks in the form of wood along with Tārā;
one should meditate upon Me alone in the center, as the supreme Goddess seated on the lap of Viṣṇu.

One should meditate upon Lakṣmī seated on the lap of the All-pervading Lord, who resides upon the pericarp of the lotus consisting of the bliss of Brahman; one should offer all those sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidhs).
Then one should offer [the oblation] consisting of flowers, as well as that consisting of incense materials;
these three types should be offered by the wise man with his own hand alone.
Thereafter, the wise one should offer the madhuparka with the *sruva* ladle;
having taken four portions of food into the *sruc* and filled it with clarified butter as before.
With that same [ladle], one should offer oblations of food while reciting the Tārikā mantra ending in "svāhā";
one should likewise perform oblations of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, equal in number to the previously mentioned fuel-sticks.
Taking a handful of flowers, one should mentally worship [the deity] residing within the fire;
this much constitutes my daily sacrifice (nityayāga), and thereafter one may cast the optional oblation (kāmyāhuti).
If he should have a desire, he should sprinkle the fire with water using the *tāra* mantra in accordance with each specific injunction and offer an expiatory oblation (*prāyaścittāhuti*).
Saying "Tara, forgive me" ten times with his mind, he should withdraw the *praṇītā* water and pour it out in a pure place (or set it down). || 40-73 ||
Having cast all the enclosing sticks (paridhis) into the fire, he should perform the pouring of the residue (saṃsrāva);
and having cast the sacrificial grass (stara) into the fire, he should fill the ladle (sruva) with clarified butter (ghṛta).
One should offer the long *pūrṇāhuti* while reciting the *tārikā* ending in *svāhā*, that supreme *Tārā* who is united with her power (*śakti*), abiding in the fire, and composed of the mind. (40.75)

And having drawn me, who was seated upon his lap, through the path of the junction of Viṣṇu’s nostrils by means of the power of the vital breath (marucchakti), he placed me within the lotus of his heart.
Then, having gone to the sacrificial ground, one should unite that ritual action performed by me while abiding in the nine lotuses and deposit it within myself, who am established in worship.
One should divide the food beforehand, even before it is served or formally offered;
with that food, one should properly worship the four-armed Viṣvaksena.
Having brought him to the edge of the mandala and summoned him from the midst of the sky,
[he saw one] with eyes, eyebrows, and beard tawny like a fresh mango leaf.
Having worshipped the god— who is clad in yellow garments, possesses four tusks, is endowed with his own two mudrās, and holds a mace and a sword— the wise one should proceed in due order.
Then, having displayed the *sāṅga-mudrā* and gone near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*),
Viṣvaksena should then be propitiated with devotion using sesame seeds and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Then, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ";
having worshipped [the deity] in the maṇḍala, one should then perform its dismissal (visarjana).
O best of gods, reciting the words "Forgive me" with his own mantra,
he should display the mudrā and visualize him as having flown up into the sky.
One should cast all the offerings for Viṣvaksena into deep water,
and one should drench that mandala with water over which the Astra-mantra has been recited.
Then one should worship all the world-protectors without exception,
with flowers, water-offerings (arghya), and gifts of food, ending with a single oblation into the fire.
Note: 65. *Brahmataru* is the *palāśa* tree; *kṣatrataru* is the tree named *mucukunda*. Regarding "the ten others": this means the remaining ten fuel-sticks (*samidh*).
81. From here onwards, five and a half verses follow the words of the one named Jaya.
Having worshipped [the deities] according to the rule with either roots, fire-offerings, or grains (vrīhis), using their respective mantras according to one's capacity,
and having dismissed them, one should then worship those weapons as well. (40.86)
One should worship all those members of the retinue according to their respective positions, beginning with the Kṣetrapālas and others, and one should offer libations into the center of the fire.

Beginning with the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti) and including all the powers of the sacred seats (Pīṭhaśaktis), as well as Gaṇeśa and the others, they should be fully worshipped and satiated with clarified butter and other offerings. (40–88)
Having performed [the rite] once or thrice, one should then pour full oblations into all [the vessels];
prior to the worship of Viṣvaksena, one should worship all [deities], beginning with Lakṣmī.
After the worship of Viṣvaksena, one should perform the worship of the world-protectors (Lokapālas) in due order;
then, having purified the altar, one should spread sacrificial grass (darbha) towards the south.
One should worship the ancestors in due order with the remnants of the food intended for their reception;
having prepared three pindas, one should offer them to the ancestors upon the sacred grass.
In that manner, one should offer water for the *arghya*—one *añjali* for each individual—or else one should give it to a Vaiṣṇava or to a distinguished Brāhmaṇa. (40–92)
Having dedicated the food intended for the ancestors, mentioning each of their names in turn,
and having offered it all into me while observing its disappearance, [one should proceed].
Having withdrawn the water for the guest-offering (arghya) and the rest, and having retracted the armor and weapon mantras,
and having also withdrawn the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should perform the subsequent sacrifice (anuyāga).
Having sprinkled with water using the Astra-mantra and having performed the circumablation with the Tāra-mantra,
one should spread a base of water with that same mantra and offer the oblations to the vital breaths (prāṇāhuti) with it.
But one who has not been initiated, while performing the subsequent sacrifices, should recite the *tārikā* conjoined with each respective mantra and should visualize me as residing within.

Divine, consisting of the bliss of Soma, having gradually attained the nature of food, she possesses the forms of potency, essence, and flavor, and consists of splendor, vigor, and strength. || 40.97 ||
One should meditate upon the Self as the imperishable enjoyer, whose nature consists of sovereignty, power, and wisdom—the lotus-eyed Puruṣottama. (40.98)
Then, while uttering the *tārikā*, one should cover the food with water;
having sipped water (*ācamana*) twice, one should thereafter perform the internal sacrifice (*anuyāga*) within oneself.
Then, at the end of the day, the wise one should practice his private recitation (svādhyāya) of the fourfold scriptures and that which arises from them, such as the Tārikās and so forth.
Furthermore, with a mind that is not attached even to all the established tenets, one should examine them with one's own intelligence for the sake of purifying one's own disposition. (40.101)

Note: 92. Regarding "to a distinguished Brāhmaṇa": this means to a specially qualified Brāhmaṇa. This [rule] pertains to cases other than those involving a wealthy patron (*dhanika*). However, regarding a wealthy patron, it is stated in the *Sāttvata-tantra* (6.167–179) that one should feed four Brāhmaṇas according to the *śrāddha* ritual, or, if they are unavailable, just one.
94. *Anuyāga* refers to the utilization of the remnants of the offerings, such as the meal and so forth.
95. *Tayopastīrya* means having sipped [water] by means of that [blade].

96. The previously mentioned acts—sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), circumambulatory sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), the *āpośana* rite, the oblation to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*), and so forth—are intended for those who have undergone initiation (*dīkṣita*). However, for those who are uninitiated (*adīkṣita*), these should be performed using only the mantras prescribed by the respective authors of the Sūtras.
99. *Apidhāyāmbhasā* means having drunk the subsequent *āpośana* water.

100. *Svādhyāya* refers to the study of the Vedas and divine scriptures. The fourfold [scriptures] are those treatises that expound the *āgama-siddhānta*, *mantra-siddhānta*, *tantra-siddhānta*, and *tantrāntara-siddhānta*.
(p. 161) Having performed the root *saṃdhyā* worship according to rule and having approached me with devotion in thought...
One should practice yoga according to the prescribed rule with a mind purified by the scriptures.
During the first and last watches of the night, one who possesses the equilibrium of the elements [should practice];
thus, O Śakra, the ritual procedure for sacrifice has been explained in detail. (40.103)
Furthermore, listen again to this summary of the ritual procedure from me;
one should perform it in brief or in detail according to the suitability of the place and time.
One should never cause a deficiency; one may worship me even with a hollowed palm.
One should worship us both together with the Puruṣa Sūkta.
Likewise, one should worship them separately with my own hymn (sūkta), or with both [mantras] for us;
or else, in the place of all mantras, one should employ the Tārikā alone.

One should perform both the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and the renunciation (saṃnyāsa) separately at the beginning and the end; or, without specifying the enjoyment [of results], one may worship with those [mantras] alone. (40.107)
One should act in such a manner as one is able;
however, one must never let a sacrifice go undone, even if it means offering only a handful of water.
Or, in the absence of material offerings, the wise one should recite the *tārikā*;
he should mentally contemplate her form, exactly as it is and of whatever nature it may be.
For one who is free from worldly desire, pure, and has truly attained the goal in that state,
all the ritual actions shown by the scripture lead only to agitation.
And for one who has become all-pervasive and has attained equanimity everywhere, who could perform what action, for whom, for what purpose, or in what manner? (40.111)
Having abandoned the two paths pertaining to all the worlds— those consisting of Agni and Soma—
one should enter the space between them and practice the upward path.
The evil path burnt by the fire of dissolution becomes cooled and free from affliction;
one becomes expert in treading upon the states that transcend the gross, the subtle, and the supreme. || 40.113 ||
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, breathing;
speaking, releasing, grasping, as well as opening and closing the eyes—(40.114)
Indeed, being absorbed in me and not consisting of this world, he performs all that [work] without being bound by any states, places, times, and so forth. (40.115)
Overcome by the sense of "I," like one who has inhaled smoke or drunk fire, he indeed dwells in the interval between the two, the sun and the moon. (40.116)

Having clearly extracted the palate [or, according to B and C: having extracted the jewel from the palate], placing it in the station of Dhruva, one should abide in a state of mind consisting of emptiness, equal to dissolution.

Thus, the yogin who conducts himself in this way, intent upon the meditation on Tārikā—he is a master of ritual action, he is indeed a follower of Sāṃkhya, he is a yogin, and he is a devotee of the Sāttvatas. || 40-118 ||
And he is to be known as a Pāśupata, and he is one who has reached the end of all philosophical systems.
Thus have I declared to you my ultimate nature;
now hear from me the remainder of what I wish to say to you in its entirety. (40.119)
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Daily Rites," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.

*Commentary:* 103. The first watch and the last watch of the night are the times for yoga. Even the sleep occurring in the middle period should be contemplated as being of the nature of yoga by means of surrendering one's own self to the Blessed One.
105. *Apacchedaḥ* means separation or interruption.

108. Regarding the phrase *śaknuyāt* ("one should be able"): because the propitiation of Me is obligatory (*nitya*), and because it is prescribed that an obligatory duty be performed according to one's capacity, the meaning is "one should propitiate Me according to one's ability.
115. Regarding the phrase *anavasyūtayā*: it means by that which is unconfined or unlimited.
116. "Smoke-drinker," and so forth. Just as one situated between smoke and fire becomes connected with both the smoke and the fire, so too does he mean one who exists between the sun and the moon.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter;
[now begins] the forty-first chapter.
Śakra:
Homage to the Mother of all embodied beings, who is eternally faultless;
who is the very form of the Self, the foundation of all pure and impure paths. 41.1
The sacrifice has been heard by me in its full detail according to the division of external and internal rites;
now I desire to hear from you the definitive teaching on initiation (dīkṣā).
Śrī said: "Nārāyaṇa alone is glorious, resplendent with the majesty of the six divine attributes;
I am his single, eternal Śakti, whose nature consists of those six attributes. (41.3)
O Vāsava, by means of divine consciousness, I, though one, divide myself fivefold:
through the forms of sound, form, and meaning, as well as through the form of mental activity.

In the same way, by means of another [form] known as initiation (dīkṣā), appearing in the form of a teacher, that which tears asunder (dyati) afflictions, karma, and so forth, and bestows the entire state of liberation. || 41-5 ||
Having exhausted all impurity, it bestows the supreme state;
therefore, initiation (dīkṣā) is described by the knowers of reality who have reached the further shore of the Vedas.
That initiation (dīkṣā) is threefold, consisting of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme;
furthermore, it is threefold according to the distinction of those to be initiated, and thus it is fourfold.

The initiate (samayin), the spiritual son (putraka), the third, the practitioner (sādhaka), and the teacher (ācārya)—these are those to be initiated; their detailed classification is found elsewhere. || 41-8 ||
Furthermore, this initiation is threefold: through the sacrifice of the great maṇḍala [or yoga], or by means of oblation alone, or even by speech alone. (41.9)
Having brought one who possesses firm resolve and has been tested over a long period—whether he be wealthy, of small means, or destitute of wealth—respectively; 41-10.
The teacher, having first fashioned a new lotus for the disciple who is bowed down and tormented by the fire of saṃsāra, and having consecrated the water-pot upon it, [should proceed].
To his disciples, whose sins had been cleansed by various kinds of expiations, who were well-bathed, wearing washed garments, and whose bodies were rendered pure; || 41-12 ||
Having brought the devotees of the Blessed One— auspicious maidens as well as women—
and having purified them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he first provided them with tooth-sticks.
Holding handfuls of flowers with eyes closed and wearing new garments,
one should fashion a single thread from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head.
Having made three strands with knots of the three qualities on that thread according to the number of the principles (tattvas),
one should contemplate the sequence of the principles from the head down to the feet.
The principles (tattvas) numbering twenty-seven, beginning with Īśvara and ending with Earth, should be known as the knots; however, the three qualities (guṇas) reside within the knots. (41.16)
Māyā, avidyā, and kriyā are proclaimed to be those bonds (pāśas);
the body, consisting of both gross and subtle aspects, bestows the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious actions. (41.17)

Note: 5. The etymological derivation of the word *dīkṣā* is given by the verse beginning with "yat" and so forth. It means "it cuts" (*dyati*) or "it shatters" (*khaṇḍayati*). The verbal root is *do*, in the sense of "cutting apart" (*avakhaṇḍane*).
6. Another etymological derivation is given as "having caused to perish" (*kṣapayitvā*).
11. *Samijjya* means having fully honored (*saṃpūjya*).
13. Regarding "women, such as maidens," he states that they too possess the qualification for Tantric initiation (*tāntrika-dīkṣā*).
15. "The three qualities" (*triguṇa*) refers to the knots consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. The number of principles (*tattva*) is twenty-seven.
(163) This [sacrificer], colored by the root [mantra] and by various qualities, and being the locus of all impurities,
himself [becomes] a body consisting of threads at the conclusion of the ritual of the *saṃpāta* oblation. (41.18)
Having repeatedly cut away [the bonds], one should offer oblations as the cause for uprooting enjoyments;
one should meditate on the Lord on the forehead, whose form is consciousness and who faces in all directions.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as established by means of its own seed-syllable, one should perform oblations according to the number of the principles (tattvas).
One should remember the Pradhāna, resembling a mass of vermilion, situated between the two eyebrows.
One should contemplate the intellect (buddhi), resembling the rays of the full moon, situated at the root of the palate;
and within the middle of the palate, one should meditate upon the ego (ahaṃkāra) as having the luster of a flower.
One should meditate on the mind, possessing the luster of a royal gem, between the palate and the ears;
it is situated between the lotuses of the throat and the heart, divided equally into five parts.
One should contemplate the five [senses], beginning with hearing, as having the form of shimmering stars;
likewise, one should remember the [five faculties] beginning with speech in the middle of the heart and navel in five ways.

One should remember the subtle elements (tanmātras) of sound and the rest at the navel, the bladder, the tip, and the middle; from the thighs down to the pair of feet, one should remember the gross elements.
Having recited the Praṇava over those [elements] which have assumed the forms of stars, one should then utter their respective seed-syllables (bīja). || 41-25 ||
Then, with the syllable *tattva-saṃjñā* followed by *svāhā*, such is the oblation of the residual drops (*saṃpātāhuti*).
At the conclusion of the homa of the residual drops, the Guru himself becomes composed of *lakṣmī*.
Then one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Tāra mantra ending in vauṣaṭ.
Thus, at the conclusion of the saṃpāta-homa, that firm thread with its knots [should be prepared].
Having offered [the oblation] contained within a pair of earthen bowls at the end of the *mada* rite,
one should then remove the blindfold from the disciple who has been brought forward.
Having properly prostrated before his own guru who has bestowed the book upon him,
that disciple, standing near the fire, should offer oblations with a mind focused on the *tāra* mantra.
Thus, through the primary limbs, the secondary limbs, and the entire retinue beginning with Lakṣmī, one indeed becomes qualified for recitation, fire-sacrifice, hearing, and worship. (41.30)
Then, for the purpose of purifying the paths during initiation, one should offer oblations with the [mantras] beginning with the Mūla-mantra;
furthermore, one should offer oblations with sesame seeds, numbering at least one hundred and up to ten thousand.
One should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with clarified butter alone and cause it to fall through a ladle;
this shall be the Mantra-initiation (māntrī-dīkṣā), which applies all mantras.

Within this much of the scope of authority, however, one should cause disciples who are solely addicted to worldly enjoyments to grasp the desired mantras, whether they be of the *prakṛta* or *prākṛta* class. (41.33)
All mantras, which arise from primordial nature, are accomplished in the presence [of the practitioner].
However, their essential principles (tattvas) are to be purified according to the method that will be explained. || 41-34 ||
The reception of mantras is prescribed for the category of the path of pure reality (śuddhatattva).
This is the Mantra-initiation; now learn from me the Initiation of Reality (tattvadīkṣā).

Oṃ! Purify the seed-syllable and the designation of reality through the sequence of the name [and the utterance of *svāhā*], by means of ten repetitions of oblations in conjunction with perfect meditation. (41–36)
When the group of principles (tattva), beginning with earth and ending with Īśvara, has been purified,
the designation of the one to be initiated should be applied according to the actual reality during the fire-oblation and other rites.

While the disciple is seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) close to him, the true guru should meditate upon the entire sequence of principles (tattvapaddhati), beginning with Īśa and ending with the earth element.
Having gazed with the two eyes of Lakṣmī, one should touch [the image] with the hand of Lakṣmī;
having withdrawn [the elements] beginning with earth, one should then create again [those] beginning with Īśa.
Note:
18. *Saṃpātahoma* is the offering of the principles (*tattva*).
19. He describes the meditation on the principles according to the distinction of their parts, beginning with "the forehead."
22. *Rājopala* means diamond (*vajra*).

39. Since it was previously stated that the Guru consists of Lakṣmī, his two eyes are called the "eyes of Lakṣmī. With the hand of Lakṣmī—that is, with the hand joined by the *tārikā*. (p. 164) Root-text:
In this way, this initiation consisting of meditation quickly brings about the awakening of the insentient principles residing within the body of the disciple. (41.40)
Then, having placed the cord for the binding-line between two shallow bowls,
one should go near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), remove them, and set them down.
Having offered a thousand oblations or at least one hundred with the *tārā-sāṅga* mantra,
one should then take a single flower and consecrate it many times.
One should strike the disciple on the heart with the *tāra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
Having recollected the disciple as abiding in the element of being (*bhūtattva*), one should mentally cause him to experience its enjoyments.

Then, having extracted [the soul] from that [earth element], one should join it to the water element once all experience of the earth has been completed; having likewise considered it thus, such is the procedure [for the subsequent elements] starting from the Lord (Īśa).
Having offered oblations with the Tārā-mantra together with its ancillaries, and having severed the earthly knot,
one should place [the vessel] in the *sruc*, fill it with clarified butter, and offer it with that same mantra.

When the Tārikā is in the state beyond [the elements], within the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) possessing the luster of a blazing flame, one should cause the subtle water-element (aptattva) to ascend; and that too one should offer as an oblation in this very manner.
One should transfer that subtle fire and offer it with the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having thus offered the succession of full oblations in this sequence, [one should proceed]. (41–47)
Having led [the disciple] from primordial nature (prakṛti) to the person (puruṣa), one should lead that person to the Lord (īśvara).
Beyond the Lord, no further reality exists within the entire collection of principles.
Power (Śakti), which takes the form of the Lord (Īśvara), has gross, subtle, and supreme aspects;
for the Puruṣa, having descended from the principle of Īśvara, becomes impure.
Having attained that supreme reality, he becomes truly pure;
as the self of the universe with eyes on all sides, he therefore becomes fit for initiation.
Then, for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation, there should be two *pūrṇāhuti* offerings;
having meditated upon the disciple as both *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts), [he offers] ghee likewise into the *sruk* ladle.
Unifying that duality, the Guru indeed stands transcending the supreme;
meditating on the nature of consciousness as sound, he abides in the supreme form of Paśyantī.
Beyond the Tārikā, [one should contemplate] the supreme state, which is unstruck (anāhata) and without elevation;
by means of that, equalizing the disciple with the Tārā ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

Then, for the sake of the disciple's stability until the falling away of the body, one should offer many oblations with the *pūrṇāhuti* mantra, beginning with *dhruva* and ending with *namaḥ*, using the *tārā* [mantra]. (51–54)
There, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* and then casting the great *mahāpūrṇa*,
the Guru [unifies] the disciple, himself, and me, the eternal Lakṣmī.
One should meditate upon everything as being unified within me, like milk poured into milk;
thus, having made the disciple consist of *lakṣmī* by means of the wind of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*).
Having drawn [the disciple] in sequence, he should cause him to hear this mantra again;
then, having established me, Tārā, within his heart, he should instruct him.

One should instruct everything concerning the primary and secondary limbs, as well as the entire scriptural sequence, and indeed the conventional dharma, such as the secrecy of the mantra and so forth. (41–58)
Then one should place the hand of Viṣṇu upon the head, the back, and within the heart; having touched that limb with the mudrā, the disciple should worship me. (41–59)
Taking the water-pot with Tārā, while mentally reciting the Tārikā mantra together with its limbs (aṅga) and subsidiary limbs (upāṅga), he went to wherever it had previously been desired by his Guru.
The guru should consecrate the disciple with a serene inner mind;
having thus attained his true form, the disciple then crosses to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Then, with great magnificence, one should perform the Guru-yāga;
having established the foundational powers (ādhāra-śakti) and so forth, and having seated the Guru therein.
One should worship with all [offerings] such as *arghya* and likewise with gold, jewels, and so forth;
thereafter, one should worship the satisfied and gratified [deity] with this mantra. (41–63)
Salutation to the Guru, who is the embodiment of the sun, moon, and fire that illuminate the dense forest of ignorance,
and who brings peace to the torment of the three fires of suffering.

Having taken the root [mantra] and then received permission, one should thereafter repeat the mantra. One should accomplish it according to one's desire, for as long as one wishes.
