Śakra said:
"O Padmā, O Sovereign, those who have been initiated by you into the initiation of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) indeed possess the right to perform worship, and no one else."
Śrī said: O Indra, out of affection for you, I shall tell you this supreme secret:
there are those on earth who have been initiated for the sake of liberation among the three castes.
For all of them are indeed disqualified from performing sacrifices for the sake of others;
among them, however, those highly fortunate ones who have dedicated their hearts to the feet of Viṣṇu [are not so].
Indeed, there are eight hundred sages in this world who are supremely devoted;
they are knowers of the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina recensions and are dedicated to the Pañcarātra.
They were knowers of the Dharma of taking refuge, devoted to the two foremost and unsurpassed [vehicles],
and relied upon the ritual actions and sūtras proclaimed by the sage Kātyāyana.
Then Kāśyapa, Gautama, Bhṛgu, Āśvalāyana, Aṅgiras,
and other such preeminent sages performed sacrifices for the sake of Hari’s supreme purpose.
Others possess the qualification for performing sacrifices, yet they are not authorized [to know this];
these are my devotees, dear to Hari, these are the Bhāgavatas.
Other Bhāgavatas do not worship us two at all;
rather, other Bhāgavatas worship with devotion the Blessed Lord Hari.
Those others in the world who are devoted to Him are called Bhāgavatas;
for the worship of the Supreme is performed by those born in the lineages of the most excellent sages, such as Kāśyapa and others.
If other devotees of the Lord perform worship to another deity out of delusion, it will result in harm through the power of the king and the kingdom.
Therefore, with every effort, those devoted to the Lord (Bhāgavatas) should always [initiate] one born of the lineage of Kaśyapa and others who has been initiated, even if he is illiterate.
He alone is worthy of propitiation, purifying, and a great knower of Brahman. || 41-65 ||
Thus have initiation and consecration been described to you, O slayer of Bala.
What more do you wish to hear regarding that which is to be accomplished through right concentration?
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Method of Initiation and Consecration," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra.
Note:

From this point onward, a section of the text intended to establish that only those born into the lineages of Kāśyapa and others are authorized to perform sacrifices for the sake of others (parārtha-yajana) is not seen in all manuscripts; rather, it is found only in the edition printed in Telugu characters. Furthermore, that section has been bracketed [deleted]. Therefore, there is reason to infer that this portion may have been interpolated by certain individuals desiring to establish the exclusive right to perform sacrifices for others within their own temples. Moreover, this section contradicts the traditional practices of the original officiating priests (ādyartvik).
Thus ends the forty-first chapter.
Chapter Forty-Two. Śakra said:
[Salutations] to the two lotus-feet, which are a boat for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.
To you, the queen of Hṛṣīkeśa, salutations again and again. || 42-1 ||

O Goddess, by your grace, I have heard the sequence of the initiation ritual (dīkṣāvidhi) in due order; now tell me, O lotus-faced one, the procedure for the preparatory rite (pauraścaraṇikī kriyā) of the Tārikā.
Śrī said: "I am the power named Nārāyaṇī, residing in Nārāyaṇa;
my supreme form is Tārikā Bhuvaneśvarī. (42.3)
Listen now to the perfection of the practice for me, who have become a single mass [of consciousness],
beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
That time has been demonstrated by those learned in the tantras for the accomplishment of Tārikā;
it is untouched by great sins or by the most notorious heinous crimes. (42–5)
Falling away from his state of disbelief, abandoning censurable practices, cultivating friendliness toward all beings, and feeling remorse for the evil he has committed; (42.6)
One should bring various high and low sins to rest through expiatory rites, remaining a celibate student, eating sacrificial food, speaking the truth, and being firm in one's vows. (42.7)
In the presence of Viṣṇu, one should mentally recite the syllable Oṃ a million times;
one should perform ten thousand oblations with clarified butter accompanied by the Mahāvyāhṛtis.

One should perform the fire-oblation with sesame seeds while reciting the Sāvitrī mantra that same number of times; thus, having set aside the two well-known great sins and heinous crimes, they are rendered neutralized.
Having performed such a rite with the triad beginning with the *praṇava*, one is liberated from great sins, extreme sins, and other such secret transgressions. (42.10)
Likewise, by means of fasts and other such illuminating practices,
or else one who knows the truth of the Aghamarṣaṇa mantra should fast for three nights.
Three times during the day and three times at night, he should enter the water with his clothes on;
immersing himself at each twilight, he should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa mantra three times.
One should thus spend those three nights performing ritual ablutions;
on the fourth day, one should indeed give a milch cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
In this way, he becomes purified of all sins without exception, as previously stated;
or else, he should sprinkle himself with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) at the three junctions of the day.
Having spent three nights in this manner, one is liberated from all sins;
or else, one may do so by means of the five [mantras] beginning with Tārā, or even just one of them, according to one's inclination.
One should indeed contemplate the Vaiṣṇava [mantra] which is pure and radiant;
by doing so day and night, one is liberated from all sins.
Those who, free from sin and devoted to dharma, go to Viṣṇu in this world—even one who merely sits in their row and eats there is liberated from all sins. (42.17)
Note:

2. *Puraścaraṇa* refers to the performance of vows, fire-oblations (*homa*), and so forth, undertaken for the purpose of ensuring that a mantra received through the instruction of a guru bestows its desired fruit.
4. Regarding the phrase "of the one who has become a *piṇḍa*": this means "of the one whose form is the *piṇḍa-mantra*."
8. A *niyuta* is ten *lakṣas*; an *ayuta* is ten *sahasras*. 9.
Regarding the phrase "having abandoned the established [practice]," the meaning is that they have not made it manifest.
11. By the phrase "through fasting and so forth," the expiation for those who have made it manifest is stated.
15. Regarding "the pentad beginning with *tāra*": this means *tāra*, the *vyāhṛtis*, the *sāvitrī*, the *tārikā*, and the *anutārikā*.
16. "One should gaze upon the Vaiṣṇava" is stated for the sake of ensuring the perfection of the performed rite.
17. He describes the majesty of the Vaiṣṇavas with the words beginning "bhuvana"; the meaning is that those who have taken refuge in Viṣṇu as their protector are the Vaiṣṇavas.

Having brought evil to destruction by means of the root dharmas esteemed by the hosts of great seers, one should thereafter take refuge in the *tārikā* (the savior), who carries one across the ocean of existence. (42.18)
Having fasted according to the rules on the seventh day of the dark fortnight, the mantra-practitioner,
remaining at the twilight, should perform the recitation of the *tārikā* on the eighth day.
Having abandoned other desires, one should perform the prescribed action without yielding,
in a divine, perfected, or likewise ṛṣi-made pure temple of Viṣṇu.
On a mountain peak, by a riverbank, in a cow-pen, or even in a grove of *bilva* trees, eating once any one of these—milk, barley-gruel, or sacrificial food (haviṣya)—[one attains success]. 42.21.
One should indeed perform the recitation twelve thousand times for seven days;
one should perform the libation with water ten parts of the recitation and also offer oblations of clarified butter.
By this procedure for the present time, if one beholds an auspicious vision at midnight on the fourteenth day during the rite of the Tārikā, [success is attained].
Either the acquisition of a jar of liquor, or the drinking of liquor, or the ritual sprinkling with desire by a woman, or else the vision of Sudṛśī. (42.24)
Either an embrace with her out of passion, or enjoyment together with her;
or the utterance of a mantra for its accomplishment, or the attainment of the fruit resulting therefrom. (42.25)
Or even the sight of a gentle, handsome couple;
or the sight of a king, or the sight of a queen.
Either the direct vision of Nārāyaṇa himself, or my own vision of him in a dream, or the sight of a devoted wife, or meeting with Vaiṣṇavas. (42.27)
And whatever other auspicious vision is described in the treatises on dreams, having obtained that [vision], he should rise up, cast off sleep, and conquer fatigue. (42.28)
Having sipped water and become pure, the practitioner should remember me while lying on his bed at night;
then, having risen in the morning and performed the sequence of the sandhyā rites, [he should proceed].

They were equal in virtue, age, and form; they were handsome, devoted to the Dharma, possessed of noble appearance rather than one that was dejected or wretched, and were both beautiful and high-minded.
Having summoned the husband and wife, who were in the prime of youth and spoke with pleasant, gentle words, he bathed them as they were the very embodiments of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
Having adorned them with garments and other finery, they practiced the deception of wealth; once they were fed and their bodies anointed with perfumes, they were satisfied with sacrificial fees.
One should pray for the accomplishment of the Tārikā with Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa as one's inner self;
at the end of the words "May it be so," one should go for refuge to those two after bowing to them.

Then, having caused the Vedic hymns to be recited for his welfare, and having gratified the foremost of the twice-born who are most learned in the Vedas and devoted to Viṣṇu, he should proceed toward the attainment of his desired goals.
If one does not see a vision in a dream on the night of the fourteenth day, then beginning from the new moon until the seventh day of the dark fortnight, [one should continue]. (42.35)
Furthermore, one who observes the vow should pass that same amount of time,
performing three thousand recitations while subsisting on a single meal per day.
In the midst of their youth, they did not neglect the arrival of the fertile season;
with wisdom, they delighted one another as husband and wife, never censuring the conduct of their beloveds.
Doing what is pleasing to women without being greedy for them, and avoiding sin, he should then reach the eighth day of the dark fortnight and perform the recitation as before. (42–38)

Performing all [rites] such as the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth, one should cause them to cease upon seeing [the signs] in a dream; one should practice in this manner for as long as the signs are not fully perceived. || 42-39 ||
When the Tārikā is accomplished, a man obtains everything;
he becomes a perfect practitioner of the scriptures and one who is skilled in the course of the supreme self.
He is a knower of the procedures of all tantras, one who has reached the further shore of all Vedānta,
a piercer of all doubts, and one who has reached the further shore of all certainties.
Note: 29. *Saṃstare* means on a bed. The accusative case in *niśām* is used to denote duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*).
33. Regarding *tāvāvām*: the meaning is that those two, the couple known as Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, are our very own forms.
36. By eating once, that is, by taking food only one time per day. (p. 168) Root verse:
He whose speech is truthful and straightforward, who is eloquent, and who has reached the further shore of the ocean of Dharma—
For he desires to employ this [means] for either another or himself. || 42-42 ||
Whether in subduing or in favoring, he always succeeds.
Śakra said:
"Obelisance to you, O beloved of Hari, whose very form is the complete aggregate of the six political expedients (ṣāḍguṇya). 42-43.
O you whose home is the lotus, O housewife of Govinda!
From the lotus of your face, I have heard the Siddhi that is the specific excellence of Tārikā.
The gross, subtle, and supreme forms have been correctly demonstrated,
as well as the threefold nature of Tārā established according to the ritual procedure.
"O Lotus-born One, you should now tell me my specific application (viniyoga).
Śrī said: "The one Swan, Nārāyaṇa, the self-controlled, whose essence is full of the six attributes... (42–46)
I am the Haṃsī-Śakti, his Vaśinī who grants all desires;
both we, the Haṃsa and the Haṃsī, are delighted in the nature of the Tārikā.
Learn from me the application of that [Goddess], who is my own essential nature, within various mantras according to their external and internal divisions. (42–48)
Whatever mantras there are, of whatever kind, whether superior or inferior; and whatever their respective applications may be, in whatever number and of whatever nature— || 42–49 ||
There are as many such applications of her as there are [beings], of this there is no doubt;
nevertheless, O Śakra, listen to some of my applications.
[He saw] those who produce immediate conviction regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
[he saw her] with a black antelope skin as an upper garment, and dwelling in a black antelope skin.

Having meditated upon her, who is clothed in a black antelope skin, whose auspicious eyes are like those of a frightened black fawn, who resembles the full moon, and who holds the gesture of Brahmā along with a rosary of beads; 42–52.
And holding two lotuses in her other two hands—
in this manner, [one should meditate on] me, the lotus-eyed one, or Janārdana, the God of gods.
Having meditated, one should recite the mantra of Tārā one hundred thousand times; then the Dharma will become manifest.
[One should offer] measures of rice grains in the form of polished *śāli* rice, numbering as many as the *vibhu* (the pervasive Lord).
One should cook that many *prastha* measures of clarified butter and *pala* measures of sugar, or likewise that many of molasses, all together in a single vessel.
An oblation of sacrificial ghee, well-boiled according to the prescribed ritual, equal in quantity to that milk,
[should be offered] on the morning of the first day of the bright fortnight when the sun has risen halfway.
One should offer the oblation situated in the great vessel with a single oblation,
using a *triṣṭubh* verse dedicated to Jātavedas, which is enclosed at the beginning and end by the *tārikā*.
Then, from sunrise until the setting of the sun, the wise one [should perform the rite] in a great sacrificial pit with a great fire by means of the application of the yantra.
And the wise one, free from fatigue, should offer oblations continuously with the *sruva* ladle itself, using consecrated clarified butter and employing such a *triṣṭubh* verse.
Beginning from morning, one should continuously feed a single Brahmin at each mealtime, starting from the morning, with śāli rice prepared with milk, curd, and clarified butter.
At the conclusion, having had the twice-born recite [the texts], he should satisfy those most learned in the Vedas,
as well as a Vaiṣṇava couple, under the names of Lakṣmī and Lakṣmīśa.
The hero who acts in this manner, supported by his resolve,
obtains an incomparable and inexhaustible treasure numbering ten million.
O Pākaśāsana, hear this most wonderful application:
first, having taken the word *tārā*, one should join it with the word *subhagā*. (42–63)
One should then join it with *svāhā*; this is the six-syllabled *Tārikā*. Having fasted on the fourteenth day, one should commence the practice on the full moon day.
One should recite that [mantra] ten thousand times while seated properly in the middle of a beautiful tree in a grove, between a full water-pot and a lamp.
Note—57. Regarding "jātavedasyā": by means of the *ṛc* beginning with "jātavedase sunavāma somam" (We shall press Soma for Jātavedas), etc. (p. 169).
Root Text:
Meditating upon me, who am radiant like the interior of a lotus, holding two lotuses, possessing two arms,
with dark-cornered eyes and dark, curly hair.
Her face was filled with a smile, she was beautiful, her breasts were full and elevated;
she was adorned with all ornaments and clothed in excellent silken garments.
Meditating thus upon her who is most beautiful and auspicious, one should perform the recitation (japa);
one should likewise offer libations (tarpaṇa) and oblations (homa), each being a tenth part [of the japa], with this Tārā-mantra.
One should offer an oblation (*bali*) consisting of *śāli* rice mixed with milk, ghee, and jaggery;
and the wise man should feed a woman endowed with auspicious marks who has been duly honored.
The student (brahmacārī) himself should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) once at night;
in this manner, he should perform this vow (vrata) for thirty nights without fail.
Undertaking the recitation, libations, fire-offerings, and so forth without interruption and without sloth,
one should complete the vow on the final full-moon day.
At the conclusion of the vow, she who is composed of the essence of Love, named Subhagā, will arrive;
that Yakṣī will say to the practitioner, "What shall I do? (42.72).
One should regard her as a mother, a sister, a wife, or a friend; having approached her with the mindset of a mother, she protects one even from all calamities. (42.73)
If she is accepted as a sister, she grants all desired objects;
if she is accepted as a beloved, she grants all pleasures for as long as one lives. (42.74)
Accepted as a friend, she indeed leads one in every direction;
one desiring liberation should constantly recite [the mantra] consisting of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme Self. (42.75)
I, being gracious, shall cause you to attain that divine Vaiṣṇava station;
as for the applications (viniyoga) pertaining to the supreme mantra which follow hereafter, they shall be explained.
All those who rely on other mantras are to be brought across [to liberation]. The path of preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) has been explained to you along with its applications;
now, for the sake of attaining conviction in her, learn from me the path to accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of the Tārā Mantra," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Note:
73. "Should conceive" (prakalpayet) means "should contemplate" (manvīta). 76. He also states that the fruit of the worship of Tārikā is liberation by saying, "that state" (padaṃ tat).
77. "Of her" means of the Tārikā. Thus ends the forty-second chapter;
[now begins] the forty-third chapter.
Śrī said: Listen, O Lord of the Gods, I shall declare the supreme accomplishment arising from various yogas, pertaining to the Tārikā which is the condensed essence of the Vidyā. (43-1)
The yogi should practice according to the prescribed rule the Tārikā within the range of the body—at the tip of the nose, at the tip of the tongue, and at the middle and root of the tongue. (43-2)

One should maintain the sequence of the principles (tattvapaddhati), beginning with earth and ending with intellect, each possessing its own nature as the cause of its respective effects, upon the throat, the chest, and the end of the breast.
When proceeding from one principle (tattva) to another principle, one should recite [the mantra] according to their number:
twice, four times, six times, eight times, ten times, and sixteen times respectively. (43–4)
One should contemplate the *prakṛti* twenty-four times; one should recollect Tārā eighty times, and there, one should meditate upon the *jīva*. (43–5)
Whatever its extent, whatever its nature, and whoever it may be—one should perform a hundred recitations there;
then one should meditate upon that Puṣkara as the support for the unmanifest consciousness, situated below it. (43–6)
Having meditated upon this as being infinite, supported by the constituent parts beginning with the *tattvas*, conveying the *tattvas*,
and shaped like a lotus, the wise one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and fifty times.

Then, that which consists of the unmanifest, time, life-force, and the imperishable (akṣara) is the stalk; but where there is space (kha), there time is darkness, having the form of an internal cavity.
Having reflected correctly upon that which consists of those three— thinking "this is he who is consciousness within"— one should perform two hundred recitations.

Recalling me, the power named Aniruddha, who consists of the Blessed One, located below the stalk, one should perform a hundred recitations while contemplating my form, time, and other attributes. (43.10)
Below that is the power of Pradyumna, and the number of recitations for it is the same;
below that is the power of Sāṃkarṣiṇī, and the number of recitations for it is likewise the same.
At the very bottom is the couple known as Vāsudeva, which has a gross form;
beyond that is the subtle, and beyond that is the supreme, which transcends everything.
Resplendent as Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, it is indefinable and incomparable;
everywhere it is the vibration of Power and the Lord of Power, untainted and pure.
Having attained this sleep consisting of yoga, one should thus enter into that very sleep;
then, rising during the latter part of the night, one should maintain these twelve [concentrations].
One may hold all these meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās) in the heart, following the procedure for their enumeration from Vāsudeva down to the earth element. || 43-15 ||
These twelve indeed are the dhāraṇās for the Tārikā, or even [for others];
this yoga is beneficial to all, insofar as one abides there with the essential principles (tattvas).
Or, having withdrawn everything— the state consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest—
and having made the mind supportless, one should enter into the state of emptiness.
I enter the Great Yoga, which is like the ocean completely full, possessing the aspect of emptiness and the aspect of equality, and is established in the meditation on emptiness. 43-18 ||

3. *Buddhi* is the principle of *mahat*.
4. Regarding "from the principle [of earth]," etc.: the meaning is that it proceeds in the manner of moving from the principle of earth to the principle of water, and so forth.

14. Regarding "twelve": the twelve *dhāraṇās* consist of the four beginning with Vāsudeva (as the individual soul), along with primordial matter (*prakṛti*), intellect (*buddhi*), and the elements (*bhūta*). 17. He states another method: "having withdrawn" (*pratisaṃhṛtya*). Having dissolved all the principles (*tattva*) back into their respective causes, one should make the mind free from objects. That experience of supreme bliss which occurs when the mind is free from objects is itself the supreme yoga. (p. 171) [Root Text]
When the yogi, while practicing yoga, becomes like the bliss of a cloudless, silent ocean, that yogi is always dear to Me.
Where no limited object of meditation whatsoever exists,
that form which is unknowable and unlimited— that clearly is my own body.
The yogi assimilates the entire object of knowledge without succession;
that vast, waveless flame is my own body. (43.21)
Wherein all beings and worlds are invoked by the mind,
then my eternal state, consisting of all existence, unfolds.
Having offered the elements, the senses, the worlds, and so forth into the ladle with the mind, and then having cast away that ladle, I become a yogin. (43.23)
Whatever is delimited by something is indeed greater than that;
for by the intellect, everything—whatever exists and whatever does not—is delimited. (43.24)
That subtle body of mine is not differentiated by anything else; it is stainless.
These two—intellect and ego—are not external entities, whether they be non-existence or existence.
My body, which has not been touched by intellect and is unstained [by passion], does not exist;
for when the ocean transgresses its bounds, it would submerge the world. (43.26)
Just as at that time there was neither high ground nor low ground, so it is with me; the entire world [is likewise].
This supreme state cannot be attained by one of small mind.
One should repeatedly sever [the mind] in order to attain this yoga, whether in a present auspicious state, or in another past or future state. (43.28)
One should remember the most essential form, the supreme state of the Supreme Lord;
for bees gather honey from all flowers. (43.29)
In that same way, yogins collect me alone within all things;
wherever the mind goes, there one should contemplate my splendor.
Having moved, where does it go? For everything is composed of that [mind].
One should contemplate the sequence of the principles as a garland strung upon my thread. (43.31)
Or, with me acting as the wall, one should perceive the world as a painting;
like a mass of foam upon the ocean, which is motionless, shoreless, and profound. (43.32)
One should remember the fourfold group beginning with the subject (pramātṛ) both in forward and reverse order;
that which arises from the form of the "I" (madākāra) and again returns to it. (43–33)
The primordial Person is my first manifestation (unmeṣa), fashioned by my own volition;
another manifestation of mine, known as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), exists upon the lower ground. (43.34)
Another, the third, situated below that on the earth, consists of externalization;
this fourth is of the nature of existence, consisting of objects of knowledge, and is the lowest of the low. (43.35)
By the power of my own resolve alone, constantly meditating with the intellect— both in regular and reverse order— upon that which is eternally of the nature of blissful consciousness.
Having abandoned these four, one attains my state, [residing] within the thirty-two lotuses that serve as the supports for consciousness. (43.37)
One should meditate upon me as having the luster of a lamp’s flame, or as Rūpasundarī,
beginning from the support-lotus down to the earth below the navel-lotus.

22. *Sarvabhāvaḥ* refers to existence as the universal self; *bhāvaḥ* means being or existence (*sattā*).
23. "May I become" and "may my self become"—these are usages in the abstract sense (*bhāve prayoga*).
24. The fact that the Goddess has the nature of consciousness (*jñānasvarūpatva*) is stated by the passage beginning with "that which is delimited," etc.

26. Regarding the point that at the stage of the maturation of yoga the entire world appears as having the very form of cognition, he provides a worldly illustration with the words "when one transcends," etc.
29. He provides an illustration regarding the fact that all entities (*bhāva*) are to be manifested by their own nature with the words "they bring together" (*saṃbharanti*).

33. "The tetrad" (*catuṣṭaya*): the meaning is the tetrad consisting of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the instrument of knowledge (*pramākaraṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the resulting cognition (*pramiti*). [The phrase] "she who is manifesting" (*prabhavantīm*) connects with the expression "the path of the principles" (*tattvānāṃ paddhatiḥ*). 37–46. The word division is "in thirty-two lotuses" (*dvātriṃśati ambujeṣu*). He points out the thirty-two lotuses starting with "the foundation" (*ādhāra*). There are six beginning with *vyucchantī*; five beginning with *paśyantī*; five beginning with *bodhayantī*; five beginning with *ghoṣayantī*; and five beginning with *grāhayantī*.
(172) The six root lotuses are to be contemplated by yogins; hear their names from me:
Vyucchantī, Vyuṣitā, Vyuṣṭā, Vyuṣuṣī, Vyoṣuṣī, and Ramā. (43.39)
From the navel-lotus and the heart-lotus, they declare five lotuses:
Paśyantī is called the navel-lotus; Paśyā consists of the other [lotuses]. (43–40)
The visible and the being-seen are the heart of those called the lotuses;
now hear of the five called the lotuses from within the middle of the space between the heart and the throat.

Awakening, the awakened, the process of awakening, and likewise the other [state], as well as resonance and manifestation—these are the designations for [the states] residing in the lotuses of the throat, the heart, and the center. (43–42)
Listen to these five known as the lotuses within the throat and palate:
Ghoṣayantī, Ghuṣyantī, Ghuṣṭā, Puṣyantī, and Puṣṭā, as well as the other, Ghoṣā.
These five, known by the name of lotuses, are situated in the palate and the region between the eyebrows;
they are the state of grasping, the state of having grasped, the desire to grasp, and the act of grasping. (43–44)

Prāṇayantī, Prāṇatī, Prāṇā, and Prāṇāvabodhinī—these supreme powers awaken [consciousness]; they reside within the lotus situated between the eyebrows. (43–46)
One should meditate upon me in the forms of the jewel-lamp flames, both in direct and reverse order; reciting the long *tārikā* mantra, which resembles the resonance of a long bell.
Thinking of me in this way, or even remembering my beautiful form, the yogi, having abandoned all affliction, attains my own state. (43–48)
Or one may observe them within nine lotuses, proceeding in both direct and reverse order:
three lotuses in the *ādhāra*, and three lotuses below the heart. (43–49)
Below the head, there are three lotuses; this is the sequence for the arrangement of the nine lotuses.
Alternatively, one may place them upon twelve lotuses, two by two, beginning with the head.
Or one should contemplate the Tārikā, the resonant sound of the syllable Om, within the six initial lotuses, or in the three—the root, the heart, and the earth—or even between the eyebrows. (43–51)
One should first contemplate that drop as being the size of a mung bean and brilliantly radiant;
then as the size of a mustard seed; and then as variegated and formless.
Whatever entity is perceived, such as a jar, a wall, or any form possessing material characteristics,
one should contemplate therein those principles (tattvas) that exist according to the scriptures.

Having made those things identical with oneself, one should contemplate them there through the sense of "I," whether they be objects in the world that possess causes or are themselves the causes of others.

Those forms which consist of the supported and the support, whether they be transparent or dense, having the nature of both the entity and its possessor, and composed of both the auspicious and the inauspicious; || 43-55 ||
Whether consisting of the productive and the non-productive, or appearing as qualities and the possessor of qualities,
or existing as the container and the contained, they are all composed of Śakti and its Possessor (Śaktimān).
They consist of the nature of the enjoyed and the enjoyer, or of women and men;
they consist of the nature of action and the agent, or of the means and the goal. (43–57)
Whatever forms of words exist in the form of feminine and masculine genders, or whatever things in this world exist as dualities— || 43-58 ||
The yogi should perceive those [elements] with his intellect as being of the nature of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
O Purandara, hear now the supreme secret of the Tantra, the sacred vow.
That which is to be practiced by the yogi in the sequence of the ritual procedure for the yoga of Lakṣmī,
as it was formerly set in motion by the Primordial God for the sake of the creation of the world.
Desiring to do what was pleasing to me, the yogi, who is expert in the *Lakṣmītantra*, assumed the form of a woman with great resolve. (43–61)
One should not, through action, mind, or speech, recall the censure of women;
where I am, there are the principles (tattvas), and where I am, there are the deities.
Root-text:
"Wherever I am, there are merits; wherever I am, there is Keśava.
Since I am in the woman, therefore the woman embodies the entire world. (43.63)
He who reviles that woman reviles Lakṣmī; he who welcomes her welcomes the three worlds. || 43-64 ||
He who hates any woman hates the beloved of Hari;
he who hates the beloved of Hari hates the entire world. (43–65)
He whose mind becomes serene upon seeing a woman like moonlight,
and who does not harbor any ill-will toward her, is considered by me to be most dear.
Just as there is no sin in Nārāyaṇa, nor in me, O Śakra, nor in a cow, nor in a Brahmin, nor in one who knows the Vedānta. (43.67)
O Śakra, likewise no evil whatsoever exists in a woman;
she is as stainless as the Gaṅgā and as meritorious as the Sarasvatī.
For just as the river Āpagā is Aruṇā, so too is Sīmantinī the most excellent;
since I am the mother of the three worlds. (43.69)
This [power] is due to my reliance upon the Noble Lady, for she is my supreme strength—the Goddess who is the mother of the three worlds and the fulfiller of all desires. (43.70)
Why should a yogi not worship a woman who is the very embodiment of his own body?
He should not commit sin against a woman, nor should he reproach her for her conduct. (43.71)
One who desires success in yoga should do nothing pleasing to a woman except for what is sinful;
he should regard her as a mother, as a goddess, or as myself.
He who, out of delusion, hates a woman and does not provide her assistance—listen to this, O Lord of Gods, for you are dear to me as I speak it. (43-73)
Having heard this, you too must practice it and never speak of it to anyone.
Any woman of beautiful form who has come within the range of your vision—(43.74)
In her, the yogi should meditate upon me while reciting the *tārikā* mentally;
with a mind free from longing, he should call to mind her form. (43.75)
One should meditate upon Prāṇa as the Sun, the Supreme Self, the Puruṣa within the heart of the woman; there, one should contemplate the fire endowed with the perfection of beauty and charm.
One should call to mind that woman endowed with every perfection;
having called her to mind and reciting the sacred syllable (*brahman*), one should indeed contemplate me through the intellect. (43.77)
Then, upon the attainment of samādhi, I become possessed therein;
the characteristic of my possession by intoxication is the loosening of all my limbs, which have become rigid. (43.78)
Having diligently propitiated me with a mind free from greed, one who practices yoga should indeed desist [from worldly activity], completely avoiding all evil. (43.79)
But this must never be done toward another's wife by one who possesses discernment; for wherever this concentration exists, she certainly becomes enamored with that [object]. (43.80)
One should practice with one's own wife or even with a common woman;
in this matter, even sexual promiscuity is not a fault, because [the practitioner] possesses the realization of my nature.
Regarding the great surge of delight that arises from enjoyments born of sensory contact, one should meditate upon my form with an undistracted mind. (43.82)
One should cultivate that state of being which consists of the intense joy felt when remembering the pleasure arising from excellent objects, such as writing or churning. (43.83)
The joy that arises when an object is seen with the eye, or when it is tasted, heard, or smelled—that is my body composed of bliss. (43.84)
Thus, this method of attainment has been declared for the ascetic who subdues the mind with respect to sounds, touches, tastes, and so forth, as they happen to present themselves by chance. (43.85)
For those enjoyments born of contact are indeed sources of suffering;
having a beginning and an end, one should not delight the mind in them.

That supreme happiness which is manifested within by the internal organ (antahkarana), when it moves in the state of purity (sattva), having cast off passion (rajas) and destroyed darkness (tamas). || 43-87 ||
That bliss of mine, whose nature is knowledge, is devoid of beginning and end;
such as it is, it is never manifested by contacts dependent upon sense objects.
The objects that bring pleasure cause suffering to follow, just as honey mixed with poison is sweet when eaten. (43.89)
What is gained by that which subsequently kills its own devourer—he who, oppressed by the heat, takes refuge in the shadow of an enraged serpent? (43.90)
p.

174) That man should enjoy those pleasures arising from touch for his own happiness—pleasures that are to be accomplished through the exhaustion and effort of suffering, and which, though seemingly pleasant, are mixed with pain. (43.91)

What happy person would resort to sense-objects, which are so subtle and subject to decay, when one has purified oneself through recitation, restricted one's diet, and thinned the body through divine beings? (43.92)
Diminishing the qualities of rajas and tamas through conduct and actions dear to Me,
the yogi should constantly subdue the mind with effort for the sake of meditative absorption.
When the mind is ever-conquered, the entire universe is thereby conquered;
when the mind is conquered, my pure body manifests of its own accord.

Śakra: O Creator, seated upon the lotus, who ordains the entire system of the machinery of distinctions between the conscious and the unconscious, and who provides all enjoyments—salutations to you! (43.95)
By what means can that mind be subdued—[the mind] which is ever inclined toward sense objects, restless, powerful, firm, swift-moving, far-reaching, and indistinct? (43.96)
Śrī said:

"O Śakra, that mind is difficult to subdue, difficult to restrain, eternally subtle, hard to understand, and prone to transgression; it is restless and can only be controlled through the practice of dispassion. (43.97)
Attachment, however, is a coloring toward an object born of nature, habituation, or association;
and its absence, which is dispassion, is produced by the knowledge of reality. (43-98)
The wickedness of sense objects is that which is known as the knowledge of reality;
the wise person should discern that wickedness in four ways through wisdom. (43.99)
One should reflect: "What is this entity, of what nature, from whence, and for whom?
Objects of sense, being of the nature of bondage, ensnare those who serve them. (43.100)
Having attained manifestation from the unmanifest, all these objects of pleasure and pain do not exist by their own inherent nature for those who merely seek sense-objects.
For they arise from the means of suffering, which involve uncertainty, exhaustion, and toil;
they would not produce happiness for you, but rather give birth to suffering.
And that pleasure, perishing in an instant, is equaled by the suffering of its own state;
this variegated nature should be contemplated by the wise person in every single phenomenon. (43.103)
This knowledge of reality has been proclaimed both by way of synthesis and analysis;
yet attachment to sense objects arises from the conviction that they are the cause of happiness. (43.104)
Because it consists of false cognition, it is sublated by cognitions of reality;
and when that [false cognition] is refuted by a definitive ascertainment, its status as a logical reason is not established at all.
No one should take up sense objects that lack a cause for their own attainment;
rather, there is this: the knowledge of reality and its repeated cultivation (or reflection). || 43-106 ||
Therefore, this is designated as "practice" (abhyāsa) by the knowers of reality in the treatises on reality, whether the object be subtle or great, minute or gross, stable or moving. (43.107)
Wherever the mind remains or is held steady—this indeed is practice for the striving yogi through the yoga of dispassion and cultivation. (43.108)
The unrestrained mind is tamed; consequently, it becomes firmly stilled.
Śakra said:
"O you whose gait is skillful in wandering through the multitude of the lotuses of reality! (43.109)
Homage to you, O dweller in the mind of the Conqueror of Madhu, seated upon the lotus!
Just as the mind is tamed through practice, so too is it subdued powerfully and firmly.
"Show me that path; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One! Śrī said:
"When the arrow, having become slender in the upward sky, falls with speed—" (43.111)
Likewise, one should restrain the mind upon a subtle object such as the star Arundhatī;
or one should contemplate the mind upon a great mountain or upon the infinite. (43.112)
Note: 100. "Viṣiṇvanti" means they bind; the root is *ṣiñ* in the sense of binding.

111–112. He explains this point with an illustration beginning with the words "viyati," etc., stating that one should first fix the mind upon objects exactly as they are perceived, and having gradually attained detachment from them, subsequently fix it upon the investigation of reality (*tattva*). Regarding the phrase "become attenuated" (*tanūbhūta*): it means being visible due to its small dimension resulting from leaping to a great distance.
p. 175) One should fix the mind precisely upon that subtle atom which exists at the base of the revolving wheel, and cause it to revolve together with the turning [wheel]. (43-113)

Likewise, one should move the mind by means of a moving tip of an *aśvattha* leaf; when it remains still, one should stabilize the consciousness; and when it moves away, one should cause the mind to follow after it. (43.114)
This method has been described to you for the sake of illustration, O Purandara;
by subduing the mind through this, one shall attain supreme yoga.

One should meditate upon that form which is both supreme and inferior, consisting of the Lord and the one to be ruled, situated in the sun; that indeed is the female form consisting of five points (bindus).
Thus, O gentle one, this form of the Tārikā has been shown to you in its entirety.
For one who has thus realized the true nature of reality, no other object of knowledge is required. (43.117)
Thus, O Śakra, this accomplishment of the *piṇḍa* has been shown to you in brief;
now hear from me the procedure for the designation of names and forms (*saṃjñāmūrtividhāna*) and the means of attainment (*sādhana*).
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Illumination of Various Yogas," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra* (or *Śrīpañcarātra*).
Note:
113. The same applies to the analogy of the wheel and so forth.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter.
Chapter Forty-four. Śakra said:
Salutations to you, who are expert in protecting the multitude of both conscious and unconscious beings!
Salutations to you, the consort of Viṣṇu, the artisan who fashions the universe. || 44-1 ||
The divisions consisting of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme self have been previously demonstrated.
O Lotus-born One, show me the division of Tārā into seed-syllables (bīja), clusters (piṇḍa), and so forth. 44-2.
Śrī said: "Nārāyaṇa alone is glorious, the embodiment of the six perfect attributes;
I alone am his supreme Śakti, the embodiment of the six attributes. (44.3)
Desiring to favor the worlds perpetually through my nature of knowledge and action, I, as that very [power], nourish and purify them by means of my form as Tārikā.
O Śakra, its state as the supreme and so forth has already been shown to you;
now listen to me as I explain the various divisions, such as the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and the clusters (*piṇḍa*).
O Śakra, that supreme *ahaṃtā* which was previously shown to be threefold in nature—just as it is, it is called the seed-syllable of Tārikā. (44–6)
Abiding in the sun and fire, crowned by Viṣṇu, Piṇḍa, Vyoma, and Īśa,
the yoga of her preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa) and her accomplishment have been revealed.
O Śakra, this Tārikā known by its name is indeed cultivated by yogins;
listen now as I speak it, fixing your attention upon it. (44.8)
Taking the single pure [syllable], O Śakra, one should join it with *svāhā*.
This is that mantra of names, worshipped by yogis, gods, Brahmā, and others [or: worshipped by Brahmin sages]. (44.9)
O Lord of the Thirty-three, even by striving yogins, or by me, Nārāyaṇa,
it is impossible to describe the power of Saṃjñā.
But the supreme imperishable is intended to be designated as merely the continuity of the auspicious;
and for this [perfection], when it is condensed, there are both the accomplishments and the means of accomplishment. (44.11)
Constantly remembering Me through practice, the yogi whose body has been made one with Me attains absorption in Me and reaches My own state of being.
Or, having been awakened by him and having attained direct realization,
I fulfilled every desire— that is, all desires— whatever that yogi wished for.
Thus, O Śakra, the mantra of the name has been briefly shown to you. Now listen to me regarding the word-mantra (padamantra), which accomplishes everything. (44.14)
Although this [object] cannot be extracted by analysis nor can it be so depicted, nevertheless,
its own nature is taught for the sake of preventing confusion regarding its form.

Oṃ 3, Hrīṃ 3, Śrīṃ [B: Hauṃ 3, Haṃsaḥ 3, Śrīṃ Namo Viṣṇave; Ī. omits Śrīṃ 3, Oṃ, Āṃ 3] 3 Oṃ Āṃ 3 Hauṃ 3 Haṃsaḥ 3 Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Namo Viṣṇave | Oṃ [F: Śrīṃ Hraṃ] Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Namo Nārāyaṇāya | Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Namo Bhagavate Vāsudevāya | Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Jitaṃ [Ī: Jitaṃ te Puṇḍarīkākṣa Mahāpuruṣapūrvaja | Namaste'stu Hṛṣīkeśa Namaste Viśvabhāvana ||] te Puṇḍarīkākṣa Namaste Viśvabhāvana |
Salutations to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, Great Being, Primordial One!

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ! O Blessed One, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Lord of Lakṣmī, Supreme Person, Origin of the World, Center of the World, End of the World, Abode of Śrī; I approach the Blessed One.
*Note:* 7. *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bījamantra*).
9. "Pure seed" is the meaning. 11. The auspicious letter is *śa*. The distinction lies precisely in its connection [to that]. *Śrīṃ svāhā* is the name-mantra (*saṃjñāmantra*).

I take refuge in the Blessed One. I have gone to the Blessed One. I entreat the Blessed One. I am meditated upon by the Blessed One. I have become an attendant of the Blessed One. I am authorized by the Blessed One. I am created by the Blessed One. By the grace of the Blessed One, I shall cause the Goddess Lakṣmī—who consists of the Blessed One and who consists of Tārikā—to revolve through her syllables. It is as follows: Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, to the Gurus and the wives of the Gurus; Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, to the Paramagurus and the wives of the Paramagurus; Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, to the Parameṣṭhin and the Parameṣṭhinī; Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, to the ancient Siddhas and the ancient Siddhas; Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutations, salutations to the Lakṣmī-yogins and the Lakṣmī-yoginīs.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ īṃ, salutations to her who bestows the perfection and abundance of all accomplishments, to the supreme state of absolute unity, to the Supreme Haṃsī, who transcends the speech and mind of all people and their own selves, whose nature is the great ocean of the mass of supreme bliss that is beginningless, motionless, stainless, and pure, to the highest of the high, to Viṣṇu and the consort of Viṣṇu, to Viṣṇu, īṃ svāhā!

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ īṃ [Ā: Īśa], salutations to Māyā, the consort of Viṣṇu, who is the supreme subtle one, the ocean of consciousness that vibrates by its own will at the commencement of the succession of the opening and closing of eyes manifested through her own sovereignty, and who is the primordial state of uninterrupted and ever-expanding aesthetic equilibrium; īṃ svāhā!

Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ īṃ, salutation to the Consort of Viṣṇu, who is the five drops (pañcabindu), whose essential nature is the state of pervasion by the Blessed One manifested through the power of her own resolve; she whose form is the manifestation of the glory of existence expanding through the penetration of her own will; she who possesses the fourfold collection of qualities and the triple mass of great waves; īṃ svāhā.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hiṃ hiṃ hiṃ, salutations to her who is the manifestation of the form of the Blessed One, eternally risen, supremely blissful, and most beautiful; she who is the abode of various siddhi-ointments; she whose power is the supreme ether, whose nature consists of the expansion of the six qualities and the essence of supreme sattva; she whose essential nature is skilled in the transformation of the various modes of pure, beautiful, and blissful networks of enjoyment; she who is subtle within her extremely subtle and gross forms; the consort of Viṣṇu; the five points; hiṃ hiṃ hiṃ svāhā!

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ āṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ namaḥ! Salutation to her who is a mass of stones consisting of the various sheaths of living beings, fanned by the wind of one’s own volitions; to her who is a great ocean of the wealth of enjoyments, instruments of enjoyment, objects of enjoyment, and enjoyers, manifested through the play of the foam-masses of the distinctions of time and its divisions; to her whose forms are both supremely subtle and gross; to the consort of Viṣṇu, the five points (pañcabindu); hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā!

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutation to her whose intellect, mind, limbs, and minor members are beautiful through her commitment to benefiting the entire world; who is the sole treasury of all prosperity, glory, victory, splendor, and power manifested by the fourfold means for the welfare of all people; who is the architect of the entire wheel of powers; who bestows enjoyment and good fortune upon all beings; who pacifies the disturbances of various worldly objects; and who dwells upon the lap of Nārāyaṇa—Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa, to Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, svāhā! Śrīṃ hrīṃ oṃ.
Thus has this most wonderful *padamantra* been shown to you;
it should be received from the mouth of a guru alone by wise men who have undergone initiation. (44.16)
While this knowledge is being studied, like a stainless mirror clearly reflecting, I shall reveal exactly who I am, what I am, and of what nature I am.
Having realized the meaning of her own true nature and being celebrated by all the Siddhas,
listen as I describe her sequence of limbs.
I am the essence of light and bliss; at its end is the All-Seeing One, who manifests true being; and near that is the Supreme Brahman.
Then, in his presence, the Blessed One, the consort of Viṣṇu, spoke this most wonderful heart-mantra, which consists of knowledge conjoined with birth: || 44-20 ||

Commentary—19. Oṃ, salutation to the Heart for the sake of knowledge, O Blessed One, Consort of Viṣṇu, whose essence is light and bliss, who perceives all, who manifests the true being [of all], and who is the form of the Supreme Brahman. The word *svāhā* indicates the genus (*jāti*). (p. 178) Root Text:

O Supreme Goddess, at the end of that state where unimpeded bliss has been attained, you abide above all as the Sovereign of All; the remainder is like the heart-mantra, endowed with its specific suffix.
And I, likewise, am within that which is complete with power and is the primordial nature of the world, in the flame of the fire of knowledge; the remainder is to be understood as before.
And [it is] consisting of the great vibration of the unfolding of the vital breath and the non-vital breath;
this armor, which transcends all stages of life, follows as a supplement to what precedes. (44.23)
Furthermore, even when agitated by transformation, its own inherent nature is thus described as "consisting of great heroism"; this is the weapon, as previously stated for the remaining cases.
"Independent in its capacity," "the progenitor of all," and finally, "consisting of awakening"—thus [is] the Eye, as the remainder of what was previously stated. (44-25)
On the peak of the five Brahmās, she who dwells in the fire of peace is this Māyā named Brahmaśrī, whose crest-jewel is Vyomeśa.
In the fourfold peak of retention, she dwells as the subtle fire;
this is Dhāraṇāśrī (or Dhāriṇī), whose crest-jewel is made by Māyāvyomeśa.
Seated upon the seat of the primary fire, crowned by Vyomeśa, she is to be known as this Śrī Puruṣa, who extends the flood of consciousness. (44.28)
Abiding in the eternal fire, crowned by Māyā and Vyomeśa, she is to be known as this Pradhānaśrī, the maker of all consciousness. (44.29)
Beginning with Vāmana and ending with the Pavitra, she is the one who enters the fire of the Pavitra;
she is the glory of the internal organ, whose crest-jewel is fashioned by Māyā and Vyomeśa.
At the end of the characteristics of the *nārāca* and *āditāla* meters, this Jñānaśrī is declared to be the Sragdharā moving through fire, adorned by Māyā and Vyomeśa. (44.31)
On the peak to the east of Vaikuṇṭha, situated within the fire that nourishes the universe,
this is declared to be Karmaśrī, adorned by Māyā and Vyomeśa.
Moving through the fire of Kapila from the beginning of Uttamā to the end of Karālā, she is designated as Bhūtaśrī, adorned by Māyā and Vyomeśa. (44.33)
These eight, preceded by Brahmaśrī and seated upon the eight lotus petals, are proclaimed as the retinue of the Tārā who is the embodiment of the Word (Padamūrti). || 44-34 ||
All of them possessed the luster of the interior of a lotus, with faces like serene lotuses,
and held a pair of full-blown lotuses in their two arms.
Brahmaśrī is auspicious, forming the Brahmāñjali mudrā with her two fore-hands;
Dhāraṇālakṣmī, who distinguishes between the pure and the impure, is present in the two front hands. (44.36)
With her two front hands, Puruṣaśrī forms the gesture of respectful salutation (añjali);
with her two front hands, Prakṛtiśrī holds a noose and a goad.
The goddess Antaḥkaraṇalakṣmī, however, bears the seal of reasoning (tarka-mudrā):
with the palms facing downward, the two fingers, the little finger and the ring finger— || 44.38 ||
One should contract and hold the other two fingers together;
likewise, one should separate and firmly hold the thumb raised high.
When the elevated surface is on the right side and facing outward, the arrangement should be made in that manner; this is indeed the Tārkikī mudrā.
When the two hands are positioned in such a manner that they form the gesture of exposition (vyākhyāmudrā), that is the mudrā of Jñānaśrī; now learn from me the mudrā of Karmalakṣmī.
O high-minded one, when the hands are always engaged in the activity of performing rites with energetic exertion, this is declared to be the mudrā of Karmalakṣmī.
Commentary:
21. Oṃ, obeisance to the head for the sake of knowledge, O Supreme Goddess, whose state of bliss is unimpeded, who abide above all.
26. Oṃ Śrīṃ: this is the mantra of the venerable Brahman-Śrī.
27. *Aṃ* 4 *yrīṃ*: the Śrī-mantra of Dhāraṇā. 28. *Mrīṃ*: the Śrī-mantra of Puruṣa.
29. *Bhrīṃ*: the Śrī-mantra of Pradhāna.
30. *baṃ phaṃ paṃ prīṃ*—this is the Śrī-mantra of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
31. *naṃ dhaṃ daṃ thaṃ taṃ trīṃ*—this is the Śrī-mantra of knowledge (*jñāna*).
32. *ṇaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭaṃ ṭrīṃ*—this is the Śrī-mantra of action (*karman*).
33. *Ñaṃ jhaṃ chaṃ caṃ ṅaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ khaṃ kaṃ krīṃ*—this is the *bhūtaśrī* mantra. (p.
179) The two primary hands of Mūlabhūtalakṣmī bestow various enjoyments.
This single peak, consisting of Mahālakṣmī, bestows all happiness.
Listen with an attentive mind, O slayer of Bala:
a man should extract that [mantra] in sequence, beginning with Garuḍa and ending with Karāla.
One should then utter the Māyā-bīja, which is situated in the fierce fire and has the Lord of the Sky (H) on its left;
this is the peak-syllable consisting of Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāśrī is its presiding deity. (44–45)
She possesses both a single and manifold nature; she is with form and yet formless;
she has infinite faces, infinite feet, and likewise infinite hands; she is the supreme one.
She is always present everywhere through the relationship of the support and the supported;
she possesses various colors and is crowded with a multitude of diverse collections of weapons.
Whether fierce or gentle, seated together, and preeminent with manifold prosperity,
she is easily accessible everywhere, auspicious, and should be meditated upon as radiant from within a lotus.
This very same [sequence], O Mahāmati, ending with Garuḍa, when reversed, should be meditated upon according to form as before, bestowing the previously mentioned fruits. (44–49)
The twenty-seven vowels of the Goddess exist as her rays;
the Bindu exists as the foundational support; and Emanation is her own powerful form.
Thus has the form of the Tārikā, known as the "Word" (pada), been revealed to you;
always fix your mind upon this with focused attention.
From the great ocean of the Lakṣmītantra, which extends over a hundred crores [of verses], this essence has been extracted and presented by me with affection. (44–52)
Formerly, while I was resting on his lap, Janārdana, the god of gods and lotus-eyed one, bestowed upon me this supreme knowledge for my delight.
Just as the hearts of men are gladdened upon seeing moonlight, so too the hearts of yogis are gladdened upon seeing this knowledge. 44–54.
There is no affliction from the restraints (yama) and so forth, nor any failure regarding the postures (āsana);
there is no distress from breath control (prāṇāyāma), for nothing at all is required here.
Seated comfortably, with a serene mind and assuming whatever posture one desires,
one attains perfection by practicing this vidyā with the mind.
Just as rivers and streams flow together into the great ocean,
so do all supreme sciences converge within the Self that is the Foot (or the Path of the Foot).
Just as there are innumerable jewels in the lord of rivers and streams, so do the wise know that there are innumerable splendors within the form of the Footprint. (44–58)
Just as food mixed with honey and honey combined with food [are mutually enhancing], so too are the seed-syllables and other elements that bestow pleasure upon Tārā. (44–59)
Seated upon the lap of Nārāyaṇa, I am the Great Sovereign of all the worlds;
consisting of every perfection, I am the intended object of meditation as the embodiment of the supreme state.
Furthermore, O Śakra, I myself have exerted supreme compassion for the sake of the welfare of practitioners and for the cultivation of the mind. (44-61)
For I, who am indivisible and perfect, desiring the welfare of others, divide this very form consisting of knowledge into a fourfold self by means of myself. 44-62.
O Purandara, you ought to hear from me correctly the ritual procedure for those four forms of mine that have been divided and consist of my own essence.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Secret," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, which is the essence of the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*. (44)
Note: 44. Regarding the Mahālakṣmī mantra, one should recite from "kṣaṃ" up to "kaṃ" and then recite "krīṃ.
52. Regarding "śata" and so forth: by this, it is stated that the fundamental Lakṣmītantra consists of one hundred crore verses.
62. "In four ways": the four modes known as Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā will be explained in the immediately following chapter.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter;
[now begins] the forty-fifth chapter.
I am the primordial Śrī, the goddess Nārāyaṇī, the first-born even of those who came before.
Lakṣmī, the Śrī who is inseparable from the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu himself, [is present]. || 1 ||
By my own power, I divide myself fourfold through myself;
those four forms are Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā.
That supreme power, Lakṣmī, who is my very self, belonging to the all-pervading Lord Hari,
divides herself fourfold for the welfare of the world.
I alone am the supreme egoity, the first body;
I am the highly fortunate one named Lakṣmī, the bestower of the fruit of all sovereignty. (4)
My second body is named Kīrti, the bestower of good renown;
my third body is named Jayā, the bestower of victory. || 5 ||
The fourth of my bodies is named Māyā, the performer of all wonders;
Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā—these are the ones who take refuge in Nārāyaṇa.
My forms, which take refuge in Nārāyaṇa, are supremely radiant;
endowed with the totality of my own powers, they are indeed formless and partless.
Just as the rays belong to the sun and the waves to the ocean,
so too does Lakṣmī abide within the sovereign power and majesty of the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Surrounded by millions of various specific glories,
such fame as that of the Lord is never divided within His body.
Indeed, there is nothing that is not pervaded by her, who possesses a universal body;
for whatever fame arises for anyone, anywhere, it is produced through her own power. (10)
Each particular form of hers has arisen from her universal nature;
thus Jayā exists as the pervasive power of the Lord of Victory.
"O Lord, O Sovereign of the Gods, know me to be whatever illusion exists in this world among the gods and others, produced by Your own Māyā. (12)
"O best of gods, apart from his partless form and my own, what else exists in this ocean of principles (tattva) in its fourfold aspect?"
Perfectly manifested by the powers of the Blessed One through yoga,
they have attained the state of having form by virtue of the capacity of their own luminous gnosis.
These deities should be meditated upon, worshipped, and honored by the best of practitioners for the sake of spiritual accomplishment.
Now, behold the form of Lakṣmī, who is the primordial source of them all. (15)
With a gentle face and gentle eyes, she has two arms and beautiful earrings;
resembling the interior of a lotus in her luster, she is adorned with a girdle and a string of jewels.
Note:

8. The meaning is that the Lord of Lakṣmī’s sovereignty, power, and so forth are dependent upon Lakṣmī. Yet, by this much, there is neither dependence nor deficiency on the part of the Blessed One; for excellence bestowed by qualities resides in the possessor of those qualities.
It increases its excellence. And the learned have said: "O Śrī, you are Viṣṇu's own;

therefore, although this Blessed One possesses prosperity dependent upon you, he remains one whose majesty is not subject to another. Although a gem is precious by its own luster, it is neither devoid of quality nor does it possess blunted independence."
"And not one possessing qualities bestowed by another.
(13) [The Lord is] fourfold, in the form of Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and so forth, and in the form of Lakṣmī, Kīrti, and so forth.
(14) The syntactical connection is that Lakṣmī, Kīrti, and the others, manifested through yoga, are to be meditated upon.
15. First, he describes the form of Lakṣmī with the words beginning "tāsām" (p. 181):
The root [verse] says:
She wears white garlands and garments, and is adorned with necklaces and armlets.
She was endowed with all the auspicious marks, possessing full, high, and firm breasts. || 17 ||
Her wide eyes were like blossomed blue lotuses, her face was graced with a beautiful smile, and she was adorned with locks of hair that moved like swarms of wandering bees. || 18 ||
She bore a wonderful and captivating tilaka upon her forehead;
her jewel-like lower lip was slightly reddened, and her teeth were like bamboo-seed pearls.
With a crescent moon upon her forehead and dark, curly hair,
the Goddess holds a noose and a goad, bestowing dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
Seated in the lotus posture and adorned with a most excellent crown,
I, the Sovereign Goddess, should thus be meditated upon as abiding within the array of Lakṣmīs.
I shall proclaim her mantra; listen as I recite it to you.
That seed-syllable named Tārikā is my supreme heart-mantra.
First, one should take the syllable *praṇava* (Om), and at its end, one should join that [name].
Then, one should add the two-syllable mantra "lakṣmyai" and finally append "namaḥ. || 23 ||
After that, one should utter the word "parama," and at its end, the Lord of Men (Puruṣeśvara); then one should utter Ānandin, Garuḍa, and Varuṇa.
At the end of this [mantra], one should recite my heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) once more;
following that seed-syllable (*anubīja*), one should again recite my supreme seed-syllable (*madbīja*). || 25 ||
At the end of that [syllable] is the wife of Vahni (the fire-goddess, Svāhā); such is my Mūrti-mantra, remembered as consisting of twenty syllables, which is directly called Lakṣmī herself. || 26 ||
O slayer of Vṛtra, learn the limb-mantras of this [Gāyatrī] exactly as they are:
having first taken the syllable Śānta (Om), one should place Puruṣeśvara at its end.
The fire, that which is situated below it, and this aggregate—these three are remembered [as the components].
At the end, having joined the six vowels from the beginning to the end [of the alphabet] with the illusion of the beginning of the Yuga and so forth, one should apply them within the heart.
One should place Candrin and Vyāpin above all;
know, O Vāsava, that these six, beginning with the Heart and ending with the Weapon-mantra, [are the limbs]. (29)
Now listen to these mantras of the companions of Lakṣmī:
*satyam*, *tatstham*, *varāham*, *māyāntam*, and likewise *amṛtam*. (Or, according to another reading: *māyāktam*. 30.
Varuṇa joined with Rāma, and the four seed-leaders—Candrī and Vyāpī should be applied in sequence upon the heads of all of them. (31)
Ṛddhi, Vṛddhi, Samṛddhi, and Vibhūti are her group of friends; the seed-syllable is TĀRAṂ, followed by their names and SVĀHĀ—this is remembered as their mantra. (32)
These four companions should have two arms and a gentle appearance;
they resemble the interior of a lotus bud and are marked with the śrīvṛkṣa and the yak-tail fly-whisk.
Seated in the lotus posture and gazing at my face—thus should those female companions be meditated upon; now hear of the four male attendants.
Note:
18. "Carāḥ" means those who move; the sense is "those whose nature is to wander. 22. "Tārikā" refers to the *hrīṃ* mantra.
23–26. *Oṃ hrīṃ lakṣmyai namaḥ paramalakṣāvasthitāyai hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā*.
This twenty-syllable mantra is the *mūrtimantra* (embodiment mantra).
27–29. Regarding the term *aṅgamantra*: this means the mantra for the limbs, beginning with the heart (*hṛdaya*). He now extracts these mantras.
By the words beginning with "śāntam," the mantras are extracted by joining each of these—*ślraṃ*, *ślriṃ*, *ślruṃ*, *śllraṃ*, *ślreṃ*, *ślroṃ*—individually with the syllable *ṭaṃ*.
30. *Ṛddhi*, *Vṛddhi*, *Samṛddhi*, and *Vibhūti* are the four female friends of Lakṣmī. Of these...
The seed-mantras are *ṛṃ*, *vṛṃ*, *siṃ*, and *viṃ*, each joined with *ṭaṃ*.
(32) The mantras beginning with *oṃ ṛṃ ṭaṃ ṛddhyai svāhā* and so forth [are the root-mantras].
(p. 182) Mūla-
Lāvaṇya, Subhaga, Saubhāgya as the third,
and Saumanasya as the fourth— these four are my attendants.
They have four arms and gentle faces, are clothed in blue silk garments,
and carry a lotus, a water-pot, and a banner marked with a lotus.
And [he holds] a blossoming *āmalaka* tree with his four auspicious arms;
I shall proclaim their mantras according to reality—learn them from me. (37)
Then the wise one, enriched by the primordial deity Soma, who is the sustainer of the world,
should take the nectar in two parts and join it with the two mountains.
One should meditate upon the seed-syllables (bījas) as being truly endowed with the moon-pervader (the nasal bindu).
The mantra is traditionally taught as consisting of the syllable *tāra* (oṃ), the seed-syllable, then the name [of the deity], and finally the word *namaḥ*. (39)
This form of Lakṣmī, together with her limbs and retinue, has been shown. Now hear about the form and other attributes of the second manifestation, known as Kīrti.
In form she is like Lakṣmī, and in complexion she has the luster of the campaka flower;
in her remaining qualities she is equal to Lakṣmī—know from me these [goddesses] as the personified mantras. (41)
First is Tāra, then my heart (Hrīṃ), then Karāla joined with Viṣṇu (Klīm), then Sragdhara mounted upon Anala (Rām) and adorned with Īśvarya (Hūṃ). || 42 ||

Then [the mantra] beginning with "namaḥ" to the one whose form is eternally arisen bliss; then the word "padaṃ," followed by the true seed-syllable mounted upon Kamalā (Lakṣmī), then the fire-syllable (Ra) adorned by Viṣṇu (Sa). (43)
One should remember this seed-syllable joined with Vyāpin at the end;
this mantra, ending with the word "svāhā," is proclaimed to consist of twenty syllables.
Now learn the limb-mantras as I speak them; listen attentively.
Having placed Karāla upon Anala and having joined them as before, [proceed]. (45)

Just as these limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) of Śrī are formed by the vowels beginning with Ānanda joined with the moon-pervader (the letter *i*), hear now the mantras of Kīrti in the form of her female friends. 46.
Dyuti, Sarasvatī, Medhā, and Śruti—these are remembered as her companions;
they have two arms, possess a golden luster, are embodiments of fame, and have smiling faces. (47)
Listen as I speak the mantras of Kīrtisakhīs, holding a fine book in her left hand and a fly-whisk in her right.
Having placed Madana, Amṛta, and Pradhāna, as well as Śaṅkara,
upon the fire, one should adorn them with Māyā.
One should bestow the moon-bearing, all-pervading [deity] while recollecting these mantras of the female companions;
now hear the names, forms, and other attributes of the attendants of Kīrti.
Vāgīśa, Jayada (or Abhayada), Prasāda, and Trāṇa—these should be meditated upon as having the hue of the *kiṃśuka* flower, possessing lovely forms that are captivating to the mind. || 51 ||
One should contemplate the Śvetāmbaras as having four arms and adorned with all ornaments;
among them, one should meditate upon [the principal deities] with their two primary hands, the left and the right.
Understand from me that with the other two [hands] he holds a conch shell with the luster of a hundred moons and a great tree called kadamba, adorned with flowers and frequented by bees.
With beautiful eyes, they hold a mirror resembling the full moon in their left hand and a bright peacock-feather fan in their right hand.
Note: 35. The attendants of Lakṣmī are beauty (*lāvaṇya*) and so forth.
38. The attendant mantras are stated by the words "the wise one" (*vibudha*) and so on: *lāṃ*, *suṃ*, *sauṃ*, *sauṃ*, *ṭaṃ*.
Seed-mantras:
39. *Oṃ lāṃ ṭaṃ*, obeisance to Lāvaṇyā, and so forth, are the mantras.
42. *Oṃ hrīṃ krīṃ traiṃ namaḥ sadoditānandavigrahāyai hrīṃ krīṃ svāhā*.
The mantra consists of twenty syllables.

45. The limb-mantras (aṅgamantra), beginning with *krāṃ* and *krīṃ*, should be understood as being like those of Lakṣmī. 46. Regarding "friend" (*sakhī*) and so forth: the meaning is, "hear [the names] of their friends, their forms, and their mantras."
49. *Madanam* and so forth. The mantras are: *mrīṃ strīṃ mrīṃ śrīṃ ṭaṃ*. 51. The attendants of Kīrti are Vāgīśa and others. "Red" and so forth.
(p. 183) The root—
It is the Boar-form, enriched by the Primordial God, immeasurable and absolute;
it is pure, mounted upon fire, wearing a garland, and of such a nature.
Having joined them with the Ādideva, one should properly join them above [or: to their heads];
at the end, the mantras accompanied by attendants are endowed with the Moon and the Pervader.
This sequence has been proclaimed for Kīrti, who is indeed my second form; now listen to me regarding the form and other attributes of Jaya, my third form. || 57 ||
Jayā is equal in form and splendor to Lakṣmī and is supremely beautiful;
Tāra and Tārikā likewise are the destroyers of birth and the four states of existence.

Subsequently, that very one, endowed with the primordial deity and possessed of sovereignty, takes the *tāra* (the syllable Om) and at its end places *kāla* together with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). (59)
The Pervasive One, the Destroyer of Birth, Sarāma, and likewise Sragdhara;
he who is accompanied by Ādideva, the Sustainer, and likewise Pradhāna. (60)
Then Varuṇa, established in immortality, was the archer adorned by Rāma;
Vairāja was enriched by the primordial deity, and Śaṅkha was adorned with sovereign power.
Then the Tārikā, the eternal one, the Viṣṇu who is the support of the entire world;
then adorned by Vyomeśa, and after that, the wife of Vahni.
This is the form-mantra (mūrti-mantra) of Jayā; now learn from me her limb-mantras (aṅga-mantras), having first taken the slayer of birth adorned with the fire of time.
One should adorn [the mantra] with the vowels as before, combined with the pervasive moon;
one should then contemplate those limbs, beginning with the heart, of Jayā.
Jayantī, Vijayā, and the third, Aparājitā;
the fourth is to be known as Siddhi—these are remembered as the companions of Jaya. (65)
Ajita conjoined with Viṣṇu, Varuṇa conjoined with Ceddha (or Siddha),
and likewise Soma alone as the pervasive one, adorned with his desired ornaments. || 66 ||
Having joined it with the *candrivyāpi* [mantra] and combined it with the name,
and having appended *svāhā* at the end, one should recollect these mantras of the female companions (*sakhī*).
Having the luster of the color of dark blue clouds,
with serene faces and eyes, all of them wearing yellow garments, their lotus-like faces radiant.
All her female companions were wearing yellow garments and golden earrings.
With white chowries in their hands and variegated cane-staffs in their grasp,
they gazed upon the faces of Jayā and Ajitā.
Pratāpin, Jayabhadra, and the third, Mahābala, along with Utsāha—this group is known as the followers of Jaya. || 70 ||
All of them wore red garments, possessed four arms and great strength;
they held bows and arrows in their hands, as well as maces and discs. || 71 ||
In this manner, those attendants are to be known—[or meditated upon]—adorned with flower ornaments:
Padmanābha mounted on fire, and likewise Ajita and Kāla.

(184) The root-mantras, the *uddāma* mantras, and those of the lords of the gods are adorned by pervading the moon; they begin with the *praṇava*, end with *namaḥ*, and are endowed with their respective names. || 73 ||
O slayer of Vṛtra, these should be known as the mantras that follow Jayā;
this is the wonderful ritual for my third form, Jayā. (74)
Listen to my arrangement for the fourth [night], concerning the illusory form;
she is the goddess who brings about all wonders for the god of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Māyā is my great power, my supreme fourth body; she is equal in form to Lakṣmī. Now hear the mantra of her embodied form.
Having first taken the *tāraka*, one should then remember the *tārikā*;
afterwards, "Oṃ" (*māyā*) and "namas," followed by "Kāla" situated within "odana. (77)
Joined with the left eyebrow, he is Sūrya; wearing a garland, he is adorned by Viṣṇu.
He alone is Narāntya, and then Madana accompanied by Gopanā. (78)
Immediately after that, Puṇḍarīka is mounted upon fire; then Rāma, enriched by the deities beginning with Tāla and Lakṣmī, is joined with the conch and endowed with sovereignty. || 79 ||
Then, one should meditate upon Kāla mounted on Anala, conjoined with Māyāvyāpin;
one should remember this divine seed-syllable of Māyā situated above the Tārikā.
The wife of Vahni (Svāhā) should follow at the end; this is remembered as the mantra of twenty syllables.
I shall now declare its limbs; listen to them from me. (81)
Having taken the seed-syllable of Māyā and having sequentially differentiated it with the vowels beginning with 'ga' (the gutturals) and so forth,
as before, the wise one should indeed perform the arrangement of the limbs.
O Lord of the Gods, Mohinī, Bhrāmaṇī, Durgā, and Preraṇī—these four should be known as the companions of Māyā, resplendent with jewels. (83)
In charm, valor, beauty, and splendor,
these goddesses, clad in white garments and anointed with unguents, are equal to Māyā.
Holding chowries and goads in their hands and seated in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), I shall proclaim their mantras; listen, O slayer of Bala! (85)
The principal [syllable] is established upon *odana* (the letter *u*), being the constant *dhruva* endowed with the deity of the letter *ra*;
it is *madana* (the letter *ma*) established upon *bhuvana* (the letter *u*), joined with the sovereignty of fire (the letter *ra*). || 86 ||
Indeed, all these, joined with *candrivyāpin* and situated upon the seat of the *praṇava*, are known as mantras that are companions of *māyā* when conjoined with the name and *svāhā*. || 87 ||
Māyāmaya, Mahāmoha, Śambara, and Kalīśvara—these four are his attendants, resembling crows and soot. (88)
They have four arms and massive bodies, with gentle faces and smiling countenances;
they are adorned with armlets and ornaments, and are clothed in yellow silken garments. (89)
Adorned with necklaces and anklets, decorated with various flowers,
white as the dust of frost, they held aloft swords and nooses in their hands.
[The first form holds] an arrow and a bow; [the second has] a parasol in its two hands.
The principal [form] is accompanied by Gopana, and immediately after that is the solitary [form]. 91.
One should place Śaṅkara, Kevala, Kamala, Candrī, and Vyāpin upon the heads of all [the deities] in sequence.
O slayer of Bala, the mantras of the four beginning with Māyāmaya consist of the syllable *tāraka* (om) at the beginning, end with *namaḥ*, and are accompanied by their respective names. (93)
O Vāsava, the meditation for all the limb-mantras has been declared to be common;
so too, O Vāsava, are the mudrās for the deities together with their limbs.
A man who worships these goddesses—whether individually or all together—should display them exactly as they were previously described by me, one by one or in their entirety. (95)
According to my understanding and according to my zeal, I apply myself with supreme splendor; these four slender forms of mine are of the nature of the rays of the Blessed One. 96.
Note: 72. Padmanābha is the letter *pa*; Ajita is the letter *ja*; Kāla is the letter *ma*; Uddāma is the letter *u*. 77. Odana is the letter *o*.
78. *Nara* is the letter *na*; *Madana* is the letter *ma*; *Gopana* is the letter *ā*. 79. *Puṇḍarīka* is the letter *śa*; *Tālalakṣmā* is the letter *ta*.
86. *Dhruva* is the letter *bha*; *Bhuvana* is the letter *u*.
By these root-mantras, that Blessed Lord, the God, abides in his full form;
from each one of them, there are innumerable powers (śaktis), each having the nature of its respective [mantra]. (97)
These [goddesses] have infinite retinues; thus, the world consists of power (śakti).
Of these four powers, one is the Supreme Goddess. (98)
I am that primordial Supreme Ego of Viṣṇu, which possesses his attributes;
I am composed of all powers and am the leader of the circle of Śaktis.
One should remember her as being interwoven within light and bliss, situated between the two—Agni and Soma—and following the central path. 100.
A wise man should contemplate with a non-externalized state of mind, having caused the sun and the moon to set upon the path of Suṣumṇā. 101.
"One should establish one's abiding in me through a practice directed toward others.
Śakra said: "O Goddess who consists of the God of gods, O Goddess seated upon the lotus! (102)
"Tell me the mudrās of the goddesses' companions and of my own hand-gestures.
Śrī said: "O slayer of Bala, the mudrās of the goddesses have already been shown to you. (103)
Now, learn from me concerning her sixteen companions:
having brought the two hands together, they should be clearly defined and well-extended. (104)
One should indeed take the pair [of fingers] from the little finger and the ring finger;
one should join them at the tips of the nails so that they become like a single mass.
With the four fingers [held] in the middle of the palm without support,
one should form the two thumbs like a staff, extended and touching at their tips.
Having rested the four fingers up to the level of the belly,
one should diligently form the two index fingers like a serpent's hood.
O Lord of the Gods, having extended the two middle fingers forward so that they touch,
