and having straightened the two little fingers while joining both hands together— 108.
And one should join them very closely from the wrists down to the base of the thumbs; the wrist [mudrā] is formed by both hands at the base of the thumbs.
One should make it fully opened; this is the mudrā called Mahāyoni, O slayer of Bala, the supreme mother of the three worlds. (110)
If she is employed according to one's desire, she can bring the entire world under her control;
a woman intent on this practice should bind [the target] from afar and display her. 111.
A man who is attached here, or one who displays himself among women, instantly causes agitation even to sages who have transcended all attachments. 112.
Even when women have turned away from the nature of desire, O Sage, they become agitated; how much more so, then, those who are already full of passion? || 113 ||
O Vāsava, this is the common mudrā for all of them; now I shall briefly describe the mudrās of the sixteen attendants.
Having placed the two hands behind [the back], one should then release them;
likewise, both the pair of index fingers and the pair of little fingers [should be released]. (115)
O Mahāmati, the middle [fingers] of those two should be clearly turned downward;
the two little fingers are joined together, and the pair of index fingers is separated.
One should hold the middle and ring fingers in pairs; they should be joined together at the nail-base up to the middle joint. 117.
O best of gods, with the face turned upward and the ground level, the two thumbs should be clearly visible, hanging down and facing downward. (118)
When [the two deities] are situated far from one another, this mudrā grants all desires;
it should be performed accompanied by their respective mantras, for this is the single [mudrā] common to all. (119)
(186) These two mudrās, which accompany one’s companions, have been declared to be common [to all].
Thus, [one should visualize] me, joined with those four [mudrās] together with their retinues. 120.
Having thus worshipped Me through My manifestations (vibhūtis), one attains Me alone at the end;
for My manifestations are infinite, resting upon the reality that is the essence of all realities.
O Vāsava, each one of them has a retinue of ten million times ten million;
these four are proclaimed to be the foremost among them.
Thus, I have described to you the summary of the mantras of the forms along with the limb-mantras and so forth; now hear from me the means of accomplishment and other details.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Forms," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
(Note:)
120. "By four" means by Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter;
[now begins] the forty-sixth chapter.
O Lord of Gods, the primary Śrī and the sequential sādhana of Lakṣmī and the others [are now described].
And learn from their mantras the various ritual actions as well. || 1 ||
Having fashioned the previously described city as four-cornered with four gates,
one should draw an eight-petalled lotus in its center, possessing a white and reddish luster.
Having first drawn four white lines as pervading [lines] starting from the wrists and the face, one should draw svastikas in the corners.
Having placed the root mantra solely upon the hand and the body,
one should subsequently place the Lakṣmī mantra likewise with both hands, first and then [last].
Then, having performed the placement of the limbs upon the hand and the body as before,
one should subsequently place that group of four goddesses which follows it.
First on the two hands beginning with the index fingers, then on the body,
on the head, in the center of the heart [or between the eyebrows], and likewise on the two thighs and the two knees.

O Vāsava, having performed the placement of the four [fingers] beginning with Lāvaṇya on the two hands starting from the ring finger (anāmā) up to the thumb, one should likewise perform it upon the body.
Then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the rule upon the right and left shoulders and the two wings [of the arms], one who desires prosperity should worship in the heart.

Having performed the Lakṣmī-mantra alone by means of the application of the *layayāga*, and having first performed the visualization (*āvalokana*) and other rites, one should then place it externally.
O Indra, the root mantra joined with the form-mantra is situated upon the pericarp;
it is the all-pervading Lord, whose body consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, and who is endowed with all mantras.
And having brought down Lakṣmī, who resides upon his lap, by means of his own mantra, he—
joined with the previously mentioned meditation— for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Then, [one should place] the four [mantras], beginning with the Heart, in the southeast, the northeast, the southwest, and the northwest; the Eye [mantra] is placed upon the expanse of the filaments.
One should place the four [deities], beginning with Ṛddhi, in sequence at the front, the right, the back, and the left side; they are two-armed and of such form [as described].
Resembling a white lotus, marked with the śrīvṛkṣa and the yak-tail whisk,
he was seated in the lotus posture, gazing at that face.
Having placed the four [deities] beginning with Lāvaṇyā in the positions of the corners starting from the northeast, they have gentle faces and four arms. (15)
Clad in blue silk garments, holding a lotus and a water-pot in his hands,
with a lotus-pond banner in his hand, and bearing a mango tree laden with fruit.
Note:
1. By the word "etc. (ādi), Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā are included. 2. He describes the construction of the city with the words beginning with "caturaśram" (quadrangular).
5. *Anugeti* means the mantra of the fourfold [powers] beginning with supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
7. He describes the placement (*nyāsa*) of the subordinate mantras (*anucaramantra*) with the words "those beginning with Lāvaṇyā.
10. "Upon the pericarp" (*karṇikopari*) means upon the pericarp of the eight-petalled lotus. *Akalaḥ* means partless (*niṣkalaḥ*).
Having placed the Astra-mantra at the main doors in the four directions and worshipped it as before;
O delighter of the gods, [worship] the goddess Lakṣmī, who is joined with the root mantra. (17)
One should display all the mudrās wherever they are prescribed;
then, having performed the recitation (japa), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains mixed with ghee.

O slayer of Vṛtra, having obtained *sāmalas*, *śrīphalas*, or lotuses along with sesame seeds, one should perform as many oblations as possible according to one's capacity; then, at the conclusion of the *homa*,
the practitioner, firm in resolve, assumes the form of Lakṣmī.
One should indeed recite it five hundred thousand times, subsisting on pure food and having the senses subdued.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with bilva, āmalaka, and lotus flowers,
according to one's capacity, either in countless numbers or by the count of ten thousand (ayuta).
At the conclusion of the fire-offering, O Śakra, the Supreme Goddess grants her vision, saying:
"Son, I have been accomplished for you; tell me what is desired in your heart."
Perform all your desired tasks with my mantra;
from this day forward, be free from doubt and devoid of the afflictions of dualities.
Having spoken thus, that goddess departed quickly to the place from which she had come;
thereafter, one should perform the rites with the permission of Lakṣmī and myself.
When pleased, he indeed bestows desired prosperity upon those who seek it;
when enraged, he can, by a mere word, render even the Lord of Wealth penniless.
One should fashion a golden image while meditating once and reciting the mantra;
then, having filled a jar with water, or with milk, or else with honey, [one should perform the rite].
Having placed the right hand [downward] and the left hand upon it,
one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while endowed with meditative concentration.

For one who is established in devotion to the Lord of Mercury (Rasendra), single-minded and composed, attains the state of being the Lord of Mercury; indeed, the water brought into his vessel becomes that very essence.
O Purandara, one who pierces a target from a lake with arrows and other weapons becomes immortal;
he makes his body free from old age and disease. (29)
First, one should take a stone the size of a thumb with the right hand,
and one the size of a jujube fruit with the left hand.
Having consecrated those two fists with mantras, two hundred and sixteen stones located on the right side attain the state of jewels.
In the left [hand] there is the state of being a pearl; both of those are of great value.
Whatever one desires according to its kind, that very jewel shall then become manifest.
In that same way, just as a pearl appears and acts as such, he takes into his hand the bones produced from cows, elephants, and horses. (33)
Having consecrated it one hundred and fifty times, it indeed attains the state of coral;
likewise, having consecrated tin, lead, or iron one hundred times, it attains that same state. (34)
O Lord of the Gods, whatever mineral he takes up and desires, from that very substance there arises gold or exceedingly pure silver. (35)
Whether angry or well-pleased, he might act in one way or another;
thus, a difference in the nature of stone-made objects is established. (36)
Note:
34. Regarding "having done" (*kṛtvā*): the phrase "if he maintains it" (*dhārayati cet*) is to be supplied.
Whatever prosperity manifests in the mind of anyone, he quickly bestows upon that person— be it wealth, grain, cattle, or other such things. (37)

Having written it upon birch bark according to the sequence of the sacrificial placement (yāganyāsa), whoever always wears it with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma), [attains success]. (38)
O Śatakratu, by having the Lakṣmī-mantra inscribed on one's limb with gold, there shall be an increase in one's lifespan, and one shall become great and victorious everywhere. (39)
Wherever he may enter, he shall receive great honor;
this worship has been proclaimed especially for those who desire prosperity,
O tiger among the gods, for Lakṣmī is my first manifestation.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Attainment of the Lakṣmī-mantra," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Note: 38. Regarding "with yellow pigment (rocana) and saffron (kuṅkuma)": the phrase "having written" connects with what precedes it.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter.
The forty-seventh chapter: The Root Śrī.
That which is indeed declared as the first glory of the arrays, known by my own name—this is said to be its accomplishment; now listen to that of the second.
Know that the entire method of ritual placement (nyāsa), the lotus-sacrifice (padmayāga), and so forth have been previously explained.
Having constructed the previously mentioned mandala, one should place white and yellow [colors] within it.
But indeed, one should fashion a lotus and immediately thereafter place Kīrti upon the lap of the Lord, as well as the heart and other limbs, just as before.
Listen now to how she gradually meditated upon her friends:
she was two-armed, golden-hued, the very embodiment of fame, with a smiling countenance.
One should meditate on him who has a fine book in his left hand and a fly-whisk in his right, possessing the luster of the *kiṃśuka* flower, with a beautiful form that is enchanting to the mind.
Therein, one should contemplate the fourfold [deities] following [the main deity], each four cubits in height and clad in white garments,
with their primary left and right hands [placed] upon them.
Learn from me that with the other two hands he holds a conch shell with the luster of a hundred moons and a great tree called kadamba, covered in flowers and frequented by bees.
Having thus meditated upon her holding a mirror resembling the full moon in her left hand and a bright peacock-feather fan in her right hand, one should then display it.

Then the practitioner should worship all the individual mudrās with water for offering, flowers, and so forth; having properly recited the mantras according to his capacity, he should then perform the fire oblation (homa).

Having offered sesame seeds sprinkled with clarified butter and accompanied by fragrant śāli rice, and having fashioned the form of the Goddess at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa) with flowers, collyrium, and garments; || 10 ||

Staying in a solitary, secluded place, observing silence and subsisting on roots and fruits, one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times; at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
O Lord of the Gods, [one should perform] one hundred thousand oblations with rice mixed with sesame seeds,
using the ghee of Kapila cows combined with an equal amount of milk.
One should then offer a thousand oblations for each of the [mantras] beginning with the heart;
afterwards, one should present the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with milk mixed with clarified butter.
When the vessel is full and [the liquid] has fallen, the Supreme Goddess arrives and, standing before the practitioner, says, "Excellent! Excellent! (sādhu sādhu).
Come, come to the supreme abode; abandon this material city!
Even while dwelling in the midst of mortals, enjoy the pleasures of the immortals. 15.
"O practitioner, perform my entire ritual with the mantra.
Having spoken thus, that goddess then departed into the sky.
The practitioner should perform whatever rite he desires by means of the Kīrtimantra;
whatever he gives to anyone shall become inexhaustible for that person as well. || 17 ||
By that, he gains renown as long as the moon, sun, and stars exist,
provided he awakens while remaining in the midst of fierce men.
If he speaks something in an assembly, he shall obtain great fame;
having surpassed all people, he attains preeminence. (19)
Having recited [the mantra] over a vessel of prepared food during a time of food scarcity, even for a very short duration,
whatever people desire shall become their food according to their wish.
If one gives [this] incessantly for seven days, it becomes inexhaustible for him;
he shall attain great fame until the dissolution of all beings.
Having taken a mere fragment of gold during a time of plenty,
and having recited the mantra a thousand times according to the rite while standing around it on all sides, || 22 ||
p.
191) It reaches its abundance at the root, and it is bestowed upon those who seek it.
For two weeks without interruption, he does not encounter any doubt.
Having taken a water-pot from the lake in the abode of the lord of the Nāgas, he shall thereby attain great renown honored by the world. (24)
One should indeed proceed to a desert region; there, on level ground or at the peak of a mountain, one should cast [the substance] after it has been consecrated a thousand times with mantras.
That lord of serpents, accompanied by his retinue,
remained there guarding the water for as long as the earth endures.
Because of that, O Vāsava, he attains great fame in the world, provided that the seed sown at the proper time germinates even if the god does not rain. (27)
Having taken a clod of earth from the edge of a pond that has been softened by the water,
or having taken a moist pot situated therein, one should recite the mantra over it three hundred times.
Having heated it with the breath from the mouth, one should recollect the Kīrtimān mantra;
indeed, if one casts it into the sky, it attains the state of a cloud.
That cloud-king shall fill the entire earth with water,
and by his command, he shall dwell in that region for as long as required.
As much water as falls during the year and becomes available for his use, by that he shall attain great fame extending throughout the three worlds. (31)
O best of gods, whatever is desired by anyone in their mind, that he accomplishes; such is the power of this king of mantras known as Kīrti.
Having written it as before and bound it upon the right hand,
one shall obtain great fame, honor, prosperity, and the goddess Sarasvatī herself. (33)
O Vāsava, best among embodied beings, this procedure for the second mantra of Kīrti has been briefly declared by me to you. 34.
By following this auspicious ritual for the Kīrtimantra, one shall attain stainless fame that bestows prosperity even upon one's progeny. (35)

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Attainment of the Kīrti-mantra," in the Lakṣmītantra, which is the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra. [In version A: the Śrīpāñcarātra; in version B: the Śrīpañcarātra. Chapter Forty-Eight.
O slayer of Vṛtra, [grant] to me the ritual for the victory of Jayā according to the third body, which is the primordial Śrī.
Listen to the manner of attaining perfection, which is praised by the hosts of Siddhas.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) as before and having worshipped Jaya in the heart,
one should construct the mandala as previously described and draw a lotus in its center.
With pollen resembling the hue of a blue lotus and possessing beautiful petals,
one should place Jayā, seated upon the lap of Viṣṇu, there, joined with his heart.
One should place the mantra-parts upon the pericarp according to the previous sequence;
however, listen attentively to the meditations for all of them as they truly are.
All the female friends were the color of dark blue clouds, with serene faces and eyes; they wore yellow garments and golden earrings.
With white chowries in their hands and colorful cane-staffs raised aloft,
they gazed upon the faces of Jayā and Ajitā.
Having the luster of the color of a jasmine bud, with serene lotus-like faces, wearing red garments, possessing four arms, and endowed with great strength. || 7 ||
The four attendants should be meditated upon as holding bows and arrows, as well as maces and discs, and adorned with floral ornaments. (8)
One should display all the mudrās that have been proclaimed for each [deity] respectively, and then worship with devotion; immediately thereafter, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
With sesame seeds mixed with white mustard, clarified butter, and guggulu resin,
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, the practitioner, having assumed his own form as the embodiment of victory, [should perform the rite].
Thinking, "Victory to me!", he perceived a great presence within his mind;
having reached a place on the shore that was secluded from people and free from fear, he remained there.
Having performed the binding of the directions with the armor- and weapon-mantras for the destruction of evil beings,
one should thereafter begin the recitation, always subsisting on milk, food, or fruit.
O Vāsava, having first prostrated before Hari with devotion using his own mantra,
he was devoted to solitude, moderate in diet, observant of silence, and intent on meditation.
One should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times, and at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa).
The sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) should be a span (prādeśa) in length and made from red sandalwood.
One should, with an undistracted mind, offer ten thousand oblations of those [seeds] smeared with ghee;
and, O Great-minded One, two million oblations of white mustard seeds mixed with honey.
Then one should offer ten thousand and a hundred thousand oblations with black sesame seeds mixed with the three kinds of honey; at the end, there should be three full oblations.
O Śakra, one should perform oblations in sequence with honey, milk, and ghee;
then the Blessed Goddess Jayā herself arrives.
"O son, perform whatever task you desire, free from hesitation and relieved of all anxiety, by means of my mantra, for I have attained success. (18)
Having spoken thus, the Śakti whose essence is Nārāyaṇa vanishes from sight;
thereafter, one should perform various kinds of rites in manifold ways. (19)
Whatever things are desired in this world, whether for oneself or for another—even regarding those, O Wielder of the Vajra, I shall speak by way of summary; listen to them in their true essence. (20)
The practitioner should meditate on the goddess with a tongue like a flame while reciting her mantra;
indeed, she causes whatever object it may be to emerge, in whatever manner required.
Having conquered that [enemy] through justice, one indeed attains victory without effort,
even over an army full of elephants, horses, and weapon-bearers, and endowed with great strength.
Having seen another person engaged in battle, prepared to strike, [p. 193] (Ā, F, Ṅ: approaching; B: risen up).
Having consecrated with recitation the bow, sword, shield, and five arrows.
Having indeed bestowed this upon someone, he who impels [the army] goes to the front of the host;
even alone, he tears it asunder and attains eternal victory.
Having meditated upon the triangular mandala of fire held in the right hand,
one should contemplate the Goddess in its center, accompanied by her retinue.
Upon seeing intoxicated elephants, lions, serpents, or thunderbolts,
they quickly turn their backs and flee once they behold that palm of the hand.
Having touched and taken up a pestle made of khadira wood that has been consecrated with a hundred mantras,
and having gone to the entrance of the cave, he should utter the fourfold mantra accompanied by the word "jaya."
O Lord of Gods, one should there gradually offer eight blows with a pestle,
using the mantra of the Goddess encased within her own weapon-mantra.
Then, with the mantra ending in the syllable *phaṭ*, he should worship the vessel of the subterranean passage;
thereafter, the most excellent of practitioners, accompanied by all the people, may enter.
Having shattered numerous mechanical devices and conquered the foremost of the Dānavas,
he established a *yojana* of safety for the people there, together with his groups of beloved women.
Having drunk the sattvic beverage with his own hand, that one of great strength departed by that very same path through which he had come to his own dwelling.
O Lord of Gods, if the minister (mantrin) sets his mind upon victory throughout the three worlds,
he shall achieve it without hesitation, with mace and discus raised in his hands.
Or else, holding a noose and a goad, one attains victory; it is not otherwise.
One should write [the mantra] on birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron, and thick ink.
Having indeed encapsulated his name and placed it in the midst of the people,
he then easily attains victory over all divine beings through mere play.
Having drawn [the design] with sandalwood paste, milk, and saffron,
whoever should wear it on the neck, the face, or on the left or right hand— || 35 ||
O Śakra, one who recites this mantra anywhere for the sake of victory will always attain victory without hesitation and without obstruction, O Lord of the Thirty-three Gods.

The practitioner should constantly employ [this mantra], and wherever he does so, he shall obtain victory. This third form of mine, which is proclaimed by the name Jaya—its ritual procedure has thus been shown to you, O Śakra. (37)

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Accomplishment of the Jayā-mantra," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. [In version A: the *Śrīpañcarātra*; in version B: the *Śrīpāñcarātre*].
The forty-ninth chapter.
O Vāsava, that fourth body of mine, which is the root-glory, is the mantra-body known as Māyā.
Now hear the procedure for that [rite], accompanied by the application of mantras.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the lineage of mantras pertaining to Māyā— known as the Form, the Limbs, the Friends, and the Servants— as before upon one's own hand, one should immediately thereafter perform it upon the body.
Having worshipped her within the heart with all enjoyments as before,
one should then construct a mandala on the outside, with an auspicious lotus in its center.
There, having brought down Māyā from the lap of Viṣṇu and from his heart, one should then worship her together with her companions, such as Aṅga and Sakhī.
Then, the four lotus-eyed female companions, Bhrāmaṇī and the others, should be meditated upon; they wear white garments (or yellow garments), are divine, and shine with jewels.
Likewise, the four attendants beginning with Māyāmaya should be meditated upon, holding chowries and goads in their hands and seated in the bound lotus posture (baddha-padmāsana).
With all their limbs complete, resembling a swarm of glossy bees, they have four arms and massive bodies; their faces are serene and their countenances are smiling.
Adorned with armlets and wearing yellow garments,
they were likewise equipped with necklaces and anklets, and decorated with various flowers.
White as the dust of snow, with sword and noose raised in their hands,
they hold an arrow and a bow in one pair of hands, and a parasol in another pair.
Having thus displayed the mudrās that are prescribed for each respective [deity],
one should thereafter perform a fire-oblation with sesame seeds mixed with white mustard.
Then, O Vāsava, having resorted to the observance and subsequently assuming the form of a goddess through unwavering devotion, he transformed his own self. (11)

Accompanied by mature and superior assistants, the observer of the vow should proceed to a place inhabited by the twice-born and recite seven hundred thousand [mantras] according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Subsisting on milk, roots, and fruits according to the requirements of place and time, he may indeed eat a single alms-meal that is unasked for, or even live on barley-gruel alone.
When the time of twilight has arrived, he should eat food prepared by his own disciples, purified by mantras, free from salt, oil, and meat. || 14 ||

The practitioner of mantras should consume the consecrated food with honey and ghee until satisfied; at the conclusion of the recitation, he should diligently perform the fire-oblation according to the rules. 15.
Balā, moṭā, māṃsī, cakrāṅgī, nāgakesara, powdered sandalwood, saffron, and the powder of turmeric. || 16 ||
Then, one should mix well-ghee with sesame seeds and honey;
having thus prepared it with ghee, one should then offer three hundred thousand oblations.
O Purandara, with the middle and ring fingers together with the thumbs,
one should finally offer three ten-thousand oblations of sacrificial fuel sticks.
First, ten thousand [oblations] of khadira wood were offered;
after that, those made of suradāru wood, and then a third ten-thousand [of another kind]. (19)
One should properly offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with a perfectly purified inner self;
when the final oblation has fallen, [the deity] comes from the midst of the sky.
Note:
By the phrase "holding chowries and goads in their hands," their two-armed nature is indicated.
Māyāmaya and the other attendants are mentioned by name here in the forty-fifth chapter.
These have been specified:
19. *rājataru* is the *karṇikāra*; *suradāru* is the *devadāru*.
Accompanied by her root retinue, Māyā spoke: "Excellent, excellent!
Now perform your desired task; go forth with my mantra. (21)
Having spoken this, the goddess should go quickly to the abode of Viṣṇu;
thereafter, that best of practitioners performs various rites.
O Śakra, listen briefly from me regarding those things which one should immediately undertake according to the desires of one's heart, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others. (23)
Having recited over an *āmalaka* and a *bilva* fruit once, one should enter the king’s palace;
having cast them before the treasury, wherever he may be stationed, he shall [attain success].
Whatever wealth he desires, whatever praiseworthy ornament, or whatever beautiful garment, may that fall swiftly from the sky. (25)
In this very way, one should likewise cast a ball of rice, or similarly sesame and rice,
into a full granary, a cow-pen, or a pit.
Whether in a royal domain or his own property, from wherever he may be situated, whatever grain, crop, or rice-filled produce he desires— || 27 ||
Then, right before those [objects], it falls from the sky exactly as desired;
in this very same way, one should likewise consecrate a pill of prepared food with the mantra.
Having thrown it into the area of the kitchen, one should draw forth prepared food in an instant;
having made a pill from cow dung itself, the size of a jujube fruit.
Having cast [the vessels] within the cow-pen after consecrating them seven times with mantras,
they became filled with curd, milk, and clarified butter at the end of a mere moment through the power of meditation alone.
Wherever the observer of the vow stands, he should look behind him at his belongings;
having properly recited [the mantra] over a jujube fruit or some other fruit, he should do so in that place.
One should cast [the seed] into Madhuvana, and it produces a harvest of fruit for the king;
furthermore, one should designate a single flower within a beautiful flower garden.
Having recited the mantra three times, the practitioner should instantly attract flowers;
wherever those arising from his body are cast, they should be consecrated seven times with the mantra.
But once a mental resolve has been formed, it shall remain in each respective place;
drawn according to one's desire, it goes to wherever that [resolve] directs.
Furthermore, that excellent practitioner never becomes aged anywhere;
having performed the rite with charcoal fragments, he who is composed should recite the mantra one hundred times.
If one casts it into the midst of water, that water is seen to blaze;
even a drop of water resting on the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, when consecrated with the mantra a hundred times, [produces this effect]. (36)
Having prepared it, one should cast it into a blazing mass of fire;
in an instant, that fire will appear like water.
And having seen a wilderness filled with sand and devoid of grass, one should cast there a blade of grass over which the mantra has been recited two hundred times. (38)
One should make that place, strewn with flowers and leaves and crowded with foliage and sprouts,
equal to the Nandana grove, surrounded by a body of water.
It was filled with various kinds of birds, endowed with city parks and groves,
complete with city walls, and possessed of temples for the deities.
Accompanied by the sounds of songs and the Vedas, and graced by beautiful women—
this wonder of kings is indeed always worthy of being seen.
In forests where water is scarce and always devoid of food, they obtain water and food at will, as well as various kinds of enjoyments. (42)
One should perform [this rite] with eight clods of earth or cow-dung consecrated by mantras, while the enemy stands face-to-face, having seized his weapon. (43)
If, moreover, he remains alone and intent upon his purpose, reciting the mantra while forming a great resolve in his mind, (then he shall succeed). 44.
And his own army, consisting of foot-soldiers, chariots, horses, and elephants, quickly becomes a host of formidable prowess. 45.
O Śakra, upon seeing that army of the enemy turning away, its vigor destroyed, he performs whatever rite he intends with his mind while reciting the mantra.
The fundamental deception,
though it is unreal, appears as if it were real.
But upon seeing a withered tree, one should strike it with one's foot.
Reciting the great mantra, he shall be filled with flowers and fruits;
uttering the mantra with both hands, he shall be endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruit.
If the practitioner of mantras, standing on a mountain peak, recites the mantra for the purpose of its destruction, he shall cause the tree to suffer and it will undergo withering. (49)
The mountain shall fall downward as long as the practitioner desires;
once satisfied, he may later raise that best of mountains from the netherworld (pātāla).
One should place the mantra within the interior of a lotus using sandalwood paste;
then, having inscribed the ancillary mantras (aṅgas) upon the petals on an auspicious day.
Having worshipped with flowers and other offerings, he should likewise encircle it with cloths;
as before, he should wear the yantra, and for him all prosperities—indeed, all supernatural powers (siddhis)—shall manifest.
In this world, these things manifest correctly for him; he is free from thorns, fortunate, long-lived, and shall attain happiness in the next world. || 53 ||
O enemy of Vṛtra, this most wonderful power of Mūrti has been shown to you only in brief; its entirety is difficult for me to describe. (54)
This collection of the accomplishments of the four goddesses has been briefly stated; it has been described in some small measure for the sake of attaining benefit for practitioners. (55)
To them he grants divine and elemental auspicious things, as well as stainless purity of mind and, at the end, the supreme state.
He reveals to his devotees the imperishable Vaiṣṇava [nature],
and me, Lakṣmī, as "Vistīrṇā" (the Vast One) through these many manifestations.
One should worship her with various dispositions, having established the mind in a state of security.
Śakra said: "Obeisance to you, the primordial goddess of the gods; obeisance to you, the beloved of Vaikuṇṭha. (58)
"Upon what mark (lakṣa) having fixed my mind, O Lotus-born One, should I worship you?
Śrī said: "Nārāyaṇa alone is the Swan (Haṃsa), the ocean of the nectar of the six divine attributes. (59)
I am his supreme power, inseparable from Viṣṇu;
I am she who sits upon his lap, as was previously described to you.
O Śakra, that very hundred thousand [gold pieces] is the cause of stability for your mind;
it is endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with gold, silver, and other precious materials.
Having fashioned me as one seated upon the lap of the Lord according to the teachings of the scriptures,
and having established me through the prescribed rites, worship me with those various mental dispositions.
Śakra said: Homage to you, O abode of the world, who delight the mind and the eyes!
Of what nature is the installation of the two of you in an image fashioned from the six qualities?
Śrī said:
Just as the god Viṣṇu is composed of all beings and possesses a body of the six divine attributes (ṣāḍguṇya), so too am I, the wondrous one, abiding as the self of all beings. (64)
Since I and Nārāyaṇa are established everywhere, what indeed could be my formal installation in reality? For all that is truly the glory of Viṣṇu.
When the mind of the ascetic has ascended to this true reality,
these conceptual constructions such as "worship" and "consecration" cease to manifest.
Listen, O slayer of Bala, to my instruction regarding the installation ceremony exactly as it is, by which, when performed, an embodied being attains the fulfillment of his purpose. (67)
Having properly fashioned our two forms according to the scriptures as described in the Yoga-tantras,
one should bathe them with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) using the two hymns accompanied by purifying grass (pavitra).
Having clothed him in a new garment, he should have him instructed by pure Brahmins who know the true nature of Dharma and are learned in the three Vedas and the Sāttvata scriptures. (69)
The root-mantra, the Tāraka, as well as the Tārikā and likewise the Anutārikā.
And they should also study the Sūkta and the Śākuna, as if they were purificatory texts.
Having reached sunset, one should wrap that solar disc with cloth while reciting the hymn beginning with "ṛtaṃ ca" and likewise the Sārasvata hymn.
One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) with verses from the Rigveda concerning gold-colored [deities];
then, when the pure sun has risen, one should perform the ritual installation of the directions (diksthāpana).
With the mantra "uttiṣṭha brahmaṇas," they should lead him to the altar;
then, having removed his garment, one should bathe him with pure water.
And on the southern part of the altar, adorned with a soft carpet,
one should lay the image with its head toward the east, preceded by the recitation of mantras as before.
Then, having taken a golden probe consecrated with mantras, one who has recited the eye-mantra should scratch the eyes with that probe. (75)
The artisan, having bathed and dressed in clean garments, being beheld with a divine vision, should open the eyes with a weapon consecrated by the Astra-mantra. (76)
One should fill it with honey and ghee and display it in that vessel;
at that time, one should present a pair of cows adorned with ornaments.
One should give all that to the artisan once it has been opened;
then, having tied the lines with a white thread on two well-washed cloths.
One should tie its protective cord (kautuka) on the right hand with a thread;
likewise, one should place the image upon a stable and auspicious throne.
When [the deity] has been worshipped with perfect devotion according to the sequence beginning with the support (ādhāra),
one should then contemplate the image with the intellect as being filled with the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya).
Having struck it with the weapon-mantra and having enveloped it with the armor-mantra,
one should bathe it with water containing all medicinal herbs alone.
Having wiped [the image] with a new, unwashed cloth, one should then remove the auspicious thread (kautuka).
Then, the knower of mantras should offer water for honor (arghya) upon the head with the Cakra-mantra.
Then, having meditated upon the image as if it were a reflection of beautiful radiance,
[one should perform the consecration] with pure, worshipped, and consecrated jars filled with ritual substances.
[The cleansing is performed] with the sixteen [deities] situated upon the sixteen petals arising from the sixteen-petaled lotus;
first with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and secondly with cow urine.
The third [layer] with cow-dung water, the fourth with the ashes of the three sacred fires (tretāgni),
and the next with earth from the tips of the horns of an elephant, a cow, or a bull, and from an anthill.
The seventh [rite] is performed with water from rice fields, rivers, lotus groves, and so forth;
the eighth is performed with water containing all medicinal herbs.
The ninth is with milk, the tenth with curd, the next (eleventh) with clarified butter;
the twelfth is with honey, and the thirteenth with the water of all seeds.
Having first consecrated each jar individually with fruits, various grains, and highly fragrant waters while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*, one completes the sixteenth.
One should respectfully bathe [the deity] with those sixteen [substances] using the root mantra,
alternating them with water, along with offerings of arghya, flowers, incense, and lamps.
Then, having rubbed it with the powders of lentils, black gram, and wheat, and having washed it with milk, one should place the supreme *tārikā* upon the head. 90.
Then, the wise practitioner should [visualize] it in these places in sequence—first subtle and then gross—at the head, the mouth, the two shoulders, the ears, the heart, the navel, and the back. (91)
One should likewise place the *tāraka* at the base of the hips, the thighs, the knees, the ankles, and the feet; and in the same manner, one should also place the *anutāraka*.
Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *Puruṣasūkta*, one should then perform the placement of the *Śrīsūkta*.
With the Yajus-mantras beginning with "May Śrī be my head," one should perform the placement according to the corresponding characteristics of the body parts.
(93) *Tippanī:* [The editor of the manuscript marked by 'ī' omits four lines from this point.]
70. The Śākuna hymn is to be found in the Ṛgveda (Maṇḍala 2, Sūkta 42, Ṛk 1). 78. *Rāji* refers to the black mustard seed.
93. "May glory be my head," and so forth; this is to be found in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (2.6.5.3).
One should perform the root-placement (mūla-vinyāsa) and the placement of the Hotṛ-priest (hotṛ-vinyāsa) as prescribed in the Yajurmayī [Tantra].
Having thus performed the ritual placement within me, the Supreme Person, one should thereafter proceed with the practice.
Having first deposited the Śrīsūkta upon my head and the Śrī-yajūṃṣi, and then having performed the Hotṛ-deposition in this manner upon the two bodies; 95.
At the conclusion of the previously described procedure, one should offer oblations into the fire-pit for the sake of universal pacification;
for as many classes of mantras as have been mentioned and those currently existing [should be employed]. || 96 ||
One should offer oblations with that many [verses] for the pacification of all defects:
the Ṛg-verses in the eastern quarter and the Yajus-formulas in the southern quarter. (97)
And in the west, O gentle one, he should likewise teach the Sāmans and the Ātharvaṇa hymns, as well as the Sāttvata mantras, to the twice-born near him.

First, one should bathe [the deity] with water from jars placed in the four directions within the pericarp of a sixteen-petaled lotus, using mantras that consist of the Tara, the Anutara, and the Pratitara.
With the mantra "vasavas tvā," [he should bathe the deity] with a jar of water and flowers;
with the mantra "rudrās tvā," [he should bathe] with scented water using a jar of golden water.
The knower of mantras should perform the consecration with the water-pitcher containing jewels, using the mantras "ādityāstvā," "viśvā," and the "tāra-tārā-anutārā" verses.
Then, having taken Śuddhodana and having consecrated him with the threefold supreme self by means of Tārā, one should likewise place the arghya upon his head.
Then, having anointed the image with ointments such as sandalwood paste,
one should worship it with offerings beginning with garments and ending with food.
Having bound the mudrā, one should thereafter worship the pedestal (pīṭha) accompanied by the Brahma-stone;
one should meditate upon the Vaiṣṇava pedestal, which consists of the entire path (adhvan) and is radiant.
One should meditate upon the divine Brahma-stone as the foundational power;
thus, the pedestal and the Brahma-stone are fashioned together in a state of coexistence. || 105 ||
One should construct those [pedestals] separately for the superior bed;
the method for the bed of a stable image is prescribed as follows.
The ascent to the palace, the placement of the pedestal and the Brahma-stone, the consecration of that very [pedestal], and thereafter the invocation of the image. || 107 ||
The placement of the twelve-limbed digits, the performance of festivals such as the three-day rite,
and likewise the concluding ablution (avabhṛtha) and other rituals— all this is prescribed here.
Listen attentively to how one should perform the installation of the *calabimba*, the sprinkling with the four jars, and the invocation after worship. (109)
Prior to the invocation, one should perform the triad of enjoyments in sequence within the unmodified,
pure, waveless, and untainted essential nature.

Having remained as the Guru in the heart-lotus of the one who has passed beyond, he should again contemplate the power (*śakti*) of Viṣṇu, which consists of pure existence and corresponds to his own nature. (111)
One should recollect that conditioned image which was previously [established], as being composed of that;
one should recollect the two states consisting of fire and moon residing within one's own body. (112)
Abiding as all-pervasive throughout the upper and lower [realms], they are supremely radiant;
as it is in the self, so it is in the reflection, and as it is in the reflection, so it is in the self.
Then, one should go out from the body by way of the right path of fire and enter the heart of the image through the left path with the mind.
Just as the incomparable Self has been personally experienced within one's own heart,
so too should one constantly recollect that Self residing within the heart.
Note:
94. Regarding "the arrangement of the Hotṛ-mantras": this refers to the arrangement of the mantras beginning with the Daśahotr, which are recited in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka. This is the meaning.

100. "May the Vasus [protect] you! "May the Rudras [protect] you! (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.7.15.5). 101. "May the Ādityas [protect] you! "May the Viśvedevas [protect] you! (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.7.15.5). (p. 199)
Having beheld that light, filled with bliss and interlaced with its own rays,
one should contemplate its oneness within each and every Supreme Brahman.
Having thus turned [the world] into a single ocean, that supreme Vaiṣṇava light should remain,
concentrating upon it and fixing his own mind in that state of motionlessness.
Then, when the mind was vibrating, he remembered that [Self] again through his intellect;
having emerged from the reflection by way of the right path, he did so with his wisdom.
One should enter one's own heart-lotus by means of the left side;
this is the yoga that sets the multitude of channels (or various forms) of the substance-image in motion. (119)
Then, for the sake of attaining the status of Lord of All, he should abide in another yoga;
from the heart-lotus, he should meditate while reciting the *tārikā*, the savior. (120)
One should ascend by the upward flow to the supreme, painless state;
then one should remember that supreme state and the enjoyment attained through one's own will.
Then, taking up that vibration which possesses the power of the sovereignty of consciousness,
one should again proceed undisturbed by that same path to the lotus of the heart.
Having emerged by way of the right [nostril], accompanied by their mutual assistance,
one should enter that lotus-heart of the image by means of the left alone.
Having meditated as before on the state of unity, having emerged by way of the upward path,
and having entered the *dvādaśānta* as before, one attains vibration (*spanda*).
Just as the reflection [enters], the wise one should enter the heart-lotus by that very same [path];
then, having emerged through the fire on the left, he should enter the heart.
One should then remember the vibration and the sovereignty of the two eyeballs;
having gazed at each other, they appear as if extending a state of oneness.
One should contemplate those two as being interpenetrated by their mutual gazing;
this is described as the yoga known as the "concentration on the Lord" (īśvarasaṃdhāna). || 127 ||
By means of which there may always be universal sovereignty over all images; now, the connection with sound is indeed the identity of the mantra and the image. (128)
That subtle power of Viṣṇu, stainless and known as Sattā,
having become identical with that universal essence, causes its own resonance to dissolve into it.
Know that to be devoid of all conceptual constructions, free from even the mere word, peaceful, supremely subtle,
and fashioned by awakening.
Then, one should remember that supreme and subtle state which is the unfolding stage of Paśyantī, characterized by the effort of a half-vibration arising from the refinement of sound and meaning.

Having ascended the path of conceptualization and being colored by various latent impressions (saṃskāras), that which arises directed toward its own denotable object after having separated it [from the universal] is indeed [the particular]. 132.
One should remember that intermediate form, which is verbal in nature, situated within the heart-lotus,
produced by various places of articulation and efforts, and impelled by the breath through the organs of speech.
Note:
Regarding "the multitude of channels" (nāḍībṛnda), the following statement from the *Pārameśvara-tantra* should be kept in mind:
"O tiger among sages, this yoga pertains both to the reflection (*bimba*) and to that which is born of matter (*dravyaja*)."
It manifests the entire network of channels from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
"O Brahmin, that by which the lordship over this entire manifestation arises—that yoga I shall now declare; listen with one-pointed attention. (15.447, 448).
122. *Spanda* means agitation. And so it is said in the *Pārameśvara*:
"Furthermore, though uninterrupted and undisturbed, he undergoes agitation by his own will.
(15.451). Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, page 200.
That which becomes manifest through its primary waves— namely, phonemes, words, and so forth—
in the form of a signifier, is known as *vaikharī* speech. (134)
Therefore, having contemplated that body as consisting of consciousness and sound, and possessing distinctions such as being supreme, subtle, and so forth,
one should then meditate upon its reflection.

Through the yoga of the withdrawal of sound, one should likewise remember that pair— the two consisting of one's own body and that reflected image— as being of the nature of unflinching consciousness and sound (or, according to some readings, sound and meaning).

By means of the application of the sequence previously described, one should indeed meditate upon the unstruck Śabdabrahman as consisting of the reflection of sound through the very sequence beginning with Paśyantī.
Having thus performed the coordination of sounds and the coordination of mantras, the wise one should begin the ritual action; this is called his yoga. || 138 ||
The supreme unstruck sound (anāhata), having reached the state of Paśyantī at the navel,
resides like a lotus fiber within the central heart-lotus.
Having remained thus, one should remember [the Self] entering within the *bimba* through the door of *vaikharī*, as the nature of the throbbing *nāda*, and likewise pervaded by all the mantras. (140)
One should meditate on the Lord of the World, whose essence is mantra, situated within the center of the heart of the image.
Thus established, the image bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 141.
Then one should perform the invocation (āvāhana) into this image of Hari-medhas,
first saying "I invoke," and likewise with the mantra for all the limbs.
One should visualize the entry and exit of Lakṣmī from the body of the Lord;
her invocation is prescribed with the first five Ṛg-verses.
One should perform the placement of the twelve parts and the digits (kalānyāsa) as in the deity-placement (devanyāsa).
One should console the two [eyes] with the mantra: "May you both be well-disposed toward us. (144)

When this much has been done for the mobile image, one who knows the procedures of the Sāttvata and other traditions should perform the installation of the stable image according to the previously mentioned path. 145.
This very triad of connections previously mentioned is the foundation for both; such is my conviction. (146)
Thus, when the two images have been perfected through ritual refinement, the wise man perceives with his intellect Lakṣmī and the Lord of Lakṣmī as being present there. (147)
With his mind fixed on them, devoted to them, sacrificing to them, intent on reciting their names,
and constantly practicing yoga toward them, he attains those very two at the end.
This supreme state, consisting of pure knowledge, is declared to be the direct foundation;
for men, nothing other than knowledge is considered to be a savior.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Installation" (or "The Illumination of the Attainment of Māyā"), in the *Lakṣmītantra*, which is the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Fifty-first Chapter: Mūla-Śakra.
Salutations to you, the source of the universe; salutations to you, the manifestation of all prosperity;
salutations to you, the fundamental cause of all spiritual accomplishments. || 1 ||
Salutations to you, O lotus-born one, who are the very self of the primordial deity, the consort of Nārāyaṇa, and the object of worship for the entire world.
Through your grace, I have heard your mantras and attained your supernatural powers (siddhis); furthermore, the method for propitiating all of them has been correctly understood by me.
Now I desire to hear the complete procedure for your well-spoken discourse, which has issued from the lotus of your mouth; I have approached you as a disciple—teach me, O Lord! (4)
Śrī said:
The Lord named Nārāyaṇa is the master of all that moves and stands; he is the self of all worlds, whose very form is the bliss of the six divine attributes.
The Lord is the source of all natures, omniscient, and the performer of all actions;
he is without blemish, faultless, and the refuge of all that is auspicious.
He is the illuminator of both darkness and light by virtue of his own self-luminosity;
he is the inner controller and the ruler, manifested through both existence and non-existence.
The powerful one, the support of all, the lord of mine who possesses all powers—
he has me as his supreme, singular, and eternal power, known by the name Śrī.
She has cast out all blemishes, she is the cow of plenty for the All-pervasive Lord,
and she manifests from the wall of His own nature as the collection of both pure and impure paths.
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, we two, who have attained equanimity in every respect and are devoted to you, are the supreme parents of the universe in the highest heaven."
Abiding in heaven with supreme splendor for the sake of favoring the worlds,
they were once filled with compassion, desiring the welfare of living beings.
"May these living beings be happy; how indeed might they attain us?"—thus, with supreme concentration, they are intent upon seeking the means [to achieve this]. (12)

We shall churn that exceedingly profound great ocean of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahma), which is filled with the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus verses; from that ocean being churned, [the essence shall emerge]. 13.
That divine pair of well-spoken verses arose like clarified butter from curds—
unstruck, unambiguous, clear, and imperishable.
Endowed with all sovereign qualities, its words and syllables are unconfused;
it is eternally intermingled with one another's syllables at both the beginning and the end.
Note: 1.

In the sense of "the source of the universe"; that is, in the sense of being the locus of the origin of the universe. 2. To her who has become the Self; that is, to her who is the beloved of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
4. *Tvatsūktasya*; [this refers to] the *Śrīsūkta*.
5. *Jagata* and so forth; the meaning is "the Lord of all that moves and is stationary.
6. *Prakṛtiḥ*; the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).

7. "By its light all this shines"—this is the expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the meaning of the Śruti here. "Existence and non-existence" means that [the Self] is determined as having the nature of the categories of existence and non-existence.
9. "All desires": the sense is that by Me alone has he attained all his desires. "On the wall of the Self."
The meaning is that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), whether pure or impure in form, has me alone as its sole support.
12. *Samādhinā*: by means of meditation (*dhyāna*).
13. *Mathnīvaḥ sma*: "we churned," meaning "we did not churn."
14. A pair of hymns: the *puṃsūkta* and the *śrīsūkta*. Unstruck (*anāhata*): unimpeded (*avyāhata*).
Not clear (*anaspaṣṭa*): exceedingly clear (*atispaṣṭa*). (p. 202)
Pierced by the power and the possessor of power, and mixed with those respective syllables,
therein the characteristic of the Person (puruṣa) is well-spoken, adorned with the qualities of the True Brahman.
The lotus-eyed Lord accepted the well-spoken description of feminine characteristics therein, which was established in his own majesty and adorned with the qualities of the true Brahman.
I, remaining undisturbed, accepted [the world] as established in my own glory—these two supreme hymns (sūkta) which are served by the hosts of great seers (maharṣi). 18.
Both when studied and when reflected upon, these lead to the supreme goal;
they are the ordinances established by the ancient authors of the ritual manuals (kalpas).
O Lord presided over by the immortals, those non-terrible [mantras] are each thousands in number;
now listen to the procedure for my hymn (matsūkta) as it is prescribed therein.
One should know me alone to be his primordial sage; the meter is said to be named Śrī;
and I am the deity, the support of all, the sovereign consort of Viṣṇu. 21.
The application of this hymn is in the worship of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
one should meditate upon me, the supreme goddess Lakṣmī, seated on the lap of Viṣṇu. (22)
She is eternally embraced by the Supreme Self with his left arm,
her own arm resting upon his shoulder, and she holds a divine lotus.
Then, being self-restrained, one should worship me, the Supreme Goddess, with Rig-verses—
me who am seated upon the left lap of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
One should perform the invocation with the first verse, remaining unwearied;
with the second, one should offer a seat to the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
One should offer the *arghya* with the third [mantra] to Īśāna, and also provide the *pādya* (with the fourth);
likewise, the *ācamana* with the fourth and the *upahāra* (offering) with the fifth.
On the sixth day, the most excellent practitioner should perform a bath together with his consort;
on the seventh, he should offer two garments, and on the eighth, ornaments.
On the ninth day one should offer fragrance; on the tenth, a heap of flowers;
on the next two days, incense and a lamp respectively; and on the final day, the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
One should perform the attainment on the fourteenth day and the prostrations on the fifteenth;
then, at the very end, one should employ the Tārikā and the Manutāra.
Restrained in mind, one should recite the mantra verse by verse according to the prescribed rule and to the best of one's ability;
thereafter, one should contemplate the dissolution of the hymn into the Tārikā.
Having meditated upon the two Tārikās as being situated within the boat, one should remember our universal course;
or else, the rite of invocation (āvāhana) is performed with the four Ṛg verses as previously [stated].
With a pure mind, one should take refuge in me, Śrī, by means of the fifth [verse];
with this verse beginning with "āpaḥ," one should perform the rites of offering water for honor, water for the feet, and water for sipping.
With "ārdrāsi" one should perform the bath; with "kardamena" the clothing;
with "gandhadvārā" the perfumes; and with "upa tvā" the adornment. || 33 ||

17. *svīcakāra* (accepted/assumed). The meaning is that he contemplated himself as the seer of those mantras (*ṛṣi*), as their subject matter (*pratipādya*), and as their deity (*devatā*). By the term *aravindākṣa* (lotus-eyed),...
It is indicated that his eyes are described by the Śruti as being "like a lotus flower with petals like those of a monkey" (tasya yathā kapyāsaṃ puṇḍarīkam evam akṣiṇī).
19. *Adhīte*: studied [verbally]. *Vimṛṣṭe*: reflected upon [according to] the meaning. By the authors of the Kalpas, such as Śaunaka and others.

22. *Aṅkasthām*: The meaning is "seated on the left lap.
28. *Parābhyām*: The meaning is "by means of the eleventh and twelfth verses."
29. "Tārikām" and so forth; the meaning is that there are two mantras, namely *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*. 31. He states another alternative: "with the Ṛg-verses.
32. "The waters."
The meaning is that [the rite] is performed on the twelfth lunar day with the verse beginning "May the waters release" (āpaḥ sṛjantu).
33. "Ārdrām" and so forth; the meaning is that [it is performed] on the thirteenth and fourteenth lunar days. "With mud" (kardamena).
"Ekādaśī" means the eleventh [day]. "Gandhadvārā" means the ninth [day]. "Upaitu" means the seventh [day]. (p.
203) "I am Kāṃsa," as well as incense, lamps, and the offering on the sixth [day].
One should prepare the madhuparka with the words, "The desire of the mind. || 34 ||
For this [formula], "hunger and thirst," is the means for obtaining [the food];
with the final one, however, there is a salutation; the remainder one should perform as before. (35)
"In this hymn, there are fifty-three names of mine;
O destroyer of Jambha, listen to their etymological explanations from me. (36)
Established within all beings during battle like a female bee in a wound,
she produced a supreme sound that flowed unceasingly like a stream of oil.
Situated between the closing and opening of the eyes of the sun and moon,
she extends from the root-support (mūlādhāra) up to the end of the twelve [finger-breadths].
Resembling many thousands of rising suns, fires, and moons,
the tranquil Madhyamā is then seen emerging from the wheel, the support of the wind.
Having reached the place of *vaikharī*, residing there within the eight locations [of articulation],
I become the mother of the phonemes and, like a cow, yield enjoyments.
Having praised me with the hymn beginning "Hiraṇyavarṇā," the noble-minded Prajāpati, through my grace, then spoke upon the dharma of the yogas.
This nine-syllabled mantra of mine, beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ," is composed of the Śabdabrahman; it is the manifest means for yogis to achieve yoga. (42)
I go further and further away from the minds of yogis than even the distance of a deer;
yet yogis of firm vows bind me by means of their own devotion. (43)
Sixty-eight thousand yogins, devoted to me,
having meditated upon me as Hariṇī, have attained supreme withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra).
She was clothed in a deer-skin, seated upon a deer-skin, her waist embraced by a deer, and she possessed long, fawn-like eyes. (45)
By recollecting me, Hariṇī, one shall attain supreme peace.
I lead Hari in his undertakings, and I am led by Hari himself. (46)
I am always the one who removes the sins of the virtuous with the luster of Hari;
this six-syllabled mantra of mine begins with the Praṇava and ends with "namaḥ. (47)
Note:
34. "Kāṃ sosmi" refers to the fourth [verse]. Its application even in the ritual rinsing (ācamana) has been stated previously.
"Ṣaṣṭhyā" means by this verse beginning with "ādityavarṇe. "Manasaḥ" means by the tenth [verse].
35. "Kṣud" and so forth means "on the eighth. "By the last one" means "by the fifteenth," as in the phrase "bring that to me. 36. "Fifty-three" means "thirty-five."

37. By the verse beginning with *nihita* and ending with *hiraṇyavarṇā*, the etymology of the name is provided. The word *hi* has the sense of *nihita*. [The phrase] *raṇe* means "I make a sound. The explanation of that immediate sound is given by the words *bhṛṅgavadhūr iva*.
*Acyuta* means "uninterrupted."

39. He explains the word *varṇa* [color/sound] with the phrase "from the wheel" (*cakrakāt*); this means from the *ādhāra-cakra*. *Śāntā*; this means the *parā* [speech]. *Paśyā*; this is *paśyantī*. 40. The locus of *vaikharī*; these are the eight [sites], beginning with the throat.

42. *Oṃ hiraṇyavarṇāyai namaḥ*—this is the nine-syllable mantra. 43. Here the name *hariṇī* is etymologically explained: first, as "like a doe (*hariṇī*) because of her running far"; and second, as "they seize and bind the yogins by means of her."

45. He states another etymology, beginning with "hariṇa," etc. One etymology is: she whose waist is like that of a deer (hariṇa), meaning it is unattached (aśliṣṭa) or unjoined; or alternatively, she whose waist is embraced by Hari, meaning by Viṣṇu.
46. Another etymological derivation is *harim*. As the learned say: "He who ordains everything according to [the creature's] gestures (*iṅgita*).
47. There are two etymological derivations: *hariṇabhāsā* and *hāriṇī*. Oṃ, obeisance to Hariṇī. (p. 204)
This excellent and direct means of practicing yoga, which accomplishes all goals,
is my eternal rosary fashioned from golden lotuses. (48)
I create beautiful forms, or I thoroughly choose the universe;
moreover, those who are bound, liberated, and so forth—the unborn ones—are constantly emitted by me.
Having thus worshipped [the deity] with a golden garland for a long time on Mount Meru, the lord of the Guhyakas attained the status of the Lord of Wealth.
My garlands shine with silver lotuses, and stainless garlands also gleam;
all these radiant garlands were created by me, the creator of the worlds.
In ancient times, the foremost of the Rudras, having approached Kailāsa with the thought "a silver garland," attained lordship over silver. || 52 ||
These two eight-syllable mantras, joined with the *tāra* and *namaḥ*, will accomplish one's desired goal through recitation, worship, fire-oblation, and meditation. (53)
As I walk about, I dissolve the evil deeds of my devotees;
and like the moon, I constantly melt the hearts of my devotees.
I am the internal bliss characterized by vibration within yogis, and I illuminate their fourth state like the moon. (55)
The supreme sage Vasiṣṭha, though struck by obstacles to his yoga, beheld within [his heart] the pure lunar sphere, a great ocean of consciousness and bliss. (56)
Having recollected me, who resides in the channel [or: who resides in the navel], he again attained his own yoga;
this six-syllabled mantra of mine instantly produces bliss. (57)

This golden [light], through the radiance of the sun, brings about the cessation of suffering for those scorched by the forest fire of worldly existence, extending from the foundational lotus to the end of the twelve [finger-breadths].
I am eternally proclaimed to be rising from the buds of sound and mental constructs,
within the supreme void beyond primordial nature and within the mandala consisting of the three Vedas.
"I abide eternally for the welfare of the worlds in the Golden One (Hiraṇmayī).
Thus do the sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas know me as Hiraṇmayī.
Having offered praise, the yogins attained their desire through the supreme yoga;
for this seven-syllabled mantra is the accomplisher of all desires and goals. (61)
Note 48: "Suvarṇasrak" and "Rajatasrak"—these are two names. 49:
By the words "I create," etc., another etymology is given; by the words "well the universe," etc., the third [is given].

Regarding the etymology: based on the recitation of names where Viṣṇu is identified as "the All" (*viśva*), the etymology should be understood either as "I choose Viṣṇu as my husband," or "I choose the entire world as my place of residence.
He states the etymology of the word *sraj* (garland) as "those that have flowed forth" (*sṛtā*).

50. The narrative is told: "Of the Guhyakas. 51. The etymology of the name *Rajatasraj* is explained: "Because they are made of silver" (*rājataiḥ*). Another etymology is "because they shine" (*rājante*). And another etymology is "because they have shone" (*rājitāḥ*).

52. An illustrative narrative is told: "Of the Rudras. 53. Om, salutation to Suvarṇasraj; Om, salutation to Rajatasraj. 54. The etymology of the name "Candra" is explained: "while walking about" (caṃkramyamāṇā). From the root *kram*, with the intensive suffix (*yaṅ*), it becomes *caṃkramya*.

Form (*rūpa*). There, taking the word *caṃ* and joining it with *drā*, the form *candra* arises. He explains the word *drā*: "I cause to flow" (*drāvayāmi*). Another etymology for *drā* is "like the moon" (*candravat*).
55. He states another etymology: "I rise up" (*udemi*). The fourth stage is the state of *turīya*.
56. He provides another etymological explanation by means of a narrative, beginning with the words "By yoga," and so forth.

57. Om, salutation to Candrā. 58. The name *Hiraṇmayī* is etymologically explained as follows: "In the support," and so forth. "Up to the end of the twelve" (*dviṣaṭkāntam*) means up to the *dvādaśānta*.
The word *yasyāḥ* ends in the vowel *ā*, as in the expression "of her who [shines] like the light of the sun.

(Verse 59) The "conceptualizations of sound" (*śabdasaṃkalpāḥ*) refer to the levels of speech beginning with *paśyantī*. The instrumental case in *tadātmanā* is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe*). An alternative etymological explanation begins with the words "from the primordial nature" (*prakṛteḥ*), and so forth.
61. Oṃ, obeisance to Hiraṇmayī. (p. 205) The Root [Mantra].
I am the witness of all beings; I perceive both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
I am Lakṣmī, eternally belonging to Hari; I am the goal of all and the measure of everything.
I am the one who bestows, the one who casts forth, the eternal, and likewise the thrice-impeller;
thus I am the very nature of knowledge, to be characterized in every measure.
In the creation of the abode of dissolution, I am the impelling force of Prakṛti;
I am the form of the states known as the characteristics (lakṣaṇa), consisting of the phases such as kalā and kāṣṭhā.
Abiding within the unmanifest, the manifest, and the existent, I am the eternal impeller;
I lead the self to its goal, I take it up, and at the end, I cast it away.
I cast away, I destroy, and alone I consume the evil of the virtuous;
I forgive, for I am indeed the forgiveness of all beings; I measure, I reflect, and I am the "Me. 66.

Having seen these matters within me, the supreme seer Kapila, of noble intellect, spoke thus to me: "O Lakṣmī, perceive my fortune! (or: "Perceive me, who am marked by the fortune of auspicious marks! Thus did the sage speak.
For this five-syllabled mantra is the means for attaining the subterranean realm (pātāla) and the provider of enjoyments belonging to the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial worlds. || 68 ||
That body of mine, consisting of knowledge, exists within the heart of Viṣṇu (or, like that of Viṣṇu).
This is the meritorious knowledge of the Self; this is the supreme knowledge of Yoga.
Just as the splendor of the stars always resides in the moon,
so do I abide as the inseparable power within the powerful Viṣṇu.
I alone move forward without a following, having become the great quality of flow;
and in the beginning, having become the river Sarasvatī, I brought forth the sage.
Formerly, while the waters of the Sarasvatī were at Viśvāmitra’s command, the river Sarasvatī, true to her vow, carried away that Vasiṣṭha who was seated within the white waters.
The sages spoke thus to me when Vasiṣṭha was swept away by the current:
"O Truth, protect Vasiṣṭha, who loves the truth, from his enemy! (73)
Note:

From this point onward, seven verses are devoted to the etymological derivation of the name Lakṣmī. He provides the derivation from the verbal root *lakṣ*, meaning "to see," as follows: "She is the witness" (*sākṣiṇī*) and "she is the fortune" (*lakṣmīḥ*) of Hari. Thus, she is Lakṣmī.

The meaning is "the attainment of all prosperity. In this regard, one should contemplate such passages as: "Through faith, a god attains godhood; for that splendor of his is immeasurable, whose [wife] is that daughter of Janaka," and so forth. Regarding the term *lakṣyam* (the object of definition): it means the object of all valid cognition (*prameya*).

63. He states the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the root *kṣip*: "the thrower" (*kṣepaṇī*). Its further explanation is "the triple impeller" (*tripreraṇī*), meaning she is the impeller of body, speech, and mind.
Here, the formation is intended to be derived from two roots: *lā* in the sense of "giving" and *kṣip* in the sense of "impelling. Thus, I am the very nature of knowledge.
She is to be defined (*lakṣaṇīyā*).

Regarding the term *laye*: I am Lakṣmī, who impels *prakṛti* during the processes of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. All entities are "definitions" (*lakṣaṇāni*) because they are perceived and measured; she is their "dispeller" (*kṣepaṇī*)—this is the etymological derivation.
65. "Lakṣmī," and so forth, is another etymological derivation (*nirukti*). Likewise, there is also "lāmī. The meaning is "I am dissolved" (*līnā bhavāmi*).

[The form] "kṣipāmi" means "I impel" or "I project. This derivation is formed by taking the verbal roots *lī* and *kṣip*. 66. He states another derivation: "kṣipāmi. He explains the derivation from the root *kṣam*: "kṣame."

He explains the etymology of the word *mī* with the verse beginning "mima" (67): "O Lakṣmī, do not look at me—that is, do not cast a sidelong glance at me," so said the sage Kapila; this is the meaning. (68) *Oṃ lakṣmyai namaḥ*.
69. Regarding the name *Anapagāminī*, it is explained as "the body" (*tanu*). Because Viṣṇu is never departing (*anapāyin*), she is named *Anapagāminī*.
71. He states another etymological explanation: *apaśca*. In the waters (*apsu*), I am the quality known as fluidity (*drava*); therefore, from them...
The meaning is "I do not go away. He states another etymological derivation: *apāvāhayam*. This is the aorist (*laṅ*) of the root *vah* with the prefix *apa*.
[In this case], having been addressed by Viśvāmitra, she said, "I drove Vasiṣṭha, his adversary, away into the water," using the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
73. Having thus derived the word *apagāminī*, he now states its opposite meaning with the words "The sages...
The syntactical connection is: "They said to me, 'Protect [me] from the enemy.
Becoming Sarasvatī, I, the Mūlasāhā, carried him away from his enemy;
for then the sages gave me the name Anapagāminī.
This nine-syllable mantra indeed wards off all calamities;
I am Aśvā Pūrvāhaṇī, and I always dwell in the city.
At the commencement of yoga, I produce a sound like the neighing of horses within the threefold [body]—known as intellect, vital breath, and physical form—which itself consists of three aspects. (76)
Having entered the center of the channel, I produce a sound like that of a chariot; having reached the opening of space, I resound like the trumpeting of an elephant.
Exerting themselves in yoga, practitioners have attained me in three ways:
the first two are mantras of eight syllables, and the last is one of eleven syllables.
For these three mantras, consisting of my own essence, are indeed the bestowers of desired objects; they hear the voice of compassion and destroy the sins of the virtuous. (79)
I pervade the universe with my qualities and am the eternal refuge;
I am the body of Hari and am served by the gods with faith according to their desires.

I am established in the state that is the support of peace; behold me, the one who sports as the universal lute (*viśvatantrī*) born from the navel, the impeller of thoughts within the mind, and likewise the creation of syllables within the mouth. (81)
Thus abiding in four states, distinguished by tranquility, passion, and so forth, I take refuge; I am the one worthy of refuge; through my powers, I sport and I delight.
"I am the radiant Śakti, the most auspicious and desired Rati"—thus do those who know the truth of the Vedānta immediately recognize me as Śrī. 83.
"O Lord of the Gods, even though I am the protector and the sovereign of the three worlds, my own lordship and sovereignty over the three worlds, including the gods and their lords,
do not equal even a sixteenth part of the excellence of my own caste. (84)
In the first three words, the syllables "śrīṃ," "hrīṃ," and "oṃ" consist of my own essence;
by these four, my body is sustained. (85)
Commentary: 74. "I drove away that Vasiṣṭha from the enemy"; that is, I caused him to depart; the meaning is that I sent him away. 75.
Om, salutation to Anapagāminī (She who does not depart). In the city consisting of the intellect and other faculties, I am she whose form is the horse and whose form is the fullness.

And I am the "Vāhanī" (the carrier). I dwell therein. Because I draw the intellect toward various objects and cause it to run, I am "Aśvā" (the horse). Because I am the city that serves as the abode of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), I am "Pūḥ" (the city). Because I carry the body by virtue of being the Self (*ātman*), I am "Vāhanī.
Therefore, my name is "Aśvapūrvā" (She who has the horse as her precursor).
76. He states another alternative: "Of horses," etc. Previously, at the commencement of yoga, [one says] "I neigh like a horse.

*Aśvapūrvāyai namaḥ* (Salutation to her who has horses as her precursor). 77. The etymological explanation of those situated in the middle of the chariot: "The channel" (*nāḍī*), etc. He provides the etymological derivation for the name "Awakener by the Elephant's Roar" (*hastinādaprabodhinī*).

"Vyoma," and so forth. *Oṃ*, salutation to her who is preceded by horses (*aśvapūrvā*). *Oṃ*, salutation to her who is in the midst of the chariot (*rathamadhyā*). *Oṃ*, salutation to her who awakens by the trumpeting of elephants (*hastinādaprabodhinī*).
79. He begins the etymological explanation of the name "Śrī" with the words "I hear" (*śṛṇomi*), etc. [The root] *śru* means "to hear"; [the root] *śṝ*...
The verbal roots are *hiṃs* (in the sense of injury) and *śṝ* (in the sense of expansion).

80. Regarding the word *śraddhayā*: the meaning is that by taking the letter *śa* and the letter *ra* from this [root], and joining the vowel *ī* from the desired word [such as *īpsita*], one forms the word *śrī*.

81. Regarding "śānta" and so forth: the sense is that by taking the letter *śa* from the word *śānta*, the letter *ra* from the word *rantī*, and the vowel *ī* from the word *preraṇī*, one obtains the word *śrī*. This is called the "creation of syllables" (*arṇasāṃ sṛṣṭiḥ*), which refers to the form of *vaikharī* speech.

82. I take refuge in Viṣṇu. She is worthy of taking refuge in (śrayaṇīyā); she is to be served by her powers such as Jayā and others. She is Remī; she destroys the sins of those who have taken refuge in her. She is Rāmī; she grants all desires. 83. She is the illuminator of power (śakti). She is most auspicious (śantamā), the most blessed. She is the embodiment of delight (rati). She is desired (īpsitā).
It is to be prayed for. Here too, by combining the letter *śa*, the letter *ra*, and the vowel *i* from the three words, the formation of the word *śrī* is intended.
85. "Or this" means the mantra *oṃ śriyai namaḥ*. "With these four" refers to *śrīṃ*, [hrīṃ, klīṃ, and aiṃ].
The meaning is by means of these four: *hrīṃ*, *oṃ*, *oṃ śriyai namaḥ*, and the root [mantra]. (p. 207) Root—
Whether recited, worshipped, offered as oblations, or meditated upon individually, in pairs, in groups of three, or all together, they shall accomplish whatever is desired.
This quartet of jewels must be guarded with great effort;
it bears fruit for one another through all its qualities without exception. (87)
[At the time of the dissolution of the universe,] my majesty is indeed measured by all measures;
for in me, at the time of the destruction of the world, the entire universe is contained.
And since I am the sovereign of the Self and all-pervading, the notion "mine" does not exist within me. (88)
Therefore, those who know me know that I am exceedingly desired like one's own self;
for this five-syllabled mantra bestows the fruit of all desires. (89)
I am the bestower of all desires and the protector of all rites;
I am beloved by the God, and the sages know me as the Goddess. (90)
For this five-syllabled mantra bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is the sound of all beings, eternally abiding within them as pure consciousness.
And though my entire body was searched by all the Vedas, they could not find where I was;
yet I, assuming the form of Brahmā, am wearing a mass of matted locks.
"I create various beings devoted to the study of their own sacred texts;
therefore, the sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas call me 'Kāma'."
For this five-syllabled mantra bestows the fruit of its own recitation; "ud" is the name of Brahman, while "vikasti" is his smile. (94)
Since that blossoming depends upon me, they therefore know me as Sosmitā (She of the Gentle Smile).
