Indeed, this seven-syllable mantra brings about abundant blossoming.
My supreme nature is both beneficial and delightful;
by taking recourse to that which consists of the quality of *sattva*, sages cross over darkness. (96)
Therefore, the sages worship me as Hiraṇyaprākārā;
for this ten-syllable mantra bestows the fulfillment of all desires. (97)
Note: 88. The etymological derivation of the name *mā* is given by the words "these" (*ime*) and so forth. It means "I measure everything," "I am measured," or "I am measured out.
It is "measured"; that is, it becomes limited. Regarding the word *ātman* and so forth; it is derived from the word *asmad*.
The meaning is explained by taking the word *mā*: "mā" means "cognition" (*dhī*). That is to say, it refers to the cognition of the "I-sense" (*ahamarthadhī*).

89. Regarding "like the self" (*ātmavat*): the intended sense is that the etymological derivation is "that which belongs to me" (*me iti*) or "my own" (*mama*). Oṃ, salutation to Māyā. 90. He explains the word *devī*: "the giver" (*pradātrī*). It is etymologically derived by taking the root *dā*, meaning both "to give" and "to place."
"Devasya dayitā" (the beloved of the god). The intention is that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied here due to her connection with a male (*puṃyoge*). "Oṃ devyai namaḥ.
Regarding "Kāṃsosmitām," the word *kāṃ* is a separate term here. He explains the etymology of the name *kā*: "to sound" (*śabdāye*).
The meaning is "she who makes sound" (*śabdaṃ karomi*).

92. Regarding the word *kāye*: the meaning is "in that which is to be established. Taking up the word *kim*, he says *anviṣye* ("I shall seek"). Thinking that *ka* is a name for Brahman, he says *brahma* and so forth. *Oṃ kāyai namaḥ*. 94. He explains the etymology of the name *Sosmita*: *uditi*. The intended meaning here is the sense of the Vedic scripture: "His name is *udit* (the risen)."
The "expansion" (*vikasti*) of that Brahman—that is, its unfolding or vastness—is itself the "smile.

*Usmitam* is the form [of the word]. That which is accompanied by this is *sosmitā*. It is thus stated that the vastness of the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa is dependent upon this. As they say: "Those glances are more numerous than those above which [the smile] is supreme..."
"That became Brahman. Om, salutation to Sosmitā.
96. The name *Hiraṇyaprākārā* is explained as "the Beneficent One" (*hitā*) and "the Wall" (*prākāra*). The word *prākāra* refers to primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Om, salutation to Hiraṇyaprākārā.
She is the liquefier of all root sins and remaining defects for those who have come to me.
By means of a stream of nectar flowing from the downward-facing lotus of his head.
I am consecrated and ever moist; my inner self is moist with compassion.
I blaze eternally within the supreme sky of all beings (or: within the sky of all elements).
I am pure, stainless, and true, illuminating the world with my radiance;
I am without crest, yet possess three crests, and am endowed with five times five crests.
Furthermore, abiding within my body, I blaze forth sevenfold and threefold;
these two six-syllable mantras bestow both liberation and radiance.
May she always be pleased with Hari, eternally satisfied among her devotees;
for I myself am eternally satisfied by nature, even without worldly enjoyments. (102)
Reflecting upon me, who am thus satisfied, the sages who have mastered the Vedas have attained that supreme,
eternal satisfaction consisting of nectar, which has knowledge as its root.
For this six-syllabled mantra satisfies the entire world;
I satisfy Viṣṇu with his qualities, and myself also with those same qualities.

I daily satiate the ocean of the body with its seventy-two thousand channels by means of vital essences, through the constant impulsion of the vital breaths (prāṇas) via the path of Suṣumṇā for those who have eternally attained the supreme state.
I have attained the state of a reflection within the stainless mirror of yoga.
With the nectar-essences of the ultimate truth, arising from the reflection of my own self and consisting of pure consciousness, I satiate the supreme being within the yogis. 107.

[The power of Time] never exhausts with its own forces that which begins with Primordial Matter (prakṛti) and ends with the Particulars (viśeṣa), which is always oriented toward transformation and has attained the state of being an effect.
I shall satisfy them with the gift of life, as rivers satisfy the ocean; and I shall always nourish the sense-faculties of living beings with affection, as one tends a lamp.
"I satisfy [the deities] with the very essence of my own consciousness, which is imperishable by nature.
Thus say the yogis who have reached the further shore of yoga. (110)
This seven-syllabled mantra indeed satiates the entire world incessantly.
Because it measures out time as it is being traversed, they call it *padma*. || 111 ||
Commentary:
98. He provides an etymological derivation for the name *ārdra*: "from afar" (*ārāt*), meaning "at a distance. Another derivation is:
"from that which is downward-facing" (*adhomukhāt*).

99. He provides the etymological derivation of the name *jvalantī*: "I blaze" (*jvalāmi*). 100. He states that its nature is that of the *Śabdabrahman* (the Word-Brahman): "Pure" (*śuddhā*). "Without parts" (*aśikhā*) refers to its supreme form (*parārūpa*). It is "three-tufted" (*triśikhā*) due to the divisions of *Paśyantī*, *Madhyamā*, and *Vaikharī*. By means of the nature of the consonants (*sparśa*),...
The twenty-five peaks:
101. This means that they are sevenfold by way of the array of the internal dhāraṇīs, and threefold by way of the *halakṣa* [syllable] nature. Oṃ, homage to Ārdrā. Oṃ, homage to Jvalantī.
102. He states the etymological definition of the name *Tṛptā*: "In Hari," etc. "Without the worldly" means "with the non-worldly.
Oṃ, obeisance to Tṛptā. 104. He states the name *Tarpayantī*: "I satisfy," etc. And satisfaction (*tarpaṇa*) is [bestowed] upon many by means of many.
He describes [the body] by means of its constituent qualities, beginning with the words "by qualities" (*guṇaiḥ*) and so forth.

105. There are seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*) in the body, as well known in the Yoga scriptures. Here, the body is treated as the ocean, the channels as rivers, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) as wind, and the essences (*rasa*) as water.
And by "determination" (adhyavasāya), what is intended is [the function of the intellect].

106. He states another method: "by the suṣumnā. 108. He states another method: "primordial matter and so forth. By the phrase "always inclined toward transformation," [he refers to] primordial matter (prakṛti).
It is stated that [the Self] has the nature of constant transformation.
109. He states another intended meaning with the words "by means of affection" (*snehena*).
111. *Oṃ tarpayantyai namaḥ*. He explains the etymology of the name "situated in the lotus" (*padme sthitā*) as "that which is being traversed" (*padyamāna*); [it refers to] the whole.
The meaning is "the object of knowledge" (*prameya*). It measures; it delimits. *Oṃ*, obeisance to her who resides in the lotus. Root-text, page 209.
Constantly measuring out all time and ever remaining present, by praising me with these names, one shall become a perfected soul who has transcended time. 112.
I eternally describe myself as the Supreme Lord, the primary source of all males, through the splendor of my own self;
my body is adorned with excellent letters in the form of lotuses.
By praising me as "Padmavarṇā," one shall attain clarity regarding the scriptures;
[I am] that first ray which emerged during the churning of the Ocean of Milk. (114)
That ray of mine, named Candra, is the precursor of her as she rises;
the sages, knowing my power, call me Candra.
That moon which is born from a ten-millionth of a ten-millionth part of my rays—this six-syllable mantra indeed bestows purity of mind. (116)
My light is being drawn away from me at all times and in all states; whatever it desires to conceal is concealed by that light.
For just as one cannot overstep the shadow of one's own head with one's feet, since it moves ahead of the foot by which one desires to overstep it. (118)
My rays, which are eternally risen consciousness-bliss and perpetually radiant, [become] faith, Soma, water, food, virility, and the oblation, respectively. (119)
These six rays of the power of enjoyment (bhogya-śakti), shining intensely within the six fires, are called "Prabhāsā" by the sages who have reached the further shore of Tantra and Vedānta. 120.

For this seven-syllable mantra is the means for accomplishing a continuous stream of splendor, as well as that brilliant fame in the world which arises from the giving of knowledge and other such deeds. (121)
That fame of mine is divided into various forms;
know me alone to be the vessel for that fame, splendor, and prosperity.
Therefore, the wise know me, who am illustrious, as Yaśasī;
for this seven-syllable mantra bestows fame upon the one who recites it. (123)
Divided into heaven, rain, earth, man, woman, and fire,
she receives the oblation that has arrived, which is designated by such names as faith and soma.
Having divided myself sixfold, I have attained the state of fire;
blazing forth, I am sung of by the sages as the radiant power of the enjoyer that illumines the Lord.
"By means of the division into Agni and Soma, I thus distribute the entire universe;
having praised me with this mantra, one shall accomplish whatever is desired. (126)
She is always cherished by the god Hari and served by the gods;
and the gods, depending upon me, remain established in their respective domains.
Note:

113. Because they are measured by a lotus (*padma*), the meanings of the word *padma* are the Lords who are primarily male. Another intended meaning is "those who have the form of a lotus. Oṃ, salutation to the one of lotus-color (*padmavarṇā*).

114. The name *Candrā* is etymologically explained as "the risen one" (*udgatā*). *Oṃ candrāyai namaḥ*. 117. Regarding the passage beginning with "being drawn forth" (*prakṛṣyamāṇā*), this is the etymological definition of *Prabhāsā*.

It describes the excellence of her radiance (*bhāsām prakarṣam*) by means of the phrase "by which" (*yena*): that very splendor by which the sun and other luminaries desire to eclipse the light of others—even that [splendor].
It is concealed by its own brilliance. 118.
He provides a worldly illustration regarding invincibility, beginning with "Just as...
119. He states another method, beginning with "Eternal... and "Faith... This [is found] in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
This is well known. The words ending in the accusative case, such as *śraddhām* and so forth, are syntactically connected with the subsequent verb *asyanti*.
(Verse 120: "In the six fires"; the meaning is "in [the worlds] beginning with heaven. The etymological derivation is "she who casts forth radiance" (*prabhā asyati*). *Oṃ prabhāsāyai namaḥ*.
121. The name *Yaśas* is thus explained: it is "fame" (*yaśas*). 122. And that fame is of various forms. He states this very point with the words beginning "of fame" (*yaśasaḥ*), etc.
123. Oṃ, obeisance to Yaśasā. According to this [mantra], [one should worship] Candrā, Prabhāsā, and Yaśasā.
"Blazing," such is the reading of the hymn (sūkta).
124. He etymologically explains the name "Jvalantī" with the words beginning with "In heaven," etc.

125. By the phrase "the power of the enjoyer," he indicates the non-distinction between the powers of the enjoyer and the powers of the objects of enjoyment (bhogya-śakti) as intended by the term *prabhāsā*.
This has been established. *Oṃ jvalantyai namaḥ*.
(Verse 127) The etymological explanation (*anirvacana*) of those [deities] favored by the gods (*devajuṣṭānām*) is given by the words "by the god" (*devena*), and so forth.
Taking the word "god" (*deva*) to refer to the senses (*indriya*), it is said: "and the gods" (*devāśca*).
Because they are specific transformations of the root-prakṛti, these [evolutes] are indeed insentient.
Therefore, having taken up my own power, which consists of the activity of pure consciousness, || 128 ||
The ear, speech, mind, and other faculties engage with their respective objects;
yet they know me as the one worshipped by the gods, who is served by the senses for the sake of their functioning [in direct perception]. 129.
By constantly contemplating me as abiding within, bestowing all powers, and cherished by the inner deity, one conquers all the gods. 130.
It is from Him alone that the consciousnesses of the great seers have arisen here, as well as the powers and the various actions of men, both high and low. (131)
The wise know me as noble, bestowing desired objects without restraint;
for this seven-syllabled mantra grants every wish. (132)
I extend the five activities through her, who is the soul of the world;
those who know reality and have reached the further shore of Vedānta declare that she is "I" and I am "she.
Indeed, this five-syllabled mantra extends the expansion of auspiciousness.
I lead both Prakṛti and Puruṣa by means of my own splendor.
And having emerged even from Time (Kāla), they then know him as Padmanemi;
for this seven-syllabled mantra bestows the abundance of all prosperity. (135)
I describe the Sun, who is of solar hue, alone in brilliance, fame, and splendor;
having become the soul of the colors situated in the sun, she is divine and consists of the three Vedas.
Illuminating all objects, even those past and future, I am the eternal eye for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings. 137.
And my first letter is the *tāra*, the primary designator;
therein, through the bliss of the quiescent and the emergent, I rejoice in the self by means of the self. (138)
Uninterrupted like a stream of oil, sounding like a long bell,
the subtle crest of the *praṇava*— that is my body consisting of sound.
One who is proficient in that Brahman will quickly attain me;
for I have manifested in the form of sound, born with the luster of the sun.
In the form of Śāntā, Paśyanti, and so forth, Vaikharī, which utters the phonemes, stands as a wish-fulfilling cow, milking forth all objects of desire. [141]
The sages know these meanings within me as "ādityavarṇa" and so forth;
for this nine-syllable mantra fulfills all desires. || 142 ||
Showering rays upon the world, and showering them ever higher and higher, by means of the wind Devamitra, the jewel, and the supporting fire. || 143 ||

129. Since the word *deva* refers here to the sense organs (*indriya*), he says "in the ear," and so forth. This is for the sake of the function (*vṛtti*); that is, for the purpose of the activity directed toward the objects. "By the senses" (*akṣaiḥ*) means by the organs. Oṃ, salutation to the one beloved by the gods (*devajuṣṭā*). 131. The etymological explanation (*nirukti*) of the name *udārā* is given by the words "from me alone," and so forth. Oṃ, salutation to the noble one (*udārā*).
133. Regarding the term *padmanemīm*, the author provides an etymological explanation (*nirvacana*) by taking *tām* as a separate name, stating:
"I expand" (*tanomi*). The five functions are creation and the rest. *Tāyai*; the meaning is "I become expanded. The verbal root is *tāyṛ*, meaning "continuity" and "protection. *Oṃ tāyai namaḥ*.
134. The etymological explanation of the name *Padmanemi*: by the words "prakṛtim" and so forth. The meaning of the verbal root *pad* is "I lead.

The meaning of the word *nemi* is "outside. Oṃ, obeisance to Padmanemi. 136. He states the name *Ādityavarṇa*: "ādityam" and so forth. I describe [him]; [he is] possessed of color, radiant with splendor.

"I perform. Intending that the word *varṇa* refers to the phoneme (*akṣara*), he says: "whose nature is the phoneme" (*varṇātmā*). 137. Regarding "the eye": the meaning of the Vedic text should be understood as "of Cakṣurmitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.
138. Thinking that the syllable *tya* is established at the beginning, he says: "being the first" (*ādibhūta*).

140. Regarding the phrase "therein, the two Brahmans": this means in the *praṇava-śikhā* (the crest of the sacred syllable). "Born with the color of the sun" means that all speech (*vāṅmaya*) is born from the *praṇava*. *Oṃ*, obeisance to her who has the color of the sun. 143. The etymological explanation of the name *Kīrti*: "scattering," and so forth. The root *kṝ* means "to scatter. Scattering is the spreading of rays.
And regarding the words:

there he says "successively," meaning in the form of *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*. In the Vedic text [cited], the word "devasakha" uses the nominative case in the sense of the instrumental by way of transposition. The explanation of "by means of the jewel" is "by means of the fire of the substratum."
Having rested repeatedly and slowly upon the leaves of the water-born lotuses at their base, (p. 211).
Then, from among the twelve, I worship the twelfth and final one.
Therefore, wise sages proclaim my glory;
for this five-syllabled mantra bestows the purity of yoga. (145)
I am successful through the powers of Viṣṇu, and I surpass the yogins who move within the inner support of the yoga-lotuses upon their petals. (146)
Successively increasing, I attain supreme expansion;
therefore, the mature yogis call this prosperity the illuminator of yoga.
Odors and the like, as well as earth and the other elements, are the gateways to my perception;
I am the eternal gateway for all meritorious fragrances. 148.
"Those brahmins who have reached the further shore of the Vedanta call me 'Gandhadvārā';
I am invincible to all the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas. (149)
I am pure consciousness and action, incapable of being sublated by anything;
for I, whose nature is consciousness and action, am the self of all. (150)

Furthermore, how will he who wishes to remove even the state of being a knower—which is indeed the state of being an agent—explain that [agency], having already known it as the agent of the negation? (151)
No one at all is capable of violating my state of consciousness;
having reflected thus on its non-existence, that very consciousness indeed exists within non-existence.
Those expert in the knowledge of Sāṃkhya call me "Unassailable.
Indeed, this eight-syllable mantra is the liberator from the path of darkness [or: from fear]. (153)
Nourished by the eternal Viṣṇu, and eternally nourished by excellent qualities, consciousness—devoid of my sense-objects—is the eternal, supreme body. (154)
She alone nourishes the sense-objects for those of inert nature by means of her non-inert forms;
yet the perfected ones, who are experts in consciousness, declare me to be eternally nourished. 155.
This eight-syllabled mantra indeed constantly nourishes consciousness;
its performers are known as "Kariṇas," who are pure in the three ways and devoted to the threefold action. (156)
I desire to see them always; with my mind I go to those who are ever held [in my heart].
Resembling the lord of snowy mountains, these lordly elephants are my vehicles.

Note: 144. Explanation of the meaning of "upaitu" in the Śruti—namely, "I worship. Om, salutations to Kīrti. 146. He etymologizes the name "Ṛddhi"—namely, "ṛddha. The meaning is "prosperous" (samṛddha). "I honor"; that is, "I please."
He explains prosperity itself with the words "on the leaves" (patreṣu).

147. *Ṛdhyāmi*; I prosper; I attain growth. *Oṃ ṛddhyai namaḥ*. 148. The word "fragrance" (*gandha*) is also indicative of form, taste, and so forth, as well as the earth and other elements that serve as their substrata.

He observes: In the passage, "He understood that food is Brahman," the sheath consisting of food (annamaya-kośa) is prescribed in the Śruti as a means to the knowledge of Brahman. Furthermore, the Śruti itself, stating "Earth is indeed food," declares that the word 'food' refers to the Earth. Therefore, in the knowledge of the Goddess, the Earth and the other elements [are included].
They serve as gateways. Oṃ, obeisance to Gandhadvārā.
151. That; removal. 152. *Tadabhāvā*; the meaning is that which consists in the absence of being overcome. Oṃ, obeisance to Durādharṣā.
154. The explanation of the eternally nourished (Nityapuṣṭā): by the words "by the eternal," etc. [It means] "by the true qualities";

that is, by qualities such as knowledge, power, and so forth. The syntactical connection is: "Even without sense objects, my supreme body, whose nature is consciousness, is nourished. Om, salutation to Nityapuṣṭā.

156. He provides the etymological derivation for the name *karīṣiṇī*: "those who act" (*kariṇaḥ*), meaning "doers" (*kartāraḥ*). The sense is that the word *karin* is derived from the verbal root *kṛ*. They are "pure in three ways," meaning pure in body, speech, and mind.
They perform "the three activities," namely those consisting of sacrifice, giving, and study.

157. Taking up the verbal root *iṣ* in the sense of "desire," he states the meaning: "I desire those. With the intention of referring to the root *iṣ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*), he says: "I go with the mind. Intending to convey that the word *karin* is well-known as referring to an elephant, he says: "The lords of elephants. *Oṃ*, salutation to Karīṣiṇī.
p.
212) O Mother, you are the primordial sovereign, the eternal agent, and forever possessed of food (or: possessed of an end).
Therefore, those who know the truth call me Karīṣiṇī.
For this seven-syllable mantra bestows the fulfillment of all desires;
and I am always the sovereign of all beings through my beloved Lord. (159)
She is the bestower of boons, the sovereign of the worlds, and is always praised by all beings;
she is the giver of prosperity, ever-increasing, and the destroyer of all sins. (160)
"Īśvarī"—this indeed is my name as established in the Veda;
for this six-syllabled mantra bestows the abundance of all sovereign powers.
Those known as terrestrial, atmospheric, and celestial, as well as those which are extraordinary and supreme—all these desires, consisting of eternal bliss, are centered in me. || 162 ||
I am the supreme ground for the delusion of all desires;
I am the object of Viṣṇu’s mind, and I transcend everything.
"Kāma of the mind"—with these very words the gods praised me.
Indeed, this nine-syllable mantra bestows the fulfillment of all desires. (164)
Furthermore, those words which are proclaimed as worldly, Vedic, or arising from external scriptures—whether they be silent sounds or articulate speech. (165)
With me as its intended object, the act of utterance of all those [sounds] is directed toward me;
every person perceives me, who abide as the Self of all, through their entire being.
Through that very sequence of uttering words in various ways, I have been brought to awareness by those who know the Vedas through their speech. (167)
This eight-syllabled mantra indeed bestows the accomplishment of all words and meanings;
it is that which perceives the world in two ways—as "being" (sat) and as "becoming" (tyat)—according to the means of valid cognition.
"The seers have declared me to be the truth: 'I am all that.
Indeed, this six-syllabled mantra bestows the fruit of all truths. (169)
Living beings, established in three ways, perceive;
O Śakra, their form is consciousness devoid of the horse (the vital breath). || 170 ||
I alone am that very form, consisting of the mass of consciousness and bliss; all these individual souls, known as the power of consciousness, are but fragments of my own power.
For that power of mine which is fiery has indeed arisen in various ways;
thus the Sāṃkhyas declare me to be the very form of the sacrificial animals.
This nine-syllabled mantra indeed bestows the fruit of perfect knowledge;
it is proclaimed as twofold food, arising from the three qualities and the six qualities.
Note:

159. He declares the name "Īśvarī" with the words beginning "of beings" (bhūtānām). Regarding the form "Īśvarā": it is derived from the root *īś* in the sense of "to rule," according to the rule *stheśabhās...* etc., which prescribes the suffix *varac*. The word *bhūta* refers to all sentient and insentient entities.
In the phrase "by the beloved lord," the third case ending is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*). "Vanitā" means she was meditated upon. *Oṃ īśvaryai namaḥ*.
(163) He states another etymological derivation for the name "Manasaḥ Kāmaḥ": "of mental desires. *Oṃ manasaḥ kāmāya namaḥ*.

165. He provides the etymological derivation of the name of Speech as "Intention" (*ākūti*), saying: "It is worldly. 166. Regarding the word "having intended": the meaning is that the term *ākūti* refers to intention (*abhiprāya*). The sense is that it is the ground of the purport of all speech. Om! Salutation to Speech, Intention.

168. He utters the name "Truth," namely "the Real" (*sat*). The Śruti passage, "It became the real and the true" (*sacca tyaccābhavat*), is intended here. *Oṃ*, salutation to Truth (*Satya*). 170. He utters the name "Form of Beasts," namely "they see" (*paśyanti*). The word "beast" (*paśu*) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*).
"By the three modes" means by the forms of gods, animals, and humans, or alternatively, by the forms of the bound (baddha), the liberated (mukta), and the eternal (nitya).
172. The fiery power (āgneyī śaktiḥ); the power of the enjoyer (bhoktṛśaktiḥ). Om, salutation to the form of the bound souls (paśūnām rūpāya namaḥ).

173. Regarding the name "fame" (yaśas) for food, he says: "the threefold quality" (traiguṇyam). Food characterized by the three qualities is the collection of objects of enjoyment belonging to Prakṛti. Food characterized by the six qualities is the collection of objects of enjoyment not belonging to Prakṛti; with reference to this, the Śruti records the song of the liberated ones: "I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food."
p.
213) For others who are bound by the fundamental three qualities (guṇas), there is likewise the other [result].
And if even of the two kinds of food, fame is the highest form; || 174 ||
Therefore, I am proclaimed by those who know reality as the Self of all beings;
worldly and transcendental enjoyments are the unfolding of my power.
That power of mine which is Soma has indeed manifested in various ways;
those who contemplate the ultimate reality know me as the glory of food. 176.
For this nine-syllabled mantra bestows all enjoyments;
I am intent upon these six paths and measured by all means of knowledge. (177)
I am the measure of all measures, and within me everything is contained;
I ferry across the entire, boundless ocean of worldly existence the whole world.
Having crossed the ocean of all defects by means of the boat of the mind toward all beings, I, having assumed the form of a cloud, flood the entire universe with water. 179.
I contemplate and I act for the benefit and pleasure of all;
therefore, yogis know me to be the mother of all beings. 180.
For this five-syllabled mantra bestows the abundance of all enjoyments;
it is the channel named Suṣumnā, the mistress of the wheel of channels.
The vehicle of liberation is known as the Mahāyāna and the Yogiyāna;
it is indeed the subtle Vaiṣṇavī power, proclaimed to be composed of the Self (manmayī). 182.
She is the object of all volitional constructions, depending upon whom everything persists;
she who, piercing upwards and downwards through every living being, follows the course of their bodies.
Pervading the supreme ether, she is celebrated as Suṣumnā, for the liberation of all living beings who are exhausted by the entirety of worldly existence. 184.
In the form of Suṣumṇā, I abide within the bodies of embodied beings, from the base of the bladder up to the head; in that power, O Purandara, [I reside]. (185)
Indeed, thirty-two lotuses known as supports are situated there;
since I am pervaded by a garland of these lotuses, I am therefore called Padmamālinī (the Lotus-Garlanded One).
I sustain Prakṛti, Puruṣa, and eternal Kāla in my own form; therefore, I am Padmamālinī.
For this eight-syllable mantra bestows the fruits of all actions;
I cause the nourishment of all through my form, glory, and splendor.
"Alone, I lead forth that which is called Time, in the form of a lotus;
because of that, the sages designate me as 'Puṣkariṇī'. (189)
Note: 176. *Somaśakti*; the power of enjoyment (*bhogyaśakti*). "Oṃ, salutation to the glory of food.

177. He provides the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) for the name "Mother" (*mātṛ*) as it occurs in the phrase "the Mother garlanded with lotuses" (*mātaraṃ padmamālinīm*)—namely, "these [beings]... (*ime iti*).
The meaning is: "I discern the six paths (adhvan), known as Bhuvana, Pada, Mantra, Tattva, Kalā, and Varṇa.

178. *Miti* means knowledge (*jñāna*). It measures (*māti*); it exists as something delimited. Having thus explained the meaning of the word *mā*, he states the meaning of the word *tṛ*: "I cause to cross" (*tārayāmi*). The verbal root is *tṝ*, meaning "to swim" or "to cross over."
179. He speaks for the purpose of bathing: "I bathe. *Oṃ mātṛe namaḥ*. 182.
He states the synonyms for Suṣumnā: "the vehicle of liberation" (*muktiyāna*). 184. The supreme ether; the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
185. *Vasti*: the lower part of the navel.
186. "Thirty-two": the *ādhāra*-lotuses well-known in the Yoga scriptures.
187. That the word "lotus" (*padma*) denotes *prakṛti* and the others has already been stated previously. Oṃ, to Padmamālinī.
Homage!
188. He provides the etymological derivation of the term *puṣkariṇī*: "It nourishes" (*poṣa*). The intended derivation is formed by taking the verbal roots *puṣ* (to nourish) and *kṛ* (to make).
189. He explains the etymology from the word *puṣkara* as a synonym for *padma*: "It is *puṣkara*. Om, salutation to Puṣkariṇī.
This is indeed the seven-syllable root-mantra, which bestows the fruit of all nourishment;
I am beloved by all the gods and am always united with Hari. (190)
She is the bestower of all desires and the support of the entire universe;
relying upon me, the primary principles such as Pradhāna and Puruṣa remain established.
Therefore, the sages designate me as "Yaṣṭi";
for this six-syllabled mantra bestows the fruit of all yogas. (192)
I am Piṅgalā by my own radiance, resembling molten gold;
and formerly, I bestowed great fortune upon the Lord of Yakṣas, Piṅgākṣa.
O Śakra, in former times the Lord of Yakṣas spoke thus to me:
"This seven-syllabled mantra indeed bestows the abundance of yogic power. (194)
I satisfy Viṣṇu with my virtues, and I am satisfied by the virtues of Hari;
when I am praised for my own deeds, there is satisfaction for all.
Contentment has been described by those who have crossed the ocean of Yoga as being "I" (Aham);
for this six-syllabled mantra is the bestower of satisfaction to the mind. (196)
I shall explain the perfected phonemes, whether they are supreme or otherwise;
these beautiful phonemes, which have no beginning in time, are my expressive symbols. (197)
Having become the eternal Sarasvatī, I describe that which is beautiful;
therefore, she is proclaimed as "Suvarṇā" by the Brahmins who know the truth. (198)
This seven-syllable mantra indeed bestows the perfection of all prosperity;
it is like a divine golden mountain filled with the moon, the sun, and the planets. (199)
"Having become the earth, I sustain [the world] for the sake of the stability of the Creator;
therefore, in former times, Viriñca praised me, who am adorned with a golden garland. (200)
This eight-syllabled mantra indeed bestows steadfastness upon human beings;
for the welfare of all living creatures, I shall now set forth the sequence of its true principles.
Furthermore, I delight them there with enjoyment and liberation as is fitting;
likewise, through the [successive] times, I restrain the series of principles along with the individual souls.
Because I am eternally beneficial to the wise and possess the form of the sun within the solar orb,
I am therefore called "Sūryā" by the wise who contemplate the ultimate reality.
For this six-syllabled mantra bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
thus, fifty-three names situated within the hymns have been proclaimed. (204)
Having attained me, the steadfast ones fulfill their respective desires;
even though the arrangement regarding the scope of their fruits has been declared by me for them. (205)
Commentary: 190. He states the name "Yaṣṭi" [meaning] "I am desired. The meaning is that she is worshipped by all the gods.
191. Intending the word *yaṣṭi* to mean "staff," he says "support" (*avalambana*). Om, to Yaṣṭi.
Salutation! 193. Piṅgalā said: "To Piṅgāya. Intending the verbal root *lā* in the sense of "to give," she said: "I have given. Oṃ, salutation to Piṅgalā.

195. The etymological explanation of the name Tuṣṭi: "I satisfy," and so forth. *Oṃ tuṣṭaye namaḥ*. 197. He utters the name Suvarṇā: "I lead to the good" (*suvarṇayāmi*). The analysis is: "I lead to the good" (*suvah nayāmi*); the change to *ṇ* is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). Furthermore, *suvah* means heaven (*svarga*); *paraṃ suvah* means the supreme state (*paramapada*). *Su* means beautiful; *varṇāḥ* means letters.
He states the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the term *vācakāḥ* as "of which [she] is the designator," beginning with the words "not this" (*anidam*), etc.
(198). He states another meaning, beginning with the word "beautiful" (*śobhanam*), etc.: "Oṃ, obeisance to Suvarṇā. (199).
The name *Hemamālinī* is explained as follows: "made of gold" (*haimam*) means "the Great Meru. Oṃ.
Homage to Hemamālinī. 201. He explains the etymology of the name "Sūryā" with the words "for the benefit" (*hitāya*). The meaning of the word *sū* is "she brings forth" (*prasūye*).
202. The meaning of the letter *ra* is "I delight" (*ramayāmi*). "According to what is fitting" means according to the distinction of those qualified [to receive it].
The meaning of the letter *ya* is "I restrain" (*niyacchāmi*).
203. He states another meaning: "and from the wise" (*sūribhyaśca*). "Beneficial" (*hitā*); the sense is that this is the meaning of the suffix *-yat*. Om, salutation to Sūryā.
p.
215) Furthermore, the greatness of these [teachings] is not yet to be fully contemplated by the wise person.
Until liberation, through non-discursive meditation, she bestows all fruits in their entirety. || 206 ||
For I, the supreme goddess Śrī, am the presiding deity of this garland of names, just as the stars are in the sky or as jewels are in the ocean. (207)
Just as enjoyments are found on the earth, as desires are in the celestial tree, as greatnesses are in cows, and as splendors are in the Brāhmaṇa; 208.
Just as the divine qualities in Janārdana, the God of gods, are infinite,
so too are the glories in this hymn of mine boundless.
For as long as time exists— characterized by divisions such as *kalās* and *kāṣṭhās*—
I am not at all able to describe his excellent qualities.
This is the final goal of those who know the Vedas; this is the path of those who know the Tantras (or mantras).
Let a human being constantly take refuge in me with this hymn.
Having recollected the meaning of the hymn and having studied the hymn for a long time, when serenity of mind has been attained, one should indeed take refuge in me as the ultimate goal. || 212 ||
Taking refuge in me constantly, whether as the God or as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), one who possesses faith and has conquered the senses should reflect in this manner. (213)
Hostility has been abandoned and favorableness embraced by me toward all beings, according to my ability and according to my understanding. (214)
I have turned away from the lower realms, from sins, and from the ocean of existence;
nevertheless, let even this engagement here for the sake of remembering you perish completely. (215)
For one who is indolent, of little strength, and lacking true understanding, the three means prescribed by the scriptures would not be capable of delivering me. (216)
Nevertheless, whatever activity occurs here is indeed the fulfillment of your command; therefore, because there is no other means, I am wretched, destitute, and without refuge. (217)
I exist by taking refuge in your shade, which removes all suffering;
our Mistress is free from limiting conditions, independent, and a treasure-house of compassion. (218)
You alone are celebrated as the refuge in all the scriptures;
and whatever is considered difficult to abandon or difficult to bear—whether it be the self or that which belongs to the self. (219)
All that has been entrusted by you to your two auspicious lotus-feet;
therefore, I choose you as the means for my attainment. || 220 ||
O Goddess, be my means; O Lotus-born One, be my refuge.
Consume all my misfortune and nourish my mind that is fixed upon you.
Note:

211. The word *yad* (that which) must be supplied as the correlative of *saiṣā*. The feminine gender in the reference *saiṣā* is in accordance with the past passive participle *prapadyeta*; for it is that which is coolness.
"Like 'the nature of water' [is its fluidity]. 213. "In this manner" means by the method that will be explained hereafter.
214. By the words "opposition" and so forth, the limbs taught in the seventeenth chapter are recalled here.
216. The meaning is that there are three means, beginning with action, knowledge, and devotion.

217. "Even so" (tathāpi) means even though those [prescribed duties] are not themselves the means. "Here" (atra) refers to among the means. "The fulfillment of the command" (ājñāparipālana) is as stated in: "Brahmins desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting."

The meaning is the observance of commands in the form of injunctions, such as: "Meditate thus upon 'Om'," "One should yoke the Self with 'Om'," "Seeking liberation, I indeed take refuge in Him," "Perform your prescribed duty," "Come to Me alone for refuge," and "One who is self-restrained attains prosperity."

218. "Chāyām" means "your compassion. 220. By the phrase "everything is entrusted," the surrender of both self and possessions is expressed. 219. By the phrase "puṣya dhiyam," devotion to the fruit [of practice] is entreated.
Having reflected thus, one should indeed take refuge in me as the goal—
the primordial God, the Lord of the world, the Sovereign, or the Supreme Person. (222)
O Śakra, at the times of performing rituals, a person should cause this supreme rite of well-being, which destroys all misfortune, to be recited according to the procedure for my hymn.
It validates all actions, nourishes the listener,
and dispels all illusion, misfortune, and impurities along with their stains.
For this, when practiced through action, mind, and speech, protects one from great evil and certainly brings about prosperity. (225)
Thus, O Śakra, this unsurpassed tantra has been told to you, wherein all the insights of the wise reside. (226)
Just as the treatise on liberation is the best among various types of scriptures, as the Brāhmaṇa is the best among bipeds, and as the cow is the best among quadrupeds; 227.
Just as gold is the best among metals and the Kaustubha gem is the best among jewels,
so too is the mother the best among elders, and the son the best among those who speak.
The mind is the foremost among the senses, just as the wind is among moving things;
Mount Meru is the best of mountains, and the triple-streamed river (Ganges) is the best of rivers. || 229 ||
Among the stages of life, the householder is foremost, just as Vasiṣṭha is among those who recite prayers;
among the principles, total renunciation is supreme, just as wisdom is the best among gains.
Likewise, this supreme tantra among all tantras for those who speak of reality has the Blessed One Vāsudeva— Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa— as its teacher.
And I have been duly celebrated here along with [Śiva] by virtue of our essential nature, qualities, and majesty;
for those who are devoted to this my doctrine possess the certainty of pure knowledge. (232)
Taking hold of this ladder, they indeed ascend to the supreme state;
this is the supreme tantra among tantras, consecrated by mantra and sealed with my own name. (233)
It should not be given to one who has not fasted, nor to an ungrateful person, nor indeed to one who does not know the ritual manual, nor ever to one corrupted by malice. (234)
This should not be given to one who is not a devotee of Vāsudeva, nor to one who lacks devotion toward me;
it should be given to one of virtuous conduct, who has bathed well, and who is an ascetic.
To one who has determined the Vedas and Tantras, especially to my devotee who bears even greater devotion toward Vāsudeva Janārdana; || 236 ||
To you, who are pure in vows, skillful, and habituated to constant practice— to you,
all this that I was asked here by you has been told.
"I am pleased with you, O Lord of Gods; what more do you wish to hear? (237)
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Power of the Śrīsūkta," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. [B:
The *Lakṣmītantra* is completed; the number of verses is 3,500.]
Commentary:
224. "He renders capable" means he makes them capable of bestowing their fruits. "Māyā" refers to the connection with *prakṛti*.
By the phrase "and misfortune (*alakṣmī*) together with the impurities," [it refers to] "the elder misfortune (*jyeṣṭhālakṣmī*), which consists of hunger, thirst, and impurity."
"I destroy [them]"—thus the meaning of the *Śrīsūkta* is recalled.
By the words "He protects," etc., the cessation of the undesirable and the attainment of the desirable are stated.
Regarding the word "of the stages" (*āśramāṇām*), the meaning is "of those belonging to the stages" (*āśramiṇām*).

The wise one named Śrīkṛṣṇa— whose spiritual intellect was attained through service to the lord of ascetics known as Śrīvāsa, and who is devoted to profound reflection on the conclusions of the traditional scriptures—
expounds the *Lakṣmītantra* by way of the pure path for the pleasure of the virtuous; may he be pleased.
She is skilled in the method of protecting her dear devotees and is beloved by Mukunda.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter.
In the manuscript designated as (Ī) held in the Royal Library of Madras, the following chapters are read as additional:
Fifty-first Chapter: Mūla-Śakra.
Their origination and dissolution, as well as their fruit, have been determined,
along with the specific modes of practice pertaining to each of them, exactly as they are. (1)
For you, there are five constant duties and also those that are occasional:
the two sections of Conduct and Action, and the two sections of Knowledge and Yoga.
Thus, this Tantra of various kinds is augmented by four sections,
and is consistent with ancient deeds, ancient traditions, and historical narratives.
This work, titled the Lakṣmī Tantra, contains the convergence of many secrets, is adorned with various statements, and correctly provides immediate conviction to human beings.
While I was in a state of meditative concentration, I perceived it exactly as it is; yet, because of its vast extent and due to the complete lapse of time, [it has not been fully recorded]. (5)
And because of the feebleness of the mind, it does not shine forth exactly as it is;
from this great ocean, O Goddess, which is filled with your knowledge.
Having extracted the essence from all [teachings] out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, please explain this compendium of the Tantra; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One! (7)
Nārada said: Thus urged, the goddess Padmā, like a milch-cow toward her calf, spoke to the subduer of Pāka with an affectionate mind.
Śrī said: "Well spoken, O child, slayer of Vṛtra!
Listen; I shall tell you in brief that which has been extracted from this tantra."
I am the eternal Ego (ahaṃtā) of all beings; by means of ascent and descent, I am remembered as the one who brings about the accomplishment of the universe.
That which is called the supreme egoity is said to be beyond the fourth state (turyātīta);
it is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode, and that indeed is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Therein, no distinction exists between us as we abide in being and non-being;
that which is called "unfolding" there is like [the swelling] of the ocean at the rising of the moon.
I am the power of Nārāyaṇa, characterized by the desire to create;
likewise, I am his fourth state (turyāvasthā), consisting of the nature that arises from transformation.
At that time, every state consisting of both the pure and the impure is contained within;
likewise, the Vyūhas, the Vibhavas, and those such as the Antaryūhas.
This nature consisting of purity, O Blessed One, which is identical with you, exists both in the manifestation and the glory, as well as in the further manifestations and so forth. (15)
In this same manner, one should understand each of my states, beginning with deep sleep;
likewise, the unmanifest, the mahat, and so forth, as well as the world of transformation.
This entity consists of both the pure and the impure, and there are indeed three states therein;
O Lord of Heaven, one should likewise raise each of these in their respective places.
These fourfold states are to be understood as existing within the elements and the stable [substratum].
Furthermore, there is another sequence in this way regarding the path consisting of both the pure and the impure. (18)

Within my own self, which consists of the ascent through the knower, the instruments, and the objects of knowledge, there are ten groups of subjects (mātṛgaṇa) according to the distinctions of the void, the vital breath, and so forth, in due order. (19)
Know that the fundamental instrument is twofold: namely, external and internal.
For in both cases, indeed, the sequence begins with silence and so forth.
The objects of knowledge have been declared to be manifold; therein one should likewise infer their state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which is the realization of the nature of the Blessed One.
This descent has been described; now hear from me the ascent as well.
Beginning from the final limit, it is established that it ends with me.

That, however, should be understood as the ascent (āroha) upon the path consisting of both the pure and the impure; a person who continuously contemplates both the ascent and the descent [attains success]. (23)
With his mind fixed on Me, his life-breath absorbed in Me, he attains My own state;
for there is no limitation of Me by form, time, or space.
O Subduer of Paka, they are pervaded by me alone, who am the embodiment of knowledge;
by my will, I manifest the entire universe upon the wall of the Self.
The establishment of the grasped and the grasper occurs through the gradation of that very form;
this transformation of the nature of the expressible has been shown to you in brief. (26)
With a concentrated mind, listen to its nature as the Speaker:
first consisting of pure consciousness, it subsequently undergoes transformation into the form of vital breath.
Through the occurrence of its respective locations, it manifests as sound;
thus, it is distinguished as the *śāntā*, the *sūkṣmā*, the *madhyā*, and the *vaikharī*. (28)
Having manifested myself as that which possesses four forms and is expressed by the fourfold speech,
I, becoming tranquil and withdrawing, enter into a subtle state of existence.
The subtle form is established in two ways: as Śakti and as Nāda.
I, who am the subtle one undergoing manifestation, attain the state of Madhyamā. 30.
The perfection of the refinement of the *bindu* is that state of the continuous flow of the imperishable (*akṣara*);
I, who am the middle [speech] undergoing transformation, attain the state of *vaikharī*. 31.
By means of the fiftyfold division and so forth, constantly meditating upon these two— the ascent and descent of the continuous stream of syllables—
one becomes proficient in the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman) and attains that which transcends the Word.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter; [now begins] the fifty-second chapter in the *Tantrārthasaṃgraha*, an extraction from the *Lakṣmītantra* within the *Śrīpāñcarātrasāra*.
Mūlaśrī said: Now listen, O child Purandara, to the path consisting of mantra.
I am of the nature of light and bliss; I am the fullness of the "I," I am Hari. || 1 ||
Know me as Mantramātā, known as Prāṇa, consisting of pure consciousness;
these [beings] surely rise from me alone and go to their setting in me.
And I am the strength of these; they know me as their own form.
I am exalted, appearing as one, as two, and indeed as three.
In four ways, five ways, six ways, and likewise seven ways;
and likewise in sixteen ways, and similarly in twenty-five ways. (4)
Furthermore, I arise in fifty ways, and again in sixty-three ways;
indeed, like a wish-fulfilling gem, I, the Sovereign Goddess, manifest in many forms.
Vowels and consonants, the combination of vowels and consonants, syllables, and likewise words, together with sentences and chapters; (6)
Furthermore, the systematic arrangement of the scriptures and systems within the daily rites and the chapters [of the treatise],
the various types of traditions, and the distinction between those that are external and those that are internal.
Know that worldly and Vedic languages, as well as various other tongues,
are all of the nature of mantra for those who know my true form.
The establishment of the apprehended and the apprehender occurs according to the degree of cultivation; likewise, proximity and distance result from the degree of cultivation. (9)
Mantras are of four kinds: seed-syllable (bīja), aggregate (piṇḍa), phrase (pada), and name (saṃjñā).
Know, O Vāsava, that among these the five jewels are preeminent.
O Pākaśāsana, those seeds are contained within my hymn like clarified butter placed in curd;
they arise from the fragments of the Sun, Moon, and Fire, and are endowed with the Nāda.
That which is the form of the sun here is declared to be the state of waking;
fire is the dream state, and the moon is the state of deep sleep, which is called the Supreme Māyā.
The fragment known as Indukhaṇḍa is the fourth; beyond that is Nāda.
Śakti is the state consisting of the tranquil self, which is the very abiding of Nāda itself. || 13 ||
Beyond that, however, is the Brahman which is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
it consists of six, four, and six vowels, arising from the Sun, Fire, and Moon.
The remaining consonants are produced from the vowels; such is the arrangement of the phonemes.
This is the supreme seed-syllable that bestows the fruit of all desires. (15)
It bestows sons upon those desiring sons, a kingdom upon one desiring a kingdom,
prosperity upon those desiring prosperity, and liberation upon one desiring liberation.
It destroys enemies and attracts whatever is desired;
this is indeed named Cintāmaṇi, for it is not merely a gem that is called Cintāmaṇi.
And following that very [mantra] is the seed-syllable beginning with Śakāra, which grants all desires;
it consists of pairs of letters derived from the Māyā-mantra, positioned at the beginning and end of the six vowels.
This arrangement of the limbs (aṅgas) should be performed, accompanied by the seed-syllables and the mudrās;
the same rule applies to the remaining four seed-syllables as well. (19)
Through immersion in the fullness of I-consciousness and through union with the primordial seed-syllable, the manifold host of mantras attains its state of being mine. 20.
Whichever deity belongs to the mantras, that deity is established in my power and partakes of my very nature;
therefore, it is indeed I who am to be meditated upon therein.
In that [practice], one should indeed recollect each respective deity in the form of a woman, endowed with their respective colors, weapons, forms, ornaments, and so forth. (22)
"Having attained the state of being mine, they likewise bestow fruits swiftly;
thus, O Śakra, this path of mantra has been described to you in brief. (23)
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter [and begins] the fifty-third chapter in the *Tantrārthasaṃgraha*, an extraction from the *Lakṣmītantra* within the *Śrīpāñcarātrasāra*.
O Purandara, I shall explain the Kriyāpāda, the root of prosperity, in brief.
With his impurities washed away, he has bathed according to the teachings of the scriptures. || 1 ||
Having reached a secluded place and preceded by the purification of the site,
O Śakra, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) through the cultivation of knowledge.

That which is known as the eightfold nature (prakṛti), beginning with earth and ending with primordial matter (prakṛti), is traditionally held to possess two forms according to the distinction between the gross and the subtle. (3)
The configuration that exists within the range of the eye is described as gross form;
therein, the state of being the cause is called the subtle *tanmātra*.
This reality consists of sixteen principles divided into gross and subtle;
one should assign the objects, the senses, and their functions to their respective places therein.
In the five [senses] beginning with the genitals and smell, three by three, one should lead them respectively by means of the five great elements beginning with earth. (6)
One should bring the conceit of the mind to rest within the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra),
and one should conceal the determination of the vital breath within the principle of the intellect (buddhi).
One should bring sattva, rajas, and tamas to rest within the unmanifest root;
in this group of sixteen, one should contemplate the eightfold root.
O Indra, the respective designations beginning with Dhruva and ending with *huṃ phaṭ* are:
flesh, fat, blood, semen, space, and the three syllables.
One should meditate upon the eight subtle [syllables], each followed by the next and joined with the Bindu;
within this group of eight seed-syllables, one should contemplate Māyā conjoined with the crescent moon.
The wise one should understand these mantras as residing within the eight powers (śaktis):
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti; || 11 ||
The wise man should remember these powers: Śāntyatītābhimānā, Prāṇā, and likewise Guṇavatī, beginning with Earth and ending with Primordial Nature (Prakṛti). || 12 ||
In that very same [group] of eight seed-syllables, one should know these mantras pertaining to the presiding deities by joining them with fire (ra), māyā (ī), and the half-moon (ardhacandra). 13.
Having meditated upon me, who possess the brilliance of a thousand suns at the time of universal destruction and resemble smokeless embers,
one shall consume the earth with the fire issuing from my mouth.
One should likewise sprinkle with water produced from one's own mouth, which has the luster of ten million moons;
in this way, the purification of the place is accomplished. Now hear about the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). || 15 ||
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter; [now begins] the fifty-fourth chapter, in the *Tantrārthasaṃgraha*, the extraction of the *Lakṣmītantra* within the *Śrīpāñcarātrasāra*.
The primary Śrī [is] the Earth, four-cornered, level, yellow, and marked with the thunderbolt sign.
Having drawn [the deity] within the body by means of the mantra, one should lead it to dissolution in its own place. || 1 ||
Then, when only the fragrance remains, one should cause that to dissolve into its own seed-syllable;
upon the cessation [of the fragrance] by means of its own seed-syllable, one should cause that [seed-syllable] to dissolve into one's own mantra.
While I have become the locus of his empowerment, he should cast me and that [empowerment],
which resembles a half-moon and is marked with a lotus, from his body into the external water by means of the mantra.
Having brought [the deity] situated in its own place into dissolution by means of one's own mantra into the mere essence (rasa),
and having established it there with that mantra, one should then lead that [essence] into dissolution within oneself.
And then, through me, fire, non-return, and primordial nature (prakṛti) in succession, the wise man should realize that everything is not manifold; he should understand the dissolution of my power.
For just as one might pour ghee into milk produced by churning it,
and there is ghee elsewhere in milk, and that ghee is yet another [instance].
Thus, the wise man should meditate upon Prakṛti as the empowered presiding deity;
likewise, he should meditate upon me, the Supreme Śakti, endowed with the sevenfold Śaktis.

Having raised [the breath] up to the end of the *dvādaśānta*, one should cast it into me, who consist of mantra; I am resplendent like ten million fires, moons, and suns, with eyes, heads, and mouths on all sides.
"For the benefit of all living beings, this body of mine consists of mantra.
Śakra asked:
"Which are the locations within this body where dissolution should be performed in successive order?"
"And what are the forms of the Earth and the other elements within the lotus? Please tell me.
Śrī said:
"The station of the Earth is from the knees upward; that of Water is remembered as being up to the waist. (10)
The place of fire is up to the navel; the place of wind is then up to the heart;
the place of ether is up to the throat; and the place of the ego is up to the base of the palate.
The great place above the eyebrows in the ether is remembered as supreme;
the great earthly orb is square and marked with a thunderbolt.
That which resembles a half-moon, is white, and is marked with a lotus is said to belong to water;
that which is triangular, marked with a svastika, and red is declared to belong to fire. (13)
Smoke-colored and joined with six dots, the circular [mandala] is called that of Vāyu;
likewise, the space [of Ākāśa] is the color of collyrium, known as the station of the mere orb.

Thus, when the summary of the reality has been made, [the breath] which has emerged from the hollow of the heart, supported by the rope of knowledge, and traveling along the central path of the *suṣumnā*— 15.
Having raised [the soul] upward from oneself by means of the series of steps that are the powers (śaktis),
one should cast it into me, who abide in the center of the great lotus at the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta).
The great lotus at the end of the twelve [fingers] is endowed with a thousand petals;
it possesses the luster of ten million times a thousand suns and the radiance of ten million times ten thousand moons.
Abiding within the duality of Agni and Soma, my body consists of great bliss; that inconceivable, incomparable consciousness is my own form. 18.
From this [source], the excellent river Jīvānanda flows forth in part;
having brought this self-bliss, it leads one to the state consisting of great bliss (mahānanda). || 19 ||

Then, one should burn from all sides that lump, which resembles a heap of salt, with networks of great flames consisting of masses of rays emerging from one's own mouth, which are composed of pure consciousness.
Then, one should flood the sixth [cakra], the red lotus, which possesses a drop and is the fire of the body, with the nectars arising from my moon-like mouth. || 21 ||
When my desire to create arises, embraced by consciousness and vital breath,
one should remember those powers impelled [by it], which reside within the body composed of mantra.

Then, one should meditate in sequence upon the creation of everything from primordial nature (prakṛti) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa), preceded by the impelling of those powers through the gateway of the impulse (codana).
Then, having thus produced the great *piṇḍa* consisting of pure *lakṣmī*, which is radiant with causes and manifestations, and which arises from the *piṇḍa*— 24. [End of verse]
By means of the path of progression previously described, one should bring [the self] back into the heart in reverse order—
from Great Bliss (mahānanda)— one's own self, characterized by the bliss of consciousness (saṃvidānanda). 25.
Then one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the hands and body,
on the joints of the fingers starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger.
On the two palms and the two backs, as well as on both hands, from the navel down to the feet, and likewise from the navel up to the head. (27)
Having placed my seed-syllable in the joints, one should place the limbs beginning with the heart;
then again, by means of the six [syllables] beginning with the heart, [one should place them] on the navel, back, hands, and thighs.
The wise one should assign the sixfold attributes, beginning with knowledge, to the feet and shanks.
When the body has thus been generated— pure, auspicious, and consisting of Lakṣmī—
one should perform the assignment of the six supports (ādhāra-ṣaṭka) through the vision of knowledge.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter [and begins] the fifty-fifth chapter in the *Tantrārthasaṃgraha*, an extraction from the *Lakṣmītantra* within the *Śrīpāñcarātrasāra*.
O Pākaśāsana, listen as I shall fully explain the primary sources of prosperity, which serve as its foundation.
Then, O Lord of Wealth, [one should meditate] within the penis, at the penis itself, and in the middle of the navel.
The wise man should meditate upon six lotuses in the pit of the heart and between the eyebrows,
[visualized] by means of the Vedas, the Rasas, the Prajāpatis, the Suns, and the Vikāras.
And [he saw] those joined with petals for the two Aśvins, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns,
conjoined with the vowels from 'ka' to 'ta', and with the two ending in the color of the sun.
One should contemplate me, the Goddess, in the form of a jewel-lamp amidst these lotuses;
wherever one’s desire may lie, remaining there, one should practice yoga.
Beginning from the first support and extending to the lotus at the end of the twelve,
one should meditate upon that single, supreme, primordial [power] residing within the body, having the form of a lamp-flame.
When the mind attains dissolution by recollecting this supreme, conscious [reality] through both direct and reverse orders,
that indeed is the supreme state of Viṣṇu.
If you have a desire for the construction of a body, listen to me regarding that body:
one should visualize the water of the Mahendra [ocean] as a pavilion within a single heart.
There, one should visualize the city as having four gates, with female gatekeepers:
Balākinī at the eastern gate, Śyāmā, and likewise Vanamālā at the others.
One should subsequently recollect the white Vibhīṣikā, described with the colors already mentioned;
and in the north, O Śakra, one should recollect the smoke-colored Śāṅkarī.
There, in the center of the pavilion, one should visualize an eight-petaled lotus, resplendent like a thousand suns, shining with its pericarp and filaments.
One should place Vāsudeva on the eastern petal, Saṃkarṣaṇa on the southern,
Pradyumna on the western leaf, and Aniruddha on the northern.
One should remember all of them bearing conchs and discs, adorned with forest garlands, possessing beauty according to the respective ages, and facing toward me. 12.
One should meditate upon Gulgulu, Gurunya, Madana, and Śalala in the corner, as they sprinkle me, Sudhā, with water. 13.
One should remember me, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds, situated in the center of the seed-syllable within the pericarp, possessing the luster of molten gold and holding two lotuses.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, adorned with all ornaments,
she is indescribable, incomparable, the faultless consort of Viṣṇu.
She sprinkles the three worlds, scorched by heat, with cool rays born from her dark outer corners— divine rays accompanied by the moonlight of her smile.

Having produced enjoyments through knowledge, one should worship the Supreme Goddess with them—enjoyments that consist of the bliss of Brahman, are truly composed of the Self (Manmaya), and are free from defects. || 17 ||
Or else, she who rests upon the lap of Nārāyaṇa, adorned by the joy of his union,
embracing the Lord incessantly with her right hand.
At that time, however, one must practice in a celestial body;
our wedlock, which is profound as the depths of the Vedas, must not be called into question. (19)

The location of the seed. [Note: Approximately twelve pages of material are missing from the original manuscript following this point. It is evident that the end of the 55th chapter, the entirety of the 56th chapter, and the beginning of the 57th chapter are lost.]
The fifty-seventh chapter:
The Root Śrī.
"The Supreme Power is indeed the Trimūrti"—this is the supreme recitation (japa). || 1 ||
Through the distinction between word and meaning, the manifestation of *lakṣmī* proceeds in two ways:
by the designations of *śāntā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*.

This manifestation of sound is fourfold, and the manifestation of meaning is likewise; it is that in which all latent impressions have subsided and which is devoid of accents, phonemes, and the like. (3)
That ancient verbal state is peaceful and has peace as its means;
it is the unrefined form of the power of sound which brings about the comprehension of meaning.
That which is the pure unfolding is proclaimed as Paśyantī;
that which has the form of conveying meaning is proclaimed as Śabda (Speech). || 5 ||
When the formative factors do not cause harm, that [state] is then the Middle Way;
thus, endowed with these formative factors, it possesses hundreds of conceptual constructions. (6)
Because she does not take pleasure in these ordinary women,
she then divides her form into parts and places it in those eight locations.
That which is called *vaikharī* is said to be the one that speaks various things through articulated phonemes;
while that which is called *śāntā* is the supreme (*parā*) which has attained equanimity everywhere.
A thousandth of a ten-millionth part of that is the speech known as Madhyamā; a thousandth of a ten-millionth part of that is the speech known as Vaikharī.
Phonemes, words, and sentences constitute the threefold manifestation of articulated speech (*vaikharī*);
this very [speech] undergoes progressive contraction by way of the path of phonemes and so forth. (10)
This fourfold power, born of the inverse and direct orders,
proceeds in four ways along with its increase through the stages of Śāntā, A-śāntā, and so forth, in succession.
Vaikharī, Madhyamā, and the others cause it to undergo an eightfold dissolution;
furthermore, that [speech] should be known as threefold: manifest, unmanifest-and-manifest, and unmanifest. (12)
That which is manifest, residing within the bodies of living beings, and which rises and sets,
is indeed made manifest by means of the lute, the flute, the drum, and other such instruments.
Then, through the efforts of living beings intent on speaking, that [sound] was likewise produced by the friction of the wind from rivers, oceans, mountains, and caves. (14)
That power of word which is manifested is said to be unmanifest;
their arising and setting are the aforementioned transposition and inversion. (15)
The fourfold object of expression (vācya) should be known as being distinguished by [the states] beginning with tranquility (śānta).
Thus established is the determination that the Power (śakti) is the Savior (Tārikā). 16.

That recitation which consists of the description of the phonemes all around is called "middling"; it is the power whose form is the phonemes, as well as that which arises from their combination. (17)
That which is bound by power, that which is permeated by power, and that which arises from the desire to speak—this is the tetrad of powers, preceded by their definitive determination. (18)

The final superimposition, which is proclaimed as occurring upon the word, consists in cognizing the denoted object separately from the word itself, once that [word] has been established in its threefold form. (19)
For that awakening which occurs through mantras is indeed the supreme and inferior recitation (japa),
which is described in the Lakṣmītantra as consisting of Agni and Soma.
Having transcended those various forms designated as the signified and the signifier, and having crossed the night consisting of *lakṣmī*, which takes the form of the *tārikā* syllable; || 21 ||
In the great ocean of the consciousness of waveless supreme bliss,
having purified all the mantras, one should be joined with the placement (nyāsa) of that state.
Having worshipped those [deities] therein, which are radiant through their respective nourishment,
one should meditate upon the deity of the mantra through both its general and specific aspects.
Thus disciplined, one should mutter the mantras; this daily recitation is worshiped when it is endowed with the sequence of consecrations and postures as prescribed in the respective scriptures. (24)
Endowed with those various states of being and meditating upon the deities of the mantra, one who sees all should perform recitation; this is remembered as the supreme recitation. (25)
Nārada said:
"This supreme secret must not be given to one who is unworthy. Having spoken thus, she vanished from sight like lightning in the sky.
Having obtained supreme wealth, Śakra rejoiced, freed from his feverish distress. Atri said:
"O blessed lady, having spoken thus, the venerable Nārada indeed ceased speaking. (27)
O fair-faced one, the fortunate Śrī was worshipped by Indra;
even Indra, filled with wonder, went constantly to the abode of Brahmā.
Being questioned by Brahmā, he then spoke to him according to the prescribed rules;
and being questioned by the Prajāpatis, Brahmā, the knower of reality, spoke to them.
Then, on Mount Malaya, the sages were made to hear it by Nārada;
Aṅgiras, in turn, caused Pāvaka to hear this supreme tantra.
Pāvaka [approached] Kātyāyana, and he [approached] Gautama in the hermitage;
then Gautama [approached] Bharadvāja, and he [approached] the great sage Garga. || 31 ||
Garga [taught] Asita Devala, and he [in turn taught] the sage Jaigīṣavya;
that sage then caused his ancestors to hear [the teaching], and thereafter he, the conqueror of greed, attained liberation.
Ekāñjanā, Nānānnapiṅgā, and she who was Mānasī’s daughter,
caused their son, the great sage Pārāśarya, to hear it.
Pārāśarya also caused his son Śuka, the supreme yogi, to hear it;
and Śuka, in turn, recited it to the Prajāpati named Svarbhānu.
Vasiṣṭha instructed the wise Arundhatī in it; she [in turn] taught it to Nārada, and from him the yogis, beginning with Kapila, obtained that system of Lakṣmī.
Śaṅkara, the moon-crested Lord, caused Pārvatī to hear it,
and Hiraṇyagarbha, the speaker of yogas, likewise [caused] Sarasvatī to hear it.
Indeed, for those goddesses who are devoted to their husbands—the wives of gods, brahmin-sages, and yogins—the perpetual study of their teachings is known as the Lakṣmītantra. (37)
Having heard this from the presence of Brahmā, O wise one, I have related it to you;
that "you are dear to me and beloved"—nothing remains [unspoken].
Listen further, Anasūyā, in brief and without malice;
having heard it, act with effort and protect it without negligence. (39)
Your state of mind shall take the form of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, having completely abandoned misfortunes and sins within the ocean of worldly existence. (40)
Whether by fate or through delusion, when one is overwhelmed by calamity,
one should likewise worship both Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
She herself abandons all misfortunes, whether they have been committed constantly or suddenly;
she is free from greed regarding their commission and is devoted to the welfare of the world.
Having personally established non-duality through one's own firm intellect, at all times, in all places, in all states, and in every way. (43)
With the certainty that the glorious Hari will protect those who have taken refuge in him,
they place themselves, their own possessions, and everything else at the feet of the Lord of Śrī.
"Choose a means; contemplate Him, the Lord of Lakṣmī, as the one to be approached.
Thus, O auspicious lady, you have [learned] everything: the scriptures, the meaning of the scriptures, and their fruit. (45)
The supreme reality has been revealed with an attentive mind;
this is the supreme Lakṣmītantra, complete with its secrets and its summary. 46.
"You must never, under any circumstances, give [this] to one who is not a devotee of Vāsudeva;
for Lakṣmī and the Lord of Lakṣmī do not depart from his mind. (47)
To whomever that [person] may be, you must speak this which is unsurpassed;
however, it must never be studied in the presence of atheists.
Likewise, it is not for those who do not observe vows or bathe [at sacred sites], nor for those who hate their mother and father,
nor for those who hate various scriptures, nor likewise for those who hate their guru.

Likewise, for those who hate their spouses and those who hate women, he indeed is one who has performed the ritual bath after completing Vedic vows and is dear to his mother, father, and preceptor. (50)
He was free from blame, a knower of the higher and lower ordinances of the scriptures,
a believer, full of faith, and beloved by both Lakṣmī and the Lord of Lakṣmī.

He is one who knows the divisions of ritual action and sacrifice, who understands the prescriptions of other tantras, who is skilled in the application of yoga with its ancillaries, and who knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures. (52)
He was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, a master of the doctrine of Paśupati,
skilled in the methods of reasoning and refutation, and an expert in the categories of valid cognition and logic.
One who knows the true essence of the meaning of all internal scriptures deserves to attain [this]:
Om, salutation to Vāsudeva, for whom Śrī is the beloved. 54.
Oṃ, salutations to the consort of Viṣṇu, to whom Nārāyaṇa is dear;
salutations to the eternally faultless one, the universal cause of all;
salutations to the waveless knowledge, whose very self is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. (55)

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Essence of the Meaning of the Secret Scripture," in the *Lakṣmītantra-uddhāra* (The Compendium of the Meaning of the Tantras), which is the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
The *Lakṣmītantra* is completed.
